2.5.2 The above table 2.5 indicates that the actual Budget Estimates (BE) for 2025-26 for various 
police-related expenditures are lower than the projected amounts for BE 2025-26. Notable reductions 
are observed in the budgets for the Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs), Central Police

Systems (CCTNS), the upgradation of Central Forensic Science Laboratories, Intelligence Bureau, 
Delhi Police and many other programs.  
 
Observation/ Recommendation 
 
2.5.3 The Committee observes, based on the above-mentioned information, that the actual 
Budget Estimate (BE) for 2025-26 is lower than the projected BE for 2025-26 across several 
key areas, reflecting a more conservative allocation than initially anticipated. The total budget 
has been reduced from ₹184,236.94 crores (projected BE 2025-26) to ₹160391.06 crores (actual 
BE 2025-26), marking a 12.94% decrease. Within the Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs), 
actual allocations fall short of projections, with reductions observed across the CRPF, NSG, 
BSF, ITBP, CISF, Assam Rifles, and SSB. This indicates a recalibration of expenditure 
priorities. Similarly, significant downward revisions have been made to allocations for the 
Intelligence Bureau (IB), NATGRID, Central Police Organizations (CPOs) and Delhi Police. 
Police infrastructure projects, particularly CAPF building projects, have experienced a 

11 
 
substantial reduction from ₹6,403.02 crores to ₹4,038.70 crores, which may potentially impact 
construction of new buildings. The Committee notes that such reductions may adversely affect 
critical schemes under these heads and may slow down modernization programs as well as 
hinder the execution of developmental projects, particularly in border areas. Hence, the 
Committee recommends that the MHA may take up the matter with the Ministry of Finance to 
seek increased allocations under these heads in alignment with their original projections. This 
will ensure that the essential developmental schemes are not affected due to insufficient 
funding. The Committee hopes that funds may be demanded for various developmental and 
expansion projects at the RE stage depending on the utilization pattern. 
 
2.5.4 The Committee observes that the significant reduction in the Grant-in-Aid to States for 
Home Guards from ₹ 566.01 crores in RE 2024-25 to ₹30.01 crores in BE 2025-26 is based on 
the expectation that all backlog claims will be cleared in FY 2024-25. However, the Committee 
emphasizes the need to reassess the funding requirements for new claims and ensure that 
States are adequately supported to maintain the operational efficiency of Home Guards. 
Similarly, with respect to the Holistic Development of Islands in Union Territories, where the 
allocation has been reduced from ₹ 88 crores in RE 2024-25 to a nominal ₹0.01 crore in BE 
2025-26, the Committee recommends expediting the preparation of EFC papers and project 
reports to ensure timely approval and funding for developmental activities in the UTs. The 
Committee further recommends closely monitoring expenditure trends and engaging with 
stakeholders to ensure that reductions across various components do not adversely impact 
service delivery or developmental goals. 
 
2.5.5 The Committee recommends the Ministry to take effective measures to address this 
issue by setting clear quarterly targets for fund utilization, enhancing planning and monitoring 
mechanisms to track progress and identifying bottlenecks in project execution at an early 
stage. The Ministry should also consider establishing a reporting mechanism to monitor 
monthly fund utilization and take corrective action wherever delays are identified. The 
Committee is of the view that by adopting these measures, the Ministry can ensure that 
allocated funds are utilized efficiently and effectively throughout the year, thereby avoiding 
last-minute spending rushes and ensuring that the major projects are executed as planned 
without any delay.

2.6.7 The Committee notes that there has been a decrease of 2.07% in allocations made for 
the Union Territories (UTs) in the year 2025-26 as compared to the year 2024-25. Further, 
there has been no substantial increase in the capital budget for the UTs (without legislatures) 
during thepast three years. In fact, it has been slightly reduced during the Financial Year

development needs of UTs, adequate capital fund is required so that the projects pertaining to 
the development of physical and social infrastructure like roads, power, water and sanitation, 
health and education in all UTs do not suffer due to lack of sufficient funds. Further, to ensure 
that the sensitive and fragile ecology of some of the Union Territories are not affected, special 
measures will have to be taken while implementing the developmental projects. This requires

recommends that the Ministry may try to address the needs of the Union Territories and any

3.2.1 The allocations under Official Language include provisions for Central Hindi Training

3.2.2  The Committee sought to know about the measures that have been worked out for the 
promotion of official language. The MHA informed about the efforts made by the Department of

standardized training modules that comprehensively cover essential disaster response skills, 
ensuring uniformity and effectiveness in community disaster preparedness including local 
committees, youths and youth organisation.  Additionally, the Committee emphasizes the need 
for regular monitoring and evaluation of program effectiveness to identify areas for 
improvement and ensure that the approved financial outlay is efficiently allocated to support 
training and resource procurement. Further, the Committee recommends promoting the 
creation of Community Emergency Stockpiles to enhance disaster preparedness. 
 
3.3.12 The Committee emphasizes the need for the Ministry to conduct comprehensive 
research to develop a long-term roadmap for disaster resilience and adaptation, focusing

disaster-resilient infrastructure, including critical facilities such as hospitals, schools and 
transport networks, to minimize the impact of disasters and improve recovery efforts. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry may include new and emerging disasters in its 
disaster management plans, such as those caused by heat waves etc.  It further recommends 
establishing a formal mechanism for the periodic review and update of the Notified Disasters 
list to ensure the Act remains relevant and responsive to emerging disaster risks through 
consultation with experts, stakeholders and affected communities.

enhanced allowances, to encourage more CAPF personnel to volunteer for NDRF assignments. 
Streamlining the nomination process and improving communication between NDRF and 
CAPFs are also crucial steps for expediting the filling of vacancies and ensuring the NDRF's

3.9.2 As per the Annual report for the Ministry 2023-24, the Government of India approved the

vulnerability to cyclones and making people and infrastructure disaster-resilient while conserving the 
coastal ecosystem in cyclone hazard-prone States/Union Territories of India. The project had four 
components namely: i) Component A: Early Warning Dissemination System ensuring last mile

Bank assistance (loan). National Disaster Management Authority is the implementing agency for the 
project.  The project was approved in following two phases as Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS): - 
 
(a)  The first phase of NCRMP was approved in January 2011 for the States of Andhra Pradesh & 
Odisha. The project was completed in December 2018 with a total expenditure of ₹ 2524.84 
crores. 
(b)  The second phase of NCRMP was approved in July 2015 for the States of Goa, Gujarat, 
Karnataka, Kerala, Maharashtra and West Bengal at a cost of ₹ 2361.35 crores with

schemeperformance, ratings, cancellation of non-started activities as well as surrendering of

4.3 Representation of Women in CAPFs 
4.3.1 The Committee sought to know about there presentation of women in all CAPFs. The MHA 
has replied that to enhance the representation of women in CAPFs, the Government has implemented 
a policy in January 2016 reserving 33% of constable positions in CRPF and CISF and 14-15% in 
BSF, SSB, and ITBP, specifically for women. This horizontal reservation aims to create a more 
gender-balanced workforce within these crucial security organizations. Recognizing the unique 
challenges and needs of women in these roles, a multi-faceted approach has been adopted to 
encourage their recruitment and retention. 
4.3.2 Several steps have been taken to foster the recruitment of women personnel in CAPF. These 
include extensive publicity campaigns through print and electronic media, waiving application fees 
for female candidates, providing relaxations in Physical Standard Test (PST) and Physical Efficiency 
Test (PET) and extending benefits such as Maternity Leave and Child Care Leave. To ensure fair and 
sensitive recruitment processes, a female member is included on all recruitment boards. Furthermore, 
CAPFs provide creches and Day Care Centers to support women employees with childcare 
responsibilities. Committees have been established at all levels to address sexual harassment 
complaints promptly and effectively. Importantly, women are afforded equal opportunities for career 
progression, including promotion and seniority, in accordance with recruitment rules, at par with 
their male colleagues. Additionally, the appointment of pregnant women is held in abeyance until 
after they have given birth, ensuring their health and well-being. 

29 
 
4.3.3 To improve women's representation in senior leadership positions, direct recruitment to Sub 
Inspector and Assistant Commandant positions occurs through the SSC/UPSC. For appointments to 
remaining senior leadership roles, women are considered for promotions based on inter-se seniority, 
ensuring equality with men. These efforts aim to create a more inclusive and equitable environment 
within the CAPFs and AR, where women can thrive and contribute to the nation's security at all 
levels. 
Observation/ Recommendation 
 
4.3.4 The Committee observes the Government's positive steps to enhance women's 
representation in CAPFs, including reservations and supportive initiatives like fee exemptions 
and childcare facilities. However, the Committee notes that actual representation remains 
below target. Therefore, it recommends targeted recruitment drives for women, particularly in 
CRPF and CISF. The Committee emphasizes uniform access to support facilities across all 
units and the importance of robust mechanisms to address workplace issues, including a zero 
tolerance policy against sexual harassment. To further improve women's progression, the 
Committee recommends creating mentorship programs and leadership development 
initiatives. It also suggests exploring flexible deployment options or soft postings during 
specific life stages to enhance retention.  
 
4.4 Cadre Review of CAPFs 
4.4.1 The Ministry has informed the Committee about the Cadre Review of CAPF, which is a 
crucial process for restructuring and optimizing the organizational framework of various cadres 
within the CAPF. This review ensures the elimination of stagnation, the creation of promotional 
opportunities and the enhancement of operational efficiency in alignment with evolving security 
challenges.  
4.4.2 In Border Security Force (BSF), the recent Cadre Reviews in certain BSF cadres have 
yielded positive outcomes by mitigating stagnation, facilitating career progression and strengthening 
the functional effectiveness of the Force. However, the impact of such reviews diminishes over time, 
necessitating periodic reassessment every five years to align with emerging requirements. It may be 
noted that while Cadre Reviews for most BSF cadres are currently under consideration of the MHA 
and the Ministry of Finance (MoF). A matter of particular concern is the Group B & C (General 
Duty) Cadre, which constitutes a significant portion of BSF's workforce. Since the establishment of 
the BSF on 1stDecember, 1965, this cadre has never undergone a review, resulting in prolonged 
stagnation, limited promotional growth and operational inefficiencies, adversely affecting the morale 
of personnel. 
4.4.3 In Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB), the Cadre Review of various SSB cadres between 2022 and 
2024, including Group A Medical Officers Cadre, Group B & C Para-Medical Cadre, Group C 
Tradesmen & Engineering Cadre and Group A, B & C Stenographers Cadre have been approved by 
the Ministry. These recent cadre reviews have effectively helped workforce stagnation, improved 
promotional avenues and enhanced job satisfaction. Notably, a one-level promotion system has been 
introduced for the Tradesmen & Engineering Cadre and a Deputy Commandant (PPS) post has been 
created in the Stenographers Cadre, strengthening the organizational capacity and operational 
efficiency of the force. 

30 
 
In Assam Rifles, the Cadre Review proposal for Group B & C personnel in Assam Rifles is currently 
under process.  
4.4.4 In Central Industrial Security Force (CISF), a Cadre Review was conducted in CISF in 2018 
to enhance career progression and create promotional opportunities across Group B & C posts. As a 
result, rationalization of Group B & C cadres happened and improved the timeline for promotions. 
25 Group A (Executive Cadre) posts (ADG-2, IG-7, DIG-8, and Commandant-8) and six Group A 
(Fire Cadre) posts were sanctioned, leading to better supervisory structures and career 
advancements. 
4.4.5 In Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), the significant impact of the Cadre Review is 
particularly related to the historic creation of 2,961 Head Constable posts in the Cadre of Cook, 
Water Carrier, Daftry, Peon, Farash, and Safai Karamchari (Ministerial). This decision has not only 
enhanced the dignity and social recognition of force personnel but has also contributed to improved 
operational efficiency and organizational functionality. 
4.4.6 In Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), a comprehensive Cadre Review for Group A, B & C 
cadres (GD & Non-GD) was approved by the MHA in 2019-20, leading to the creation/upgradation 
of 1,971 posts, improving career progression across various ranks and the abolition of 2,941 
redundant posts, optimizing personnel deployment. Further, in 2023, additional cadre reviews were 
approved, leading to the upgradation of 1,055 posts in Group C Tradesmen & Followers staff, 
facilitating promotion and upgradation of 221 posts in Group B & C Para-Medical cadre, enhancing 
career prospects. 
Observation/ Recommendation 
4.4.7 The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Ministry in conducting Cadre 
Reviews across various CAPFs to enhance promotional avenues and improve operational 
efficiency. It notes that while some forces, such as SSB, CISF, CRPF and ITBP, have benefited 
from recent Cadre Reviews, others, particularly BSF’s Group-B & C (General Duty) Cadre, 
have not been reviewed since its inception in 1965. The Committee emphasizes that Cadre 
Reviews should be undertaken at regular five-year intervals as their effect diminishes over 
time. It observes that timely Cadre Reviews, as seen in recent cases, have significantly 
contributed to better workforce planning, increased job satisfaction and improved operational 
effectiveness.  
4.4.8 The Committee feels that the MHA along with the Ministry of Finance (MoF) may 
expedite the approval of pending Cadre Reviews, particularly for BSF, Assam Rifles and any 
other forces and to establish a structured mechanism to ensure periodic reviews without 
unnecessary delays. The Committee recommends that financial and structural planning for 
Cadre Reviews be carried out proactively, with dedicated task forces ensuring smooth 
execution. The Committee further recommends that the MHA may explore innovative 
strategies, such as lateral mobility programs, training-based advancements and inter-force 
career progression frameworks, to enhance career growth opportunities across the CAPFs and 
Assam Rifles.

4.5 Welfare and Rehabilitation Board (WARB) for CAPF 
4.5.1 The Ministry has informed the Committee about various welfare measures undertaken to 
provide financial, educational, and employment support to the families of CAPF personnel killed in 
action, as well as for the rehabilitation of retired personnel. It has highlighted that the Welfare and 
Rehabilitation Board (WARB), established in 2007, oversees the welfare and rehabilitation needs of 
retired CAPF personnel, their familiesand the dependents of deceased personnel, including those 
who are disabled. To facilitate this, 06 Central Welfare Officers (CWOs), 32 State Welfare Officers 
(SWOs) and 156 District Welfare Officers (DWOs) have been deployed across States and UTs to 
provide necessary assistance. 
4.5.2 The Ministry has further informed that financial support is extended through multiple 
schemes, including ex-gratia payments, pensions, gratuity and insurance benefits. Ex-gratia 
payments provide immediate financial relief, while families of deceased personnel receive monthly 
pensions and lump-sum gratuity payments. Additionally, group insurance scheme payments are 
disbursed to the next of kin. Educational support includes scholarships, fee waivers and reservations 
in educational institutions for the children of deceased personnel. Employment opportunities are 
facilitated through compassionate appointments and under the CAPF Punarvaas initiative, the data of 
retired and willing CAPF personnel is made available to private security agencies via the Private 
Security Agency (Regulation) Act (PSARA) website for recruitment. 
4.5.3 The Ministry has also highlighted the Bharat Ke Veer portal, which allows individuals to 
contribute directly to the accounts of the next of kin of deceased personnel or to a dedicated corpus 
fund. Furthermore, a 50% GST subsidy has been introduced for purchases from Kendriya Police 
Kalyan Bhandar (KPKB), with ₹125 crores allocated to support CAPF personnel, retirees and their 
families. The Ministry has informed that additional welfare measures include a 5% quota for 
compassionate appointments, financial aid and free education in CAPF public schools for the 
children of martyrs. The Prime Minister Scholarship Scheme provides ₹30,000 for boys and ₹36,000 
for girls pursuing professional degrees. Other benefits include a ₹33,756 children’s education 
allowance, ₹1,01,256 hostel subsidy and reservation of 26 MBBS and 3 BDS seats for the wards of 
CAPF personnel. 
4.5.4 The Ministry has further informed that ₹50 crores has been sanctioned for ex-gratia lump-
sum compensation to CAPFs in the current financial year. This includes ₹35 lakhs for personnel who 
die in active duty and ₹25 lakhs for those who die on bonafide Government duty. Additionally, 
approval has been granted for the 50% GST subsidy on KPKB purchases from April 1, 2024, to 
further support CAPF personnel and their families.

rehabilitation of CAPF personnel and their families. It notes the financial, educational and 
employment support provided, including ex-gratia payments, scholarships, compassionate

Committee observes that these measures play a crucial role in ensuring the well-being of 
serving and retired personnel, as well as the families of those who have laid down their lives in

4.6 Housing Facilities and Food Quality for CAPFs 
4.6.1 Recognizing the critical need to improve housing satisfaction among CAPF personnel, which 
stood at 47.95% as of December 2022, the Ministry has initiated several measures to address this 
issue. Forces such as the SSB have reported even lower satisfaction levels, highlighting the urgent 
need for intervention. A significant challenge identified is the unwillingness of personnel to accept 
accommodations in semi-urban or remote areas due to the distance from essential amenities like 
schools and hospitals. To address this, the MHA launched the "CAPF e-AWAS" portal to optimize 
the allocation of existing housing units across different forces. This portal aims to enhance the 
housing satisfaction ratio by allowing personnel from one force to seek accommodations available 
with another. The Ministry has informed that several new houses have been constructed and 
additional projects are currently in pipeline.  
4.6.2. The Ministryinformed the Committee that the mess menu is determined by a representative 
board comprising members from all ranks. This board decides the menu on the basis of instructions 
regarding daily calories intake per day. Food supplies, including rations, dairy products, and 
vegetables, are sourced either from local Army Service Corps (ASC) depots or through monthly 
purchases overseen by a designated board. A separate quality control board ensures the quality of all 
purchased items. To enhance nutritional value, millets have been incorporated into the mess menu. 
Unit doctors conduct regular inspections to ensure that cooks and mess staff maintain strict hygiene 
standards during food preparation. To facilitate feedback and address concerns, monthly mess 
meetings are held, providing a platform for all dining members to voice their opinions. Feedback 
received through these channels is addressed promptly to maintain high standards of food quality, 
hygiene and overall arrangements.

construct housing units for CAPF personnel in urban or well-connected areas to improve the 
current housing satisfaction level. It emphasizes on utilizing rapid construction technologies to 
expedite the process and ensure timely completion of projects. The Committee recommends 
that the "CAPF e-AWAS" portal be enhanced to improve the allocation of existing 
accommodations by ensuring it serves as an accurate inventory of residential houses and 

33 
 
Separated Family Accommodation (SFA) across all CAPFs. The Committee wishes to 
emphasize that achieving a housing satisfaction target of 70-80% in the coming years is 
essential for enhancing living conditions for CAPF personnel and their families. 
4.6.4 The Committee notes with satisfaction the Ministry's explanation of the mess menu 
determination process, highlighting the representative nature of the board responsible for 
menu planning and its adherence to daily caloric intake guidelines. The Committee also 
appreciates the multi-faceted approach regarding food supplies, involving both local Army 
Service Corps (ASC) depots and a designated procurement board. The Committee commends 
the incorporation of millets into the mess menu to enhance nutritional value. Further, the 
Committee acknowledges the importance of regular hygiene inspections by unit doctors and 
the implementation of monthly mess meetings to gather feedback from dining members. The 
Committee recommends the continuation and strengthening of these practices to ensure

4.8 K9 Unit/Canine Squad 
4.8.1 During the meeting of the Committee, a query was raised about the usage of K9 units/canine 
squad in the CAPF. It was informed by the Ministry about the usage of K9 in the CAPF, also known 
as canine squads, for various security and operational tasks. These units are integral to the forces' 
capabilities, providing support in areas such as explosive detection, tracking, and anti-Naxal 
operations. These dogs are trained for tasks like infantry patrol, anti-sabotage sniffer duties and 
detecting bombs and improvised explosive devices (IEDs). K9 units are used in high-risk operations, 
such as counter-terrorism and counter-insurgency missions and play a crucial role in detecting 
explosives and narcotics, helping to prevent attacks and maintain security in sensitive areas. 
Additionally, their ability to navigate challenging terrains and detect hidden threats makes them 
invaluable in border security and surveillance operations. 
4.8.2 K9 units often work alongside other specialized units within CAPF, such as the Rapid Action 
Force (RAF) and Commando Battalion for Resolute Action (CoBRA), to provide comprehensive 
security solutions. Some K9 units, like those in the National Security Guard (NSG), are equipped 
with advanced technology such as two-way audio-video K9 augmentation devices, allowing handlers

to see what the dogs see in real-time, enhancing operational effectiveness. This integration of 
technology not only boosts the efficiency of operations but also ensures the safety of both the 
handlers and the dogs. The training process for these units is rigorous, with handlers undergoing 
extensive training to work effectively with the dogs, ensuring seamless communication and 
operation. The integration of advanced technology and continuous training helps K9 units face 
operational challenges like harsh environments and complex scenarios.

provide indispensable support in explosive detection, tracking, anti-Naxal operations and 
counter-terrorism missions. The Committee also commends the rigorous training of these 
canine squads, which enables them to excel in infantry patrol, anti-sabotage sniffer duties and 
detecting bombs and improvised explosive devices (IEDs), making them crucial in high-risk 
operations. The Committee recommends the formation of more K9 squads, considering the 
exceptional services rendered by these units and their potential to further enhance security 
capabilities.

4.18 MODERNIZATION OF PRISONS  
 
4.18.1 The Ministry has been implementing the "Modernization of Prisons" project over five 
financial years, from 2021-22 to 2025-26. This project aims to enhance security infrastructure and 
logistical facilities in jails through technological interventions and the creation of high-security 
infrastructure. It also focuses on correctional administration through programs and initiatives 
centered on skilling, rehabilitation and behavior change. The Government prioritizes correctional 
administration and inmate rehabilitation to promote reintegration into society, with the goals of 
decriminalization and de-radicalization. This project modernizes prisons by enhancing security and 
introducing technology into daily administration to improve the safety and security of jails and 
inmates. 
 
4.18.2 According to the Ministry, this project encompasses several key components designed to 
enhance security and promote rehabilitation. These include upgrading video conferencing 
infrastructure, implementing body-worn cameras and developing motivational videos to encourage 
inmates to abandon criminal lifestyles. Jamming solutions and security poles will bolster security 
measures. Furthermore, the project emphasizes correctional programs such as counseling and 
therapies, facilitated by hiring instructors, teachers, behavioral experts, correctional administration 
experts and psychologists to support inmates. A significant aspect of the project involves 
establishing high-security prisons in States to securely house hard-core criminals and prevent them 
from influencing other prisoners. Initial funding has been released to these identified States for this 
purpose. The budget allocated under this head is shown in the table mentioned below:-

construction after overcoming administrative delays, substantial funding is required in FY 2025-26 
to ensure effective scheme implementation. 
4.18.4 The Committee notes that as of 2022 over 75% of prisoners in India were undertrials which 
mean that their cases are pending for a long time.  In many of these cases it has been seen that the 
undertrial prisoners have been acquitted by Courts after remaining in jail for a long time. The Rules 
and Regulations applicable to the undertrials are more or less similar tothat of the hardened 
convicted criminals.  The jails are becoming a nursery and training centre for committing heinous 
crimes due to the intermingling of the hardened criminals with undertrials, who are in jail for less 
heinous crimes or petty offences.  This is mainly due to the fact that the undertrials and heinous 
criminals are housed in the same jail. The undertrials who are acquitted by the Court have to live 
with the stigma that they were in jails.  
4.18.5 In this regard, the Ministry has informed the Committee that the undertrials and convicted 
prisoners are to be kept separately in prisons as per the Model Prison Manual, 2016 and the Model 
Prisons & Correctional Services Act, which mandate the classification of prisoners into different 
categories, including convicted prisoners, undertrials, habitual offenders and high-risk prisoners. 
High-risk prisoners are to be housed in high-security prisons to prevent their negative influence on 
others. However, since prisons fall under the State List, the implementation of these provisions is the 
responsibility of State and UT Governments. To address the issue of undertrials, Section 479 of the 
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), allows for the release of undertrials who have 
served half of their maximum sentence or one-third in the case of first-time offenders. Prison 
superintendents are required to file bail applications for eligible undertrials. On Constitution Day, 
26th November 2024, MHA launched a Special Campaign to ensure the effective implementation of 
this provision, leading to the filing of 933 bail applications and the release of 336 eligible prisoners. 
States and UTs have been directed to continue this initiative and submit monthly reports to the 
Ministry. 
4.18.6 With respect to the usage of mobile phones in the jails, the Ministry informed the Committee 
that the MHA has issued guidelines to States and Union Territories (UTs) through the Model Prison 
Manual and the Model Prisons and Correctional Services Act. These guidelines emphasize the use of 
modern jamming solutions and search equipment to tackle the mobile phone usage within prisons. 
The Model Prisons and Correctional Services Act categorizes the use of mobile phones and other 
contraband as a "prison offense" prescribing punishments for such offenses. To support these efforts, 
the MHA is providing financial assistance to States/UTs under the Modernization Prisons Project. 
This funding is used for installing security equipment such as mobile phone jammers, baggage 
scanners and other search devices to prevent the use of contraband items like mobile phones inside 
prisons. 
 
 

53 
 
Observation / Recommendation 
4.18.7 The Committee appreciates the Ministry for its ongoing efforts in the modernization of 
prisons, which focus on enhancing security and promoting rehabilitation through technological 
advancements, infrastructure improvements and effective correctional administration. 
However, considering the funding gap caused by the transition to the CNA TSA Hybrid Model 
1A, the Committee emphasizes the need for a smooth transition and calls on the Ministry to 
proactively address challenges to ensure the timely disbursement of funds. 
4.18.8 The Committee appreciates the Ministry's adherence to the Model Prison Manual, 2016 
and the Model Prisons & Correctional Services Act in ensuring the separation of undertrials 
and convicted prisoners. It emphasizes the necessity for full implementation of those guidelines 
by States and UTs, even though the prison administration falls under the State List. The 
Ministry’s efforts to address undertrials’ detention through Section 479 of the Bharatiya 
Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) and the Special Campaign launched on Constitution 
Day are acknowledged by the Committee. The Committee suggests continued monitoring and 
collaboration with States and UTs to ensure the timely release of eligible undertrials and the 
submission of monthly progress reports.  
 
4.18.9  The Committee recommends that there may be separate centers of detention for 
undertrials. It should not be referred to as jails,instead they may be called correction centers 
or detention centers. Jails should be used only to accommodate the hardened convicted 
criminals.  This may go a long way in preventing the undertrials becoming hardened criminals, 
providing more scope for reforming the undertrials and escaping the stigma of jailed 
prisoners. 
4.18.10  Further, the Committee recommends the allocation of dedicated funds for capital 
expenditure alongside revenue expenditure to facilitate substantial and long-term 
improvements in prison infrastructure. It also recognizes the significant role of skill 
development and rehabilitation programs for prisoners and encourages the Ministry to ensure 
these initiatives receive sufficient funding and are effectively implemented in all States and

4.18.11 The Committee notes that the Ministry has issued guidelines to the State and UTs 
through the Model Prison Manual and the Model Prisons and Correctional Services Act. The 
Committee recommends that these guidelines be fully implemented across all jurisdictions to 
address mobile phone usage in prisons. It also suggests enhancing the penalties prescribed in 
the Model Prisons and Correctional Services Act for using contrabandin prisons.

5.1.3 The Committee notes, from the perusal of the overall budgetary provisions and 
expenditure provided by the Ministry that most of the Union Territories have performed well 
with regard to the utilization of funds against allocation made in RE 2024-25. Although the 
funds utilization in Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu and Lakshadweep are

5.1.4 The Committee feels that people’s representatives in a democratic setup are well 
acquainted with the priorities, needs and aspirations of the people of their constituency. They 
can play an important role in representing the needs of the local population of their 
constituencies to the UT Administration. The Administration of UTs can seek participation of 
the people’s representatives of the Union Territories while planning and implementation of 
developmental projects of the UTs.

5.2.3 The Committee notes that water supply, power, medical and public health, roads and

the BE 2025-26 and the utilization of entire allocation within the Financial year. 
 
(i) Air Connectivity 
 
5.2.4 Andaman and Nicobar Islands are the largest archipelago system in the Bay of Bengal which 
is situated thousands of Kilometers away from the mainland of India. It is connected to the mainland 
through air and water route.The Committee enquired about the proposal to enhance the capacity of airport in Port Blair amid increased tourism in the UT and proposals for establishment of new airports in the UT to improve connectivity of far flung islands of the UT with mainland. The Ministry has informed that a new Integrated Terminal Building (NITB) at Veer Savarkar 
International Airport, Sri Vijaya Puram, has been made operational since August 2023. The annual 

61 
 
passenger handling capacity has increased from 0.75 Million Passengers Per Annum (MPPA) to 5 
million MPPA.  
 
5.2.5 In addition, Helicopter and Dornier Aircraft services are also available. Further, under RCS-
UDAN, 18 seater small fixed wing aircrafts are expected to be operationalized from the airports at 
Sibpur, Car Nicobar and Campbell Bay by March, 2025. 
 
5.2.6 During the course of meeting of the Committee held on 21st February, 2025, the 
representatives of UT of A&NI informed that approx. 3,32,000 tourist  came to the A&N islands 
during 2023 and it was increased to 7,21,000 tourists in the year 2024. The A&N Islands are 
connected to 18 destinations from different parts of the country through flight operations. 
International flight to Malaysia has also been in operation. 
 
Observation / Recommendation 
 
5.2.7 The Committee notes that a new Integrated Terminal Building (NITB) at Veer 
Savarkar International Airport, Sri Vijaya Puram has been made operational since August 
2023 and the annual passenger handling capacity of the airport has increased from 0.75 
Million Passengers Per Annum (MPPA) to 5 million MPPA. The Committee feels that 
commencement of international flights from A&N Islands must have also given a boost to the tourism sector by attracting more number of foreign tourists. The Committee would like to be apprised about the impact of development in tourism sector on revenue generation in the UT and on socio economic growth of the local people of the A&N Islands. The benefits of economic growth in the UT must also percolate to the local population as they equally deserve to reap those benefits. The Committee also feels that 
there are a number of islands in the UT of Andaman and Nicobar Islands which are not 
inhabited but have beautiful beaches and potential for eco tourism. The Committee 
recommends that UT administration may explore the opportunity of development of the 
tourism related activities in these islands and develop them as tourist destination for the 
growing number of tourists in the UT. 
 
(ii) Power consumption and Renewable Energy 
 
5.2.8 The information was sought on the status of power consumption and power supply in the UT 
of Andaman and Nicobar islands. It has been informed that all inhabited islands in UT of A&N 
Islands are electrified. The available capacity is 99.55 MW (including Solar & Hydro sources) 
against the power demand of 65 MW. Renewable energy sources constituted ~10.35% of total 
generation (382.48 MU) during FY 2023-24. Further, feasibility study for Solar & Wind has been 
conducted by The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI) and National Institute of Wind Energy (NIWE) 
respectively to harness Renewable Energy. 
 
5.2.9  The Committee is of the view that the UT of A&N Islands has huge potential for the 
generation of electricity through renewable energy sources like solar energy, wind energy and hydro 
energy, to cater to the need of the islands of the UT. The Committee sought to know from the UT of 
A&N Islands about the measures that have been taken and proposed to be taken to harness 
renewable sources of energy in the UT. The UT of A&N Islands replied that the A&N Islands 
administration is undertaking various measures to harness renewable sources of energy viz. Solar 
Roof Top (RTS) in Govt. buildings, Grid connected Solar Rooftop, RTS in RESCO Mode in 

62 
 
Residential buildings, Ground Mounted Solar PV projects with BESS, Floating Solar PV project, 
Wind Turbine Generator (WTG) etc. It has been also informed that enhanced allocation under the 
sub head ‘Power’ for the upcoming fiscal year is proposed to be utilized as below: 
 
1. Implementation of PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana 
2. Payment for HSD towards power generation 
3. Power Purchase 
4. Procurement of Spare Parts, Lubricant oil 
5. Procurement of DG Sets / Transformer 
 
Observation / Recommendation 
 
5.2.10 The Committee notes that renewable energy sources constituted only 10.35 % of total 
power generation during FY 2023-24, which is very low. The Committee should be informed 
about the outcome of feasibility study for Solar & Wind energywhich has been conducted by 
The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI) and National Institute of Wind Energy (NIWE) 
respectively to harness Renewable Energy. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
Ministry of Home Affairs along with the UT administration may approach the concerned 
Ministry/ Department to bring the new proposals of producing electricity through renewable 
energy resources at the earliest, to reduce the dependence on non-renewable sources of energy 
and preserve the fragile island from the negative impact of climate change.

3. Development of eco hut, watch towers and eco-tourism facilities under various forest

Observation / Recommendation 
5.2.12 The Committee notes that the various projects and schemes to be initiated in the UT of 
Andaman & Nicobar Islands in Financial Year 2025-26 under the Forestry and Wildlife Sector 
are related to construction works. There are not many activities relating to wildlife 
conservation. The UT has very rich wildlife as well as marine life. Giant leatherback Sea turtle 
is one of the species which is facing the threat of extinction in the UT. The Committee feels that 
enough hatcheries should be maintained to protect eggs of sea turtles. Efforts must also be 
made to have regular coordination and collaboration with concerned organizations for 
protecting natural habitat and nesting grounds of sea turtles.

Observation/ Recommendation 
 
5.3.6 The Committee notes that that the UT of Chandigarh had projected a demand of 
₹7924.58 crores (Gross basis), but the Government of India has allocated ₹6983.18 crores 
(Gross basis) for the Financial Year 2025-26. There is a shortfall of ₹941.40 Cr. (Gross and Net 
Basis) as compared to the allocations made and demand projected. The Committee feels that 
such substantial shortfall in allocation can hamper the progress of ongoing infrastructure 
projects in the field of health, urban development and education as envisaged by the UT 
administration for the upcoming Financial Year. The commencement of new projects could 
also be affected by the shortage of funds as focus will be on completion of ongoing projects 
rather than initiating any new schemes. The Committee, therefore, recommends that efforts 
must be made by the UT administration to strictly monitor the progress of projects and 
utilization of funds, so that it can seek additional fund at RE stage as per revised requirement.   
 
5.3.7 The Committee notes that UT administration of Chandigarh has earmarked ₹76.60 
crores for the infrastructure development in technical and higher education sector and 
Government schools for the Financial Year 2025-26. The Committee recommends that efforts 
must be initiated by the concerned agencies to adhere to the completion of 
construction/extension of the proposed buildings at the earliest.  
 
5.3.8  The Committee is of the view that in any school availability of fundamental facilities is 
paramount to fostering a conducive learning environment. These facilities not only ensure the 
safety and well-being of students but also contribute significantly to their academic growth and 
overall development. Improvement of infrastructure should be topmost priority for the 
education sector. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs may provide 
sufficient funds to the UT administration at RE stage for the education sector for improvement 
of basic facilities like sufficient number of classrooms, toilets, libraries, laboratories and sports 
facilities at city Government schools. Measures should also be taken towards creation of smart 
classrooms by digitizing the existing ones and provision of nutritious food for mid day meals.  
  
5.3.9 The Committee was informed that the teachers and parents are slightly agitated over 
some issues related to school education in the Union Territory of Chandigarh. The Committee 
recommends that the Administration may consult with all the stakeholders involved and 
address their issues they are facing in a positive way.

(v) Waste Disposal and Management 
5.5.17 To improve the infrastructure for waste disposal and management, the UT of Ladakh has 
taken following steps: 
Urban Areas: 
i. Solid Waste Segregation and Collection: A comprehensive door-to-door waste collection 
system across both Leh and Kargil Towns has been implemented. All streets and main 
bazaars in Leh and Kargil, with a frequency of twice a day are being swept. 
 
ii. Development of Waste Management Facilities: An Integrated Solid Waste Management 
Plant in Leh with a capacity of 30 TPD (20 TPD for dry waste and 10 TPD for wet waste) 
became operational in 2020 to process both types of waste separately.  Construction of Solid 
Waste Management Plant in Kargil with a capacity of 25 TPD (15 TPD for dry waste and 10 
TPD for wet waste) which was completed in November 2024 is currently operating on a trial 
basis. 
 
iii. Liquid Waste Management: A 3 MLD (Million Liters per Day) Sewage Treatment Plant is 
already operational in Agling, Leh, and  the capacity of the plant will be increased upto 10.5 
MLD. In Kargil to address future population growth. 
 

77 
 
iv. Legacy Waste Management: The legacy waste at Bombgarh in Leh, which accumulated to 
approximately 58,910 tons, has been successfully remediated. 
 
v. Policy Framework and Governance: A comprehensive ban on single-use plastics in Leh 
and Kargil Towns have been implemented. Installation of Sewage Treatment Plant (STP) has 
been made mandatory for all established guest houses, hotels and building with more than 10 
rooms to ensure effective wastewater management. A series of policies including Solid 
Waste Management, Plastic Smart Ladakh Strategy, and the Strategy on Construction and 
Demolition Waste have been introduced.  On directions from National Green Tribunal 
(NGT), a ban on open burning of municipal and plastic waste has been imposed.  Solid 
Waste Management Bye-laws has been notified in Leh and Kargil. 
 
Rural Areas:  
i. Solid Waste Collection Centers and Plastic waste Segregation centers are in place in all the 
31 blocks of UT of Ladakh.  
ii. Door to door waste collection is being done which is facilitated by the fleet of 35 waste 
collecting vehicles.  
iii. Community Sanitary Complexes have been constructed in almost all the villages and 
especially at the places where tourist footfall is high and at places where people throng for 
religious pilgrimage/gathering. 
iv. Biodigesters have been installed at important tourist/religious places. 
v. Integrated Household Latrines have been given to all the eligible beneficiaries.  
vi. The UT of Ladakh has achieved 100% Grey Water Management in all rural areas. 
vii. Out of 240 villages, 203 villages have been declared as Open Defection Free Plus (ODF 
Plus) Model Villages. 
5.5.18 In addition to the above, Regular Information, Education, and Communication (IEC) 
activities, such as workshops and murals, are being conducted to educate tourists and locals about 
responsible waste management and reducing single-use plastics.

like implementation of a comprehensive door-to-door waste collection system across Leh and 
Kargil Towns and construction of Solid Waste Management Plant in Kargil with a capacity of

The Committee observes, based on the above-mentioned information, that the actual 
Budget Estimate (BE) for 2025-26 is lower than the projected BE for 2025-26 across several 
key areas, reflecting a more conservative allocation than initially anticipated. The total budget 
has been reduced from ₹184,236.94 crores (projected BE 2025-26) to ₹160391.06 crores (actual

actual allocations fall short of projections, with reductions observed across the CRPF, NSG, 
BSF, ITBP, CISF, Assam Rifles, and SSB. This indicates a recalibration of expenditure 
priorities. Similarly, significant downward revisions have been made to allocations for the 
Intelligence Bureau (IB), NATGRID, Central Police Organizations (CPOs) and Delhi Police. 
Police infrastructure projects, particularly CAPF building projects, have experienced a 
substantial reduction from ₹6,403.02 crores to ₹4,038.70 crores, which may potentially impact 
construction of new buildings. The Committee notes that such reductions may adversely affect 
critical schemes under these heads and may slow down modernization programs as well as 
hinder the execution of developmental projects, particularly in border areas. Hence, the 
Committee recommends that the MHA may take up the matter with the Ministry of Finance to 
seek increased allocations under these heads in alignment with their original projections. This 
will ensure that the essential developmental schemes are not affected due to insufficient 
funding. The Committee hopes that funds may be demanded for various developmental and 
expansion projects at the RE stage depending on the utilization pattern.

Home Guards from ₹566.01 crores in RE 2024-25 to ₹30.01 crores in BE 2025-26 is based on 
the expectation that all backlog claims will be cleared in FY 2024-25. However, the Committee 
emphasizes the need to reassess the funding requirements for new claims and ensure that 
States are adequately supported to maintain the operational efficiency of Home Guards. 
Similarly, with respect to the Holistic Development of Islands in Union Territories, where the 
allocation has been reduced from ₹88 crores in RE 2024-25 to a nominal ₹0.01 crore in BE 
2025-26, the Committee recommends expediting the preparation of EFC papers and project

stakeholders to ensure that reductions across various components do not adversely impact 
service delivery or developmental goals.

the Ministry to ensure that these allocations are utilized efficiently, particularly in areas like 
narcotics control and cybercrime, where technological advancements are crucial. For instance, 
the Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) has been allocated ₹193.77 crores for 2025-26, which 
should be utilized effectively to enhance drug detection capabilities and operationalize new 
field units. Similarly, the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) has been allocated 
₹142.81 crores, which should focus on expanding cyber awareness programs and establishing 
specialized units like the Cyber Commandos.The Committee notes that the drug menace is 
affecting the young population of our country in a bad way.  The Ministry of Home Affairs 
should take more steps to address the issue in association with NCB. 
(Para 4.13.4) 
 The Committee recommends the NCRB to effectively utilize its increased budget for 
2025-26, to enhance its data analysis capabilities. It emphasizes the importance of leveraging 
advanced technologies, such as artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning, to improve the 
depth and accuracy of crime statistics. The Committee urges NCRB to ensure that all crime 
data is published regularly and made accessible to law enforcement agencies and public. It also 
notes the publication of agitation data by the NCRB and suggests continuing of this 
publication. The Committee further recommends that NCRB to collaborate with international 
agencies, to adopt best practices in crime data collection and analysis.  Additionally, it suggests 
that the Directorate of Coordination and Police Wireless (DCPW) may focus on upgrading 
communication systems to ensure seamless coordination among law enforcement agencies. The 
Committee emphasizes that each CPO should provide regular updates on expenditure and 
project implementation to ensure that the allocated funds are used effectively to enhance 
public safety and security. The Committee notes that cybercrime in the country has increased 
manifold. A notable characteristic of cybercrimes is that they often involve multiple State and 
police jurisdictions.  Therefore, it is essential that the Police authorities must get the power of 
seamless jurisdiction to deal with the Cyber Crimes.  The Committee recommends that a 
separate Central Police Force may be established on the lines of NIA or CBI to deal with Cyber 
Crimes. 
 (Para 4.13.5) 
 
 
 
 

104 
 
FORENSIC SCIENCES FACILITIES AND INFRASTRUCTURE 
 
 The Committee notes the significant efforts to enhance forensic capabilities, 
particularly through the strengthening of DNA and cyber forensic facilities under the 
Nirbhaya Fund. It recommends the Ministry to continue to invest in modernizing forensic 
infrastructure, focusing on advanced technologies to improve analysis efficiency. The 
Committee suggests the Ministry to ensure that all forensic laboratories, both central and 
State, are equipped with the latest equipment and trained personnel to handle complex cases 
effectively. It emphasizes the importance of maintaining a centralized database of forensic data 
to aid in investigations and policy-making. Additionally, it suggests that the Ministry to 
consider establishing more regional forensic laboratories to increase accessibility and reduce 
the burden on existing facilities. The Committee notes that new Criminal Laws mandates 
forensic investigation for offences involving punishment of 7 years or more.  The Committee 
also notes that there are very few forensic science laboratories.  The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that every district of the country must have a forensic laboratory to deal with the 
criminal investigation. The Committee is aware that criminal investigation is a State subject 
but given the financial health of the States, the Union Government should financially support 
the establishment of forensic laboratories in each district of the country. 
 (Para 4.14.6) 
The Committee also recommends that the Ministry needs to prioritize the establishment 
of off-campuses of the National Forensic Sciences University (NFSU) and Centers of Excellence 
to provide quality training and education in forensic sciences. It suggests that mobile forensic 
vans be deployed to enhance on-site forensic capabilities, particularly in remote areas. 
 (Para 4.14.7)

The Committee notes the significant efforts of the Ministry to enhance border 
infrastructure across various international borders. The Committee recommends that the 
Government needs to expedite the completion of ongoing fencing projects, ensuring that all 
allocated funds are utilized efficiently. It also recommends conducting regular assessments to 
identify gaps in border infrastructure and ensure that allocations are aligned with strategic 
priorities. The Committee also wishes the Ministry to prepare the data of influx of immigrants 
like Bangladeshis, Rohingyas and from other countries. The Committee notes that Rohingyas 
are entering and settling illegally in various parts of the country. The Committee recommends 
that the Ministry of Home Affairs should take effective steps to identify the illegally settled 
Rohingyas and repatriate them to their parent countries. 
 (Para 4.15.6) 
 
The Committee suggests that the Ministry needs to consider establishing more 
integrated check posts to facilitate smoother trade and travel while maintaining security 
standards. The Committee recommends that the MHA needs to continue to enhance border 
security through the expansion of smart fencing projects, which are part of the Comprehensive 
Integrated Border Management System (CIBMS). These initiatives should use advanced 
technologies such as thermal imagers, fiber-optic sensors, radar and sonar systems to create an 

105 
 
invisible electronic barrier that aids in real-time surveillance and intrusion detection, thereby 
strengthening India's border security. 
(Para 4.15.7)

enhance women's safety through various schemes under the Nirbhaya Fund. Initiatives such as

Forensic Science Labs reflect a holistic approach to combat violence against women. The 
Committee observes that the allocation for ERSS Phase II in 2025-26 will focus on upgrading 
the existing system to ensure a standardized and efficient emergency response mechanism 
nationwide.  However, the Committee notes the underutilization of funds allocated under these

investigating officers, prosecutors and medical officers to improve the handling of forensic

powered surveillance systems and mobile apps, to enhance women's safety in public spaces.  
 
(Para 4.16.6)

the criminal justice system through the Inter-Operable Criminal Justice System (ICJS). This

pillars of the justice system. The Committee recommends that MHA needs to prioritize the 
effective implementation of ICJS across all States and Union territories by ensuring timely 
allocation and utilization of funds. It suggests that the Ministry of Home Affairs work closely 
with the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) and the National Informatics Centre (NIC)

recommends that necessary capacity building and training programs for officials involved in

undertrials. It should not be referred to as jails, instead they may be called correction centers

with the Administration of the UT of  Lakshadweep to discuss and find an amicable solution to 
these issues pertaining to the UT of Lakshadweep. 
 
(Para 5.6.15) 
 

115 
 
Demand No. 57 –  Transfers to Delhi 
 
5.7.4 The Committee recommends that the Ministry must ensure that regular and periodic 
monitoring of ongoing and new schemes/projects proposed under Central Assistance to UTs 
for which an allocation ₹951.00 crores has been made to the UT of Delhi by the Union 
Government, so that these projects can fully utilize the fund allocation and avoid cost overruns 
and strictly adhere to their completion time line.  
 
(Para 5.7.4) 
  
The Committee notes that Chandrawal Water Treatment Plant project is proposed to 
be executed in six packages and expected to be completed by September, 2027. Earlier, the 
project was expected to be completed in October, 2024. This shows that the completion of the 
project has been delayed. Considering the shortage of water in different parts of Delhi, the 
Committee observes that the project is vital for Delhi as it will help in improving water supply 
system for population of 22 lakh i.e. about 11% of Delhi population. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends that the MHA may take up with the UT of Delhi for periodic monitoring of the 
progress of work so that the timelines are met without cost overruns. Adequate funds may be 
sought from the Ministry of Finance as per the requirement.  
(Para 5.7.8) 
 
 
The Committee is of view that a substantial number of private coaching centres and 
hostels for boys and girls are being run in Delhi without any strict norms and regulations. 
These are not providing adequate space and basic living conditions to the young population 
who come from far-flung areas for fulfilling their future employment aspirations.  The 
Committee would like to be apprised about the number of such coaching centres and hostels 
that are being run in Delhi and what kind to accommodation and other basic facilities are 
being provided by them to the students and residents of these facilities. The Committee may 
also be informed about the provision of licensing of such centres and the last inspection done to 
review the conditions of these centres and hostels.  
(Para 5.7.10) 
 
  
The Committee also like to be informed about the maintenance of any kind of record of 
around 25-30 Lakh floating population in the region of Delhi and what kind of basic facilities 
are available for them. 
(Para 5.7.11) 
 
 
Demand No. 58 - Transfers to Jammu & Kashmir 
 
 The Committee notes that the UT administration of Jammu and Kashmir has achieved 
successful and nearing completion of various projects in the sectors of road, rail and air 
connectivity, power generation and provision of drinking water in rural households. The 
Committee feels empowerment in infrastructure projects creates conducive environment for 
investments in industries and create opportunities for entrepreneurship in underdeveloped 
regions. The Committee recommends that UT Administration should take measures to 

116 
monitor the progress of ongoing projects in these sectors and speed up the projects which are 
in pipeline.  
(Para 5.8.6) 
The Committee is heartened to note that the tourists’ arrival in J&K for the last two 
years have increased manifold. The Committee takes notes of the steps taken for the 
development and promotion of tourism in the UT of Jammu and Kashmir. The Committee is 
of the view that the tourism and hospitality sector, apart from generating large revenue, is a 
major source of livelihood for the people of J&K by creating employment opportunities and 
boosting local businesses. It also contributes towards regional and rural development of the 
UT. The Committee recommends that UT administration should chalk out a road map to take 
initiatives to position J&K as a world class tourism destination, improve the tourist experience 
and create sustainable economic opportunities for the local population.  
(Para 5.8.10) 
The Committee is of the view that the industrial sector in Jammu & Kashmir needs to 
be enhanced for generation of employment for the local youth. The Committee recommends 
that initiatives should be taken to improve infrastructure i.e. investing in transportation, 
power supply, and internet connectivity to make region more attractive for businesses and 
investors.  At the same time, by encouraging entrepreneurship, promoting tourism, enhancing 
education and skill development, the employment potential of Jammu and Kashmir can be 
significantly increased. Providing loans on subsidised rates can also improve employment 
scenario in the UT.  
(Para 5.8.18) 
The Committee recommends that the Administration of Jammu and Kashmir should 
take more concrete steps towards providing employment opportunities to educated youth of 
the UT. Additional initiatives should be taken for implementation of self-employment schemes 
across various sectors to establish sustainable income generating ventures for unemployed 
youth.  
(Para 5.8.19) 
Handicraft sector in the UT of Jammu and Kashmir is one of the largest employment 
generation sources in the region. The UT administration should strive for Geographical 
Indication (GI) tagging of each and every crafts of the region as it can  promote cultural 
heritage and economic growth as with GI tagged product, the producers are able to get 
significantly better prices for their products.  
(Para 5.8.20) 
Demand No. 59- Transfers to Puducherry 
The Committee notes that 98.17% of funds have been utilized by the UT of Puducherry 
(till 31 stJanuary, 2025) in the FY 2024-25, but the allocation at BE stage in FY 2025-26 has 
been reduced to ₹3427.18 crores against the projected amount of ₹3766.33 crores, under 

117 
“Central Assistance”. The shortfall in allocation for programme/activities under this head for  
the Financial Year 2025-26 should be reviewed vis-à-vis actual progress of implementation and 
if required additional fund must be sought at RE 2025-26 stage. The Committee, recommends 
that in future, the Ministry of Home Affairs should impress upon the Ministry of Finance to 
increase the allocation of funds in accordance with the projected demand of the Government of 
Puducherry as the UT has been a maintaining a very healthy utilization pattern.  
(Para 5.9.5) 
The Committee notes that the Airport Authority of India has approved the plan for the 
expansion of Puducherry Airport, and finalized a Master Plan. The Committee recommends 
that the MHA may take up with the UT of Puducherry, concerned Ministries/ Departments, to 
expedite the further necessary activities in this direction and made efforts to provide requisite 
funds for the plan. The Committee would like to be apprised about the progress made in this 
regard. 
(Para 5.9.6) 
The Committee appreciates that the UT administration is working towards developing 
Puducherry into a sustainable tourism destination. The Committee is of the opinion that 
Puducherry has multiple tourist attractions and some unique identity owing to history of 
French influence. Tourism has a potential to become a major source of employment and 
income/revenue generation with active participation of the private sector and local host 
communities.  The UT should take steps to fully develop the tourism potential of UT of 
Puducherry in a planned and integrated manner and to augment the infrastructure facilities 
for tourists and promote socio economic development through tourism while preserving and 
protecting the environment and heritage. 
(Para 5.9.10)

CHAPTER-I 
 
OVERVIEW 
 
1.1 Introduction 
 
1.1.1 The North Eastern Region (NER) comprises eight States namely Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, 
Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim and Tripura, with a total area of almost 8 per cent of 
India. It is characterized by its rich bio -diversity and heavy precipitation a nd has immense potential for 
development. The region shares International Borders with several neighbouring countries - Nepal, 
Bhutan, China, Myanmar and Bangladesh. As per the India State of Forest Report, 2021, the forest 
resources in the North Eastern States account for 23.75% of the total forest cover of the country. As per 
Census 2011, the population of the region is about 4.5 crores, constituting 3.78% of the total population 
of India. The rural population makes up 81.64% of the total population of the  region, while the urban 
population accounts for 18.36%.  
 
1.1.2 The Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region (DoNER) was constituted, first as a 
Department in 2001 and then as a Ministry in 2004, for better coordination between the State 
Governments of North Eastern Region and the Central Ministries/Departments of Government of India. 
It is the only Ministry with a territorial jurisdiction and functions to coordinate the developmental efforts 
in the North Eastern Region (NER). 
 
1.1.3 The Ministry of DoNER aims to transform North Eastern Region through development, in 
sustainable yet accelerated manner, affording comprehensive growth and access to ease of living to all 
its citizens. The following are the main objectives of the Ministry: 
(i) Synergize policies, plans and execution for rapid development of NE  Region through 
Collaborating with Central Ministries, States, Agencies & Expert Stakeholders; 
(ii)  Ensuring full utilization of 10% Gross Budget Support (GBS) and other budgetary resources for 
NER; 
(iii) Promoting investment in the NER, including public, private, corporate & multilateral funding; 
(iv) Developing infrastructure to mitigate connectivity and social sector deficits of the region; and  
(v) Strengthening institutions and networks for livelihood, social services, skills and capacity. 
 
1.1.4 The Ministry has also been implementing various Schemes for development of North East Region 
viz. North East Special Infrastructure Development Scheme (Roads) -NESIDS (Roads), North East 
Special Infrastructure Development Scheme Other Than Road -NESIDS (OTRI), Schemes of North 
Eastern Council (NEC), Prime Minister’s Development Initiative for North East Region (PM -DevINE) 
scheme and Special Development packages (SDP). Ministry also coordinates with other stakeholders, 
who can be from non -government sector or multilateral sector, to work for the development of NER. 
During 2024-25, MDoNER has taken some major initiatives for faster implementation of projects for the 
development of NER.

1.2.1
 The Ministry is mandated to deal with the following matters: - 
(i) Matters relating to planning, execution and monitoring of developmental schemes and projects
of NER including those in the sectors of Power, Irrigation, Roads and Communications.
(ii) I mplementation of various schemes like Non -Lapsable Central Pool of Resources (NLCPR),
North East Special Infrastructure Development Scheme (NESIDS), Hill Area Development
Programme (HADP), Schemes of NEC, North East Road Sector Development Scheme
(NERSDS), etc.
(iii) Matters pertaining to various organizations under its administrative control, such as North
Eastern Council (NEC), North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation Limited
(NERAMAC), North Eastern Handloom and Handicrafts Development Corporation
(NEHHDC), Cane and Bamboo Technology Centre (CBTC), and North East Development
Finance Institution (NEDFi).
(iv) L ivelihood Programmes of North East Rural Livelihood Project (NERLP) and North Eastern
Region Community Resource Management Project (NERCORMP).
1.2.2 As per Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) recommendation, in the budget of FY 2023-24, 
the NERSDS Scheme has been merged in NESIDS as a NESIDS (Roads) component which also 
includes committed liabilities of NLCPR, NER SDS-Programme/EAP and HADP. HADP scheme has 
been closed.

in the North Eastern Region. Besides, calling the progress of expenditure out of the earmarked outlay 
for NER, a set of Ministries/Departments has been assigned to senior officers of the Ministry for regular 
and continuous interactions with respective Ministries/Departments. Moreover, all non- exempted 
Ministries/Departments have appointed nodal officers in their respective Ministries to coordinate over 
10% GBS with the Ministry of DoNER and to apprise them about the major initiatives undertaken in 
NER.  
1.4.2
 The Ministry formulates thematic reg ional plans for coordinated development and welfare of 
people in NER. It works towards resource mobilization for NER through convergence, expert 
partnerships and Public Private Partnership (PPP).  

4 
1.4.3 In addition to the routine interactions, the Ministry also convenes sectoral review meetings with 
key Ministries such as Railways, Road Transport & Highways, Civil Aviation, Power, Environment, 
Forest & Climate Change, Tourism etc. for effective implementation of schemes and time -bound 
completion of major infrastr ucture projects in NER. Ministry of DoNER is represented in Inter -
Ministerial Groups of major Ministries such as the Ministries of Road Transport and Highways 
(MoRTH), Railways, Micro, Small & Medium Enterprises (MSME), Home, etc. and is also consulted 
at policy formation and project implementation stage through EFC/ SFC and Cabinet notes.  
1.4.4
 The Ministry has five Inter-Ministerial Committees (IMC) viz. IMC on Roads, IMC on Health 
& Nutrition, IMC on Medicinal Aromatic Plants, IMC on HADP and IMC on STINER wherein issues 
of importance in these domains are discussed with the Stakeholder Ministries/Departments.  
1.5
 Gross Budgetary Support (GBS): Earmarking of Union Budget by Central Ministries/ 
Departments for North Eastern Region 
1.5.1
 In October 1996, the Central Government announced ‘Some initiatives for North Eastern 
Region (NER)’, one of these measures was the policy decision to earmark at least 10% of Plan Budgets 
of the Central Ministries/Departments for the development of NE States. Accordingly, it was decided 
that Central Ministries/Departments, unless specifically exempted, will set aside 10% of their Plan 
Gross Budgetary Support (GBS) for the NER to ensure a quantum jump in budgetary resource flows to 
the region and to fill the backlog and gaps in basic minimum service and infrastructure. Subsequently, 
allocation of funds under 10% GBS for the NER introduced in 2014-15 (Statement-23), is being done 
annually on a lump sum basis by the non-exempted Central Ministries/Departments at the BE/RE stage 
under Major Heads 2552 (for revenue expenditure), 4552 (for capital expenditure) and 6552 (for loan 
expenditure) under their respective functional schemes. The details of expenditure of non- exempt

for the North East (NLCPR) 
1.6.1
 The scheme of Non-Lapsable Central Pool of Resources (NLCPR) has been a scheme for gap 
funding for creation of infrastructure in the States of NER. The NLCPR Scheme of the M inistry has 
been re-structured as North East Special Infrastructure Development Scheme (NESIDS) to meet the 
gaps in social and physical infrastructure in the region. NESIDS is a 100% Centrally funded Central 
Sector Scheme. Hill Area Development Pilot Schem e for development of backward districts of 
Tamenglong and Noney in the state of Manipur is a sub- scheme of NESIDS, which was introduced 
during 2018-19 and is under implementation. Under NLCPR -Central - a Central Sector Plan scheme, 
projects of Union Ministries/Departments, which exceeds 10% GBS expenditure in a year, pertaining 
to subjects listed in the Union and Concurrent Lists, are being funded. However, no new projects are 
sanctioned under NLCPR - Central and only on -going projects are funded under the Scheme. Union 
Cabinet approved the continuation of Schemes of MDoNER during the remaining period of 15th 
Finance Commission i.e. from 2022-23 to 2025-26.

1.7 Central Pool of Resources for NER 
1.7.1 In 1997-98, when it was found that the actual expenditure of Ministries/Departments for NER 
was less than the mandatory ceiling of 10 per cent, the Government decided to create a "Central 
Resource Pool" into which the unutilized portion of the 10 per cent earmarked GBS would accrue at 
the end of the financial year.  Since 1998 -99, the annual surrendered amounts out of the earmarked 
outlays of all the non- exempted Central Ministries/Departments for NER have been accounted as 
accruals to this Pool and the annual expenditure of the Ministry under the NLCPR scheme is being 
accounted as withdrawal from the Pool. However, this is a notional pool, maintained on a proforma 
basis by the Ministry of Finance. The Ministry of DoNER monitors Ministry -wise expenditure/ 
surrendered amounts for the purpose of ascertaining the accrual to the NLCPR pool in consultation 
with the Ministry of Finance.

1.8
 North Eastern Council (NEC) 
1.8.1 T
he North Eastern Council (NEC) was constituted as a statutory advisory body by an Act of 
Parliament under the NEC Act, 1971 (84 of 1971) marking the beginning of a new chapter of concerted 
and planned endeavor for rapid socio- economic development of the North Easter Region (NER). Over 
the last fifty years, the Council has played a significant role in ushering development into the region at a 
time when most of states were in their formative stages. Road and air connectivity was supported, 
foundations for important regional Institutions were established, and various socio- economic 
infrastructures were created across the length and breadth of the Region, making a difference in the lives 
of the people and thereby earning a lot of goodwill in the local community. Presently, NEC is looking to 
continue its efforts, especially in terms of gap-filling in areas which have escaped the attention of various 
development agencies, and creating convergence at different levels. NEC is also looking at building 
capacities, sharing best practices and introducing cutting edge technologies among the NE states.

(i) During January to December, 2024, under Schemes of NEC, a total of 51 projects worth
₹ 216.33 Crore were sanctioned and 116 projects worth ₹ 1248.99 Crore were completed.
(ii) During the same period, twelve  (
 12) projects worth ₹  780.94 Cr. were sanctioned, five  (5)

1.9 North East Cane and Bamboo Development Council (NECBDC) 
1.9.1 North East Cane and Bamboo Development Council (NECBDC) [erstwhile Cane and Bamboo 
Technology Centre (CBTC)] is an ISO 9001:2008 certified organization and was established in the year 
2000 as part of Cane and Bamboo Technological Up-gradation and Networking Project of United Nations 

7 
Development Programme (UNDP). NECBDC was registered as a Society on 21 st July 2004 with the 
Secretary, NEC as the Chairman and Mission Directors of State Bamboo Mission of the eight North 
Eastern States as Members of the Governing Body of NECBDC. NECBDC has been steadfast in its 
commitment to developing the bamboo and cane sector, particularly for the NER. NECBDC has created 
16 cane and bamboo clusters (02 in each NE state) on different themes. It is also developing cane and 
bamboo clusters and promotion of eco tourism bamboo based housing techniques. 
1.10 North E astern Handicrafts an d Handlooms D evelopment C orporation Limited 
(NEHHDC) 
1.10.1 The North Eastern Handicrafts and Handlooms Development Corporation Ltd (NEHHDC) was 
incorporated on 31 st March, 1977 at Shillong, Meghalaya with the mandate of promotion and 
development of Handlooms and Handicrafts Sector in the North Eastern Region. NEHHDC has been 
providing marketing support through procurement of Handicrafts and Handlooms products directly 
from the Artisans, Weavers and Self -Help Groups at clusters and selling the same through its Sales 
Emporia located at Shillong, Guwahati, Kolkata, New Delhi and Gujarat and through Sales Promotion 
Offices located at Chennai and Bangalore and also through the conduct of various exhibitions and 
marketing events all over the country. NEHHDC promotes crafts of all 8 states by providing market 
linkages to the artisans and through its emporiums “Purbashree” & e-commerce platform mobile outlets 
and exhibitions. It also provides skill development in various job roles under various Centra l 
Government Schemes. 
1.11 North E astern R egional A gricultural Mar keting C orporation L imited 
(NERAMAC)  
1.11.1 North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation (NERAMAC) Limited was 
incorporated in 1982 as a CPSE. It functions under the administrative control of the Ministry of 
Development of North Eastern Region (MDoNER). NERAMAC, a marketing organization dedicated 
to the agricultural sector of the North Eastern Region, has been envisaged and is functioning as not just 
a marketing agency for farmers and ent repreneurs, but also undertakes agri -horti projects, skill 
curriculum supplies inputs, GI produce promotion activities, agri -events and assists in setting up of 
horticulture value chain (food processing) etc. to holistically approach the aspect of Agri -horti 
development. It supports farmers right from the fields to the market (end consumers) for their produce. 
1.11.2 A revival package for NERAMAC was approved in August 2021. The Corporation has 
performed remarkably in the last two financial years by registering the high turnovers with net profits 
of ₹4.27 Cr. in the FY 2022-23 and ₹1.27 Cr. in the FY 2023-24. In the financial years 2024-25, the 
Corporation is also expected to achieve the targets set under the revival plan. 
1.12 Prime Minister’s D evelopment Initiative for North East Region (PM-DevINE) Scheme 
1.12.1 The Union Cabinet approved the PM-DevINE Scheme on 12.10.2022, as a Central Sector 
Scheme with 100% Central funding, with a total outlay of ₹ 6,600 crore for the 4 year period from 
2022-23 to 2025-26. PM-DevINE aims at rapid and holistic development of the North-E ast Region by 
funding infrastructure and social development projects based on felt needs of the States. It strives to fill 
gaps in various sectors and will not be a substitute for existing Central and State Schemes. 

8 
1.12.2 The objectives of PM-DevINE are to: 
a. Fund infrastructure convergently in the spirit of PM Gati Shakti
b. Support social development projects based on felt needs of the NER
c. Enable livelihood activities for youth and women
d. Fill the development gaps in various sectors
1.12.3 An Empow ered Inter -Ministerial Committee (EIMC) under th e ch airmanship of Secretary, 
Ministry of DoNER screens, appraises and recommends project proposals for implementation by 
appropriate agency. The Committee also monitor progress of sanctioned projects to ensur e proper 
utilization of the allocated funds under the scheme. 
1.13  N orth East Special Infrastructure Development Scheme (NESIDS) 
1.13.1 NESIDS is a central sector scheme, which aims to support filling up the infrastructure gaps in 
identified sectors of the NER such as drinking water supply, power, road connectivity, tourism and 
social infrastructure in the areas of primary and secondary sectors of education and health. The NESIDS 
scheme was approved during 2017-18 and was implemented till 31.03.2022. The approval for extension 
of NESIDS Schemes w.e.f. 01.04.2022 till 31.03.2026 has been accorded by the Government on 4 th 
January, 2023. During the process of extension of the NESIDS w.e.f. 01.04.2022, the erstwhile 
NESIDS has been restructured into two components viz. NESIDS (Roads) and NESIDS (Other than 
Road Infrastructure).
