Proposed Amendments to the Recommendations in the Two Hundred and
Fifty Fourth Draft Report on ‘Cyber Crime – Ramifications, Protection
and Prevention’
Respected Chairman,
I would like to place on record my appreciation for the diligence with which the
committee has produced draft report #254. The draft report has outlined in great
detail, the significantly increased threat to our national assets, infrastructure,
and the financial, physical and psychological well-being of our citizens, all of
which are paramount and must be secured at all costs.
The objective to create a robust legal and institutional framework to protect the
nation from cybercriminals, financial fraudsters and malicious actors is well
served by the report’s recommendations however they also bring to light some
imperative concerns within the realm of privacy, personal and creative
freedoms, and Fundamental Rights guaranteed by the Constitution of India.
In this regard, my colleagues from the Congress party have already placed
before the committee, a set of recommendations with which I am in agreement
and I wholly endorse. I do not wish to repeat them here. However, I would like
to add the following points for your perusal:

1. Mandatory Pre-certification for OTT content (Para 3.2.17)
As per the draft report “The Committee, recommends that the
Government may consider amending the IT Rules, 2021 to introduce a
mandatory pre-certification process for OTT content, by establishing an
OTT content regulatory ecosystem within the ambit of CBFC, bringing
it in line with CBFC practices for films and ensuring that explicit or
culturally sensitive material is reviewed prior to public release”.
As regards the above recommendation, I suggest the following:
•“Aside from the extremely grave objections cited by my colleagues
in their recommendations addressing the issue of the Fundamental
Rights of Freedom of speech and expression being curtailed by the
above recommendation, its implementation is likely to prove
practically inefficient and virtually impossible. The number of
films produced by the entire Indian film industry is far exceeded by
the number of films, videos, reels, and other content produced
across the range of OTT platforms. Funnelling all these through a
single, central board equivalent to the CBFC will create a massive
backlog and regulation will become extremely problematic”.
•“This will also seriously affect the OTT industry in terms of the
frequency and ease of content distribution which will in turn affect
employment opportunities in which a large number of youth are
now engaged”.
•“Since the stated objective appears to be primarily curbing access
to adult content by minors, it would be more feasible to allow these
platforms to continue self-regulating and self-rating while
interfacing with them to apply more stringent parental controls”.
•“Instituting a joint forum at which stakeholders can formulate
norms and guidelines that are conducive to required cultural and
social standards as agreed upon by the said stakeholders (if
required to be separate from those of other countries) should be
considered and such guidelines released as directives to be
followed by the OTT platforms. Infringement of the guidelines can
be made to attract relevant penalties.”

•“It is also to be noted that OTT platforms are not the primary
platforms for minors to access adult material. These are already
better regulated than other social media apps and platforms on
which such material is far more easily accessible”.
2. Regulation of Financial Influencers (Para 3.8.9)
As per the draft report “The Committee further recommends SEBI for
exploring the possibility of "verified tick" (a verification mark
indicating that an account or entity has been authenticated and
confirmed as legitimate by a platform or service) for the SEBI
registered investment advisors on social media platforms”.
As regards the above recommendation, I suggest the following:
•“In addition, a mandatory legal provision may be made for
financial influencers to disclose all conflicts of interest on each
video in a standardised, visible manner so as to warn the consumer
of any beneficial interest in disseminating financial advice. Non-
compliance should attract punitive legal action”.
3. Definition of Cybercrime and Organised Cybercrime
As per the draft report, “The National Cybercrime Reporting Portal
(NCRP) defines the Cybercrime as “any unlawful act where a
computer, computer network, or electronic device is used as a tool or
target to commit or facilitate a crime.” This definition includes both
traditional crimes that are facilitated by technology, as well as new age
crimes that specifically target digital systems. Traditional crimes in
cyber space include theft, fraud, forgery, defamation and mischief, all
of which can be committed using electronic devices or networks. There
are some new-age crimes that are emerging, these offenses are
specifically enabled by technology, such as hacking, denial-of-service
attacks, phishing, malware distribution, cyber terrorism, etc.”

As regards the above recommendation, I suggest the following:
• “Crimes committed by minors against minors (which form a
significant part of Cybercrimes) must be differentiated within the
ambit of Cybercrimes as applicable laws will be different”.
• “A clear differentiation between less serious crimes such as uploading
defamatory content and more serious crimes such as disseminating
child pornography for example, should be made and commensurate
laws applied”.
• “Crimes infringing on the privacy of an individual that are enabled by
technology should be given adequate recognition and punitive
measures for the same should be clearly defined”.
• “The definition of Organised Cybercrimes should be made to include
large organisations (corporate and political entities) directing
Cyberattacks on individuals and other organisations so as to cause
them physical, psychological, defamatory, criminal or financial harm.
For example, the use of corporate machinery and finance to engage
trolls and other technological means to attack the reputation of another
corporate entity in an organised fashion”.
4. Size and Origin of IT intermediaries and appointment of local
grievance officers (Para 4.1.8)
As per the draft report “The Committee, therefore recommends
establishing a mandatory national registration system for all IT
intermediaries operating in India, regardless of size or origin, requiring
them to appoint local grievance officers and nodal contact persons with
clear timelines for responses. Further, for SSMIs, (Facebook,
WhatsApp, Telegram etc), the Committee suggests increasing the
number of nodal officers by appointing regional representatives to

facilitate faster and region specific coordination with law enforcement
agencies”.
As regards the above recommendation, I suggest the following:
• “Many IT Intermediaries are small enterprises that may not be able to
afford such appointments and services. It is advisable to allow those
smaller than a defined size to operate without appointments of such
nodal contact persons or local grievance officers and enforce this
recommendation for such intermediaries that are in the position to
afford the same. This distinction can be made according to
standardised norms”.
In addition, I suggest the following recommendations in reference to
regulatory measures mentioned in the draft report:
• “Especially with regard to operators of YouTube channels, news
portals, influencers, comedians, musicians, film makers and digital
news portals, safeguards should be provided for their ability to express
and disseminate their views without oppression by regulatory
mechanisms, harassment by agencies and other means of suppression.
These measures should be clearly articulated and laid out”.
• “Regulatory measures should not be allowed to become excuses for
pressurising or arm-twisting individuals, intermediaries, SSMI/SMI
and IT companies into suppressing material, altering content or
limiting the views of any content for political or ideological reasons.
They should be confined to regulating the entities within the limits of
legality and for the express purpose of curbing Cybercrime of any
kind. A clear policy regarding this distinction should be articulated
and instituted.”

The above suggestions do not in any way, dilute the pressing need to ensure
Cyber security for our citizens, they simply attempt to balance the realistic
environment with the need to regulate and control the players within it.
Our constitution guarantees us the Fundamental Right to Free Speech and
Expression, both of which have flourished in creative form both as part of our
freedom movement and as an integral part of the fabric of our Nationhood since
India’s Independence. It is imperative for us to preserve and strengthen these
Rights that are the bedrock of our democracy while simultaneously doing all we
can to protect and secure our citizens.
It is in this belief that I place on record my agreement and strong endorsement
of the concerns expressed by my colleagues in the Congress Party regarding the
balance between securing our Fundamental Rights and the protection of our
Nation and its Citizens from the menace of Cybercrimes of all kinds. I do hope
that you will accept these recommendations in the same spirit.
Yours sincerely,
Priyanka Gandhi Vadra

Informatics Centre (NIC) on the subject 'Cyber Crime – Ramifications, Protection 
and Prevention’.  
 (On arrival of witnesses) 
3.  The Chairman welcomed Whole Time Member, Securities and Exchange 
Board of India (SEBI); Chief Information Security Officer, National Stock 
Exchange (NSE) and Chief Risk Officer, National Payments Corporation of India 
(NPCI) and other senior   officers to the meeting of the Committee.   The proceeding 
of the meeting was commenced with the presentation of the SEBI followed by NSE 
and thereafter, NPCI. 
4.       After the introduction of the representatives of the organisations, the Whole 
Time Member, SEBI gave a brief overview of the role of SEBI in combating cyber 
crime.  He informed the Committee about how the innocent retail investors are often 
subjected to fraud by using social media platforms; a series of measures that aims at 
enhancing investor protection and market integrity; as a policy move, SEBI has 
prohibited registered intermediaries from associating with unregistered 
“fininfluencers” to curb financial misinformation.   He also informed that on the 
enforcement front, SEBI has conducted inspections and search -and-seizure 
operations in cases of market manipulation and expanded investor awareness 
initiatives through intermediaries and m utual fund associations. He mentioned that 
to counter fraudulent investment software apps (applications), SEBI has introduced 
an optional centralized fee collection system for registered advisors and is going to 
introduce a UPI -based validation mechanism t o ensure investor funds are routed 
only to SEBI -registered entities. The Committee was apprised that the lists of 
legitimate investment software apps are now available on NSE and BSE websites, 
and SEBI is working with app stores and social media platforms to implement 
verified identification marks. It was also informed that SEBI has a cybersecurity and 
resilience framework for all registered intermediaries, with safeguards, and to secure 
IT system whenever there is a cyber attack.  
5.       The next present ation was made by the Chief Information Security Officer, 
National Stock Exchange (NSE). The presentation covered in detail about key 
aspects of the NSE which included information  on Indian capital market ecosystem; 
layers of control which are put up to m ake it resilient and available for all the 
investors and customers at all points of time; technology operations initiatives i.e. 
intelligent monitoring and quick incident response, automated operations, 
identification of single point of failure, contingenc y drill, seamless switchover, 
process improvements to better efficiencies, increase flexibility and enhancement 

154 
 
of  IT service performance; technology infrastructure of NSE with state of the art co-
location facility, Multi -tier security with appropriate se gmentation fully resilient 
Infrastructure, fault tolerant servers with an uptime guarantee of 99.999%, etc.   He 
also informed about the threat intelligence backdrop, specific to capital markets; the 
potential impact of cybercrime on market integrity; globa l threat updates and 
evolving attack vector patterns over time like DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service), 
ransomware, data based attacks, application attacks;  supply chain attacks; cyber 
security tools of NSE and its cyber security framework. 
6.       After the completion of the presentation by NSE, the representative of 
National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) made a presentation before the 
Committee. The Committee was informed about the various key aspects, including 
the role of NPCI in the payments ecosystem and an overview of the Unified 
Payments Interface (UPI) landscape which has played a significant role in driving 
digital payments and it accounts for roughly 80% of all payments nowadays.   The 
representative also briefed the Committee on prevaili ng scams, particularly current -
day frauds and investment scam flows, challenges in the system and nuances of 
money movement. The Committee was apprised of the actions taken by NPCI to 
combat fraud, like device binding and 2FA, cooling period & Debit/Credit  side 
limits, a real time Fraud Risk Monitoring (FRM) Solution with AI/ML based risk 
scoring, close coordination with agencies like I4C, FIU, DoT, IB, Banks, fintechs 
and Law enforcement agencies, sending information on suspicious MULE accounts 
to Banks, implementation of an early warning system for UPI payments. Further, the 
Committee was informed about the ongoing fraud awareness campaigns and media 
engagement initiatives aimed at educating users and enhancing security. The 
presentation was concluded with  an emphasis on targeted awareness campaigns, 
collaborative efforts for strengthening the digital payments ecosystem and stringent 
law to ensure convictions and create a deterrent for fraudsters.  
7.       After the presentation, the Chairman and Members of the Committee raised 
some issues that inter-alia included seeking clarification pertaining to unregistered 
identities promoted on social media platforms; unregistered influencers; fake 
investment apps whether SEBI proposed to take any legal action on such platforms; 
any cyber drills conducted by SEBI in collaboration with major financial 
institutions; awareness programmes for investors from villages and small towns; 
action against shell companies. The information was also sought regarding any plan 
of SEBI to strengthen its surveillance of social media platforms which are 
increasingly being used by pump and dump schemes; plan to improve infrastructure 
status of local offices of SEBI in small cities;  whether SEBI has found any cyber 
security weakness or loophole that high frequency trading firms could use to unfairly 
affect the market, steps taken by SEBI to keep a check on such firms. The 
representative of NSE was asked whether NSE has implemented an y partnership 
with cyber security firms or any academic institutions to build threat intelligence or 
R&D in market security.  During the meeting queries were raised about NPCI’s 
coordination with banks and RBI in case of cyber frauds involving Bhim, UPI or  

155 
 
Rupee platforms; matters related to linking UPI and demat accounts; the provisions 
to deal with authorized push payment frauds and mule accounts and similarly, the 
responsibility of account holder if he receives money in his account without his 
knowledge or permission. 
8.  The representatives of SEBI, NSE and NPCI replied to some of the queries 
raised by the Chairman and Members of the Committee. On other queries, they were 
asked to furnish written replies to the Secretariat within five days.  
(The witnesses withdrew) 
(The Committee re-assembled at 02:30 p.m. to hear the views of National 
Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC) and National 
Informatics Centre (NIC) on the subject). 
9.     The Chairman welcomed the Director General, Na tional Critical Information 
Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC), and Deputy Director General, National 
Informatics Centre (NIC) and other senior officers to the meeting of the Committee 
and asked them to make a presentation on the subject ‘Cyber Crim e - Ramifications, 
Protection and Prevention’ one after the other.  
 10.     After the introductions of the team of officers from NCIIPC, representative of 
the Centre made a presentation before the Committee. The presentation covered an 
overview of NCIIPC, including its mandate and functions. It inter- alia included the 
significance of protection of Critical Information Infrastructure (CII); the critical 
sectors identified in India; various CII protection -related activities and support from 
the NCIIPC such as capacity building/raising cyber security awareness, sharing 
vulnerabilities/ threats, risk assessment and practical suggestions for mitigation, 
cross sectoral exchange/ dissemination of best practices, etc. The Committee was 
also apprised about the Auto mated Threat Dissemination Platform (ATDP), an 
indigenously developed platform for sending real time cyber threat intelligence to 
more than 180 organisations; incident response activities; cyber security gap 
analysis; and risk assessments undertaken by NCI IPC for Critical Sector Entities 
(CSE); new protection strategies, mechanisms developed for monitoring CIIs and 
the Sectoral Coordinator -based System for monitoring critical sectors; constitution 
of the Information Security Steering Committee (ISSC) by org anisations having 
protected systems.  
11.     At the end, the DDG, NIC apprised the Committee that the NIC provides 
technology-driven solutions to enhance capacities at Central, State, and District 
levels, offering services through its organizational struc ture, and services/enterprise 
level applications to many sectors in Government of India & State Governments. 
The presentation on the subject also highlighted information on National Data 
Centres and the Government of India’s National Cloud initiative- MeghRaj, aimed at 
optimizing e -Governance; Information and Communication Technology (ICT) 
Network; National Knowledge Network - multi-gigabit PAN -India 
network;  maintaining a secure digital environment for government infrastructure. It 
was informed that NIC's cyber security framework covers computer network, 

156 
 
sensitive information and data, software applications, individual devices, data and 
services in cloud environments, managing user access to systems & data. NIC 
implements a comprehensive cybersecurity strat egy through technical, 
administrative, and physical measures, as well as continuous maintenance, 
monitoring, and deployment of specialized tools, ensuring robust protection for 
government IT infrastructure. 
12.     The Chairman and Members of the Committee  also raised several issues 
relating to the NCIIPC, which inter alia included recent vulnerability assessments; 
details of cyber attacks on critical infrastructure —such as their origin, mitigation 
efforts; and response strategies; cyber intrusions/attacks by some hostile countries 
and changes in cyber threat levels and mitigation measures to counter these attacks. 
Updates were sought on data protection protocols, safeguards against insider threats 
and the role of AI in countering such risks. Additionally, q ueries were also raised 
about NCIIPC’s balance between intelligence gathering and collaborative protection, 
adherence to quarterly ISSC meetings by 114 notified entities, measurable 
improvements in cyber security, and frameworks for evaluating cyber maturi ty 
levels in these organizations. 
13.       The Chairman and Members of the Committee raised some issues with the 
representative of National Informatics Centre (NIC) regarding clearance and 
approval process for infrastructure upgrades and cyber security pr otocols; whether 
the existing data centres are adequate; suggestions for expansion to meet growing 
cyber resilience needs. Clarification was also sought on whether existing data 
centres function as data recovery centres.  
  
14.     The representatives of NCIIPC, NIC and MHA replied to some of the queries 
raised by the Chairman and Members of the Committee. On other queries, they were 
asked to furnish written replies to the Secretariat within five days.  
                                                (The witnesses withdrew) 
15.     A Verbatim record of the proceedings of the meeting was kept. 
16.     The meeting adjourned at 04:56 p.m.

2.       At the outset, the Chairman welcomed the Members to the meeting of the 
Committee and stated that the Committee has already heard the views of the related 
Ministries and some Organisations on the subject 'Cyber Crime – Ramifications, 
Protection and Prevention’. He apprised them that as per the agenda, in the present 
meeting, the Committee will hear the views of two domain experts on the subject, 
namely Dr. Pavan Duggal, Founder & Chairman, Internat ional Commission on 
Cyber Security Law and Shri Trishneet Arora, CEO of TAC Security who have been 
invited to share their views on the subject.  
 (On arrival of witnesses) 
3.       The Chairman welcomed Dr. Pavan Duggal, Founder & Chairman, 
International Commission on Cyber Security Law and Shri Trishneet Arora, CEO of 
TAC Security to the meeting of the Committee and requested them to present their 
views on the subject 'Cyber Crime – Ramifications, Protection and Prevention’.  The 
proceedings of the meeting commenced with the presentation by Dr. Pavan Duggal. 
4.       Dr. Pavan Duggal informed the Committee that cyber crimes has become an 
epidemic and it is thriving due to fear and panic among general public and these 
factors are being misused by cyber crim inals to commit frauds. He made a detailed 
presentation before the Committee and informed the Committee about the best 
practices adopted by major countries in preventing cyber crime which includes 
robust laws & public -private collaboration; harmonized regu lations & focus on 
privacy; comprehensive strategy & cyber hygiene culture; intelligence -driven 
defence & innovation. The Committee was also provided information on cyber 
crime caseloads and convictions; international nature of cybercrime & preventive 
steps; global Treaties and Conventions; international agencies in cybercrime 
prevention; global cybercrime bodies & coalitions; best practices by Indian States 
and Police agencies like cybercrime portals & helplines, cybercrime training & 
capacity building, sp ecialized units & policies, use of advanced 
technology;  limitation of IT Act, 2000 to deal with cyber crime; challenges in 
enforcement & obtaining evidence; role of Government Ministries in preventing 
cyber crimes; etc. 
  

159 
 
5.       To strengthen cybercrime  legislation, he suggested that a dedicated 
comprehensive cybercrime Law is to be formulated to consolidate offences and 
expand definitions for modern crimes like ransomware, DoS (denial of Service), and 
phishing, explicitly criminalize modern cybercrimes and provide graded 
punishments for organized or repeat offenders and mandate cybersecurity audits and 
breach disclosure for companies, with penalties for negligence. He also suggested 
for aligning with global cybercrime frameworks, incorporating provisions  like 
expedited data preservation and cross-border data sharing into Indian laws, ensuring 
crime definitions match global standards for easier cooperation.   Other suggestions 
inter alia  included specialized cybercrime courts; strengthening of data protecti on 
and privacy; need for legislation on misuse of Artificial Intelligence; strengthen 
provisions for courts to award restitution or compensation to cybercrime victims as 
part of sentencing; strengthening of legal & regulatory framework; capacity building 
for law enforcement agencies; public awareness and digital literacy; improving 
cyber hygiene across organizations; etc.  
6.       The next presentation was made by Shri Trishneet Arora, while making his 
presentation he highlighted the financial frauds, Stat e-sponsored cyber threats by 
hostile neighbouring countries; threats to critical infrastructures; technology gaps; 
involvement of multiple ministries and organisations to deal with cyber frauds, cyber 
threats and cyber security; need for comprehensive sing le nodal agency to deal with 
matters related to cyber security; best practices adopted by major countries, like 
creation of cyber security ministry. He suggested there is a need to assess the current 
state of cyber security of nationwide critical infrastru ctures, like, energy, power 
grids, ports, airports, defence system, etc.   He also suggested that only Indian origin 
cyber auditing companies be considered for auditing of national critical 
infrastructures, creation of an organisation to help victims especi ally women who 
become victims of cyber crime, online harassment; nation -wide cyber awareness 
campaign; provision for enforcement of cyber insurance for common citizens in case 
one falls victim to cyber frauds; provision for cyber ambulance facility, etc.

personnel of law enforcemen t agencies, cyber army and commandos for cyber 
security, time taken by Indian law enforcement agencies and US agencies to 
investigate cyber crimes, provision of cyber insurance and cyber ambulance, cyber 
threats to power grids, etc.

1.1 Overall Assessment of Demand for Grants (2025-2 6) of the MHA 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.1.1 The Committee observes, based on the above-me ntioned information, that the actual 
Budget Estimate (BE) for 2025-26 is lower than the projected BE for 2025-26 across several key 
areas, reflecting a more conservative allocation th an initially anticipated. The total budget has 
been reduced from ₹184,236.94 crores (projected BE 2025-26) to ₹160391.06 crores (actual BE 
2025-26), marking a 12.94% decrease. Within the Cen tral Armed Police Forces (CAPFs), actual 
allocations fall short of projections, with reducti ons observed across the CRPF, NSG, BSF, 
ITBP, CISF, Assam Rifles, and SSB. This indicates a  recalibration of expenditure priorities. 
Similarly, significant downward revisions have been  made to allocations for the Intelligence 
Bureau (IB), NATGRID, Central Police Organizations (CPOs) and Delhi Police. Police 
infrastructure projects, particularly CAPF building  projects, have experienced a substantial 
reduction from ₹6,403.02 crores to ₹4,038.70 crores , which may potentially impact construction 
of new buildings. The Committee notes that such red uctions may adversely affect critical 
schemes under these heads and may slow down moderni zation programs as well as hinder the 
execution of developmental projects, particularly i n border areas. Hence, the Committee 
recommends that the MHA may take up the matter with  the Ministry of Finance to seek 
increased allocations under these heads in alignmen t with their original projections. This will 
ensure that the essential developmental schemes are  not affected due to insufficient funding. The 
Committee hopes that funds may be demanded for various developmental and expansion projects 
at the RE stage depending on the utilization pattern. 
(Para 2.5.3 of   252
nd   Report)  
Action Taken  
1.1.2  Recommendations of the committee have been noted. The matter will be taken up with the 
Ministry of Finance at RE 2025-26 Stage, if the additional funds will be required.

respect to the Holistic Development of Islands in U nion Territories, where the allocation has

3.1   NATIONAL DISASTER RESPONSE FORCE (NDRF)  
Recommendation/Observation 
3.1.1   Acknowledging that the NDRF is entirely dep endent on deputation from CAPFs and 
currently faces a 21% vacancy rate, while CAPFs themselves are experiencing staffing shortages, 
the Committee recommends the Ministry to conduct a thorough review of the deputation 
policies. The Committee is of the view that the rev iew should assess the impact of the current 
seven-year deputation tenure and explore incentives , such as flexible terms or enhanced 
allowances, to encourage more CAPF personnel to vol unteer for NDRF assignments. 
Streamlining the nomination process and improving c ommunication between NDRF and CAPFs 
are also crucial steps for expediting the filling o f vacancies and ensuring the NDRF's operational 
readiness.    
(Para 3.3.13  ibid)  
Action Taken  
3.1.2   NDRF is a 100% deputationist force. The posts on deputation in NDRF are filled up on 7-
year rotational basis from CAPF’s. It is a dynamic and continuous process. Each NDRF 
Battalions has fully functional team strength at al l points of time. Besides, concerned CAPFs 
HQrs are being requested to fill up the vacancies of NDRF BNs time to time. 
3.1.3  So far as incentives are concerned, it is apprised that recently Govt. of India has approved 
Risk and Hardship allowance @ 40% of R2H2 Cell of R HA matrix to eligible NDRF personnel 
vide MHA DM Division letter dated 18 July 2024. 
Further Recommendation 
3.1.4 The Committee notes the submission that NDRF battalions maintain fully 
functional strength at all times and that CAPFs are  being requested periodically to fill 
vacancies. The Committee also takes cognizance of t he approval of Risk and Hardship 
allowance to NDRF personnel. However, the Committee is of the considered view that these 
measures, though positive, may not sufficiently add ress the structural challenge of 
persistent vacancies arising out of the exclusive r eliance on deputation from CAPFs, which 
themselves face acute shortages. The Committee, therefore, reiterates that a comprehensive 
review of deputation policies is imperative. In add ition to allowances, the Ministry may 
consider measures such as flexible deputation tenur es, streamlined nomination procedures, 
career progression incentives, and exploring a limi ted cadre of permanent staff in critical 
operational and technical roles. This would ensure both the long-term stability of 
manpower and enhanced operational readiness of NDRF. 
  

70 
 
3.2   Cadre Review of CAPFs 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.2.1  The Committee appreciates the efforts made b y the Ministry in conducting Cadre 
Reviews across various CAPFs to enhance promotional  avenues and improve operational 
efficiency. It notes that while some forces, such a s SSB, CISF, CRPF and ITBP, have benefited 
from recent Cadre Reviews, others, particularly BSF’s Group-B & C (General Duty) Cadre, have 
not been reviewed since its inception in 1965. The Committee emphasizes that Cadre Reviews 
should be undertaken at regular five-year intervals  as their effect diminishes over time. It 
observes that timely Cadre Reviews, as seen in rece nt cases, have significantly contributed to 
better workforce planning, increased job satisfaction and improved operational effectiveness.  
(Para 4.4.7   ibid ) 
Action Taken  
3.2.2  (i) Cadre Review is an important process thr ough which a cadre is upgraded and aligned 
with the changing work environment and requirements  for the next five years. This involves a 
better restructuring of posts, which leads to incre ased promotion opportunities and enhanced 
operational efficiency. 
3.2.3  (ii) Recent Cadre Reviews of some BSF cadres viz. N ursing & Paramedical Cadre, 
Tradesman Cadre, Stenography cadre etc. have clearl y shown positive outcomes providing 
personnel with greater career advancement opportuni ties, improved promotional flow, and 
strengthened capacity of the cadre to perform its duties more effectively. 
3.2.4  (iii)  As needs evolve over time, it becomes  essential to periodically update the structure of 
a cadre. Conducting a Cadre Review every five years  is a progressive step that helps maintain 
the cadre’s vitality and functional strength. 
3.2.5  (iv) The review process for many BSF cadres viz. Gr oup-‘B’ and ‘C’ (General Duty) 
Cadre, Veterinary Cadre, Ministerial Cadre, Water W ing Cadre and Engineering Cadre is 
currently underway with the Ministry of Finance and  all efforts are being made to strengthen 
these cadres further. 
3.2.6 (v) Steps are being taken for fast-tracking t he approval of the Cadre Review of BSF’s 
Group-‘B’ and ‘C’ (General Duty) Cadre, as well as other cadres, which will strengthen their 
overall functionality, resulting in greater benefits for the Force and the Nation. 
Further Recommendation 
3.2.7 The Committee notes the Ministry’s acknowledg ement of the importance of Cadre 
Reviews and the positive outcomes already visible i n certain BSF cadres, as well as the 
assurance that the review process for BSF’s Group-‘ B’ & ‘C’ (General Duty) Cadre and 
other cadres is underway. While appreciating these efforts, the Committee is concerned 
that the delay in completing the Cadre Review of BS F’s Group-‘B’ & ‘C’ (General Duty) 
Cadre, pending since 1965, has deprived a large seg ment of personnel of timely 
promotional avenues, retirement benefits and affect ed morale of the force. The Committee, 
therefore, reiterates that Cadre Reviews must be co mpleted in a time-bound manner with 
strict monitoring and accountability mechanisms. Th e Ministry may also consider 

71 
 
institutionalizing an automatic review cycle with c learly defined timelines to ensure 
sustained workforce planning, job satisfaction, and operational effectiveness. 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.2.8   The Committee feels that the MHA along with the Mi nistry of Finance (MoF) may 
expedite the approval of pending Cadre Reviews, par ticularly for BSF, Assam Rifles and any 
other forces and to establish a structured mechanis m to ensure periodic reviews without 
unnecessary delays. The Committee recommends that f inancial and structural planning for Cadre 
Reviews be carried out proactively, with dedicated task forces ensuring smooth execution. The 
Committee further recommends that the MHA may explo re innovative strategies, such as lateral 
mobility programs, training-based advancements and inter-force career progression frameworks, 
to enhance career growth opportunities across the CAPFs and Assam Rifles.  
(Para 4.4.8  ibid ) 
Action Taken  
3.2.9 At present, proposals for the review of impor tant cadres of the BSF are under 
consideration with Ministry of Finance and steps ar e being taken for fast-tracking the approval 
of above cadres. Periodic reviews to restructure a cadre are being carried out by evaluating the 
staffing needs and promotional avenues in a cadre w hich will ensure equitable, fair and timely 
career advancement opportunities for all eligible officials/officers. 
3.2.10  With regards to Assam Rifles, Group B & C posts, is under inter-ministerial consultation. 
Further Recommendation 
3.2.11  The Committee notes the Ministry’s assuranc e that proposals for Cadre Reviews of 
BSF are under active consideration with the Ministr y of Finance and that steps are being 
taken to fast-track approvals. The Committee also n otes that Cadre Reviews of Assam 
Rifles, Group B & C posts, is under inter-ministerial consultation. While appreciating these 
initiatives, the Committee emphasizes that delays in approvals continue to adversely impact 
career progression and morale of personnel. The Com mittee, therefore, reiterates its 
earlier recommendation that a structured and time-b ound mechanism be instituted jointly 
by MHA and MoF for Cadre Reviews across all CAPFs a nd Assam Rifles, with defined 
milestones and regular progress reporting. 
 Further, the Committee urges the Ministry to 
operationalize innovative career growth measures su ch as lateral mobility, training-linked 
promotions, and inter-force career progression fram eworks, so that personnel are not 
entirely dependent on delayed Cadre Reviews for advancement opportunities.

3.3.3   Suggestion of the committee is also noted. 
 
Further Recommendation 
3.3.4 The Committee takes note of the Ministry’s re sponse that periodic review meetings 
are being held at senior levels to streamline procu rement process of modernization plan 
and address bottlenecks. While this is a welcome st ep, the Committee observes that review 
meetings alone may not ensure systematic monitoring  and evaluation of modernization 
expenditures. The Committee, therefore, recommends that a robust monitoring framework 
with clearly defined performance indicators, timeli nes, and periodic progress reports be 
instituted to track the utilization of funds and ou tcomes of the modernization plan. 
Further, the Committee reiterates that enhanced and  continuous training programmes 
must be integrated into the modernization process t o ensure that personnel are fully 
equipped to operate and maintain the advanced technologies and equipment procured. 
3.5   Traffic Management in Delhi    
Recommendation/Observation 
3.5.1   The Committee notes the efforts made by Delhi Police in leveraging technology for traffic 
management. It appreciates the implementation of au tomated challan systems and surveillance 
cameras to monitor traffic violations. The Committe e wishes to know how the challan collected 
from the traffic violators are used. The Committee recommends further investment in intelligent 
traffic systems to enhance real-time traffic monito ring and management. The Committee further 
recommends the Delhi Traffic Police to adopt intern ational best practices in traffic management, 
where sensors and AI are used extensively to optimi ze traffic flow. Moreover, the Committee 
observes the importance of public awareness campaig ns to promote safe driving practices and 
recommends collaboration with other agencies to dev elop comprehensive traffic management 
strategies. 
(Para 4.11.2  ibid)  
Action Taken  
3.5.2  Delhi police has installed 334 Nos. RLVD (fu nctions on a sensor-based radar system) 
and OSVD cameras and is procuring 328 more such ins truments for automated challan; and has 
also procured 1500 e- challan machines. 
3.5.3  The compounding fees collected under Motor V ehicles Act, 1988 to compound the traffic 
offences is deposited in the "Major Head 0041. Taxe s on Vehicle 101-1MV fees and fine” with 
GNCTD. 
3.5.4  Delhi Traffic Police is currently working on  ITMS (integrated traffic management 
system) project, an Al based system to monitor the traffic movement, violations, and accidents 
caused due to high speed. The DPR has been prepared . The best international practices will be 
adopted. 

73 
 
3.5.5  Road Safety Cell is continuously working on public awareness campaigns to promote 
safe driving practices in close cooperation of the other agencies. 100 Nos. VMS (Variable 
Messaging Signboards) have also been installed at various locations. 
Further Recommendation 
3.5.6 The Committee appreciates the initiatives tak en by Delhi Police, including the 
installation of RLVD (Red Light Violation Detection /OSVD (Over Speed Violation 
Detection) cameras, procurement of e-challan machin es, progress on the AI-based ITMS 
(Integrated Traffic Management System) project, and  the ongoing public awareness 
campaigns. The Committee also takes note of the cla rification that the compounding fees 
collected under the Motor Vehicles Act are deposite d with GNCTD (Government of 
National Capital Territory of Delhi). However, the Committee emphasizes the need for 
ensuring that a portion of these revenues may be ea rmarked specifically for road safety, 
traffic infrastructure development, and awareness i nitiatives. The Committee further 
recommends that the ITMS project be expedited with clearly defined timelines, while 
incorporating global best practices in AI-based tra ffic optimization. Additionally, the 
Committee stresses on enhanced inter-agency coordin ation, data-sharing mechanisms, and 
periodic impact assessments of awareness campaigns to ensure sustained improvements in 
traffic management and road safety in Delhi. 
3.6   BORDER INFRASTRUCTURE AND MANAGEMENT  
Recommendation/Observation 
3.6.1 The Committee notes the significant efforts o f the Ministry to enhance border 
infrastructure across various international borders . The Committee recommends that the 
Government needs to expedite the completion of ongo ing fencing projects, ensuring that all 
allocated funds are utilized efficiently. It also r ecommends conducting regular assessments to 
identify gaps in border infrastructure and ensure t hat allocations are aligned with strategic 
priorities. The Committee also wishes the Ministry to prepare the data of influx of immigrants 
like Bangladeshis, Rohingyas and from other countri es. The Committee notes that Rohingyas are 
entering and settling illegally in various parts of  the country. The Committee recommends that 
the Ministry of Home Affairs should take effective steps to identify the illegally settled 
Rohingyas and repatriate them to their parent countries. 
(Para 4.15.6  ibid)  
Action Taken  
3.6.2  Sufficient funds are released to executing a gencies for timely completion of all ongoing 
border infrastructure projects including fencing al ong Indo-Pakistan and Indo-Bangladesh 
borders. Further, regular assessments are done by B order Security Force for identification of 
gaps in border infrastructure and all necessary steps are taken for covering these gaps. 
3.6.3  Foreign Nationals staying in India without v alid travel documents are treated as illegal 
migrants. Since illegal migrants (including Rohingy a and Bangladeshi illegal migrants) enter 
into the country without valid travel documents in a clandestine and surreptitious manner, data 
of such migrants is not centrally available. Detect ion and deportation of illegal nationality 
verification is a continuous process. Central Gover nment has been vested with power under 
Section 3(2)(e) and 3(2)(c ) of the Foreigners Act,  1946 to restrict movement and deport foreign 

74 
 
nationals staying illegally in the country. Under s ection 5 of The Passport (Entry into India) Act, 
1920, Central Government may also by an order direc t the removal of any person from India 
who enters India without passport. These powers of the Central Government have also been 
entrusted under Article 258(1) of the constitution of India to all the state Governments since 19 th  
April 1958. Further, under Article 239(1) of the co nstitution of India, the Administrators of all 
the Union Territories have also been directed to di scharge the functions of the Central 
Government relating to the aforesaid powers. Instru ctions regarding  action to be taken against 
illegal migrants is issued by the Central Governmen t to State Government/ UT Administration 
from time to time. 
Further Recommendation 
3.6.4  The Committee appreciates the Ministry’s ass urance regarding timely fund release, 
regular assessments by BSF, and the legal framework  in place for dealing with illegal 
migrants. However, the Committee is concerned about  the absence of availability of data 
on illegal immigrants, particularly Rohingyas and B angladeshis, which hinders effective 
policy making 
 and targeted action. The Committee, therefore, reco mmends that the 
Ministry should coordinate with State Governments a nd UT Administrations, to track 
detection, detention, and deportation of illegal mi grants. Further, the Committee 
emphasizes that ongoing fencing and infrastructure projects must be completed within 
strict timelines, with periodic progress reviews. T he Committee also recommends that the 
Ministry strengthen coordination with neighboring c ountries to expedite nationality 
verification and repatriation processes, while ensu ring that national security and 
demographic concerns are effectively addressed. 
3.7   SCHEMES FOR THE SAFETY OF WOMEN 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.7.1 The Committee recommends that the Ministry ne eds to expand training programs for 
investigating officers, prosecutors and medical off icers to improve the handling of forensic 
evidence and sexual assault cases. It emphasizes th e need for increased awareness and capacity-
building initiatives to address violence against wo men effectively. The Committee also suggests 
the MHA to consider integrating more technology-dri ven solutions, such as AI powered 
surveillance systems and mobile apps, to enhance women's safety in public spaces.   
(Para 4.16.6  ibid)  
Action Taken 
 
3.7.2 Under the umbrella scheme "Safety of Women”, the Government is undertaking training 
for Investigating Officers, Prosecutors, and Medica l Officers from States/UTs in collection, 
storage and handling of DNA evidence and use of Sex ual Assault Evidence Collection Kits. So 
far 35,306 Investigating Officers, Prosecutors and Medical Officers have been trained by the 
Bureau of Police Research and Development (BPR&D) a nd the LNJN National Institute of 
Criminology and Forensic Sciences (now Delhi campus  of the National Forensic Sciences 
University). The Ministry of Home Affairs has also distributed 18020 Sexual Assault Evidence 
Collection Kits to the States/UTs as part of this t raining. The NFSU is also undertaking training 

75 
 
of forensic scientists in view of the new criminal laws and so far, NFSU has trained 996 
personnel. 
3.7.3  The Committee’s recommendation regarding mor e technology driven solutions has been 
duly noted. 
Further Recommendation 
3.7.4   The Committee appreciates the significant p rogress made by the Ministry under the 
"Safety of Women" scheme, including large-scale tra ining of Investigating Officers, 
Prosecutors, Medical Officers, and forensic scienti sts, as well as the distribution of Sexual 
Assault Evidence Collection Kits. However, the Comm ittee notes that training and 
distribution efforts must be accompanied by periodic evaluation of their effectiveness at the 
ground level to ensure uniformity and quality in ha ndling of sexual assault cases. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that an institutio nalized monitoring and feedback 
mechanism be established to assess the impact of su ch training and ensure capacity-
building translates into better conviction rates and victim support.  
3.8  Demand No. 53 –Chandigarh 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.8.1  The Committee notes that UT administration of Chand igarh has earmarked₹76.60 crores 
for the infrastructure development in technical and  higher education sector and Government 
schools for the Financial Year 2025-26. The Committ ee recommends that efforts must be 
initiated by the concerned agencies to adhere to th e completion of construction/extension of the 
proposed buildings at the earliest.  
(Para 5.3.7 ibid)  
Action Taken  
3.8.2  The Engineering Department (i.e. the executing agen cy) has been directed by the UT 
Administration for strict adherence of time schedule so that the projects are completed on time.  
Further Recommendation 
3.8.3  The Committee notes the assurance that the U T Administration has directed the 
Engineering Department i.e. the executing agency to  strictly adhere to the prescribed 
timelines for infrastructure projects in the educat ion sector. While appreciating this step, 
the Committee emphasizes that timely completion mus t be complemented with close 
monitoring, transparent reporting, and quality chec ks to ensure that the infrastructure 
created is durable and aligned with educational nee ds. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that a structured monitoring mechanism w ith periodic progress reports be 
instituted, and accountability fixed for delays.  
  

76 
 
3.9 Demand No. 57 – Transfers to Delhi 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.9.1  The Committee is of view that a substantial number of private coaching centres and hostels 
for boys and girls are being run in Delhi without a ny strict norms and regulations. These are not 
providing adequate space and basic living condition s to the young population who come from 
far-flung areas for fulfilling their future employm ent aspirations. The Committee would like to 
be apprised about the number of such coaching centr es and hostels that are being run in Delhi 
and what kind of accommodation and other basic faci lities are being provided by them to the 
students and residents of these facilities. The Com mittee may also be informed about the 
provision of licensing of such centres and the last  inspection done to review the conditions of 
these centres and hostels. 
(Para 5.7.10 ibid ) 
Action Taken  
3.9.2  New Delhi Municipal Council (NDMC) has sanct ioned one building for Hostel for 
boys/girls for YMCA at Jai Singh Road, New Delhi. 
3.9.3  No license is issued by them in respect of p rivate hostels/stay homes for boys and girls 
and no survey has been carried out by NDMC in this regard in its jurisdiction.   
3.9.4 However, NDMC maintains three working women h ostels viz. Akansha, Indira Niketan 
& Swati and three old age home viz. Ashirwad, Sandh ya & Aradhna. No license is issued by 
NDMC in its jurisdiction for Coaching Centres.  
3.9.5 Also, Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) do es not regulate Hostels & Coaching 
Centres. 
Further Recommendation 
3.9.6  The Committee notes with concern that neithe r NDMC nor MCD regulates or 
licenses private hostels and coaching centres in De lhi, despite the fact that a large number 
of students from across the country rely on such fa cilities. The absence of any survey, 
licensing framework, or regulatory oversight raises  serious issues relating to safety, 
adequacy of living conditions, and well being of st udents. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs, in co ordination with the GNCTD and local 
bodies, should initiate the formulation of a compre hensive regulatory framework for 
private hostels and coaching centres in Delhi. This  may include mandatory registration, 
periodic inspections, regulation of rent and minimu m standards for accommodation, 
hygiene, and safety to ensure the welfare of students.

Report 
 
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the Ministry of 
Development of North Eastern Region on the recommendations contained in the Two Hundred Fifty 
Third Report of the Committee on Demands for Grants (2025-26) of the Ministry. The Two Hundred 
Fifty Third Report was presented to Rajya Sabha/laid on the Table of Lok Sabha, on 10th March, 
2025. 
 
2. Action Taken Notes as received from the Ministry of DoNER in respect of the 
recommendations contained in the Two Hundred Fifty Third Report have been categorized as 
follows: 
Chapter I: The recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the 
Government: Para Nos. 2.2.7, 2.4.4, 2.4.5, 2.4.6, 3.1.8, 3.1.9, 3.1.10, 3.1.11, 3.2.3, 3.2.4, 
3.2.5, 3.3.4, 3.8.3, 4.2.6, 4.2.7, 4.2.8, 4.2.9, 4.3.4, 4.3.5., 4.4.3, 4.4.4, 4.5.2, 4.6.7, 4.6.8, 
4.8.11 and 4.9.2 (of Two Hundred Fifty Third Report). 
Total recommendations-26 Accepted. 
The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry has accepted its recommendations as 
mentioned in Chapter-I of the Report. 
 
Chapter II: The recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire 
to pursue in view of the Government’s replies: Para Nos. 1.5.3, 2.1.3, 3.6.5, 3.7.4, 3.7.5, 
3.7.6, 3.8.4, 3.9.3, 3.9.4, 4.1.13, 4.7.2, 4.8.7, 4.8.10, 4.10.6, 4.10.7, 4.11.4, 4.11.5, 4.12.2, 
4.13.3, 4.13.5 and 4.13.6 (ibid) 
Total recommendations – 21. Not to be pursued further. 
The Committee is convinced with the explanations furnished by the Ministry and, therefore, 
does not want to pursue the recommendations further. 
 
Chapter III: The recommendations/observations in respect of which the Committee is 
not satisfied with the replies of the Ministry: Para Nos. 3.2.6, 3.6.4, 4.1.12, 4.8.8, 4.8.9, 
4.10.8, 4.12.3, 4.13.4 (ibid) 
Total recommendations – 8. Not convincing replies. 
The Committee expresses its concern over the non-implementation of its recommendations 
contained in Chapter-III and desires that the Ministry should furnish convincing action taken 
steps in respect of those recommendations. 
 
Chapter IV: The recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the 
Government have not been received. 
Total Recommendations – NIL

CHAPTER I 
 
Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government 
 
1.1 Utilization of Funds 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.1.1 During the deliberations of the Committee, the Secretary, DoNER informed the Committee 
that the utilization as on 27.02.2025 is ₹ 3352 Crore i.e. almost 85% of utilization. The Committee 
hopes that the Ministry may utilize the full budget by the end of March, 2025. 
 
(Para 2.2.7 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.1.2 The total expenditure during 2024–25 stood at ₹3,452.99 crore, representing 86.20% of the 
Revised Estimates (RE). This marks a significant increase of 74.68% over the  
₹1,976.76 crore spent in 2023–24. Notably, the 2024–25 expenditure is the highest ever recorded by 
MDoNER, surpassing the previous peak of ₹2,669.72 crore in 2019–20 by 29.34%. MDoNER will 
make all possible efforts to further improve the utilization of allocated funds during 2025-26. 
 
1.2 Outlays for Financial Year 2025-26 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.2.1 The Committee notes that due to classification in Head of Account MH 4552 under various 
schemes, the major part of the budget outlay has been reflected under the Capital Section. Hence, the 
total Revenue outlay decreased to ₹ 1,882.76 crores in BE 2025-26 from ₹ 2,040.68 crores in BE 
2024-25.The Committee also notes that under the head ‘Schemes of NEC’, there is a shortfall of ₹ 
178.66 crores in BE 2025-26 compared to the projected demand of ₹ 909.30 crores. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry coordinate with NEC to prioritize the expenditure out of the 
present budgetary allocation and seek more funds at the RE 2025-26 stage to meet the shortfalls. The 
Committee also recommends that the requirement of additional funds under the Capital Section may 
also be realistically assessed at the RE stage and additional funds, if required, may be sought.  
(Para 2.4.4 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.2.2 The Committee’s recommendations have been noted for compliance. 
1.2.3 The requirement of additional funds shall be taken up by MDoNER with the Ministry of 
Finance at the RE stage in FY 2025-26 based on various factors such as progress in expenditure, 
reduction of outstanding UCs, unspent balances, projections and demands made by the concerned 
Divisions etc. and other related considerations. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.2.4 The Committee notes that during 2022-23 and 2023-24, percentage of funds utilization is not 
satisfactory which proves the slow pace of work on the proposed projects. The Committee 

3 
 
appreciates the fact that during 2024-25 almost 85% fund has been utilized till 27.02.2025 and 
hopefully 100% utilization by the end of this Financial Year.  
(Para 2.4.5 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.2.5 There were multiple reasons for underutilization of funds during 2022-23 and 2023-24. The 
fund flow was hampered due to issues faced in transition to Central Nodal Agency (CNA) system, 
which was adopted from 01.04.2022. Unspent balances with the States/ Implementing agencies were 
also a factor as the CNA system does not allow fresh releases until the previously released amount is 
utilized. Allocations for Prime Minister’s Development Initiative for North-East Region (PM-
DevINE), which was announced in Union Budget 2022-23, largely unutilized during 2022-23 and 
2023-24 as the operational guidelines could be notified only in August 2023. Utilization of allocated 
funds was also hampered due to delay in project implementation by State Government/ 
Implementation Agencies because of short working season on account of inclement weather 
conditions; difficulties in transportation of material due to difficult terrain; land acquisition issues; 
local law and order issues etc. and also because of delay in submission of demand/ claims by the 
State Governments. 
1.2.6 The total expenditure during 2024–25 stood at ₹3,452.99 crore, which is 86.20% of the 
Revised Estimates (RE). MDoNER will make all possible efforts to further improve the utilization of 
allocated funds. 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.2.7 The Committee would like to be apprised about the budgetary allocation to the NER from 
2005-2014 and 2014-2024 alongwith a comparative study of the socio-economic as well as 
infrastructural development between the period from 2005-14 and 2014-24. 
(Para 2.4.6 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.2.8 Details of budgetary allocations for MDoNER, from 2004-05 to 2013-14 and 2014-15 to 
2024-25, are at Annexure-I. 
1.2.9 The budgetary allocation to the North Eastern Region (NER) from 2005-2014 and during 
2014-2024 (FY- wise) is enclosed at Annexure –II. 
 
1.2.10 Further, it is also submitted that the socio-economic and infrastructural development in the 
NER has been a priority for the Government. Over the years, substantial investments have been 
made to improve connectivity, education, healthcare, and livelihood opportunities in the region. Key 
infrastructure projects include the expansion of road, rail, and air connectivity. Despite challenges 
posed by difficult terrain and dispersed population, the concerted efforts of the Centre and State 
Governments have resulted in measurable progress across various sectors in the NER. 
1.2.11 During 2005-2014, Growth in the NER is as follows: 
 In 2005, the Special Accelerated Road Development Programme for North East (SARDP-
NE) was launched to improve 8,737 km of roads. The first phase of approved work was of 
2,304 km. 

4 
 
 Major railway projects were taken up, including electrification of the 800 km Barauni–
Katihar–Guwahati route, construction of a rail-cum-road bridge over the Brahmaputra at 
Bogibeel, and gauge conversion of the Lumding–Silchar and Rangia–Murkongselek lines. 
New railway lines for the state capitals of Assam, Tripura, Manipur, Nagaland, Mizoram and 
Arunachal Pradesh, besides opening up the possibility of a rail link at a later date due to 
Chittagong Port from Sabroom were also planned. 
 Several schemes for development of airports in the NER had been taken up at Agartala, 
Barapani, Dibrugarh, Dimapur, Guwahati, Silchar, Imphal, Jorhat and Rupsi. 
 Foundation stoneslaidfor the 3,000 MW Dibang Multipurpose project- the country’s largest 
hydroelectric project and a 750 MW gas-based thermal power plant in Tripura. 
 The Government approved the 600 MW Kameng hydroelectric power project and resumed 
work on the 2,000 MW Subansiri Lower hydroelectric project. 
 90% assistance under Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan was given to States as compared to 65% for 
other States. 
 NEIGRIHMS, Shillong was made operational and Indian Institute of Management was set up 
at Shillong. 
 North Eastern Region Livelihood Project (NERLP) launched in 2012 focused on women-
led SHGs, rural enterprise development, and micro-finance. 
 During 2014-2024, Growth in the North Eastern Region (NER) is as follows: 
 North Eastern Region Power System Improvement Project (NERPSIP) was approved in 2014 
with World Bank assistance. 
 Expansion of National Highways: The length of National Highways in the NER has seen a 
significant rise, increasing from 10,905 km in 2014 to 16,207 km by 2024. 
 Sela Tunnel: Constructed at a cost of ₹825 crore, the Sela Tunnel provides all-weather 
connectivity between Tezpur and Tawang. 
 Railway Infrastructure Growth: NER has added 1,909 km of railway tracks, with 19 major 
railway projects worth ₹81,941 crore currently underway. Additionally, 972 km of railway 
track has been converted to broad gauge. 
 Key Railway Projects Since 2014: 
o Agartala–Sabroom New Line (112 km) at ₹3,904.61 crore 
o Commissioning of the Bogibeel Rail-cum-Road Bridge (2018) 
o Completion of Agartala (Tripura) – Akhaura (Bangladesh) Railway Link at the cost 
of ₹1,100 crore 
 Connectivity to State Capitals: Three State Capitals- Arunachal Pradesh, Tripura and 
Mizoram are connected by broadgauge rail. The railway network project to connect Imphal 
(Manipur) is in the advance stage of completion. 
 Aviation Sector Boost: The number of airports in the region has grown from 9 in 2014 to 17 
in 2024.  

5 
 
 Waterways Expansion: With an investment of ₹1,040 crore, the number of national 
waterways in the NER has expanded from 1 to 20. Notable milestones include: 
o MV Lal Bahadur Shastri’s successful cargo voyage from Patna to Pandu via 
Bangladesh (2022) 
o Launch of MV Ganga Vilas, the world’s longest river cruise, operating from Varanasi 
to Bogibeel via Bangladesh (2023) 
 Hydropower Projects: 
o Kameng Hydro Power Project (600 MW) in Arunachal Pradesh made operational  
o Dibang Multipurpose Hydroelectric Project (2,880 MW) under development in 
Arunachal Pradesh 
 Medical Infrastructure: The first AIIMS in the NER was established in Guwahati in 2017. 
Assam will have South Asia’s largest Cancer hospital network with 14 hospitals.

Recommendation/Observation 
1.3.1 The Committee acknowledges that North Eastern Council is one the important agencies for 
overall inclusive growth of North East Region. The Committee hopes that the increased allocation of 
₹ 822.00 Cr. in B.E. 2025-26 will provide a much needed support to the agency for carrying out 
socio-economic development, regional planning and welfare activities in the region. 
(Para 3.1.8 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.3.2 MDoNER in association with North East Council (NEC) will make every effort towards the 
full utilization of the budget allocated for FY for 2025-26. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.3.3 The Committee suggests that the North Eastern Council and the Ministry of DoNER must 
take necessary steps to enhance the infrastructure capacity and technological upgradation in the 
North East Region. The Committee notes that under North Eastern Council, 61% of budgetary 
allocation has been utilized till Dec, 2024. The Committee hopes that the Ministry will make 
necessary efforts to clear liabilities of all the ongoing projects in the Financial Year 2025-26 itself so 
that they may not spill over to the next financial year. 
(Para 3.1.9 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
1.3.4 Plan is being formulated to enhance the infrastructure capacity and technological 
upgradation in the NER. Under Schemes of NEC, the utilization of funds is 99.55% & under 
NESIDS Roads, the utilization is 99.98% as on 31.03.2025. NEC will clear all liabilities in FY 
2025-26. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 

6

implementation of its schemes due to various reasons. However, the Committee recommends that 
the following challenges can be resolved with proper management, administrative efficiency and 
planning-

(ii) Lack of experts for preparation of DPR. 
(iii) Delay in submission of UC and QPR. 
(iv) Delay in submission of Completion Certificate after the actual physical completion of 
the projects. 
(v) Change of location of project sites proposed by implementing agencies. 
(Para 3.1.10 ibid)

2025-26 to meet the shortfalls. 
(Para 3.1.11 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
1.3.8 The recommendation of the Committee has been noted for compliance.

accommodation for working women, including those from SC/ST backgrounds, in areas where 
employment opportunities exist. Currently, there are 523 Sakhi Niwas functional across the country. 
Shakti Sadan offers shelter and rehabilitation for women in distress, including trafficked and 
socially marginalized women. 404 Shakti Sadans are operational across the country.

2.13.12  5. The Govt. of India has taken significant steps to enhance the safety and security of 
women through the creation of a dedicated, non-lapsable corpus known as the Nirbhaya Fund. 
Established in response to growing concerns about crimes against women, this fund has grown 
remarkably over the past decade from supporting a few projects initially to now overseeing 50 
projects with a total outlay exceeding ₹11,300 crore. These initiatives are implemented both 
nationally and regionally, targeting key areas such as behavioural change, legal and institutional 
reform, capacity building and infrastructure development. All the initiatives can broadly be divided 
into three spheres, one being assuring a safe and secure environment in which a woman lives and 
works, the other is to support effective implementation of legislation, and finally, creating a wide 
enabling infrastructure to afford to women speedy justice and support in any crisis. Projects under 
this fund are being executed by various Ministries and Departments including the Ministry of Home 
Affairs, Ministry of Railways, Ministry of Road Transport & Highways, Department of Justice, 
Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, Ministry of Tourism, Ministry of Panchayati 
Raj, Ministry of Housing & Urban Affairs, Ministry of External Affairs and several State 
Governments across the country. 
2.13.13  6.Under the Nirbhaya framework, an Empowered Committee (EC) of officers constituted 
under the chairpersonship of Secretary, Ministry of Women & Child Development (MWCD), 
appraises and recommends proposals submitted by Ministries/ Departments/ Stale 
Governments/UTs for funding under Nirbhaya Fund. After the projects are appraised and 
recommended by the EC, the responsibility of its execution lies on the concerned Ministries or State 
Governments who utilise funds from their own budget after obtaining approval of their respective 
financial authorities to release the same to the State Governments/ other Implementing Agencies 
(IAs) to implement the approved projects. 
2.13.14  Some of the key initiatives under the fund have been enumerated below: 
i. Launched in February 2019, the Emergency Response Support System (ERSS) provides a 
nationwide, technology-enabled emergency response mechanism accessible a pan-India, single, 
internationally recognised number, i.e., 112. Operational across all 36 States and Union 
Territories, ERSS includes computer-aided dispatch systems and has handled over 43 crore calls 
since inception. ERSS has been integrated with 139 Rail Madad Helpline service (all 36 
States/UTs), 1077 National Disaster Helpline (35 States/UTs), 1098 Child help Line (all 36 
States/UTs) and 181 Women Help Line 181 (35 States/UTs). 
ii.      The system has recorded a national average response time of 18.55 minutes. The 112 India 
mobile app, with over 44 lakh downloads, further enhances accessibility. The ERSS forms the 
backbone of India's emergency safety infrastructure for women-available 24/7 in any location, 
be it home, workplace, or public space. 
iii.    In addition to ERSS, there is fully functional dedicated Women Helpline (WHL) functional 
since April 2015 with the aim to provide emergency and non-emergency response to women 
affected by violence across the country by referral service. Under the scheme, a toll-free 24-

31 
 
hours telecom service through short code 181 is provided to women seeking support and 
information. It is operational in 35 States/ UTs. So far, WHL has handled over 2.1 crore calls 
and assisted over 87.28 lakh women till April 2025 across the country and 69,904 women have 
been assisted specifically in North East states. The Government is in process of automating and 
integrating Women Helpline (181) with Emergency Response Support System (112) to obviate 
the problem of multiplicity of helpline numbers, and also further linking it with OSCs 
iv. The Government launched the scheme of One Stop Centre(OSCs) in April 2015 to provide 
integrated support and assistance to women affected by violence or in distress, both in private 
and public spaces under one roof and facilitate immediate, emergency and non-emergency 
access to a range of services including police, medical, legal aid and counselling, psychological 
support. At present, 820 OSCs are functional across 38 States/UTs, covering entire geographical 
area of the country. These centres have assisted over 11.19 lakh women so far. In North East 
region, a total of 125 OSCs are operational that have assisted 42,763 women till 31st March 
2025. 
2.13.15   7. To address the issue of Women's Safety in Railway Stations across the country, the 
Ministry of Railways has put in place an Integrated Emergency Response Management System

are being installed at 983 major Railway Stations to provide 24x7 security to women passengers at

systems in all public places where women work and live so that perpetrators are kept at bay. 
Keeping this 'mantra' in mind that Government is implementing Safe City Projects in 8 major cities

3.5 Healthcare and Education 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.5.1 The Committee notes that as per the information provided by the Ministry of Development of 
North Eastern Region, the Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) (Per Thousand), 2020, is far less in the States 
of Mizoram (3), Nagaland (4), Sikkim (5) and Manipur (6) as compared to the other North Eastern 
States namely, Assam (36) Meghalaya (29), Arunachal Pradesh (21) and Tripura (18). The IMR 
count of the States of Assam and Meghalaya is even greater than national average which is 28. The 
Committee is of the view that death of infants is a key yardstick to determine the larger healthcare 

41 
 
situation and facilities of an area. Multi-departments efforts, provision of health and wellness centres 
with trained professionals and easy accessibilities of healthcare facilities to pregnant women and 
post natal care to new-borns can pave a way for minimising the number of infant deaths in the States 
which have high infant mortality rate. Similarly, best healthcare practices adopted in the States of 
Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim and Manipur can be adopted in other North Eastern States to improve 
their health infrastructure. The Committee recommends that the MDoNER should take initiative to 
study basic health care facilities available in those States where IMR is quite high and ensure to 
provide sufficient health care facilities to those States to reduce IMR drastically. 
 
(Para 4.10.8 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
3.5.2 The details of basic health care initiatives/programmes taken up by the Governments of 
Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim and Manipur where IMR is 3,4,5, and 6 respectively, are as under:

Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (F-IMNCI) and Integrated 
Management of  Neonatal and Childhood illness (IMNCI); (b) High Immunization Coverage; (c) 
Institutional deliveries; (d) effective  Antenatal and Postnatal Care (ANC/PNC); (e) Extended 
Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyaan (e-PMSMA); (f) SAANS campaign (Social 
Awareness and Action to Neutralize Pneumonia Successfully); (g) Community Health Care 
Workers (HWOs, ANMs and ASHAs); (h) Improved nutrition and Breastfeeding practices; (i) 
Access to Quality Healthcare in remote Areas;  (j) Intersectoral Coordination and Community 
Participation; (k) focus on education; (l) involving NGO and Church for influencing people in 
general; etc. 
(ii) Nagaland: (a) Maternal Nutrition during pregnancy; (b) Feeding practices at Birth and 
Childhood; (c) Facility and community level interventions viz. facility based new born care, 
focus on quality ANC and Identification and Tracking of High Risk Pregnancies, focus on care 
around birth, leveraging presence of Church Organizations (FBO) in improving demand  
generation, streamlining comprehensive VHSND (Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Day) 
services. 
(iii) Sikkim: (a) Promotion of Institutional Delivery; (b) Emphasis on facility based new-born 
care at different levels; (c) Appropriate Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF); (d) Universal 
Immunization Programme (UIP); (e) Home based new born care (HBNC); (f) Capacity building; 
(g) Education and awareness; (h) Monitoring and supervision; (i) Improvement in health seeking 
behaviour; (j) Use of Technology (Whatsapp); (k) One year maternity leave to take care of the 
infant: 
(iv) Manipur: (a) Institutional deliveries,; (b) Strengthening of the Village Health Sanitation 
and Nutrition Days; (c) Traditional practice of rooming the mother and the newborn till the

1 hour (Colostrum); (e)”Chak  Umba” a local ritual in which complimentary feeding is 
started along with continuation of breastfeeding; (f) Keeping the baby warm through local 
practice  of wrapping the infants and holding the infants either in the back or on the 
chest; (g) Diet rich in high protein/Iron intake by the community across state; (h) 
Functionality of Special Newborn Care Units (SNCUs), Newborn Intensive Care Unit (NICU),

Newborn Stabilization Unit (NBSU) & Newborn Care Corner (NBCC), etc. in Medical Colleges,

Special Package for Bodoland Territorial Council (BTC), Karbi Anglong Autonomous 
Territorial Council (KAATC) and Dima Hasao Autonomous Territorial Council (DHATC) 
The Committee notes that despite the measures taken by the Ministry for monitoring 
and review, no fund had been utilized under Bodoland Territorial Council (BTC) and Dima 
Hasao Autonomous Territorial Council (DHATC) till December, 2024. The Committee would 
like to be apprised about the reasons for non-utilization of funds by these Councils. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry should identify the specific bottlenecks faced by 
BTC and DHATC and take targeted corrective measures in coordination with the State 
Government and implementing agencies to ensure that the sanctioned funds are effectively 
utilized within the prescribed timelines. 
(Para 3.2.4) 
 
Agriculture and Allied Sectors 
 
 The Committee notes the efforts made by the Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers 
Welfare (MoA&FW) in implementing the Mission Organic Value Chain Development for 
North Eastern Region (MOVCDNER) across all the eight states of the North East. The 
Committee notes that Sikkim has achieved the distinction of being the first fully organic State 
in the country. The Committee desires to know about the economic impact of complete organic 
framing conversion in Sikkim on the income levels and livelihoods of farmers. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry may undertake a detailed assessment or impact study to 
evaluate how 100% organic farming has influenced farmers’ earnings, productivity, and 
market access, and share the findings with the Committee. Such insights would be useful for 
replicating the successful elements of Sikkim’s model in other North Eastern States. 
(Para 3.3.5) 
 
Infrastructure and Power 
 
 The Committee takes note of the information furnished by the Ministry of Road 
Transport and Highways (MoRTH) regarding the implementation of 62 mega infrastructure 
projects amounting to ₹56,160.20 crore in the North Eastern Region. While appreciating these 
efforts to enhance regional connectivity, the Committee desires to be apprised of the 
proportion of the total MoRTH budget that is being spent on projects in the North Eastern 
Region. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry furnish year-wise details of 

47 
 
expenditure incurred on these 62 projects out of the total sanctioned cost of ₹56,160.20 crore, 
indicating the financial progress, completion status, and physical milestones achieved.  
(Para 3.4.5) 
 
 The Committee notes that under the Bharatmala Pariyojana, projects covering a total 
length of about 3,035 km at an estimated cost of ₹69,569 crore are in progress in the North 
Eastern Region. The Committee seeks clarification from the Ministry as to whether this 
amount of ₹69,569 crore is distinct from or inclusive of the ₹56,160.20 crore worth of 62 mega 
infrastructure projects earlier mentioned (under Para 3.4.2) by the Ministry of Road 
Transport and Highways (MoRTH). The Committee further recommends that the Ministry 
may furnish a comprehensive breakup of all ongoing and sanctioned projects, along with their 
corresponding financial allocations in the North Eastern Region. 
(Para 3.4.8) 
 
Healthcare and Education 
 The Committee notes that the Ministry has shared the initiatives undertaken by the 
States of Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, and Manipur which have resulted in significantly low 
Infant Mortality Rates (IMR) with other States of North Eastern Region. In addition to this, 
the Committee recommends that the Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region 
(MDoNER), in coordination with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), 
should facilitate a coordinated mechanism for the implementation of best healthcare practices 
of these better-performing States in other North Eastern States where IMR remains high. The 
Committee further recommends that the Health Secretaries of all North Eastern States be 
taken on board to ensure effective inter-State knowledge sharing, capacity building, and 
adoption of proven interventions aimed at reducing IMR across the Region. 
(Para 3.5.4) 
 
Internet and Artificial Intelligence 
 The Committee notes the initiatives undertaken by the Department of 
Telecommunications (DoT) through BharatNet and mobile tower projects for enhancing 
broadband and internet connectivity in the North Eastern States. The Committee would like to 
be informed about the timeline by which internet coverage will be achieved across the entire 
North Eastern Region. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should prepare a State-
wise roadmap with specific targets and completion timelines, ensuring that even the most 
remote and difficult terrains are brought under seamless digital connectivity at the earliest. 
(Para 3.6.3) 
 
Social Justice and Women Empowerment 
  The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Development of North Eastern 
Region (MDoNER), in coordination with the concerned Ministries may take a consolidated 
assessment of the socio-economic outcome of the initiatives taken for the development  and 
employment generation in the North-Eastern Region. Assessment may include clear indicators 
such as income enhancement, entrepreneurship development, skill upgradation, and livelihood 
and employment creation. This will help in assessing the real effectiveness of the empowerment 
measures being implemented in the region. 
(Para 3.7.10)
