CHAPTER-I 
OVERVIEW 
 
1.1  CONSTITUTIONAL AND FUNCTIONAL MANDATE 
 
1.1.1 The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) is entrust ed with the responsibility of ensuring 
internal security, border management, administratio n of Union Territories, Centre–State 
relations, disaster management, citizenship matters  and related subjects. The Ministry plays a 
pivotal role in maintaining public order, strengthe ning national integration and ensuring 
coordinated security responses across the country. 
 
1.1.2  Though 'Public Order' and 'Police' are the r esponsibilities of States as per the Seventh 
Schedule to the Constitution of India, Article 355 of the Constitution enjoins the Union to protect 
every State against external aggression and interna l disturbance and to ensure that the 
Government of every State is carried on in accordan ce with the provisions of the Constitution. 
While discharging its duties, the Ministry of Home Affairs continuously monitors the internal 
security situation, issues appropriate advisories, shares intelligence inputs, extends manpower 
and financial support, guidance and expertise to th e State Governments for maintenance of 
security, peace and harmony without encroaching upon the constitutional rights of the States. 
 
1.1.3  The Detailed Demands for Grants (2026-27) re flect the Ministry’s wide-ranging mandate 
covering Secretariat administration, Modernisation of Prisons and Other Administrative Services 
including Civil Defence and Fire Services, Miscella neous General Services and Police 
Infrastructure, among others. 
 
1.2 GOALS AND OBJECTIVES 
 
1.2.1 The MHA administers and implements a wide ran ge of schemes and programmes. In 
brief, the goals and objectives of the Ministry for the year (2026-27) are as follows: 
 
(i) Continuous monitoring of  internal security situati on and issuance of timely 
advisories; 
(ii) Consolidation of gains towards achieving a Naxal-fr ee Bharat through 
coordinated security and development initiatives in  Left Wing Extremism 
affected areas; 
(iii) Implementation of a zero-tolerance policy against t errorism including 
strengthening of counter-terrorism architecture and  intelligence coordination 
mechanisms;  
(iv) Adoption of a Whole-of-Government approach to disma ntle narco-terror 
networks and combat drug trafficking; 
(v) Strengthening border management through integrated border infrastructure, 
coastal security, surveillance technologies and Vibrant Villages Programme; 

2 
 
(vi) Modernisation of the criminal justice system throug h implementation of new 
criminal laws and digitization to ensure a transpar ent, time-bound and victim-
centric criminal justice system; 
(vii) Further development of the Inter-Operable Criminal Justice System (ICJS) for 
seamless data exchange among police, courts, prison s and forensic 
institutions; 
(viii) Strengthening forensic science and investigation in frastructure under the 
National Forensic Infrastructure Enhancement initia tives, including 
modernization of Central Forensic Science Laboratories (CFSLs); 
(ix) Further expansion of evidence-based investigation s ystems, and enhancement 
of training and skill-development programmes for police personnel; 
(x) Enhancing cyber security architecture and strengthe ning institutional 
mechanisms to address emerging digital and financial cyber threats; 
(xi) Strengthening disaster preparedness and response ca pacity through capacity 
building, early warning systems and coordinated dis aster management 
frameworks; 
(xii) Modernization, capacity building and welfare measur es for Central Armed 
Police Forces (CAPFs), including provision of secur ity, administrative and 
residential infrastructure; 
(xiii) Ensuring timely reimbursement to States under Secur ity Related Expenditure 
(SRE) and providing Special Infrastructure Support to LWE affected States; 
(xiv) Conduct of Census 2027 and related preparatory acti vities, including 
technological upgradation for census operations; 
(xv) Operationalisation and strengthening of Bhartiya Bh asha Anubhag and 
promotion of Official Languages to support translat ion services and linguistic 
diversity; 
(xvi) Strengthening cooperative federalism through the In ter-State Council and 
Zonal Councils; 
(xvii) Implementing initiatives for women's safety and emp owerment to ensure a 
secure environment for women; 
(xviii) Fostering international cooperation on security iss ues, including counter-
terrorism and transnational crime; 
(xix) Supporting prison reforms and modernization of pris ons, including schemes 
for support to poor prisoners; 
(xx) Streamlining immigration processes through technolo gy-driven systems 
including the Immigration, Visa, Foreigners Registr ation and Tracking 
(IVFRT) and related platforms;  
(xxi) Timely disbursement of funds to freedom fighters an d their eligible 
dependents; 
(xxii) Supporting holistic development of islands and bord er areas in Union 
Territories to enhance local governance and infrastructure; and 
(xxiii) Fostering community engagement programs to promote peace, harmony and 
social cohesion;

CHAPTER-II 
 
OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF DEMANDS FOR GRANTS (2026-27) OF 
THE MHA 
 
2.1 OVERVIEW 
 
2.1.1 There are eleven Demands for Grants which are  administered by the Ministry of Home 
Affairs (MHA). The detailed Demands for Grants of t he Ministry of Home Affairs are divided 
into three volumes: Vol. I, Vol. II-A and Vol. II-B. The Detailed Demands for Grants (Volume-I) 
contains three Demands (Nos. 49-51), namely the Min istry of Home Affairs (Demand No. 49); 
the Cabinet (Demand No. 50); and the Police (Demand No. 51). 
 
2.1.2. The Detailed Demands for Grants (Volumes-II- A and II-B) relate to the five Union 
Territories (without Legislature), namely Andaman &  Nicobar Islands (Demand No. 52), 
Chandigarh (Demand No. 53), Dadra & Nagar Haveli an d Daman & Diu (Demand No. 54), 
Ladakh (Demand No. 55) and Lakshadweep (Demand No. 56) and  three Union Territories (with 
Legislature), namely Delhi (Demand No. 57- Transfer s to Delhi), Jammu & Kashmir (Demand 
No.58- Transfers to Jammu & Kashmir) and Puducherry  (Demand No. 59- Transfers to 
Puducherry). 
 
2.1.3 The provisions for the Union Territories (wit hout Legislature) form part of the Demands 
of the Ministry of Home Affairs. However, various p rogrammes/schemes are the subject matter 
of different Ministries, which are responsible for scrutinizing, sanctioning and implementing the 
schemes/projects falling under their respective pur view. Provisions for the Union Territories 
(with a Legislature) cover Assistance to the Union Territories of Puducherry, Jammu & Kashmir 
and NCT of Delhi, in the form of the Grants and Loa ns. In respect of these three Grants, the 
Ministry of Home Affairs releases the Grants on a q uarterly basis and has a limited role in 
scrutinizing, sanctioning and implementation of the schemes/projects.

3.1 OVERVIEW 
3.1.1 Ministry of Home Affairs contains provisions mainly for various administrative functions 
in respect of MHA Secretariat, Office of Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India, 
various offices functioning under Department of Off icial Language, Zonal Councils, National 
Disaster Response Force, National Disaster Manageme nt Authority (NDMA), Director General 
of Fire Service, Civil Defence & Home Guards, Natio nal Human Rights Commission, National 
Fire Services College and Departmental Accounting Organisation of MHA.  
3.1.2 Apart from the above, provisions have been ma de for schemes like Relief & 
Rehabilitation for repatriates and migrants, Pensio n and other benefits to Freedom Fighters, 
Helicopter subsidies for North-East, Jammu & Kashmi r, Ladakh and Himachal Pradesh and 
various schemes of Disaster Management and Establis hment of Bhartiya Bhasha Anubhag 
(BBA).  
3.2 OFFICIAL LANGUAGE 
3.2.1 The allocations under Official Language inclu de provisions for Central Hindi Training 
Institute (CHTI), Central Translation Bureau (CTB),  Technical Cell, Regional Implementation 
Offices (RIOs) and other schemes / programmes being  implemented by the Department of 
Official Language. 
3.2.2  The Committee sought to know about the measu rable outcomes proposed to be achieved 
under the head “Official Languages” during 2026–27 and the specific targets fixed for 
translation, capacity building and inspection activ ities. The Ministry informed that the following 
outputs have been proposed for the year:  
(i)
 Under translation activities, the Indian Languages Section proposes to translate 
approximately 20,000 letters into various regional languages, while the Central 
Translation Bureau has fixed a target of translating 40,000 pages during 2026–27. 
(ii) Under capacity building, the Department aims to exp and the Hindi Shabd Sindhu 
repository from 7 lakh to 7.5 lakh words and prepar e a Medical Shabd Sindhu 
dictionary in 15 Indian languages. It has also prop osed to impart Hindi training to 
25,000 personnel through the Central Hindi Training Institute and provide training to 
1,175 personnel through the Central Translation Bureau. 
(iii) With regard to inspections, the Parliamentary  Committee on Official Language has 
proposed to inspect approximately 7,000 offices. Fu rther, approximately 852 
offices/banks/undertakings are to be inspected by t he Regional Implementation 
Offices. 

21 
 
3.2.3 The Committee further sought to know the addi tional measures and initiatives 
undertaken for promotion of Official Language Hindi  apart from quarterly and annual assessment 
reports. The Ministry informed that the Department of Official Language has undertaken the 
following initiatives: 
(i) Development and upgradation of the Artificial Intel ligence-based translation software 
“Bharati - Bahubhashi Anuvada Sarthi” (earlier Kant hastha), integrated with e-Office 
and expanded to include 15 Indian languages, with p rovision for instant translation 
facility. 
(ii) Establishment of the Indian Languages Section to fa cilitate multilingual 
correspondence between the Central Government and S tate Governments in their 
respective official languages through a universal translation system. 
(iii) Continuous expansion of the fully digital Hindi-to- Hindi dictionary “Hindi Shabd 
Sindhu”, which presently contains over seven lakh words across diverse domains. 
(iv) Inspired by the Hon’ble Prime Minister’s “Panch Pra n,” the Department has organised 
a series of All India Official Language Conferences  and Regional Official Language 
Conferences to strengthen implementation of the Off icial Language Policy and confer 
Rajbhasha awards for exemplary performance. 
(v) Conduct of Technical Conferences for capacity enhan cement of officers of the Central 
Secretariat Official Language Service. 
(vi) Functioning of over 550 Town Official Language Impl ementation Committees 
(TOLICs) across the country, including five oversea s TOLICs, to promote the use of 
Hindi in official work. 
(vii) Periodic review of implementation through the Centr al Hindi Committee, chaired by 
the Hon’ble Prime Minister, and additionally, under  the chairmanship of the Secretary, 
Department of Official Language, a meeting of the C entral Official Language 
Implementation Committee (COLIC) is organized every year.  
(viii) Launch of the e-Saral Hindi Phrasebook containing m ore than 14,000 official-use 
sentences including terms drawn from domains such a s administration, agriculture, 
banking and finance, healthcare, industry, information technology, law, and tourism. 
3.2.4 From the information provided by the MHA, it may be seen that while the allocation in  
RE of 2025-26 was ₹ 97.06 crores, in BE 2026-27 an allocation of ₹ 98.16 crores has been made 
under the head ‘Official language’. 
Observations/Recommendations 
3.2.5  The Committee notes the measurable targets fixed by  the Department of Official 
Language for 2026–27, including translation of 20,0 00 letters and 40,000 pages, imparting 
Hindi training to 25,000 personnel, training of 1,1 75 officials by the Central Translation 

22 
 
Bureau, expansion of the Hindi Shabd Sindhu reposit ory to 7.5 lakh words, preparation of 
a Medical Shabd Sindhu dictionary in 15 Indian lang uages, and inspection of 
approximately 852 offices/banks/undertakings by Reg ional Implementation Offices. The 
Committee appreciates the outcome-oriented approach  reflected in the fixing of 
quantifiable physical targets and expects effective  implementation of the proposed targets. 
Further, the Ministry may explore expansion of domain-specific terminologies, particularly 
in emerging sectors such as digital governance, art ificial intelligence, cyber security and 
health sciences, so as to strengthen the practical usability of Hindi in technical and 
administrative communication. 
3.2.6 The Committee further notes the technological  interventions undertaken by the 
Department, particularly the upgradation of the AI- based translation platform “Bharati – 
Bahubhashi Anuvada Sarthi”, its integration with e- Office, and the establishment of the 
Indian Languages Section to facilitate multilingual correspondence between the Centre and 
States. The Committee is of the view that while the se initiatives are commendable, the 
Ministry may consider instituting a robust performa nce-monitoring framework to assess

 The Committee notes the significant increase in ope rational commitments of the

across multiple States/UTs and its participation in  international humanitarian assistance

responsibilities, no additional battalion has been raised during the last three years and the

3.9  HOME GUARDS  
3.9.1 The Ministry informed the Committee that the increase between BE 2025–26 and RE 
2025–26, as well as BE 2026–27, is due to additiona l demand by the Directorate General, Fire 
Services, Civil Defence and Home Guards (DGCDFS&HG)  for reimbursement to States/UTs 
and clearing of backlog claims. The Committee was a pprised that Home Guards constitute a 
voluntary force raised by States and Union Territor y Administrations under a broad policy 
framework laid down by the Ministry of Home Affairs . The force supplements State/UT police 
forces in maintaining law and order, traffic manage ment, protection of public property, guarding 
borders and performing election-related duties. The  central provision is meant for assisting 
States/UTs in raising, training and equipping Home Guards. 
3.9.2 In response to the Committee’s query regardin g enhancement of working conditions, 
training, equipment and deployment constraints, the  Ministry informed that the following 
measures have been proposed/initiated by Directorat e General (Fire Services, Civil Defence and 
Home Guards), MHA. As Home Guards fall under the ju risdiction of respective States/UTs, 
implementation would be undertaken by them: 

31 
 
(i) Introduction of Digital Platform - “Seva Path” 
The proposed Model Home Guards Bill, 2025 envisages  a dedicated digital platform for 
transparent and efficient allotment of duties. The platform provides for term-wise 
engagement of Home Guards for a five-year period, e nsuring equitable deployment, 
improved workforce planning and enhanced accountability. 
(ii) Digitalisation of Wage Disbursement 
States/UTs may introduce digital systems for disbur sement of wages/honorarium through 
Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) to ensure transparenc y and timely payments. Coordination 
with Government banks is also proposed to extend ac count-linked benefits on lines similar 
to those available to Armed Forces/CAPFs. 
(iii) 
Group Medical Insurance and Health Coverage 
States/UTs may introduce Group Medical Insurance sc hemes or extend coverage under 
existing Central/State health schemes such as Ayush man Bharat to ensure comprehensive 
health protection for Home Guards. 
(iv) 
Modernisation of Training Modules 
A review of training syllabi is under process to al ign with contemporary requirements, with 
emphasis on disaster management, community engageme nt, internal security support and 
awareness of flagship schemes. A conference with St ate/UT authorities has already been 
convened in this regard. 
(v) 
Integration with SDRF as First Responders 
It has been recommended that Home Guards may be tra ined and utilised as first responders 
at the district level, particularly in disaster pre paredness and response, considering their 
wide presence across districts. 
(vi) 
Review of Uniform and Equipment Policy 
A national-level committee has been constituted to standardise uniforms and modernise 
equipment, ensuring climate suitability and functio nal adequacy for duties relating to 
disasters, elections and internal security. 
 
Observations/Recommendations 
3.9.3  The Committee notes that although the alloca tion under the head “Home Guards” 
has improved in BE 2026–27, it remains modest in co mparison to the expanding role of 
Home Guards in elections, disaster response and int ernal security duties. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry, in consultation with States/UTs, may undertake a 
comprehensive assessment of financial and operation al requirements so that central 
assistance is commensurate with the increasing depl oyment responsibilities of the force.

Path” platform and digitalisation of wage disbursem ent, may be implemented in a time-

32 
 
bound manner across States/UTs to ensure transparen cy, equitable deployment and timely

protective gear and essential equipment to enable e ffective discharge of duties during

Observation/ Recommendation 
4.2.5 The Committee notes that the allocation for C entral Armed Police Forces (CAPFs) 
has shown a steady increase over the last three yea rs, with the total outlay rising from 
₹1,04,824.10 crores in Actuals 2024–25 to ₹1,16,789 .30 crores in BE 2026–27. The 
Committee observes that the increase is largely att ributable to higher provisions under 
allowances, medical expenditure, provisioning items , ICT and Machinery and Equipment, 
reflecting the growing operational commitments and administrative requirements of the 
Forces. The Committee further notes that while Reve nue expenditure constitutes the 
predominant share of the allocation, enhanced provi sions have also been made under the 
Capital Section towards machinery & equipment and motor vehicles.  
In view of the expanding role of CAPFs in border ma nagement, counter-terrorism, 
internal security and election duties, the Committe e recommends that sustained emphasis 
may be placed on modernisation of equipment, techno logy upgradation and infrastructure 
strengthening to enhance operational efficiency and  response capability. The Ministry may 
periodically review the ratio of Revenue to Capital  expenditure with a view to ensure the 
capital investments in modern equipment, mobility a nd surveillance systems keep pace

4.5.1 The Committee noted that allocation under “We lfare Grant and Miscellaneous” has 
declined from ₹1,422.65 crores in RE 2025–26 to ₹1, 090.00 crores in BE 2026–27. The Ministry 
informed that the primary reason for the reduction is that the provision for Medical Treatment

stage based on expenditure trends. Any additional r equirement in 2026–27 will similarly be

4.5.2 The Committee was informed that CAPFs have au gmented their health infrastructure 
through recruitment of doctors and paramedical staf f, construction of new 10, 20 and 50-bedded 
hospitals and upgradation of various field hospital s. Preventive and fitness-based medical 
initiatives, including sports, yoga protocol, physi cal training and mental health interventions, 
have been given emphasis. Further, the Central Arme d Police Forces Institute of Medical 
Sciences (CAPFIMS) has been proposed as a tertiary and speciality healthcare facility for CAPF

treatment is available in 2,027 CGHS-empanelled hos pitals and 33,135 AB-PMJAY empanelled 
hospitals that have signed MoUs with the National H ealth Authority. Approximately 42 lakh 
Ayushman CAPF IDs have been generated. Retired pers onnel and their spouses are eligible for

4.5.3 The Ministry further apprised the Committee t hat comprehensive welfare measures are in 
place for families of CAPF and Assam Rifles personn el who lost their lives in the line of duty. 
The Welfare and Rehabilitation Board (WARB), establ ished in 2007, oversees welfare and 
rehabilitation of retired CAPF personnel, their fam ilies and dependents of deceased or disabled 
personnel. WARB functions through 06 Central Welfar e Officers, 32 State Welfare Officers and 
201 District Welfare Officers across the country. N ext of Kins (NoKs) of CAPF and Assam

Sector Undertakings and circulates vacancy notifica tions to retired personnel. The “CAPF

personnel killed in action.

ranks below DIG, grant of Risk and Hardship Allowan ce for deployment in J&K, Ladakh and 
LWE areas, additional HRA for personnel posted in K ashmir Valley, air courier services in 
difficult areas, air travel facilities for non-enti tled personnel and the CAPF e-Awas Portal for 
online allotment of residential accommodation. The Ministry informed in its presentation that as 
on 31.12.2025, the total authorised dwelling units (DUs) for CAPFs, Assam Rifles (AR) and 
NSG stand at 2,68,346, against which 1,35,544 dwell ing units are presently available. In 
addition, 10,430 dwelling units are under construct ion. The housing satisfaction level has been 
indicated at 50.14% in respect of available accommo dation and 54.03% considering ongoing 
construction. The Kendriya Police Kalyan Bhandar (K PKB) provides concessional canteen 
facilities with 50% GST concession w.e.f. 01.04.202 4. Stress management initiatives including

Observation / Recommendation  
4.5.6 The Committee appreciates the comprehensive w elfare framework put in place for 
families of CAPF and Assam Rifles personnel killed in action and for rehabilitation of 
retired personnel. The Committee notes the institut ional mechanism established through 
the Welfare and Rehabilitation Board (WARB) and the  deployment of Central, State and 
District Welfare Officers across the country. The C ommittee recommends that the 
Ministry may evolve a structured outcome-monitoring mechanism to periodically assess the 
effectiveness of financial assistance, pensionary b enefits, scholarship schemes and re-
employment initiatives, so as to ensure timely deli very and long-term socio-economic 
stability of beneficiary families. 
4.5.7 The Committee recommends that re-employment i nitiatives under the “CAPF 
Punarvaas” scheme may be strengthened through great er coordination with Public Sector 
Undertakings and private sector entities, and that data regarding placements and self-
employment outcomes may be periodically compiled an d reviewed. Special emphasis may 
be placed on skill development and counselling supp ort for widows and dependents to 
enable sustainable livelihood opportunities. 

41 
 
4.5.8 The Committee observes that the availability of housing units remains significantly 
below the authorised strength, with only 1,35,544 dwelling units presently in place against a 
sanctioned capacity of 2,68,346 units. In addition,  10,430 units are currently under 
construction, which, when completed, will marginally improve the situation. At present, the 
housing satisfaction level stands at 50.14%, reflec ting the considerable shortfall in meeting 
the sanctioned requirements. Upon completion of the  ongoing projects, this figure is 
projected to rise to 54.03%, indicating some progre ss but still underscoring the persistent 
gap between authorised strength and actual availabi lity. The existing housing gap requires 
sustained and time-bound augmentation.  
The Committee recommends that personnel deployed in  hard-duty, border and 
high-risk operational areas may be accorded priorit y in allotment of residential 
accommodation. Completion of ongoing housing projec ts may be closely monitored and 
that a phased roadmap may be prepared to progressiv ely enhance housing satisfaction 
levels across the Forces. 
4.5.9 Further, the Committee recommends that given the increasing operational stress 
and deployment in difficult terrains, access to qua lity and timely medical care assumes 
critical importance for CAPF personnel and their fa milies. Periodic review of empanelled 
hospitals, claim settlement timelines and beneficiary coverage may be undertaken to ensure 
comprehensive and timely medical support to serving  and retired personnel and their 
dependents. 
4.5.10 The Committee also take notes of the enhance ment of Central ex-gratia 
compensation and the assurance of a minimum financi al support package from various 
sources. While acknowledging the existing structure , the Committee recommends that the 
Ministry may examine the feasibility of evolving a broad and simplified categorisation of 
ex-gratia compensation so as to ensure clarity, uni formity and equity. The framework may 
remain sensitive to operational realities while avoiding over-fragmentation of categories.

Observation/ Recommendation 
4.8.6 The Committee notes that increasing represent ation of women in police forces is 
essential for promoting gender-sensitive policing, improving public trust and enhancing 
response to crimes against women and vulnerable sec tions. The Committee is of the view 
that Delhi, being the National Capital with a diver se and dense population, requires a 
strengthened and balanced force structure reflectin g adequate representation of women 
personnel at all levels.  
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Minis try, in coordination with 
Delhi Police, may prepare a phased and time-bound r oadmap to enhance the strength of 
women personnel to at least 33 percent of the total  sanctioned strength. Focused 
recruitment drives, adequate training capacity, pro vision of suitable infrastructure 
including separate accommodation and facilities, an d enabling service conditions may be 
ensured to achieve this objective in a sustainable manner. 
4.8.7 The Committee observes that hesitation among citizens to visit police stations often 
stems from perceptions of inaccessibility, lack of transparency and discomfort in 
interacting with personnel. Such barriers have pote ntial to discourage reporting of crime, 
weaken community participation and reduce trust in law enforcement.  
The Committee, therefore, recommends that Delhi Pol ice may adopt a citizen-
centric policing model to make police stations more  approachable, transparent and 
responsive. In this regard, the Ministry and Delhi Police may explore and adopt best 
practices such as establishing dedicated One-Stop Citizen Service Desks at police stations to 
assist visitors with inquiries and reporting proced ures; deploying Community Liaison 
Officers for outreach and follow-up with local comm unities; creating Victim Support 
Corners to provide private and supportive spaces fo r women, children and senior citizens; 

50 
 
instituting structured feedback and grievance redre ssal mechanisms with defined 
timelines; and prominently displaying service chart ers outlining procedures and rights of 
complainants.  
4.8.8 The Committee recommends expansion of mobile and community policing 
initiatives through regular engagement in markets and residential areas, and strengthening 
of online reporting and appointment systems to faci litate access without requiring physical 
visits. Regular training of personnel in communicat ion skills, sensitivity and public 
interface management may also be undertaken, and pe riodic community satisfaction 
surveys may be conducted to assess and improve service delivery. 
4.8.9 The Committee observes that cases relating to  missing persons, particularly women, 
children and vulnerable individuals, have significa nt social and security implications in a 
metropolitan city like Delhi. The Committee is of t he view that a data-driven and research-
oriented approach is necessary to understand the un derlying socio-economic, demographic 
and behavioural factors contributing to such cases.  
The Committee, therefore, recommends that Delhi Pol ice may undertake a 
comprehensive sociological study in collaboration w ith reputed universities and research 
institutions to analyse patterns and root causes of  missing persons’ cases. The study may 
include comparative analysis of missing rates in De lhi vis-à-vis other metropolitan cities in 
India as well as selected international cities, wit h a view to identifying best practices and 
systemic gaps. The findings of such a study may be utilised for policy formulation, 
preventive strategies, improved tracking mechanisms and community-based interventions. 
4.8.10 Further, the Committee observes that effecti ve implementation of provisions 
relating to plea bargaining under the Bharatiya Nag arik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) can 
play a significant role in reducing pendency of cas es, expediting disposal of minor offences 
and easing the burden on investigating agencies, co urts and correctional institutions. The 
Committee also observes that structured use of plea  bargaining mechanisms may 
contribute to faster resolution of cases, reduced u ndertrial prisoners and improved 
efficiency of the criminal justice system.  
The Committee, therefore, recommends that Delhi Pol ice may take proactive steps 
to sensitise investigating officers and supervisory  officers regarding the scope and 
procedural requirements of plea bargaining under th e BNSS. Awareness measures may be 
undertaken, in coordination with prosecution and le gal services authorities, to ensure 
informed participation of eligible accused persons.  Periodic review of cases disposed off 
through plea bargaining may also be conducted to as sess its effectiveness in reducing case 
backlog and custodial burden. 
4.8.11 The Committee, further, notes the increasing  deployment of CCTV cameras, body-
worn cameras, traffic surveillance systems, IoT-ena bled devices and integrated 

51 
 
communication platforms by Delhi Police as part of modernization and smart policing 
initiatives. While appreciating the technological a dvancements, the Committee also 
observes that robust data protection and cybersecur ity safeguards are critical to prevent 
misuse, unauthorised access, data breaches and comp romise of sensitive operational 
personal information. The Committee, therefore, rec ommends that Delhi Police may adopt 
a comprehensive data security framework covering en cryption standards, secure data 
storage, controlled access protocols, periodic cybersecurity audits and real-time monitoring 
of surveillance systems. 
4.8.12 The Committee recommends that private indivi duals and establishments installing 
CCTV systems may be encouraged or mandated to procu re devices only from 
manufacturers that comply with notified data securi ty, encryption and secure server 
standards. Periodic advisories and awareness campai gns may also be issued to promote 
adoption of secure systems and prevent misuse, hack ing or unauthorised access to 
surveillance data.

Observation/ Recommendation 
4.9.5 The Committee notes that 62 major traffic con gestion points have been identified 
across Delhi and corrective measures are being unde rtaken in coordination with civic 
agencies. The Committee recommends that a time-boun d action plan with clearly defined 
responsibilities for each stakeholder agency may be  prepared for all identified hotspots. 
Periodic public reporting of progress and measurabl e indicators such as reduction in 
average travel time, queue length and accident rate s may be introduced to assess 
effectiveness of interventions. A long-term urban m obility perspective, including 
coordination with urban planning authorities, may a lso be integrated into traffic 
management strategies to ensure sustainable deconge stion and a system of traffic flying 
squads may be put in place so that the same may be deployed at designated points during 
peak hours. 
4.9.6 The Committee observes that unregulated parki ng around office complexes, courts, 
hospitals and commercial establishments significant ly contributes to congestion and 
obstruction of roads. The Committee recommends that  Delhi Police, in coordination with 
Municipal and Urban Development authorities, may un dertake a comprehensive parking 
management strategy, including strict enforcement a gainst illegal parking on roads and 
residential areas, promotion of designated parking zones and use of technology-enabled 
parking monitoring systems. The Committee further r ecommends that commercial 
establishments may be mandated to ensure adequate o ff-street parking facilities to reduce 
spill-over onto public roads. 
4.9.7 The Committee notes with concern the increasi ng instances of unnecessary honking 
in the National Capital, leading to noise pollution  and public inconvenience, particularly in 
residential areas and near schools, hospitals and c ourts. The Committee recommends that 
Delhi Police may intensify enforcement of existing provisions relating to use of horns and 
pressure horns, especially in notified “No-Horn Zon es”. The Committee further 
recommends that sustained sensitisation and public awareness campaigns may be 
undertaken to discourage habitual and non-essential  honking, and that technology-enabled 
enforcement measures may be explored to ensure comp liance and promote responsible 
road behaviour. 
4.9.8 The Committee also notes instances of motorcy cles fitted with modified or non-
standard silencers that produce excessive noise, le ading to sound pollution and causing 
disturbance and unease to commuters and residents. The Committee recommends that 
Delhi Police may strengthen enforcement against suc h violations through regular checking 
drives, strict penalties and coordination with tran sport authorities to ensure compliance 
with prescribed vehicle noise standards.  

54 
 
4.9.9 The Committee observes that begging at traffi c signals not only poses safety risks 
but also disrupts traffic flow. The Committee recom mends that Delhi Police may work in 
coordination with Social Welfare Departments and Ci vil Society Organisations to address 
this issue through a humane and rehabilitative appr oach. Sustained enforcement at major 
intersections may be combined with rehabilitation, counselling and livelihood support 
initiatives to address the root causes of the problem.

The Committee, therefore, recommends that BPR&D may  further scale up and 
institutionalise specialised training programmes on  the new criminal laws, with particular 
emphasis on investigation procedures, evidence coll ection, digital documentation, forensic 
integration and trial processes under the revised l egal framework. Refresher courses, 
scenario-based simulations and field-level practica l modules may also be incorporated to 
ensure uniform understanding and application across States and Union Territories.  
In view of the rapidly evolving nature of crime, pa rticularly cyber-enabled and 
technology-driven offences, the Committee further r ecommends that dedicated courses on 
Artificial Intelligence (AI), Big Data Analytics, C ybercrime Investigation, Digital Forensics 
and Technology-driven Policing may be introduced an d mainstreamed in police training 
curricula. Advanced certification programmes and pa rtnerships with technical institutions 
may also be explored to equip officers with analyti cal and technological competencies 
required for modern policing. Periodic evaluation o f training outcomes may be undertaken 
to assess impact and identify emerging skill gaps.

separate accommodation and suitable custodial arran gements for these categories so that 
such measures would help safeguard the rights of un dertrial prisoners, reduce the risk of 
negative influence of convicted criminals and contr ibute to better prison management and 
discipline. 
4.16 SUPPORT TO POOR PRISONERS 
4.16.1 The Committee sought details regarding the n umber of prisoners benefitted under the 
Support to Poor Prisoners Scheme, the average proce ssing time for assistance and challenges 
encountered in timely delivery of support. The Mini stry informed that since inception of the 
Scheme, 262 prisoners have been provided financial assistance. It was further stated that the 
Guidelines and Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) o f the Scheme have recently been revised 
to ensure time-bound and effective implementation. 
4.16.2 As per the revised SOP, cases of undertrial prisoners who are not released within seven 
days of grant of bail are required to be reported b y Jail Authorities to the concerned District 
Legal Services Authority (DLSA). Verification and i nteraction by Jail Visiting 

70 
 
Lawyers/Paralegal Volunteers is to be completed wit hin five days. Thereafter, the cases are 
placed before the District Level Empowered Committe e, which is mandated to meet twice a 
month (on the 1st and 3rd Mondays of each month or the next working day) to consider eligible 
cases. The Committee is required to take a decision  and ensure availability of funds to the Court 
within a further five days. The Ministry stated tha t these clearly defined timelines are intended to 
minimise delays and procedural bottlenecks in extending assistance. 
4.16.3 With regard to challenges in timely delivery  of support, the Ministry informed that 
several States/UTs have reported that a significant  number of prisoners are not eligible under the 
Scheme due to their involvement in multiple cases o r in heinous offences such as terrorism-
related offences, offences affecting national secur ity, dowry death, rape, human trafficking and 
offences under the POCSO Act, NDPS Act, Unlawful Ac tivities (Prevention) Act, Prevention of 
Corruption Act and Prevention of Money Laundering A ct, for which benefits under the Scheme 
are not admissible. 
Observation / Recommendation 
 
4.16.4 The Committee notes that while the Support t o Poor Prisoners Scheme provides 
important financial assistance to undertrial prison ers who are unable to furnish bail, the 
number of beneficiaries since inception remains lim ited. The Committee appreciates the 
revision of Guidelines and Standard Operating Proce dure to ensure defined timelines at 
each stage of processing. The Committee recommends that greater awareness regarding 
the Scheme may be generated among prison authoritie s, legal aid institutions and eligible 
prisoners to ensure that deserving beneficiaries are not left out due to lack of information. 
 
4.17 VIBRANT VILLAGES PROGRAMME 
4.17.1 The Ministry has informed the Committee that  Vibrant Village Programme is for 
comprehensive development in phased manner of selec ted border villages. This includes village 
infrastructure development, road connectivity and o ther developmental works. The Ministry also 
informed that the Vibrant Villages Programme-II foc uses on improving living conditions and 
livelihoods in selected border villages. Its core a reas include village infrastructure, road and 
telecom connectivity, electrification, basic servic es, livelihood support, and integration of border 
populations with the nation. 
Vibrant Villages Programme–I 
4.17.2 The Committee was informed that the Vibrant Villages Programme (VVP) was launched 
with the objective of enhancing vibrancy in border villages and reversing outmigration by 
providing adequate incentives and improving living conditions. The Programme covers 662 
villages across 4 States and 1 Union Territory, wit h an approximate population coverage of 1.5 
lakh persons. The financial outlay for FY 2023–26 i s ₹4,800 crores, including the road 

71 
 
component, with an additional allocation of ₹440.82  crores for construction of Long Span 
Bridges (LSBs). 
4.17.3 The Ministry informed that since its launch in Kibithoo, Anjaw district, Arunachal 
Pradesh in 2023, several outreach and development a ctivities have been undertaken. Seventeen 
Union Cabinet Ministers have visited 34 VVP villages across 8 districts, and 92 officials from 17 
Ministries have visited 259 villages. More than 8,5 00 activities have been organized in the 
identified villages. Under VVP-I, 263 projects amounting to ₹116 crore have been sanctioned for 
development of tourism infrastructure. In addition,  112 road works amounting to ₹2,513 crore 
have been approved. A total of 2,663 projects worth  ₹1,172 crore have been sanctioned by the 
Ministry of Home Affairs under VVP-I and through co nvergence with Central Ministries and 
Departments for comprehensive development of these villages. The Programme aims to 
strengthen socio-economic resilience, prevent borde r depopulation and reinforce the first line of 
defence through community development initiatives. 
Vibrant Villages Programme–II (VVP-II) 
4.17.4 The Committee was further informed that Vibr ant Villages Programme–II has been 
approved as a Central Sector Scheme with effect from April 2025, with a total financial outlay of 
₹6,839 crores for the period FY 2024–29. VVP-II cov ers 1,954 villages across approximately 
100 districts in 17 States and Union Territories lo cated along land borders other than the 
Northern Border already covered under VVP-I. 
4.17.5 The objectives of VVP-II include strengtheni ng internal security by assimilating border 
populations with the national mainstream and encour aging their role as the “eyes and ears” of 
border guarding forces; improving living conditions  and livelihood opportunities; and weaning 
communities away from inimical activities while controlling trans-border crime. 
4.17.6 The strategy under VVP-II includes saturatio n of villages abutting International Land 
Borders (ILBs) with connectivity infrastructure suc h as telecom, roads, power and television; 
creation of diverse and sustainable livelihood oppo rtunities; development of infrastructure 
including education and tourism; and undertaking bo rder-specific outreach activities. The 
Programme seeks to enhance socio-economic developme nt, improve connectivity and 
infrastructure and reinforce community participatio n in national security objectives in border 
areas. 
Observation / Recommendation 
4.17.7 The Committee appreciates the Vibrant Villag es Programme (VVP) as a significant 
initiative aimed at comprehensive development of bo rder villages through phased 
infrastructure augmentation, livelihood generation and enhanced connectivity. The 
Committee notes that VVP-I has led to substantial p rogress in road connectivity, tourism 
infrastructure and convergence-based developmental activities and that VVP-II expands 
the scope of coverage to additional border regions.  The Programme’s emphasis on socio-

economic resilience, prevention of outmigration and  integration of border populations with

AIR CONNECTIVITY 
 
5.2.5  Andaman and Nicobar Islands constitute the l argest archipelago system in the Bay of 
Bengal and are located thousands of kilometres away  from the Indian mainland. The UT is 
connected to the mainland primarily through air and  water routes. The Committee took note of 
the increased tourism activity in the region and en quired about the steps taken to augment air 

78 
 
connectivity, including the enhancement of airport capacity in Port Blair and proposals for 
establishing additional airports to connect remote islands of the UT with the mainland. 
 
5.2.6 The Ministry informed the Committee that a Ne w Integrated Terminal Building (NITB) 
at Veer Savarkar International Airport, Sri Vijaya Puram, has been made operational since 
August 2023 with an annual handling capacity of 50 lakh passengers. To meet future demand, an 
alternate Greenfield Airport at Sri Vijaya Puram ha s been planned. The Committee appreciated 
this operationalisation, noting that the new termin al has enhanced passenger-handling capacity 
significantly.  
 
5.2.7 The Committee was further informed helicopter  services are operational from Sri Vijaya 
Puram to Car Nicobar, Diglipur, Mayabunder, Rangat,  Kamorta, Katchal, Chowra, Teressa, 
Shaheed Dweep, Swaraj Dweep and Campbell Bay. Under  the Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik 
(UDAN) scheme, the UT has also planned connectivity  to Diglipur, Car Nicobar and Campbell 
Bay through 19-seater fixed-wing aircraft. Seaplane services under the UDAN scheme have been 
approved and are under consideration for operationa lisation, with a view to improving last-mile 
connectivity to the remote islands. 
 
Observation/ Recommendation 
 
5.2.8 The Committee also deliberated upon the conce rns raised by Members regarding 
high airfares to the UT and the limited availabilit y of commercial seats. The Committee 
recommends that larger aircraft may be deployed on these routes to increase passenger 
capacity and help reduce airfares. Early operationa lisation of the approved seaplane 
services under the UDAN scheme may be ensured to im prove last-mile connectivity to 
remote islands of the Union Territory. Appropriate fare rationalisation measures may be 
explored so that air travel remains affordable for residents and tourists.  
 
TOURISM 
 
5.2.9 Tourism development plays a crucial role in t he economic, social and cultural growth of 
the Union territory of Andaman and Nicobar Islands.  Due to its natural beauty, biodiversity and 
strategic location, tourism is one of the most impo rtant sectors for the islands’ development. It 
has vast potential of generating revenue for the is lands. It creates direct employment in hotels, 
tour operators and transport services. At the same time, it creates avenues for fisheries, 
handicrafts, local markets and can encourage entrepreneurship among local population. 
 
5.2.10 The Committee noted with interest the sharp rise in tourist arrivals in the Andaman and 
Nicobar Islands, increasing from 7.22 lakh in 2024 to 8.23 lakh in 2025. The Administration 
informed that five major resort projects under the Public-Private Partnership (PPP) mode have 
been successfully bid out, drawing strong market re sponse from reputed international hospitality 
groups. The Committee further noted the proposal to  open eleven uninhabited islands for 

79 
 
regulated day-tourism in coordination with the Fore st Department. While welcoming these 
initiatives aimed at enhancing tourism infrastructure and revenue, the Committee emphasized the 
importance of maintaining world-class standards consistent with global eco-tourism benchmarks.  
 
Observation / Recommendation 
 
5.2.11 The Committee recommends that PPP tourism pr ojects adhere to internationally 
recognised environmental and construction norms. Co mprehensive environmental impact 
assessments and carrying-capacity studies may be co nducted prior to project 
implementation. Provisions for local employment gen eration and skill development may be 
incorporated in the agreements so that the local po pulation benefits from tourism 
development. A robust monitoring mechanism may be i nstituted to ensure that ecological 
sustainability is not compromised in the expansion of tourism activities. 
 
5.2.12 The Committee recommends that the impact of development in tourism sector on 
revenue generation in the UT and on the socio econo mic growth of the local population of 
the A&N Islands may be assessed. The benefits of ec onomic growth in the UT must also 
percolate to the local population as they equally d eserve to reap those benefits. The 
Committee recommends that the UT Administration exp lore opportunities for developing 
tourism-related activities in islands that are pres ently uninhabited but have scenic beaches 
and potential for eco-tourism, and develop them as tourist destinations for the growing 
number of visitors to the UT.

5.2.16 The Committee notes that the geographical lo cation of the Andaman and Nicobar

television, radio, social media, sirens, megaphones  and mobile-based systems such as SMS

inhabited islands with participation of about 59,60 0 persons, in addition to multiple 
community-level drills and training programmes during the year.

2025-26 to ₹1.66crores in BE 2026-27. The UT has pr oposed installation of 35 additional 
automated tsunami sirens at VSAT-based locations co -located with GPS observatories of 
INCOIS, with centralised activation at the Director ate of Disaster Management, Sri Vijaya 
Puram. 
 
Observation/ Recommendation 
 
5.2.18 The Committee observes that timely dissemina tion of early warnings and 
community preparedness of disaster management are c ritical in an island territory 
where evacuation windows are limited. The Committee  recommends expansion of 
automated siren coverage to all vulnerable coastal locations, periodic audit of 
dissemination response time across communication ch annels and establishment of 
maintenance protocols for warning infrastructure. R egular mock drills and capacity-
building programmes may continue to ensure sustained preparedness.

diesel dependence and simultaneously grid connectiv ity works be completed on priority.

ROAD CONNECTIVITY 
 
5.2.36 The Committee noted that under the current g uidelines of the Pradhan Mantri Gram 
Sadak Yojana (PMGSY), road connectivity under PMGSY  is generally provided to habitations 
with a minimum population of 250 persons. However, The UT administration brought to the 
Committee’s attention during meeting that approxima tely 60 habitations in the Andaman and 
Nicobar Islands fall below this threshold, with pop ulation clusters ranging between 100 to 150 
persons. These habitations, many of which are located in tribal and geographically isolated areas, 
continue to face acute connectivity challenges. The  Committee also observed that such a 
constraint is not unique to the Andaman and Nicobar  Islands, but is also relevant to other Union 
Territories with sparsely populated settlements such as Ladakh. 
 
Observation/ Recommendation 
 
5.2.37 The Committee recommends that the Ministry o f Home Affairs may pursue this 
matter with the Ministry of Rural Development that it may examine the feasibility of 
relaxing the existing population norms under PMGSY for islands’ territories and other 
similarly placed regions. A dedicated flexi-provisi on may be incorporated in the scheme to 
allow inclusion of habitations that are critically in need of road connectivity despite having 
population below the threshold.

 To enhance healthcare accessibility in high-risk zo nes, 27 ambulance stations with 108 
ambulance services are strategically positioned acr oss Ladakh to enable rapid 
emergency response. Tele-medicine services are also  operational, extending healthcare 
services up to the village level. 
 
5.5.6 The Committee also sought information regardi ng the effective implementation of 
Ayushman Bharat-PMJAY in Ladakh and the challenges faced therein. The Ministry informed 
that Universal Health Coverage (UHC) was launched i n convergence with PM-JAY in December 
2020 to ensure coverage of remaining families. At p resent, 12,120 families are covered under 
AB-PMJAY, fully sponsored by the Government of Indi a. Outreach initiatives such as 
“AapkeDwar Ayushman” and Health Mela campaigns have  been conducted in remote areas 
including Nubra, Zanskar, Nyoma, Hanle, Chumathang,  Drass and Batalik to enhance awareness 
and facilitate enrolment. Internal block-wise and t ehsil-wise targets have been fixed for issuance 
of Ayushman Golden Cards to enable access to cashle ss treatment. In view of the absence of a 
tertiary care centre in Ladakh, the UT Administrati on provides travel expense support to 
beneficiaries referred outside the UT for advanced treatment. 
 
5.5.7 Further, with regard to budgetary allocation,  the Committee noted that ₹68.44 crores has 
been provided under Medical and Public Health in BE  2026-27. The Ministry informed that 
₹67.19 crores of this allocation pertains to the re venue component, primarily for heating charges 
of District Hospitals, PHCs, CHCs and GNM School an d for procurement of medical supplies 
and essential drugs. An amount of ₹1.25 crores unde r the capital component is earmarked for 
completion of ongoing works at SNM Hospital, Leh an d Sub-District Hospital, Drass. The 
Ministry further stated that additional funds, if r equired, would be projected at the Revised 
Estimates stage. 
 
Observation/ Recommendation 
 
5.5.8 The Committee appreciates the efforts made to  strengthen healthcare delivery in 
the remote and high-altitude regions of Ladakh, inc luding upgradation of PHCs and Sub-
Health Centres into Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, deploy ment of medical personnel, 
operationalisation of tele-medicine services and es tablishment of structured referral 
mechanisms. However, the Committee observes that La dakh continues to face unique 
geographical and climatic challenges which directly  impact healthcare delivery. The 
absence of a tertiary care centre within the Union Territory compels patients to travel 
outside the UT for advanced treatment. While travel  assistance is being provided, such 
referrals may cause delay in critical care, particu larly during winter months when 
connectivity is severely affected. 
 

97 
 
5.5.9 The Committee further notes that a substantia l portion of the allocation under 
Medical and Public Health for 2026-27 is towards re venue expenditure, including heating 
charges and procurement of essential supplies, whil e the capital component remains 
limited. Considering the strategic and sensitive lo cation of the UT and its dispersed 
population, strengthening of permanent health infrastructure assumes special importance. 
 
5.5.10 The Committee recommends that the feasibilit y of establishing tertiary-level 
healthcare facilities in Ladakh may be examined on priority so as to reduce dependence on 
referrals outside the UT. Availability of specialis t and super-specialist may be strengthened 
through incentive-based postings, rotational deputa tions or tele-specialist support. Capital 
investment in critical health infrastructure, parti cularly in District Hospitals and 
emergency care facilities, may be enhanced in a pha sed manner. Emergency response 
systems may be further strengthened keeping in view  extreme weather conditions and 
accessibility constraints. Implementation of Ayushm an Bharat – Pradhan Mantri Jan 
Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY) and Universal Health Coverag e (UHC) may be periodically 
reviewed to ensure universal coverage and timely se ttlement of claims.  Sustained and 
focused attention to healthcare in Ladakh remains e ssential in view of its terrain, climatic 
conditions and strategic importance. 
 
TOURISM 
 
5.5.11 The Committee noted that the allocation unde r Tourism has marginally increased to 
₹14.36 crores in BE 2026-27 from ₹12.09 crores in R E 2025-26. The Committee sought details 
of the initiatives proposed for sustainable tourism  development and capacity building, 
particularly in ecologically sensitive zones. 
 
5.5.12 The Ministry, in its reply, informed that to urism in Ladakh is being developed around 
four strategic pillars, namely Adventure Tourism, N ature-based Tourism (including Dark Sky 
Reserves and ecologically sensitive landscapes), Cu ltural Tourism (including the Buddhist 
Circuit and heritage sites) and Experiential Touris m. Project proposals are being prepared for 
central funding based on these pillars to strengthe n infrastructure, enhance visitor experience and 
ensure sustainable tourism growth in high-altitude and remote areas. 
 
5.5.13 The Ministry further informed that locally, the UT Administration promotes ecologically 
sustainable tourism through policy incentives such as the STP Incentive Scheme 2025 and the 
Ladakh Homestay Policy, complemented by initiatives  such as the PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli 
Yojana. Capacity-building programmes are being cond ucted to train local youth, tourist guides, 
homestay operators and hospitality workers. Astro-t ourism initiatives centred around the Dark 
Sky Reserve at Hanle are also being promoted to pre serve night skies, promote scientific 
awareness and diversify rural incomes. 
 
5.5.14 To safeguard fragile ecosystems, the Adminis tration has proposed tourism carrying-

98 
 
capacity studies for key destinations including Pan gong Tso, Hemis National Park, Changthang 
and Zanskar. These studies are intended to provide data-driven guidance on visitor limits, 
infrastructure requirements and environmental safeg uards to ensure that tourism growth does not 
compromise ecologically sensitive landscapes. 
 
5.5.15 The Committee also sought information regard ing concrete steps taken to develop 
cultural and adventure tourism while ensuring envir onmental safeguards and community benefit 
sharing. The Ministry informed that the Registration and Renewal Guidelines for Adventure Tour 
Operators (ATOs), 2024 have been notified to regula te adventure tourism activities. Operational 
standards have been prescribed to ensure environmen tal protection, tourist safety and adherence 
to best practices. The Ladakh Mountaineering Policy , 2024 has also been introduced to promote 
safe and environmentally responsible mountaineering. 
 
5.5.16 The Ministry further stated that the Departm ent actively organises and supports 
adventure-based events and festivals such as the Ch adar Trek on the frozen Zanskar River, Ice 
Climbing Festival, Suru Summer Festival (2025 marke d its inaugural edition following Suru’s 
inclusion in National Geographic’s “25 Best Destina tions” for 2024,Ladakh Aero Festival, Pre-
Paragliding Accuracy World Cup and the Ladakh Marat hon internationally recognised as the 
“World’s Highest Marathon.”.  
 
5.5.17 In the area of cultural tourism, the Departm ent has undertaken construction of museums 
across different parts of Ladakh and extends suppor t to museums that preserve and display 
artefacts, manuscripts and religious and cultural heritage.The Department of Tourism and Culture 
also aids monasteries for civil works, beautificati on and visitor amenities, thereby improving 
infrastructure while preserving the sanctity and cu ltural significance of these sites. Additionally, 
the Department actively supports and promotes tradi tional festivals that showcase Ladakh’s rich 
cultural heritage and attract domestic and internat ional tourists. These include, but are not limited 
to, the SpitukGustor Festival, Dosmochey Festival, Hemis Tsechu Festival, ThikseyGustor 
Festival, Sindhu Darshan and the Ladakh Nomadic Fes tival. These festivals serve as platforms 
for cultural preservation, community participation and inclusive economic benefits for local 
artisans, performers and service providers. 
 
5.5.18 In addition to supporting traditional festiv als and heritage infrastructure, the Department 
of Tourism, UT Ladakh, has strengthened cultural to urism promotion through the launch of 
‘Celebrate Ladakh’ Tourism Calendar, focusing on fe stivals as key cultural tourism products and 
positioning Ladakh as a year-round destination. Und er this initiative, the department has declared 
nine UT-Level Festivals with fixed locations and da tes for the next three years, ensuring planned 
promotion, coherent branding and enhanced national and international visibility, while all other 
local and regional festivals continue to be celebra ted in accordance with community 
traditions.Collectively, these initiatives reflect a balanced approach towards tourism development 
in Ladakh, integrating environmental sustainability , safety standards, cultural preservation and 
meaningful community benefit sharing. 

99 
 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
5.5.19 The Committee notes the structured approach adopted by the UT Administration 
in developing tourism around adventure, nature, cul tural and experiential pillars, along 
with policy frameworks for regulating adventure act ivities and promoting community 
participation. The Committee particularly appreciat es the focus on carrying-capacity 
studies and dark sky preservation initiatives in ec ologically fragile zones. The Committee is 
of the view that carrying-capacity assessments must  be completed in a time-bound manner 
and integrated into planning and regulatory decisio ns. The Committee is of the view that 
infrastructure expansion, waste management systems,  water usage regulation and carbon 
footprint mitigation must receive priority attention. 
 
5.5.20 The Committee recommends that sustainable to urism principles may be adopted 
through guidelines, continuous environmental monito ring and stronger community-based 
tourism models to ensure equitable benefit sharing.  It also recommends that skill 
development initiatives be scaled up to maximise lo cal employment and reduce external 
dependence. The Committee underscores that tourism growth in Ladakh may remain 
environmentally responsible, culturally respectful and community-centric.

WATER SUPPLY, SANITATION AND SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT 
 
5.5.26 The Committee noted that the allocation for Water Supply and Sanitation has declined 
from ₹11.30 crores in RE 2025-26 to ₹9.80 crores in  BE 2026-27. The Committee sought to 
know how the UT Administration proposes to address drinking water scarcity and sanitation 
challenges in remote and high-altitude habitations in view of the reduced allocation. 
 
5.5.27 The Ministry, in its reply, informed that th e reduction under this head is primarily on 
account of Fuels and Lubricants. The enhanced provi sions in RE 2025-26 were made to clear 
pending liabilities of the previous year. The alloc ations in BE 2026-27 have been rationalized in 
order to adhere to the revenue and capital expendit ure ceilings prescribed by the Ministry of 
Finance. 
 
5.5.28 It was further informed that the allocation under this head is largely utilized for revenue 
expenditure towards fuels and lubricants for water tankers, procurement of water-supply-related 
spare parts and stores, repair and maintenance of w ater supply schemes and tankers and payment 
of electricity dues for water lifting points. 
 
5.5.29 To address drinking water supply and sanitat ion requirements in remote and high-altitude 
habitations, the Ministry stated that any additiona l requirements will be met, as far as feasible, 
from the Tribal Area Component. Further, initiative s under Central Sponsored Schemes such as 
Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) and AMRUT are being implem ented. Accordingly, drinking water 
supply and sanitation requirements will be addresse d through coordinated funding and 
implementation by the UT and CSS schemes in synergy. 
 
5.5.30 With regard to sustainable water management,  the Ministry informed that the 
Administration of the Union Territory of Ladakh is addressing water supply challenges and 
ensuring sustainable water resource management thro ugh a comprehensive, climate-resilient and 
institutionally coordinated approach, keeping in vi ew the region’s low rainfall, cold desert 
ecology and increasing impacts of climate change. 
 
 Under the Jal Jeevan Mission, the UT Administration , through the District Water & 
Sanitation Missions (DWSMs), is implementing measur es for planning, execution, 
monitoring and long-term sustainability of drinking water schemes.  
 The DWSMs play a pivotal role in district-level con vergence, source sustainability 
planning, monitoring of scheme performance and stre ngthening community institutions, 

102 
 
particularly Village Water & Sanitation Committees (VWSCs). 
 Sustainable water supply is being ensured through i dentification, protection and 
augmentation of reliable sources such as springs, g laciers, snow-fed streams and 
groundwater, supported by spring-shed management, c atchment area treatment and 
recharge interventions.  
 In view of climate variability and declining snowfa ll, the Administration, under the 
guidance of DWSMs, is promoting storage-based solut ions, including construction of 
reservoirs, winter water harvesting systems and ado ption of locally appropriate 
innovations such as artificial glaciers and ice stupas, which help store excess winter water 
for summer use. 
 The DWSMs are also responsible for regular water qu ality monitoring and surveillance, 
ensuring compliance with national drinking water qu ality standards through laboratory 
testing, field-level inspections and community-base d water quality monitoring. Capacity 
building of local manpower for operation and mainte nance, promotion of water 
conservation practices and community ownership of assets are being actively pursued. 
 Further, the Administration is ensuring inter-secto ral convergence at the district level 
through DWSMs with schemes related to watershed dev elopment, afforestation, rural 
livelihoods and climate adaptation, thereby strengt hening the resilience of drinking water 
systems in Ladakh’s fragile Himalayan ecosystem. 
 
5.5.31 Through these coordinated institutional and technical interventions, the Administration 
aims to ensure safe, adequate and sustainable drink ing water supply, while enhancing long-term 
resilience against climate change impacts in the Union Territory of Ladakh.

management be adopted to safeguard Ladakh’s fragile  Himalayan environment while 
meeting the needs of remote and tribal habitations.

5.6.9 The Committee notes that transport connectivi ty in Lakshadweep is a lifeline

ensured alongside infrastructure expansion. The Com mittee recommends that the 
Administration may explore support mechanisms such as UDAN, viability gap funding or 
seat subvention for commercially priced yet sociall y essential routes such as Agatti-Kochi. 
The proposals submitted under Sagarmala may be fina lised expeditiously and acquisition 
of all-weather vessels may be prioritised to reduce weather-related isolation.  
URBAN DEVELOPMENT, HOUSING, WATER SUPPLY AND FLOOD CONTROL  
5.6.10 Urban development and basic civic infrastruc ture remain critical sectors for the Union 
Territory of Lakshadweep in view of its limited lan d availability, fragile coastal ecosystem and 
vulnerability to climate-related risks. Allocation under Urban Development, Housing, Water 
Supply and Flood Control has been ₹61.28 crores in BE 2026-27.  
5.6.11 With regard to water security, the Ministry has informed that the UT continues to rely 
significantly on desalination technologies, includi ng Low Temperature Thermal Desalination 
(LTTD) plants, in addition to rainwater harvesting systems. The Ministry has informed that 
ongoing projects aim at ensuring year-round availab ility of potable water across inhabited 
islands. Funds are also being utilised for maintena nce and upgradation of existing distribution 
networks to reduce transmission losses. Further, de salination plants have been installed in all 
islands, except Andrott, where the Low Temperature Thermal Desalination plant (LTTD) is 
expected to be completed by April, 2026.  
 
5.6.12 Further, in the area of coastal protection a nd flood control, scientific shoreline 
management plans have been prepared in consultation  with expert agencies. Anti-sea erosion 
measures are being addressed through scientific sho reline management plans prepared by 

111 
 
National Centre for Sustainable Coastal Management (NCSCM), following the discontinuation 
of hard coastal structures as per Ministry of Envir onment, Forest and Climate Change 
(MoEFCC) directions. Diaphragm walls along peripher al roads are currently proposed to protect 
land and infrastructure from wave action and erosion. 
 
Observation/ Recommendation 
5.6.13 The Committee observes that in small island territories, urban development and 
water supply are directly linked to public health, tourism sustainability and environmental 
stability. Any delay in desalination or drainage pr ojects can have immediate consequences 
on quality of life and economic activity. The Commi ttee notes that the success of urban 
development interventions in Lakshadweep depends on  sustainable planning, strict 
adherence to Coastal Regulation Zone norms and time ly completion of projects. Water 
security measures, particularly desalination, requi re continuous technical supervision and 
maintenance.  
5.6.14 The Committee recommends that ongoing desali nation and water augmentation 
projects be completed in a time-bound manner and th at regular monitoring of water 
quality and supply hours be managed properly. Urban  drainage and flood mitigation 
works may be prioritised in vulnerable islands to a ddress climate-related risks. Coastal 
protection projects may comply with environmental s afeguards and adopt eco-sensitive 
methods. Periodic reporting on physical and financi al progress of urban infrastructure 
projects may also be placed before the Monitoring a uthority to ensure effective utilisation 
of funds.

consideration of geographical constraints and limit ed institutional alternatives. 
Infrastructure redevelopment in such a context must  be undertaken in a phased and 
coordinated manner to ensure uninterrupted academic  functioning. The Committee 
recommends that reconstruction, demolition or reloc ation of school infrastructure may be 
undertaken only after ensuring fully functional int erim arrangements and appropriate 
public communication so that academic activities are not disrupted.

aligned with emerging economic sectors in the islan ds so as to improve local employability. 
The Committee also takes note of the suggestion mad e during deliberations to explore

5.6.22 During the meeting, Members raised concerns regarding continuity of services in certain 
islands, particularly in cases where reconstruction  or redevelopment of hospital buildings is 
proposed. Concerns were also expressed regarding av ailability of specialist doctors, adequacy of 
diagnostic facilities and hardship faced by patient s referred to mainland hospitals, especially in 
Kochi. Members opined that in an island territory, health services function as an essential lifeline 
and must remain uninterrupted at all times. 
 
 
 
 

114 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
5.6.23  The Committee notes that due to limited tertiary ca re facilities within the islands, 
residents are significantly dependent on referral s ervices. Any disruption in primary or 
secondary healthcare facilities can therefore have serious consequences. The Committee 
also observes that shortage of specialist doctors a nd trained paramedical staff affects 
quality of care and increases dependency on mainland institutions. 
 
5.6.24 The Committee recommends that any reconstruc tion, relocation or redevelopment 
of hospital infrastructure be undertaken only after  ensuring fully functional interim 
healthcare arrangements and proper public communica tion. Deployment of specialist 
doctors and medical teams from mainland tertiary in stitutions on short-term rotational 
basis may be explored to bridge manpower gaps. Tele medicine facilities may be 
strengthened and adequate diagnostic equipment prov ided in island hospitals so as to 
reduce unnecessary referrals. A structured patient- support mechanism, including 
assistance for accommodation and logistics in mainl and cities such as Kochi, may also be 
explored to minimise hardships for referred patient s and their attendants. Periodic 
monitoring of health service delivery indicators ma y be undertaken to assess improvement 
in access and quality of care.

5.6.29 The Committee notes that power supply in Lak shadweep is predominantly 
dependent on diesel-based power generation due to t he absence of mainland grid 
connectivity. While allocations have been provided for operation and maintenance of 
power stations and for introduction of renewable energy projects, recurring expenditure on 
fuel continues to impose a significant financial bu rden. The Committee also observes that 
logistical constraints and weather-related disrupti ons can affect timely fuel supply, thereby 
impacting reliability of power in the islands.  
5.6.30 The Committee recommends that although steps  have been initiated for solar power 
generation with battery storage systems, the scale of renewable integration requires further 
augmentation to ensure long-term sustainability and  energy security. The UT 
Administration may adopt a phased and time-bound st rategy to progressively reduce 
dependency on diesel-based generation by expanding solar power projects integrated with 
adequate battery energy storage systems. Capital in vestments may be prioritised towards 
strengthening renewable base-load capacity and modernising transmission and distribution 
infrastructure. An island-wise energy transition plan with measurable targets for reduction 
in diesel consumption and improvement in system eff iciency may also be prepared. 
Periodic monitoring of fuel expenditure vis-à-vis  renewable energy generation may be 
considered to ensure fiscal prudence, reliability o f supply and long-term sustainability of 
the power sector in the Union Territory.

Observations /Recommendations  
 
5.8.25  The Committee notes with satisfaction the significa nt growth in tourist arrivals 
from 2022 to 2024, with total footfall increasing f rom 1.88 crores to 2.36 crores. The sharp 
increase in foreign tourist arrivals from about 20, 000 in 2022 to over 65,000 in 2024 is 
particularly noteworthy and reflects growing intern ational confidence in the Union 
Territory as a tourist destination. 

130 
 
 
5.8.26 The Committee further observes that although  there was a decline in tourist 
arrivals in 2025 compared to 2024, largely attributable to the Pahalgam incident, the sector 
demonstrates resilience with recovery visible from June 2025 onwards. The cumulative 
footfall of approximately 1.78 crores by December 2 025 indicates restoration of confidence 
and sustained interest among visitors. 
 
5.8.27 The Committee is of the view that tourism co ntinues to be one of the key drivers of 
economic activity and employment generation in the Union Territory. The upward trend in 
tourist arrivals during recent years has contribute d significantly to livelihoods in 
hospitality, transport, handicrafts and allied sect ors. With regard to development of new 
destinations, the Committee notes the allocation of  ₹26.24 crores under the State Capex 
Budget and ₹20.33 crores under the Swadesh Darshan Scheme for development of 
infrastructure at Kokernag, Bhaderwah, Doodhpathri and adjoining areas. The Committee 
appreciates the efforts made to diversify tourism b eyond traditional hubs such as Srinagar, 
Gulmarg and Pahalgam. 
 
5.8.28 The Committee observes that sustained growth  in tourist footfall necessitates 
comprehensive planning to avoid over-concentration and ecological stress in popular 
destinations. The Committee recommends that develop ment of emerging destinations must 
be accompanied by adequate infrastructure, waste ma nagement systems, carrying capacity 
assessment, connectivity improvement and local comm unity participation. A long-term 
sustainable tourism strategy be prepared integratin g environmental safeguards and 
tourists carrying capacity norms. Infrastructure de velopment initiatives at emerging 
destinations may be expedited in a time-bound manner with clear outcome indicators.  
 
5.8.29 The Committee further recommends greater emp hasis may be placed on high-value 
tourism segments such as eco-tourism, adventure tou rism and winter tourism. Skill 
development and entrepreneurship support may also b e provided to local youth to 
maximise livelihood benefits. Measures for periodic  monitoring of tourist satisfaction, 
safety perception and infrastructure adequacy could be initiated. The Committee reiterates 
that tourism has emerged as a vital sector for econ omic revitalisation of Jammu & 
Kashmir and sustained focus on diversification, inf rastructure strengthening and 
confidence-building measures will be essential to maintain the growth momentum.
