implemented under Schemes of NEC and out of these 18 projects worth of ₹114.72 
crores have been completed as on 31.01.2026. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry may further strengthen its institutional mechanisms to ensure effective 
aggregation, value addition, branding, and logistics support for agricultural and allied 
products of the region. In this connection, the Committee also recommends that the 
Ministry may also take steps to facilitate better integration of farmers with national and 
international markets through improved cold-chain infrastructure, digital 
marketplaces, and collaboration with Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs) to ensure 
remunerative prices and sustainable livelihoods for farmers in the region. 
(Para 4.1.15 ) 
 The Committee takes note of the fact that the initiatives undertaken by the 
Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region in coordination with the Ministry of 
Food Processing Industries, Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises, and 
Ministry of AYUSH to promote value addition in agricultural and allied products in the 
North Eastern Region through various schemes and projects are appreciable. It feels 
that periodic review of the implementation status of these initiatives may further 

66 
 
improve their outcome. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry may 
further strengthen convergence among the concerned Ministries and ensure effective 
implementation of these schemes in the region. The Committee also emphasizes the need 
to expand processing infrastructure, skill development, and advanced technology 
support for farmers and local entrepreneurs so as to enhance value addition, improve 
marketability of regional products, and generate better income opportunities in the 
North Eastern Region. 
(Para 4.1.16 )  
 The Committee notes the efforts undertaken to promote organic farming in the 
North Eastern Region through the Mission Organic Value Chain Development for 
North Eastern Region(MOVCDNER)which is being implemented by the Department of 
Agriculture and Farmers Welfare since 2015–16. The Committee also notes that out of 
total released amount of ₹146014.47 Lakhs to all the eight States of North Eastern 
Region under MOVCDNER from 2015-16 to 2025-26, they have been able to utilize 
₹129297.24 Lakhs till 31.12.2025. This reflects that all the NER States are committed 
towards promotion of organic farming. The Committee also acknowledges the progress 
made in bringing substantial area under organic cultivation, formation of 427 Farmer 
Producer Organizations, and development of their own organic product brands by 
States. While appreciating these initiatives, the Committee observes that true potential 
of organic farming can be realised by efficient branding and marketing and access of 
these products to end consumers, the Committee recommends that the Ministry of 
Development of North Eastern Region may evolve a mechanism in coordination with 
concerned Ministry and State Governments incorporating best and latest technologies 
and idea to strengthen the organic value chain and enhancing processing, certification, 
branding and market access for organic produce.  
(Para 4.1.17) 
Tourism 
 The Committee notes the initiatives undertaken by the Ministry of Development 
of North Eastern Region in coordination with the Ministry of Road Transport and 
Highways, Ministry of Railways and Ministry of Civil Aviation to improve connectivity 
to major tourist destinations in the North Eastern Region through expansion of road, 
rail, air and digital infrastructure. The Committee also notes the progress made under 
schemes such as Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana, UDAN (Ude Desh ka Aam 
Nagrik) and BharatNet, the Committee recommends that the Ministry of DONER 
should strengthen coordination with the concerned Ministries and State Governments to 
expedite ongoing connectivity projects and ensure improved last-mile connectivity to 
key tourist destinations. The Committee also recommends to develop integrated 
transport and communication infrastructure to promote tourism and facilitate balanced 
socio-economic development in the North Eastern Region. 
(Para 4.2.7) 
 The Committee appreciates the Ministry of Development of North Eastern 
Region (MDoNER) for the identification of Model Tourism Circuits across all eight 
states and the establishment of a High-Level Task Force to drive sustainable, high-value 
tourism. To ensure this initiative achieves its full economic potential, the Committee 

67 
 
recommends that the Ministry accelerate the replication of the integrated development 
model currently being piloted in Meghalaya (Sohra) and Tripura (Matabari) across the 
remaining six identified circuits. By adopting a convergence approach—linking 
infrastructure and connectivity with localized skilling and community-led 
entrepreneurship—the Ministry can effectively transform these unique ecological and 
cultural corridors into world-class destinations that provide inclusive growth and long-
term employment for the youth of the North East Region. 
(Para 4.2.8) 
 
 The Committee notes that while the North Eastern Region possesses immense 
tourism potential, the data on tourist arrivals during 2024 indicates significant regional 
imbalance in the distribution of domestic and foreign travellers across the States. While 
some States have witnessed encouraging growth, others continue to experience low 
tourist inflow or negative growth rates. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region, in coordination with the Ministry of 
Tourism and the concerned State Governments, should formulate targeted strategies to 
promote lesser-visited destinations through improved connectivity, infrastructure 
development, focused marketing, and promotion of niche tourism such as eco-tourism, 
cultural tourism, and adventure tourism, so as to ensure balanced and sustainable 
tourism development across all North Eastern States. 
 
(Para 4.2.9) 
Transport and Connectivity 
 
The Committee notes that the length of National Highways in North Eastern 
Region was 10,905 Kms in 2014 and it has increase to 16,207 kms in 2025. The 
Committee appreciates the 48% expansion of the National Highway network since 2014 
and the successful delivery of strategic landmarks like the Maitri Bridge (connectivity 
from NE region to Chittagong port in Bangladesh) and Dhola-Sadiya Bridge (direct 
inter-state connectivity between Assam and Arunachal Pradesh), which have 
fundamentally transformed regional connectivity. To build on this momentum, the 
Committee recommends that Ministry of DoNER should intensify its role as a central 
coordinator to expedite the remaining road components of the Kaladan Multimodal 
Transit Transport Project which will establish connectivity from Kolkata Port to Sit we 
Port in Myanmar and further link the NER through Mizoram and the Trilateral 
Highway which is aimed  at linking country’s NER to Southeast Asia, ensuring these 
vital corridors are fully operationalized.  By leveraging dedicated funding, the Ministry 
can effectively transition the Act East Policy from infrastructure milestones into a 
robust, integrated economic gateway for the North East. 
(Para 4.3.7) 
 
Railways 
 The Committee is of the view that the railway connectivity is still lacking in 
North Eastern Region. For better mobility of people and goods, it is socially and 
economically important to integrate North Eastern Region with national railway 
network. Improved railway connectivity may also help in faster movement of defense 
personnel and supplies in the region. The Committee recommends that Ministry of 

68 
 
DoNER may closely with the Ministry of Railways to expedite the ongoing railway 
projects. This proactive coordination will help in reducing carbon footprint of logistics 
sector, and seamless integration of the North Eastern cities into the national rail grid. 
 
 (Para 4.4.4) 
Industrial, Infrastructure and Skill Development 
 
The Committee recommends that Ministry of DoNER should accelerate the 
Amended BharatNet Program (ABP) to ensure that high-speed fiber connectivity 
extends beyond administrative hubs to the remaining non-GP (Gram Panchayat) 
villages on a priority basis. By establishing a robust monitoring mechanism for these 
government-funded connectivity projects, the Ministry can ensure that physical 
infrastructure translates into reliable, last-mile connectivity, thereby unlocking the 
region's potential for e-governance, digital education, and tele-medicine. 
 
(Para 4.5.8) 
 
  
The Committee recommends that Ministry of DoNER may collaborate with the 
Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship to address the geographical 
imbalance in training infrastructure—specifically by establishing Jan Sikhshan 
Sansthan (JSS) centers in Arunachal Pradesh and Sikkim and expanding the low 
apprenticeship engagement in smaller States like Nagaland and Mizoram. By aligning 
these skill-building initiatives with the region’s emerging logistics and digital sectors, the 
Ministry can ensure that the local workforce is not only certified but also effectively 
integrated into high-value employment opportunities within the growing NE economic 
corridors. 
 
(Para 4.5.9) 
 
 The Committee appreciates the Ministry’s strategic push in securing investment 
interests through the Rising Northeast Investors Summit 2025 and the forward-looking 
integration of Industry 4.0 technologies. To capitalize on this unprecedented private 
sector interest, the Committee recommends that Ministry of DoNER should provide 
technical assistance to North Eastern States for the swift on boarding of knowledge 
partners and the detailing of the 30 identified high-tech project concepts. By 
synchronizing Uttar Poorva Transformative Industrialisation (UNNATI) Scheme’s 
fiscal incentives with the implementation of the Logistics Roadmap, the Ministry can 
ensure that the transition toward AI-powered systems and smart cold chains effectively 
reduces the cost of doing business, thereby converting regional investment leads into a 
sustainable and technologically advanced industrial base. 
 
(Para 4.5.10) 
 
Healthcare and Education 
 
 The Committee appreciates the comprehensive coverage of maternal and child 
health initiatives under the National Health Mission (NHM) and recommends that 
Ministry of DoNER may serve as a strategic facilitator to ensure these services reach the 
"last mile" in the North Eastern Region. To maximize the impact of schemes like Janani 

69 
 
Suraksha Yojana (JSY), Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK), and Surakshit 
Matritva Aashwasan (SUMAN), the Ministry should prioritize strengthening the 
underlying physical and digital infrastructure—such as all-weather road access to 
health centres and reliable tracking systems for high-risk pregnancies—which are often 
the primary barriers to institutional care in hilly terrains. By ensuring that financial 
incentives reach beneficiaries and Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs) promptly 
and that rural health facilities are fully equipped, the Ministry can effectively bridge the 
gap between national policy and regional health outcomes, ensuring dignified and 
quality healthcare for every mother and child in the North Eastern Region. 
 
(Para 4.6.12) 
 
 The Committee notes with satisfaction the robust growth in medical education 
across the North Eastern Region, highlighted by a 172.7% increase in medical colleges 
and a 206.1% surge in under Graduate (UG) seats since 2013-14. However, the 
Committee observes a significant intra-regional disparity, with Assam accounting for 
over 50% of the total medical colleges and seats, while states like Sikkim remain without 
a government medical college and others like Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Nagaland 
and Tripura are limited to a single institution. To rectify this imbalance, the Committee 
recommends that Ministry of DoNER, in coordination with the Ministry of Health & 
Family Welfare, prioritize the establishment of new government medical colleges in 
these underserved States and focus on doubling the Postgraduate (PG) seat capacity, 
which has lagged behind UG growth at only 108.2%. By strengthening the tertiary 
healthcare education pipeline in every North Eastern State, the Ministry can ensure a 
more equitable distribution of specialist doctors and a stronger, self-reliant healthcare 
workforce across the entire region. 
 
(Para 4.6.13) 
 
 The Committee appreciates the multi-layered strategy for improving 
immunization coverage through Mission Indradhanush and the digital integration via 
the U-WIN (Universal Immunization Win platform) portal, but recommends that the 
Ministry of DoNER leverage its regional coordination role to address the logistical "last-
mile" challenges unique to the North Eastern terrain. To ensure the success of National 
Immunization Days (NIDs) and other activities/programmes, the Ministry should 
provide targeted support for strengthening the cold chain infrastructure in remote hilly 
districts and incentivize Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs) with terrain-
specific mobility allowances to reach unvaccinated children in unserved/underserved 
areas. 
 (Para 4.6.14) 
  
 The Committee notes that  there are 54574 primary schools in North Eastern 
Region whereas in comparison there are only 5325 higher secondary schools,   
indicating a drop in institutional availability to students as they progress. Therefore, to 
address this imbalance and reduce potential dropout rates, the Committee recommends 
that Ministry of DoNER prioritize the upgradation of existing secondary schools to the 
higher secondary level through targeted infrastructure funding and establishment of 
more higher secondary schools.  By focusing on States with steep institutional gaps and 
ensuring that these upgrades are geographically distributed to ensure "last-mile" access 
in hilly terrains, the Ministry can safeguard that the region’s youth have the necessary 

70 
 
institutional support to complete their schooling and transition into higher education or 
skill development programs. 
 
 (Para 4.6.15) 
ART AND CULTURE  
 The Committee appreciates the work done by the Ministry of Culture and the 
Zonal Cultural Centres in preserving regional heritage through the Guru–Shishya 
Parampara Scheme and national festivals like OCTAVE and Rashtriya Sanskriti 
Mahotsav (RSM). To further strengthen these efforts, the Committee recommends that 
Ministry of DoNER help local artists turn their traditional crafts and performances into 
sustainable livelihoods by integrating them directly into the region's Model Tourism 
Circuits. By creating permanent village-level performance spaces and providing better 
financial support to NGOs for documenting endangered art forms, the Ministry may 
ensure that the North East’s rich cultural identity is not only preserved for future 
generations but also becomes a key driver of local economic growth. 
 
(Para 4.7.10) 
 
 The Committee appreciates the market linkage provided through "Karu Biponi" 
a craft outlet in Santiniketan, West Bengal for exhibition and sale of handicrafts and 
handlooms products from North Eastern Region. It also appreciates organising of craft 
exhibitions and sale stalls and cultural festivals at Shilpgram Crafts Village, Guwahati, 
Stone Sculpture Garden, Dimapur and other venues, providing artisans with direct 
market access, publicity and exposure. The Committee recommends that Ministry of 
DoNER may scale these efforts by establishing a robust e-commerce platform 
specifically for North Eastern handlooms and handicrafts to reach global buyers. 
Further, the Ministry may focus on creating permanent hubs in major Indian metro 
cities and providing artisans with training in digital marketing and quality 
standardization. The Ministry may push for expanding Geographical Indication (GI) 
tagging among the North Eastern States to improve the marketability of products. 
 
(Para 4.7.11)

REPORT 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Home Affairs, having been authorised by the Committee, 
present this 26th Report of the Committee, relating to situation in Jammu and Kashmir. 
2. The Committee, in its meetings held on the ,1Oth May, 18th July anJ 17th August, 1995, had 
discussed the situation in Jammu and Kashmir (Annexure- I) and had decided that a Study Group ofthe 
Committee may visit the State to have an on-the-sport assessment of the situation prevailing over there. In 
pursuance of this decision, I constituted a Study Group (Annexure-H) to undertake the proposed visit. 
Accordingly, the Study Group visited the State from the 15th to 19th September, 1995, and had interac­
tion with the representatives of various political parties, persons from cross sections of society, represen(f­
tives of the Army, the State Government and the Governor of the State, (Annexure-III), to find out the 
ground realities. 
3. In its meeting held on the 14th December, 1995, the Committee considered the draft Report on the 
subject and adopted the same. 
4. The main observations, conclusions and recommendations of the Committee are contained in 
succeeding paragraphs. 
5. Background 
5.1 The State of Jammu and Kashmir comprises three regions, namely (i) the sub-Himalayan Jammu; 
(ii) the Himalayan Kashmir; and (iii) the trans-Himalayan Ladakh. All the three regions are marked by 
geographical, cultural, religious and linguistic diversities. 
5.2 The State of Jammu & Kashmir has been in the news ever since its accession with the Union of 
India as Pakistan had an eye on it from the very beginning and wanted to annex it by any means. She first 
sent her invaders in the Valley, then launched aggression against India twice, in the years 1965 and.l971. 
On both the occasions her designs were frustrated. But one-third of the State's area remained under Pak 
occupation. Having failed to annex the State through military means, she embarked on overt and covert 
support to militancy in the state which erupted in the State during late 1988. She started training th.e 
Kashmiri youths, arming and inducting them into the valley. The militants resorted to indiscriminate 
killings, forcing many people, including the minorities, to migrate out of the valley, followed by large: 
scale killing of teachers, doctors, mediapersons, and rape of women. They destroyed a number of schools, 
hospitals, places of worship, damaged the roads and bridges, assassinated various political leaders . They 
issued diktats through the media, asking the people to do or not to do certain things. Some religious 
leaders also towed their line. It not only took a heavy toll of human life and property, but had an adverse 
impact on the total economy also. Entire development process was trampled. All the business activities 
came to a stand-still and tourism, the main affected. The administration was also badly affected. The 
officers usually were confined to their homes and offices. The police and the political parties became 
inactive. 
5.3 The security forces have been struggling to throw out the infiltrators, to wipe out militancy and 
restore normal life in the State. They have been able to improve their grip on the situation, but at the cost 
of tremendous sacrifices. A large quantity of arms, explosives and incriminating materials have been cap­
tured from the militants. Of late, Pakistan has started inducting a large number of foreign mercenaries, 
including a number of Pakistanis themselves, some Afghans, Libyans, Sudanese, Iranians, etc. They have 
been able to commit some incidents of sabotage, subversion, kidnapping etc., but really they are unable to 
fight the security forces. 
Jammu Region 
5.4 Th1s Region has an area of 12,837 square miles, comprising six districts and 31 tehsils. As per 
the 1981 census, population of the Region is 26,90,616. At Jammu Members of the Study Group held 

2 
wide ranging discussions with the representatives of the State Government, various political parties, the 
Kashmiri Pandit migrants and the Muslim migrants. 
5.5 The representatives of the State Government briefed Members about the proxy war unleashed 
by Pakistan and the militancy related-incidents, which have by now registered a receding trend. Due to 
heavy materials coming from across the borders the militants still have considerable striking power. They 
strike at the security forces, without getting directly involved. They are also using sophisticated arms like 
solar powered rockets and night vision devices. In the hilly areas of Udhampur and Doda districts they 
have an edge over the security forces, as they can watch their movement from the hill tops. They also 
drew attention of Members to the water and power scarc1ty, shortage of ambulances in the medical insti­
tutions/hospitals, shortage of residential quarters for doctors/para medical staff and emphasized the need 
for improvement in the television and communication services. The region had been promised seven low 
power TV transmitters, but actually ten such transmitters are needed. 
5.6 The representatives of Congress (I) favoured setting up of regional councils in the Jamtnu and 
Kashmir regions, on the pattern of the Autonomous Hill Development Council set up recently at Leh. 
They were also in favour of holding elections but did not favour the demand for autonomy to the State. 
They drew attention of Members to the cumbersome formalities involved in the Prime Minister's Rozgar 
Yojana. 
5.7 The representatives of National Conference favoured a political solution to the State's prob­
lem. They stressed that commitments made to the people of the State under the Agreement of 1952 should 
be fulfilled. They also impressed upon the involvement of all in any political process and equal treatment 
to all the three regions in respect of autonomy. Before holding elections, the State should be given eco­
nomic and political packages and an agency to monitor spending of development funds should be set up. 
5.8 The representatives of Bhartiya Janata Party stated that the Central funds are going into the 
hands of militants and the State administration is demoralised because of the nexus between the police 
and persons with crime records. There is no link between the administration and the people. Recruitments 
are being made on the commands of militants. They were of the view that while elections to the local 
bodies could be held, conditions are not conducive for free and fair elections to the State Assembly. They 
also wanted the migrants' issue to be settled before the elections, as the 1991 census was not conducted 
in the State. They demanded minority status and benefits of the Minorities Commission for Hindus, like 
other minority communities. They pointed to rising unemployment among the educated youths in the 
Region and referred to 105 days' old relay dharna by the engineering graduates at Jammu. They de­
manded waiving of wealth tax and relaxation of upper age limit for Government jobs in the Jamme 
Region, on the pattern of the Kashmir Valley, setting up of regional councils in all the three Regions, 
abrogatio n of Article 370 of the constitution and full integration of the State with the rest of the country. 
5.9 The representa tives of Janata Dal stated that almost 80% of the Central funds and assistance go 
to militants, who use the same for furthering militant activities in the State . They favoured elections to the

6. Conclusions and Recommendations 
6.1 Most of the people's representatives the Members interacted with, conveyed the impression that 
people of the State have started rt?alising that Pakistan has been exploiting them for vested interests. They 
are fed up with militancy now. All the nationalist forces in the State should strive to bring Kashmiris back 
into the national main-stream and strive to restore popular Government. 
6.2 The general law and order situation in the State has registered a distinct improvement. There is 
a discernible change in the mood of the people, who earlier hestiated to speak against militants, but ·are 
now coming forward with vital clues and information to the security forces about them. Pakistar never 
wanted normalcy and restoration of popular Government in the State. Pakistan sponsored militants try to 
negate all efforts towards bringing back normalcy in the State, through their subversive activities. Gov­
ernment should deal with Pak agents and foreign elements with a firm hand. 
6.3 The Doda.Revenue District in Jammu Region has large concentration of militants, due to the 
vast hilly areas and dense forests. The security forces have to operate under great constraints. Govern­
ment ~should explore the possibility of dividing the district into different police districts, though it may 
remain one revenue district. 
6.4 Unemployment among the educated youths continues to be most critical area for the State. 
Government have taken a number of measures to ease the situation. Since the State has traditionally a low 
industrial base, a lot more needs to be done to restore its economy through development process by 
bringing back the misled youths into the mainstream of developmental activities. Small-scale industries 
based on agriculture, food processing, handicrafts, sericulture and horticulture should be developed in a 
big way, so as to generate more employment opportunities. At the same time, cumbersome procedures 
involved in getting benefits under Prime Minister's Rozgar Yojana, JRY and similar other schemes, 
should be simplified. Minorities should get adequate reapresentation in Central services, including Para 
Military Forces. Government should ensure greater transparency in the administration and remove all 
allegations of corruption. Age relaxation for Government employment and waiver of Wealth Tax given in 
the Kashmir Valley, should be extended in the Jammu Region as well. Benefits of liberalisation should 
percolate down to the unemployed youths and the poor people. Benefits of Rural Development Pro­
grammes/Schemes sponsored by the Government of'India, should also percolate· down to the village~. 
Government should make distribution of Central funds for development programmes more transparent 
and balanced and see to it that these are not misappropriated. Government should also look into com­
plaints of recruitment of militants' relations/sympathisers in services and introduce some wage employ­
ment programmes, the main thrust being given to the Prime Minister's Rozgar Yojana and Jawahar Rozgar 
Yojana. 
6.5 Tourism industry has been the backbone of State's economy. A large number of people of the 
State are directly or indirectly dependent on it. But this sector has also received a severe blow due to 
militancy. Government should take steps to diversify the tourism industry and promote pilgrim tourism in 

9 
the State. Pending return of peace and nonnalcy in the State, Government should develop alternate tourist 
resorts in Jammu and Ladakh Regions. 
6.6 Government should create conditions conducive for safe rt;turn of migrants to their homes, who 
are living in pathetic and miserable conditions in Jammu and other parts of the State and eliminate all 
distinctions of caste and community among the migrants. Pending their return, they should be ptovided 
better educational facilities, better hygienic conditions, with all the basic amenities and other facilities 
and steps should be taken for protection of the property and business establishments left behind by them. 
One-room tenements or house rent allowance in lieu thereof should be provided to migrants living out­
side the camps. Action to clear pending housing proposals for the migrants should be expedited. The 
traders among them should be provided marketing facilities and soft loans. The agriculturists among 
them should be provided compensation for loss of crops. The amount of monthly relief being paid to 
migrants should be enhanced adequately. 
6. 7 Severe shortage of drinking water in all the three Regions of the State was also brought to 
notice of Members of the Study Group. The State has got vast potentials for generation of hyde! power. 
But the present installed capacity of the hydel power plants is not adequate to meet State's requirements 
of power. Provisions of drinking water and power generation should be taken up in the right earnest. 
Steps should be taken to complete the ongoing hydel power projects and constrUction of over-head water 
tanks in Kargil, to tide-over the drinking water scarcity. 
6.8 Health institutions in the State lack infrastructural facilities. The Jammu Region is facing short­
age of ambulances. Most of the existing ambulances remain out of order and are lying in workshops, for 
repair. Government should take urgent measures to augment health services in the State, with special 
emphasis on the remote, snow-bound and inaccessible areas. 
6.9 The Jammu-Srinagar national highway remains closed for about four months in a year due to 
heavy snow falls, which creates problem~ in the transportation of foodgrains and Oth T essential COm­
moditieS. Provision should, therefore, be made for winter stocking of foodgrains and other essenti.U 
commodities in advance, i.n the Valley as well as in the Kacgil and Ladak? Regions. 
6.10 The State has a rail line upto Jammu which is being extended further upto Udhampur. The 
Railways have also plans to lay a rail line upto Srinagac. Work on this line should be expedited. It should 
be taken up from both the ends to provide employment opportunities to the local people. 
6.11 Road sector should also be given priority. Repair of damaged roads and bridges should be 
taken up immediately. Pending proposals for construction/repair of roads should be cleared. Government 
should also consider opening of trade route and Mansarovar Yatra through Demchok. 
6.12 Subsidised helicopter services to remote and border areas like Tangdhar, Kargil, Poonch and 
Rajouri shoulc;l be introduced. Steps should be taken to improve communication and telecommunication 
facilites in the remote, snow-bound and inaccessible areas. 
6.13 Educational institutions have been the most affected and so the students the worst sufferers of 
militancy. Government should ensure provision of buildings, teachers, etc. Special drive to educate women, 
especially in the remote areas of Kargil, Tangdhac, etc. should be taken up. Problem of posting of quali­
fied teachers in the Degree College at Kargil should be looked into. 
6.14 Srin!lgar being the capital of the State, can offer facilities for export of certain handicrafts items 
to other countries, especially the CIS countries. Government should explore the possibility of declaring 
Srinagar Airport as an International Airport. Earlier there used to be a Passport Office in Srinagar which 
has been closed and people of the State, especially the haj pilgrims , have been put to great inconvenience 
due to long procedure of verification involved in the Jammu Passport Office. Steps should be taken to 
reopen the Passport Offir.e at Srinagac. Government should also take steps to provide relief to victims of 
recent floods in the State. 

10 
6.15 Some inaccuracies in the recent delimitation work were also placed before Member s. The State 
has 87 constituencies for the Legislative Assembly. The division between the three Regions is: Jammu 37, 
Ladakh 4 and Kashmir 46. A demand was made for increase in the number of Assembly seats for Jammu 
and creation of one separate seat for Zanaskar in Kargil district. Government should look into the feasibi­
lity of rational ising allocation of Assembly seats in the State. 
6.16 The crisis in the State has turned into a proxy war by Pakistan. The international media projects 
distorted versions of the activities of militant outfits. People complained of unresponsive portrayal of 
militant activities by the l~al media, including Doordarshan . Government shou ld take steps to sensitise 
the local media to portray better perceptio n of the situation and start effective campaigning against mili­
tant outfits . The minds of the people in the State are being vitiated by exposure to venomous propaganda 
over Pak TV. Government should, therefore, consider setting up of more LPTs/VLPTs and creation of 
prog.ramme generation facilities in the State, to deviate people 's minds from the Pak TY. 
6.17 The people habitating certain areas deserve some concessions due to the unique topographic 
conditions, vivid cultural traditions remoteness, inaccessibility and vastness of the terrain . The people of 
Ladakh were earlier granted exemption from payment of income tax, on the pattern of North-eastern 
States of the country, whiah was subsequently withdrawn . This facility should be restored. The monthl y 
stipend should be extended not to a few, but to all Scheduled Tribes Students. Similarly, all the Scheduled 
Tribes employee s should get benefits of reservation policy and housing loans. Government should also 
consider to grant more powers to the Leh Autonomou s Hill Deve lopment Council. Pending proposals for 
construction of sports stadia and a youth hostel at Leh should be cleared. Government should also con­
sider to include the remaining two blocks along the China border under the Border Area Dev(dopmen t 
Programme. Further, the Pahari s of Tangdhar Valley and the Argons of Ladakh have been struggling for 
Scheduled Tribes status . The Gujars ofTangdhar have been granted such status and provided with facili­
ties available for Scheduled Tribes. Such status of Scheduled Tribes should also be granted to the Pahari 
and the Argon communitie s. 
6.18 Main concentration should be focused on creating conditions for restoration of a political proc­
ess in the State. Though the fear of gun still exists, yet political process is the only solution. All the hurdles 
coming in its way should be removed. All the political parties and democratic forces should be brought 
across the table to eliminate fear of the gun, to help usher in peace and for effective restoration of demo­
cratic process. All the available resources should be mobilised to re-activate political institutions. Govern­
ment should consider constitution of a Advisory Committee comprising eminent political and social worK­
ers, to assist the Governor in ensuring greater transparency between the people and the administration, so 
that people 's confidenc e in the admini stration is restored. Some apprehensions were expressed that once a 
political proce ss is initiated, militants might step up their subversive activitie s. But the adminis tration 
should be well set for initiation of such a process. 
6.19 Kashmi r problem is essentially a political problem to be resolved politically. The demand for 
complete autonomy is a complex and sensitive issue, to be resolved through a process of understanding, 
reconc iliation and acco mmodation. A break-through can be achieved through initiation of negotiations 
with elected representat ives of the people, to the exclusion of separatist elements. 
6.20 Kashmir has been a perennial problem between India and Pakistan. Under the Shimla Agree­
ment of 1972, both the countries had resolved to settle their differnces by peaceful means, through bilat­
eral negotiations or by any other peaceful means mutually agreed upon. But Pakistan has always tried to 
internationa lise the issue by raising it at any internation al fora. The State has been a part of India cultur­
ally, historically and geographically. Its accession wilh the country is unquestionable . The country's right 
extends over whole of the State and not just upto the Line of Control. Government have to change their 
strategy, with the changing scenario and keep exposing P'lkistan at all the available fora, for having un­
leashed proxy war in the State. At the same time, pressure on mihtants and foreign elements, using extreme 
force against th6 separatists, should be maintained. Steps should be taken to effectivel y curb infiltration of 

11 
arms and militants from across the borders. The security forces should be motivated to deal with the 
situation, with due consideration for human rights. 
6.21 With the adoption of a more imaginative and consistent policy, taking special steps for reha­
bilitation of migrants and fulfilling the people's aspirations, Government can hope to restore democracy 
and peace in the State.

REPORT 
I, the Chainnan of the Committee on Home AffairS, having been authorised by the Committee to 
present the Report on its behalf, present this Twenty-seventh Report of the Committee, relating to the 
Private Security Guards and Agencies (Regulation) Bill, 1994* 
2. In pursuance of the Rules relating to Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the 
Chainnan, Rajya Sabha referred** the Private Security Guards and Agencies (Regulation) Bill, 1994, as 
introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the 14tli December, 1994 and pending therein, to the Committee for 
examination and report. 
3. With the increase in th~ number of business establishments, growth in crime rate and increasing de­
mands for surveillance, there has been a oroliferation of private security agencies in the recent years. There 
has also been a growing concern about the mann~r of functioning of these agencies. Unless suitable safe­
guards are devised, their activities are likely to have wide-ranging security implications, including the 
danger of their employees encroaching upon the duties of police. The Bill, therefore, seeks to regulate the 
private security agencies, by providing for a controlling authority to be appointed by the State Govern­
ments. 
4. The Committee invited the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs to make a presentation on various 
provisions of the Bill. Accordingly, he made a presentation before the Committee on the 21st November, 
1995. During his presentation he explained salient features of the Bill and the circumstances necessitating 
the present legislation. He infonned the Committee that at present there is no law to regulate the functioning 
of private security agencies. Hence, this proposed Bill. 
5. The Committee took-up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill in its meeting held on the 29th 
January, 19% . 
6. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on the 9th February, 19%. 
7. The principal changes suggested by the Committee in the Bill and the reasons therefor are set out 
hereinafter:-
ClauseS 
Clause 5 of the Bill lays down the eligibility criteria to be a private security guard. Sub- clause (iii) 
provides that if any person has been convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for two years or more, he 
will not be eligible to engage himself as a private security guard. The Committee is of the view that 
conviction in itself should be deemed to be a disqualification and the provision of period of imprisonment, 
therefore, may not be necessary. Hence the Committee recommends that the words and sentenced to impris­
onment for two years or more in this Sub-clause be deleted. 
As regards Sub-clause (iv) of Clause 5, the Committee is of the view that to becoll1e eligible to be a 
private security guard, a person should have undergone at least three months' training instead of one 
month, as provided in this Sub-clause. The Committee also feels that mere mention of "train ing of the type 
imparted to Home Guards" will not be sufficient. Such training should be imparted by some recognised

2 
institute, on the pattern of that being provided by the Central Industrial Security Force, Home Guards, 
N.C.C., etc. Hence the Committee recommends that Sub-clause (iv) of this Clause should be amended 
suitably, to make provision to this effect. 
Further, the Committee feels that in this Clause, there is no mention of recruitment of private Security 
guards from amongst Ex-servicemen, as has been done in the case of Supervisors in clause 6. Hence, the 
Committee recommends that Clause 5 should be renumbered as Clause 5( 1) and another Sub-clause, i.e. 
Sub-clause (2), should be added to this Clause, to provide that a person who has served in one or more of 
the Forces like the Army; Navy; Air Force; any other Armed Force of the Union, Police; Home Guards and 
fulfils the eligibility criteria to become a private security guard under Sub-clause (1) above, should be 
given priority for engaging as a private security guard. 
Clause6 
Clause 6 provides that every private security agency shall employ a prescribed number of supervisors 
from amongst the persons who have served in one or more of the Forces like Army; Navy; Air Force; any 
other Armed Force of the Union; Police; Home Guards, for a minimum period of five years. The Commit­
tee feels that besides the minimum period of service, the persons to be employed as supervisor should also 
possess good character. His character and antecedents should be got duly verified. Moreover, eligibility 
criteria as in the case of employment of private security guards under Clause 5 should also be specifically 
prescribed. The Committee recommends that Clause 6 be modified accordingly. 
ClauseS 
Clause 8 of the Bill intends to make companies, not registered in India, eligible to obtain licences for 
private security agencies, after obtaining prior permission of the Central Government. The Committee is of 
the considered view that under no circumstances, a company not registered in India, should be permitted to 
get a licence for a private seturity agency. Hence, the Committee recommends that in Clause 8, the words 
"unless it obtains prior permission of the Central Government", be deleted. 
Clause 13 
Clause 13 provides that every private security agency shall maintain a register containing the names, 
addresses and salaries of private security guards under its control. Further it provides that every private 
securicy agency and private security guard shall furnish to the Controlling Authority the returns speeified 
by it. But there is no mention of the Supervisors . The Committee feels that a similar register pertaining to 
Supervisors should also be maintained and they should also be made liable to furnish the specified returns. 
Hence, the Committee recommends that Clause 13 be amended suitably. 
8. Clauses 2 to 4, 7, 9 to 12 and 14 to 20 were adopted by the Committee without any change. 
9. Clause 1, the Enacting Formula and the Title were adopted with some changes which are of conse­
quential or drafting nature. 
10. The Committee recommends that the Bill, as reported by it, be passed.

ac~used person by a private Registered Medical Practitioner should be valid. only if no 
hosp ital run by Government or a local authority is located within a periphery of sixteen 
kilometers from the place of crime. 
Clause 11 
This Clause seeks to amend Section 54 of the Code so as to provide that a copy of the 
report of the medical examination of the arrested person should also be furnished hy the 
registered med ical practitioner to the arrested person or his nominee. on request, after his 
medical examination has been conduc ted. The Committee is of the view that the provision 
for furnishing a copy of the medical repo rt to the arrested person or to his nomin ee, by the 
Registered Medical Practitioner. should be mandatory . 
Clause 18 
This Clause seeks to insert a new section 144A in the Code to enable the District 
Magistrates to prohibit mass drills (or training) with arms in public places. The Committee is 
of the view that enough provisions already exist in Section 1~ of the Code to deal with 
such situations and there is no need to insert a new Section to the Code. The Committee 
therefore, doe s not approve the proposed amendment. 

4 
Clause 19 
This Clause seeks to insert a new Section 164A in the Code to provide for rnedi<:al 
examination of the victim of a rape by a Registered Medical Practitioner employed in a 
hospital run by the Governm~nt or a local authority and, in the absence of such a 
Practitioner, by any other Registered Medical Practitioner. The Comr:nittee is Of the view 
that the medical examination of such a victim should be held within twenty-four hours of 
commission of the offence. Further, the word, 'forwarded' in sub-clause (2) of this Clause 
should be substituted by the word 'sent'. 
Clause 20 
This Clause seeks to add a new Sub-section (3A) to Section 173 of the Code, to enable 
the police to take note of the desire of the parties to compound offences compoundable 
under Section 320, even at the stage of investigation. The Committee is of the view that this 
provision could be misused. by forcing the parties to agree to a compromise and. therefore, 
disapproves the proposed amendment. 
Clause 21 
This Clause seeks to amend Section 176 of the Code to provide that in the case of death 
of disapperance of a person. or rape of a woman while in the custody of the police, there 
shall be a mandatory judicial enquiry and, in case of death, examination of the dead body 
shall be conducted within twenty-four hours of the death. The Committee is of the view that 
incidents of death, disappearance and rape, occurring in judicial custody, should also be 
brought within the purview of this Clause. · 
Furiher, in case of death in the police or judicial custody, compensation to the bereaved 
family in the form of either employment to one of its eligible members or adequate family 
pension, say rupees fifteen hundred per mensum, should be given. For this, relevant 
provision should be incorporated in the Code. 
Clause 22 
This Clause seeks to insert a Proviso to Sub-section (1) of Section 190 of the Code so as 
to enable a Magistrate to pass an order of remand for further detention of an accus'ed person 
in custody for a period not exceeding .a week, after recording the reasons therefor, after 
submission of police report under Section 173 (2) of the Code and before taking cognizance 
of an offence disclosed by the police report under Section 190. The Committee is of the view 
that sufficient powers are vested with the Magistrates under Section 167 of the Code. The 
Committee, therefore, does not approve the proposed amendment. 
Clause 23 
This Clause seeks to amend Sub-section (3) of Section 197 of the Code, with a view to 
extending protec tion to_such other public servants, besides members of the Armed Forces, 
as are charged with' mainterHince of public order, in the matter of prosecution in respect of 
offences al!eged to have been committed while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of 
their duties. The Committee is of the view that this provision is likely to be misused ~tnd, 
therefore, disapproves the same. 
Clauses 47 & 49 
The Committee is of the view that amendments proposed in Sub-clauses (a) and (b) of 
Clause 47 and Sub-clause (a) of Clause 49 are only consequential in nature. In view of the 
Committee's recommendation in respect of Clause 18 of the Bill, the Committee disapproves 
the amendments proposed to be made through these Sub-clauses.

INTRODUCTION 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Home Affairs having been authorised by the 
Committee, present this Twenty-ninth Report of the Committee on the Action Taken by 
Government on the recommendations/observations of the Committee, contained in its 
Fifteenth Report on the Demands for Grants (1995-96) of the Ministry of Home Affairs. 
2. The Fifteenth Report was presented to the Rajya Sabha on the 8th May, 1995. The 
Committee directed Government to furnish a note indicating Action Taken by it on various 
recommendations of the Committee contained in that Report. 
3. The Committee in its meeting held on the 16th January, 1996, decided to consider 
the Action Taken Note furnished by Government. Accordingly, the Committee, in its 
meeting held on the 6th March, 1996 considered the Action Taken Note and sought 
clarifications from the Secretary of the Ministry of Home Affairs thereon. 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on the 
29th March, 1996.

REPORT 
CIVIL DEFENCE 
Recommendation (Para 11)-Tbe strength of Civil Defence volunteers is far behind the 
targeted strength (3.77 lakhs against 6.76 lakhs). Volunteers are not inclined to join Civil 
Defence as it provides scope for mobilisation mainly during hostile enemy action. The 
Committee wonders whether it would be helpful to provide some kind of incentives to the 
volunteers to encourage them to join Civil Defence, since majority of these disciplined men 
make no dig on the State exchequer in the form of salary and allowances. The Committee 
also recommends that the training imparting capacity of the National Civil Defence College, 
Nagpur should be enhanced and made relevant to the modem warfare. 
2. Action Taken by Government-State Governments are primarily responsible for 
raising the volunteers to their targeted strength and providing them adequate training. 
Government is reminding them continuously in this regard remedial measures/incentives as 
mentioned below are under consideration of Government to attract volunteers from 
public:-
(i) Amendment to the Civil Defence Act, 1960 to enable deployment of volunteers 
during natural calamities such as earthquake, flood etc. It will keep them operation­
ally fit and help to ttain them for war at all times. This will also bring them in close 
contact with public and build up their image; 
(ii) Enhancement of daily allowance and parade allowance from Rs. 221- and Rs. 20/­
per day to Rs. 50/- and Rs. 47/ respectively; and 
(iii) Issue of Uniforms to the volunteers. 
StatesiUTs are not utilising their allotted vacancies in various courses run by 
National Civil Defence College, Nagpur. States have been impressed upon to utilise 
their allotted vacancies. An exercise to improve the infrastructure of the college to 
increase its course capacity is also under consideration. Constant revision of syllabi to 
include modern state of art subjects is an on-going process. 
3. The Committee welcomes the measures proposed by Government to attract volunteers 
to join Civil Defence. It hopes that final decision on these proposals will be taken at the 
earliest. It also hopes that Government will make all efforts to impart the necessary training 
to all volunteers recruifed to the Civil Defence in the National Civil Defence College, Nagpur. 
HOME GUARDS 
4. Recommendation (Para 14)-Against the authorised strength of 5,73,793, the raised 
strength of Home Guards is 4,18,493. The Committee, therefore, in view of the multiple 
rble being performed by the Home Guards, is of the opinion that either the requirements of 
the States in regard to their authorised target strength be revised or all efforts be made by 
the Ministry to raise the strength to its targeted level within a specified time-frame. 
5. Action Taken by Government- The responsibility for raising and training of Home 
Guard Volunteers is that of the StatesiUTs. StatesiUTs have been reminded to make up 
their deficiencies. Out of a total deficiency of 1.57 lakh Home Guards, West Bengal and 
Bihar alone account for 1.03 lakh. Leaving these two, there is no significant shortfall in any 
of the remaining States. To attract people to join this force, the upward revision of 
allowances payable to Home Guards is under consideration. The Ministry is also of the firm 
opinion, not to decrease the Centre's share for reimbursement of 75% for North-Eastern 
States and 50% for the remaining States which have been unilaterally reduced by the

2 
Finance Ministry to 40% in respect of States in the current fmancial year (1995-96). For 
1996-97 this percentage has been further reduced to 25%. The Home Ministry feels that this 
reduction will lead to loss of initiative with States. 
6. The Committee, in view of the significant role assigned to Home Guards reiterates, 
that all efforts may be continued to raise the force to its full authorised strength. The 
Committee also expresses its conformity with the Ministry that the share for reimbursement in 
respect of North-Eastern States and other States should be retained to 75% and SO% 
respectively. Further, the Committee is of the view that guidelines should be issued to aU 
States to reserve vacancies for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, as per percentage of 
their population in the respective States. 
INTER-STATE COUNCIL 
7. Recommendation (Para-B)-The Committee reiterated its recommendation contained 
in its First and Ninth Reports for frequent meetings of the Sub-Committee of the Inter-State 
Council to examine and make concrete suggestions on the recommendations of the Sarkaria 
Commission on Centre-State Relation. The Sub-Committee has not met since 24th April, 
1993. 
8. Action Taken by Government-All efforts are being made to convene the meeting of 
the Sub-Committee to complete consideration of the recommendations of the Sarkaria 
Commission expeditiously. It is also proposed to call a meeting of the Inter-State Council 
early, to consider and finalise the recommendations which have been made by the Sub­
Committee. The Prime Minister and Chairman of the Inter-State Council has been requested 
accordingly. 
9. The Committee is pained to express, that for one reason or other, the meeting of the 
Sub-Committee has not been held, despite repeated recommendations of the Committee. It is 
now over three years since the Sub-Committee last met. The Committee, once again expresses 
its serious concern over inordinate delay in holding the meeting of the Sub-Committee and 
calls upon Government to convene the meetings of the Sub-Committee and the Inter-State 
Council at the earliest. 
UNDER UTILIZATION OF PLAN FUNDS UNDER REGISTRAR-GENERAL OF INDIA 
(PARA 22) 
10. Recommendation (para 22)-The Committee is not at all convinced with the reasons 
given by the Ministry regarding the under-utilisation of Plan Funds for 1992-93, 1993-94 and 
1994-95 by the Registrar-General of India and finds it casual and perfunctory. The 
Committee feels that responsibility should be fixed for non-utilisation of plan fund because 
of administrative slackness. The Committee is, therefore, constrained to express its 
unhappiness over this. 
11. Action Taken by Government- The proposal for creation of a large number of posts , 
required for implementing the schemes were put forward to Home (Finance). The 
competent authority decided to refer the proposals to Staff Inspection Unit (SIU) for their 
assessment. A few skeleton posts were, however; sanctioned to initiate the projects. Final 
Report of the SIU is still awaited. As the required posts were not sanctioned, the fund 
allotted for the purpose remained unutilised. Similarly, funds remained unutilised due to 
non- purchase of equipments for various reasons under a few schemes. 
12. The Committee is surprised to note that though funds have been allotted to 
implement various schemes under the Registrar-General of India, sanction of posts to 
undertake these activities was not given. Even after a lapse of couple of years, the final report 
of the SIU is still awaited, resulting in abandonment of plan schemes. The Committee is, 
therefore, constrained to express its unhappiness over these administrative delays and hopes 
that the requisite number of posts will soon be sanctioned and filled to carry out these 
important schemes.

CENSUS STAFF 
13. Recommendation (para 23)-The census staff which is engaged on temporary basis 
for decennial census work is relieved of their duties when the census work is over. The 
Committee would like the Government to examine the possibility of re-employing such 
persons in some Government Establishments on humanitarian grounds. 
·14. Action Taken by Government-Government has already granted certain concessions 
and benefits to the retrenched census employees recruited in 1991 census in recruitment to 
Government Service. These include relaxation of age for appearing in exams conducted by 
Staff Selection Commission and Railway Service Commission, consideration for absorption 
in vacancies in group 'C' posts arising in the census organisation etc. on fulfilling other 
eligibility conditions. 
15. The Committee appreciates that Government is concerned and sympathetic towards 
the retrenched census employees and hopes that these concessions/benefits will continue. 
MODER.NlSATION OF POLICE FORCE 
16. Recommendation (para 30)-The Committee endorses the view of Government for 
enhancement of the amount sanctioned under the modernisation of Police Force in view of 
the new challenges thrown up by the law and order situation in various States, cost 
escalation and the need for upgradation of equipments to keep pace with the technological 
changes. The Committee also supports the idea of spending the allocated amount on one or 
two items selected by the States themselves, instead of distributing them under the 
prescribed six items, as it would enable them to spend the amount as per their requirement. 
The Committee strongly feels that the criteria for allocation for various States, which were 
fixed long ago, may be reviewed so as to make it need-based while taking care of some 
other aspects like strategic location of a State, level of modernisation of police in the State 
etc. 
17. Action Taken by Government-A proposal for enhancing the annual allocation from 
Rs. 30 crores to Rs. 50 crores for modernisation of State Police Force for the period 1995-
2000 was referred to the Ministry of Fioance (Deptt. of Expenditure). However, it has been 
disapproved. The Matter of allowing the State Governments to spend their respective annual 
allocation under the scheme on one or two items to be selected by them (individual State 
Governments) is being considered separately. The criteria for State-wise allocation of funds 
is also being reviewed. 
18. The Committee is not at all convinced with the decision of the Ministry of Finance , in 
disapproving the proposal for an enhancement of allocation for modernisation of State Police 
Force. It, therefore, urges upon the Ministry of Home Affairs to endeavour afresh for an 
upward revision of the allocation. The Committee also calls upon the Government to take an 
early decision on the convenience of State Governments to spend their respective annual 
allocation on one or two items of their .individual choice; and on the criteria for allocation 
among all States. 
TRAINING OF CENTRAL PARA-MILITARY FORCES 
19. Recommendation (para 31)- Training to Central Para-Military Forces should not 
mean only physical training and training in equipment but also include behavioural training 
and awareness of human rights. The Committee, therefore, recommends a composite 
training aimed at integrated development of the personality of such personnel in view of the 
changing socio-economic scenario. 
20. Action Taken by Government-Behavioural aspects and human rights have been 
included in the curricula of all the training courses for different levels being conducted by 
CPMFs. In the light of observation of the Committee, BPR & D has been requested to 

4 
evolve composite training programme aimed at integrated development of CPMF personnel. 
The recommendations/observations of the Committee have further been communicated to 
all CPMFs for re-orienting their training courses where necessary. 
21. The Committee appreciates the efforts made by Government on its recommendation 
in imparting a composite training to CPMF personnel to develop their all round personality. 
But, it feels that a close monitoring of these training courses is immensely required to make 
them effective. It, therefore, impresses upon Government to conduct these courses in true 
spirit. 
HOUSING FOR CENTRAL PARA-MILITARY FORCES (CPMFs) 
22. The current annual level of funding on Police Housing, which is around 60-70 crores 
is highly inadequate. The Committee, therefore, is of the considered opinion that mere 
increase of a few crores of rupees is not a solution to this acute housing problem and some 
concrete steps need to be taken to improve the situation. The Ministry would have to take a 
holistic approach in this regard. The Committee, therefore, calls upon the Ministry to study 
the cases of a few States who have set up State Police Housing Boards and have also taken 
commercial loans to tackle the situation. ln this connection, the Committee understands that 
the Director-General CRPF has submitted a proposal regarding setting up of a Housing 
Corporation for Central Police Organisation which may be given due consideration. 
23. Action taken by Government- For exploring the possibility of setting up of Housing 
Corporations, an exercise was undertaken in the Ministry to evaluate whether it would be 
possible to supplement Government funding for Police Housing with commercial borrowings. 
The interest burden only, however, appeared to be much higher than the total projected 
budget allocation and the proposal was not processed further. Nevertheless, in deference to 
the wishes of the Committee, some selected State Governments have been requested to 
indicate the details of their Police Housing Corporations/Boards and source of funding, 
including commercial borrowings, if any. On receipt of the information, possible modalities 
would be studied in depth, and the viability of setting up of a Housing Organisation would 
be analysed afresh. 
24. The Committee is happy to note that Government has started afresh, an exercise to 
explore the possibility of setting up of Housing Corporation/Board and taking of commercial 
loans for Police Housing. It, however, impresses upon the Government to complete the 
exercise in a time-bound manner, so that the scheme evolved could be implemented as early as 
possible.

COXST AL SECURITY 
28. Recommendation (para 40)-The Committee expresses its serious concern over the 
state of affairs in regard to coastal security and desires that adequate number of vessels, fully 
equipped with latest gadgets and equipments, required for the purpose of effective patrolling 
of coastal areas be procured and put into service at the earliest, so that, the smuggling of 
arms, ammunition explosives etc., through sea could be prevented. 
29. Action Taken by Government-Following the Bombay bomb blast incidents of 1993, 
the Ministry of Home Affairs Core Group carried out a threat assessment. With a view to 
checking smuggling, particularly of arms and explosives effectively, the Core Group decided 
upon a 3-tier defence mechanism i.e. intensive surveillance by Naval Vessels on the high 
seas, joint Coast Guard-Navy surveillance in the territorial waters and patrolling by joint 
detachments of Navy, Coast Guards, Customs and State Police through trawlers in the 
shallow waters along the shore. This exercise is going on. Subsequently, it was felt that it 
would be more cost effective if the entire responsibility of coastal surveillance were to be 
entrusted to the Coast Guards. Coast Guards were accordingly r~quested to prepare a paper 
in consultation with the Ministry of Defence, containing proposal for such a new scheme 
under which the entire gamut of functions required for effective coastal surveillance is 
coordinated by the Coast Guards. A scheme has since been prepared by the Coast Guards 
and is awaiting a joint presentation by the Coast Guard and Navy to the Defence Secretary. 
This Scheme is based upon a holistic view of the problem. The scheme envisages:-
(i) Setting up of a Centralised intelligence agency for collection and collation of 
information from different sources; 
(ii) Intensification of surveillance by l:lpgrading the equipments; 
(iii) Working out an appropriate mechanism for command and control to facilitate joint 
operations; and 
(iv) Building up of an appropriate communication structure. 
30. The Committee has noted the various steps taken by the Government to strengthen 
the security, particularly the coastal security, in the country. The Committee, however, is of 
the considered view that the measures thus far taken are far from adequate and the 
authorities which are responsible for taking decisions are not yet fully alive to the need and 
importance that the internal security of the country requires. In fact the Home Secretary in 
his presentation before the Committee on March 6, 1996, was candid enough to admit that 
the Security aspect hitherto had not been given the necessary importance which it really 
deserved. Regarding Coastal Security he admitted that there are no vessels for surveillance 
and boats are still being hired from fishermen for the purpose. The State Governments hire 
them and the cost is reimbursed to them. He informed the Committee that Pakistan was 
trying to undermine the security of this nation by using various means-land-means, sea­
means and air-means. He added that the Home Ministry had not been able to impress upon 
the Ministry of Finance for allocation of adequate funds required to strengthen the various 
security measures. The Home Secretary added that there was tremendous need to improve 

6 
the police forces in the North-Eastern sector of the country. In his view the present police 
forces in this part of the region, barring Assam, were basically meant for 6,000 or 10,000 
people only. In his view the local police forces should have been strengthened all these years 
which had been neglected to some extent. At present, Rs. 30 crores were being given per 
year for this purpose as against Rs. 50 crores requested by the Ministry of Home Affairs. 
However, the Ministry of Finance felt that it was not necessary to provide financial resources 
to that extent. The Home Secretary in his presentation further added that in his view it had 
still not dawned on them that security needs should be given top priority and anything else 
should follow after that. 
31. The Committee notes with great concern the views expressed by the Home Secretary 
and the fact that security aspects are not receiving the importance that they deserve. The 
Committee is of the view that the -'ational security is paramount and should be given due 
priority and adequate funds should be made available to the agencies which are responsible 
for national security in the country. 
PROBLEM AREAS OF BSF AND CRPF 
32. Recommendation (para 42)-A few critical areas which include ralSlng of more 
battalions, modern methods of surveillance, replacement of old and unsafe aircrafts,

RAPID ACTION FORCE (RAF) 
35. Recommendation (para 43)-The Committee in its First and Ninth Reports relating 
to the Demands for Grants of the Ministry, had recommended raising of more battalions of 
RAF. The Ministry in its Action Taken Note has stated that the Committee's recommenda­
tion has been noted and has not given any categorical reply in this regard. The Committee 
takes serious note of the Ministry's evasive reply and once again reiterates its earlier 
recommendation that raising only ten battalions of RAF may not be sufficient and there is 
need for further raising of such battalions. 
36. Action Taken by Governmem-In deference to the recommendation of the 
Committee and depending upon the pressing need and the long-term threat to internal 
security proposals have been initiated for budgetary allocations in 1996-97 for raising of two 
additional RAF battalions. 
37. The Committee feels satisfied that the Ministry has ultimately accepted its 
recommendations and decided to raise two more battalions of RAF for dealing with situation... 
arising out of communal tension, including riots and riot like situations ~ore effectively. 
ABERRATIONS IN THE ROLE OF CPMFs 
38. Recommendation (para 45) - The Committee expresses its deep concern over the 
serious aberrations in the roles of Central Para-Military Forces. The Committee is of the 
considered view that deployment of these forces outside their originally prescribed duties 
should be done sparingly and only in exceptional circumstances. 

7 
39. Action Taken by Government- The Government agrees with the Committee. As 
far as possible, CPMFs are deployed on their defined primary tasks. However, over the last 
few years, there has been increasing demand from various Stat~s and Union Territories. The 
deployment in North-East and Jammu and Kashmir have increased to an unprecedented 
level, thereby reducing the availability of Force for deployment. Expansion of CPMFs has 
not been able to keep pace with the increasing demand for their deployment. This imbalance 
in the demand and availability ratio has at times made it inevitable to deploy other CPMFs 
outside their original duties in exigencies. However, efforts are made to relieve CPMFs from 
such deployment at the earliest so that they return back to their normal functions. 
40. The Committee is satisfied that Government agrees with its recommendation and is 
making efforts to relieve CPMFs from duties other than their originally prescribed duties.

43. The Committee expresses its satisfaction.

FREEDOM FIGHTERS' PENSION 
50. Recommendation (para 53)- Committee expresses its deep concern over the state of 
affairs in grant of pension to the genuine freedom fighters and hopes that the Ministry would 

8 
take all necessary remedial steps to overcome these shortcomings. The Committee also 
endorses the recommendations made. by. the Committee on Petitions, Rajya Sabha in its 97th 
Report on the "thorough review. of the entire procedure relating to grant of pension to 
freedom fighters" to improve the situation. 
51. Action Taken by Government - It has never been the intention of the Central 
Government to deny pension to the genuine freedom fighters. The application for grant of

52. The Committee while taking a note of this clarification, urges upon Government to

great sacrifices for the sake of country's freedom from the. British Empire. 
DEPLOYMENT OF CISF PERSONNEL BY DELID POLICE 
53. Recommendation (para 57)- In view of the manpower constraints being faced by 
Delhi Police, 22 companies of CISF are presently performing armed guard duties at the 
residences of the protected persons. A proposal for sanction of additional staff for this 
purpose is pending consideration of the Government. The Committee again stresses that 
Para-Military Forces should not be deployed on duties other than their prescribed ones , 
except in exigencies and that too not for a long period. It hopes that Government would 
take an early decision in regard to the proposal pending before it so that the CISF personne l 
could perform their normal prescribed duties. · 
54. Action Taken by Government - The recommendations have been noted. The 
proposal received from the Delhi Police involves creation of 6560 posts with a tot al

required. Efforts to obtain the approval of the Ministry of Finance continue to be made and 
will be intensified to secure an early decision. 
55. The Committee notes that the proposal is pending before the Ministry of Finance for 
more than a year. It, ·therefore, expresses its displeasure over the delay in examining the 
proposal and arriving at a decision. The Committee urges upon the Government to make all 
efforts to secure an early decision so that CISF personnel could be relieved to perform their 
normal prescribed duties. 
DELHI POLICE AS MODEL POLICE 
56. Recommendation (para 59)- Delhi Police is taking a number of steps including 
training courses to improve behavioural pattern of its personnel towards persons belonging 
to weaker sections of the society. The Committee hopes that the measures being taken by 
the Delhi Police would improve the behavioural aspect of its personnel and thereby taking it 
closer to the ~eaker sections of the society in ameliorating their problems and difficulties. 
57. Action Taken by Government - Training of Delhi Police personnel - initial as well 
as in-service are being carried out as per recommendations of the Jain Committee and Delhi 
Police Commission. Inputs on human rights, communal amity, police-public relations, police 
attitude towards the public in general and weaker sections in particular have also been 
included in the training curricula. Similarly, reorientation courses on these lines are also

immediately to some Judges. Accordingly, clauses 2 and 3 of the Bill were adopted by the Committee

consequential or drafting nature.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS 
Public EnterpriseS Selection Board 
Vacancies of Chairman and Members In PESB 
1. Recommendation : The Committee, in para 9 of the Sixteenth Report had expressed 
concern that the post of the Chairman PESB has been lying vacant since 1.11.1993. Out of 
the three members , there was only one member and the second member ha~ been appointed 
only recently. This , in the view of the COmmittee, meant, that only one member held :(61 
meetings and made recommendations for 49 Chief Executives and 93 full time Functiomd 
Directors and part time Chairman. This in view of the Committee, assumed significance in 
view of the fact that a total of Rs. 164332 crores (1993-94 figures) of the public money is 
invested in as many as 246 Central Public Enterprises. The Committee had been informed 
that efforts were being made to locute silitable persons to fill up vacancies of the Chairman 
and the member of PESB . The Committee felt that necessary action to fill 'up the vacancies 
had not been taken with due seriousness and recommended that such important posts l{e 
filled up without further delay. 
2. The Ministry, in its Action Taken Note, had reported that out of the 3 posts of 
members, two members were in position now; the second member having joined on 2.2.95. 
The Observations of the Committee regarding the filling up of posts have been brought to 
the notice of the Cabinet Secretary und thqt the matter has also been taken up by him at the 
appropriate level. The Action Taken Note also mentioned that the Members PESB generally 
does not act alone in making recommendation for appointments in Public Enterprises . 
Besides, the Members in the PESB, the Secretary of the Administrative Ministry concerned 
with the public enterprise is also associated. The Secretary of the Ministry, in his deposition 
before the Committee informed that Mr. N. Vittal has been appointed the Chairman, PESB 
with effect from 4th January, 1996. As on 6.3.96 there were two vacant posts of members in 
the PESB and that those might be filled up in about two months' time . He also submitted 
that non-availability of suitable persons was the reason for delay in filling up of vacant posts 
in PESB. 
3. The Committee in its 16th Report had noted with concern that the post of Chairman 
of the PESB had been lying vacant since November 1, 1993. Similarly, full complement of 
members were not in position. The Committee . had, therefore, recommended that such 
important posts should be filled up without further delay. 
4. The Department of Personnd in its Action Taken Note, submitted in November , 
1995, had stated that Committee's observations regarding filling-up of the posts had been

top level of posts in the PESB, namely, Chairman and the members rests with the Cabinet

responsibility of recommending Board level appointments for the Central Public Sector

Committee emphasises the importance and the need of selecting qualified and suitable persons 
to man the top level posts in the PSUs. This would be possible only if PESB itself bas full 
complement of its· members. However, the Committee notes with deep regret that Government 
has handled the matter of manning the PESB with rather cavalier fashion. Over the years 
only lAS officers have been selected as Chairma&inembers of the Board and these too who 
are either retired or were due to J."ftire In the near future. Therefore, it is no w~nder thqt 
performance of the majority of PSUs h~d not been satisfactory. The Committee would, 
therefore, reiterate that timely action should be taken to fdl-up the posts in the PESB, which 
should not necessarily be from the lAS alone.

mo~th, giving details of the action taken by them on its recommendations. This would 
enable the PESB to regularly monitor the progress made by the various Administrative 
Ministries/Departments in implementing the recommendation made by it. 
11. ·The Committee is pleased to note that a monitoring mechanism at the level of PESB 
has been instituted as per its recommendation. The Committee hopes that the PESB will be 
able to monitor effectively whether-. or not. its recommendations are being implemented by the 
concerned Ministries/Departments expedi.tiously.

INTRODUCfiON 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Home Affairs having been authorised by the 
Committee , present this Thirty-First Report of the Committee on the Action Taken by 
Government on the recommendations/observations of the Committee, contained in its 
Seventeenth Report on the Demands for Grants (1995-96) of the Ministry of Law, Justice 
and Company Affairs. 
2. The Seventeenth Report was presented to the Rajya Sabha on the 8th May , 1995. 
The Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs furnished replies indicating Action Taken 
on the recommendations contained in that Report, on the 25th October, 1995, 12th January 
and 1st March , 1996. The recommendations of the Committee were contained in Paras 12 to 
15, 20 to 22, 25 to 33, 35, 39 and 40 of the Report. 
3. The Committee in its meeting held on the 16th January, 1996 decided to take up 
consideration of the Action Taken Notes furnished by the Ministry of Law , Justice and 
Company Affairs (Departments of Legal Affairs; Justice; Company Affairs and Legislative 
Department) and seek clarifications thereon from the Secretaries of the respective 
Departments of the Ministry. Accordingly, the Committee considered the Action Taken 
Notes and sought clarifications from the Secretaries/representatives in respect of Action 
Taken replies on the recommendations relating to their respective Departments in its 
meeting held on the 7th March , 1996. 
4. The recommendations/observations contained in this Report are based on the Action 
Taken Notes furnished by the Ministry and the presentations made by the Secretaries/ 
representatives of the Ministry before the Committee on the 7th March, 1996. 
5. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on the 29th 
March, 1996.
