MEGBALAYA 
38. The State of Meghalaya, which was created as a full-fledged State in 1972, has an 
area of 22,429 ·sq. kms. and a population of 760,626 (1991 Census). The State is 
predominantly inhabited by Khasi, Jaintiya and Garo tribes. The State has not witnessed any 
insurgency. However, there have been ethnic conflicts between the tribals and non-tribals. 
the presence of non-tribal traders and businessmen is resented to by the tribal people who 
fear that they will be swamped by the non tribal people. 
3~. The Khasi Students' Union (KSU), Garo Students' Union (GSU), the ' Federation of 
Khasi, Jaintiya and Garo people (FKGP) and Ka Seng Ki and Nongkhaii etc. have been 
agitating against the so called exploitation by outsiders, for eviction of illegal non-tribal 
traders, bifurcation of the joint cadre of All India Services between Assam and Meghalaya 
and checking the influx of foreigners into the State. There have also been incidents of 
assault and intimidation, the non-tribal traders/businessmen being main targets. Recently, 
the Hynniewtrep Achik Liberation Council (HALC) is reported to be indulging in 
extortions, kidnappings and jail-breaks. Some other North-Eastern insurgent groups like 
NSCN(I), ULFA and BSF are reported to be using Meghalaya as a transit route to 
Bangladesh. Shillong is also reportedly being used by these insurgent groups as a meeting 
place. To contain ethnic violence in the State, the State Government undertook thorough 
introspection into functioning of the police department at various levels. A number of 
welfare measures like Meghalaya Police Special Security Scheme (MPSSS), expediting the 
payment of pension and other benefits to the retiring Police Personnel , holding of retirement 
parade on the day of retirement or immediately after retirement of the ~olice personnel have 
been undertaken, to boost the morale of the police force. The wives of the senior police 
officers have also formed an Association, called the Police Officers Wives Association for 
Care (PSWAC). There has been a remarkable improvement in the disposal of cases at the 
investigation stage. The introduction of the City Patrol Scheme in Shillong has widely 
improved the response time of the poiice to .attend to any situation. One India Reserve 
Battalion has been sanctioned to Meghalaya in February 1986 by the Ministry of Home 
Affairs to cope up with the incidence of robbery/dacoity on the national highway. To 
effectively deal with infiltration of foreign nationals , some proposals, like creation of posts of 
riverine police, creation of 10 additional check post, creation of Moblile Task Force , 
creation of additional posts of special Anti-Infiltration squad for Ri-Bhoi and South .. Garo 
Hills districts; creation of infiltration Heaquarters staff; have been pending with the Central 
Government. Besides extortion, there have been cases of reported seizure of yellow cake 
(suspected uranium) ; influx of narcotics like heroine , ganja, hashis, SPM, RPM capsules, 
ephairon syrup, morphine sulphate, etc. The withdrawal of five companies of CRPF from 
Shillong city has led to lesser availability of police force in the city. To control and prevent 
crime in the State, the State Government has taken some additional measures like setting up 
mobile patrol , highway patrol in vulnerable crime affected areas, especially of check posts on 
the national highways and esc.orting night buses with armed guards etc.

ARUNACHAL PRADESH 
54. Arunachal Pradesh is the largest State in the North Eastern Region, with an area of 
83,743 sq. kms. and a population of 8,58,392 (1991 Census). It is primarily a tribal State, the 
major tribes being Adi, Nishing and Apatani. The "State has international borders with 
Bhutan, China and Myanmar and inter-state borders with Assam and Nagaland. The entire 
terrain in the State is mountainous and is divided by various small and large rivers. The road 
communication in the State is difficult in normal times, which becomes almost impossible 
during the monsoons. The overall law and order situation is satisfactory and the State has 
remained an island of peace in the otherwise disturbed North -Eastern Region.

Secretary, I.G. Police and other Officers of the State Government at ltanagar, the Capital of

56. The Chief Secretary informed that Arunachal Pradesh was the . most strategic State 
of the region , having boundaries with three countries -namel y, China, Bhutan and 
Myanmar. 
57. There is no direct flight to Delhi and it takes eight hours .to travel by road to 
Guwahati. It is also the most difficult State in the region , which, till date, enjoys the 
reputation of 'island of peace'. There are certain aspects about the State which deserve 
special attention: 
(i) There has been a persisting and severe discrimination with the $tate for the reason 
that this is a predominantly tribal society which should have enjoyed the status of 
Scheduled Tribes , but the same has been denied to it in a number of ways; 
(ii) The boundary question-the boundary of the State was arbitrarily decided in 1951, 
by the then Governor of Assam when the State's areas in the plains were 
transferred to Assam; and 
(iii) Then there is the Chakma problem-the single most longest problem. The Ministry 
of Horne Affairs is bent upon granting citizenship rights to Chakmas, instead of 
deporting them back. Their stay in the State is a violation of all the protections 
given to the State under different laws. The State has not been involved in any 
insurgency issue so far. However, NSCN activities have been noticed in its eastern 
borders, with Nagaland and Myanmar. Similarly, due to Assam problem the Bodo 
activists have been entering into the State, leading to incidents of firing. 
58. The. IGP, Arunachal Pradesh informed members that the Bodo and ULFA 
insurgents enter Arunachal Pradesh when there is a pressure from Assam. They are setting

(iv) Communal riots in 1980: 
There were bloody ethnic clashes between tribals and non-tribals in Tripura in 
1980 in which civilians from both sections of the society took part and killed each 
other. People were not satisfied with the role played by the security personnel. 
They also narrated some incidents of torture, rape and killing of tribals people and 
deaths in police custody. Many tribal inhabitants. had deserted their homes and 
most of the educational institutions were closed down. The economic scenario in 
the tribals areas was in disarray. If remedial measures were not undertaken, 
indigenous tribal people will face extinction from the State. 
110. The Democratic Youth Federation , Tribal Youth Federation , Students ' Federation 
of India and Tribal Students Union in their joint representation made the following 
submissions:-
(i) closing of Indo-Bangladesh Border , since most of the extremist groups are taking 
shelter in Bangladesh; 
(ii) deployment of more para-military forces , as the extremists are armed with most 
sophisticated . arms. They also requested that Central Government must start 
dialogue with Bangladesh Government to rescue the Joint Secretary of Tribals 
Students Union , who is also an MLA and his bodyguard ; 
(iii) to equip the State police force with sophisticated weapons on the pattern of other 
extremists affected States like Assam , Nagaland and Manipur; 
(iv) adequate financial assistance for rehabilitation of surrendered extremists; and 
(v) adequate financial aid for overall development, especially the tribal area of the 
underdeveloped Tripura. 
111. The General Secretary of Tripura Motor Karmi Samiti submitted that the life and 
property of motor transport workers and vehicle owners is insecure. During the last three 
years a number of motor workers had been kidnapped , murdered and subjected to inhuman 
treatment by the extremists. The Government is unable to provide them adequate 
protection. The Government could not make the national highways and other motorable 
roads free from extremist disturbances , while huge amounts are being spent in the name of 
surrendered extremists. 
112. The General Secretary of the Indian National Trade Union Congress pointed to the 
extreme lawlessness and police inaction in the State. According to them , nepotism, political 
favouratism is rampant in t.he State in matter of employment and financial facilities. They 
also referred to the incident of attempt to murder the President of INTUC, Tripura branch 
and setting on fire the boundary fencing of his house on 13th September, 1995. Though the 
culprits were identified by CID, the police has still not arrested them. 
113. The Tripura Upjati Juba Samiti (TUJS) in its representation complained of serious 
law and order situation in the State and stated that the ADC areas have been under the 
control of extremists since 1993. Not a single school in the hill area is running for the last 
three years. No developmental activity could be implemented. Village after village have 
become deserted. More than 50 thousand tribals have migrated to Assam, Mizoram and 

26 
Bangladesh. A number of their workers and supporters have been killed by the extremists or 
by their cadres. They also narrated some incidents of lawlessness and extremist violence. 
They also alleged that Government has entered into a pact with A TTF (Tigers) not to 
operate in sout hern sub-division and not to use police and CRPF against the extremists. 
They, therefore, requested for the declaration of disturbed area, bann ing of extrem ists and 
dateline for surrender to improve the law and order situation in the State. 
114. The Tripura Pradesh Congress Committee (TPCC) alleged that a reign of terror 
has been Jet loose in the State and referred to the incidents of terrorisif)g and obstructing the 
candidates and voters during Panchayat and Nagar Palika elections, booth capturing and 
rigging. They also alleged diversion of Central Development Funds by State Governments in 
the name of surrendered extremists who are re-engaging themselves in looting, arsoning , 
kidnapping and rape etc. They also referred to the kidnapping business by way of 
negotiation and release of kidnapped persons on payment of huge ransoms. The outlawed 
groups are collect ing donations in the interior areas of the State. The Central Arm ed Forces 
are being wrongly deployed and are being misled by State Police. State Government did not 
accept an all party suggestion to declare the names of extrem ists and to fix a last date for 
their surrender. The so called extremists are torturing and killing members of a particular 
community and forcing them to leave Tripura. Many villages have become deserted and 
villagers have taken shelter in relief camps at various places. More than four thousand of 
Congress workers and supporters have been killed. They therefore, suggested for imm ediate 
declaration of disturbed area, empowering the central forces to take charge of the secur ity of 
the people and preventing the State Government from divert ing central funds for rewarding 
so called extremists. 
115. The Committee under stands that NH-44 is the life line, not only for the State of 
Tripura but also for Meghalaya and part of Assam, i.e. Cachar and Karimganj District. 
However the condition and maintenance of it is very dismal. Attacks by extremists and 
extortions, are also chronic problems not only for Tripura but for Meghalaya also. The 
Committee, therefore, recommend s that the highway may be maintained prop erly and 
extortions etc. on it be checked to instil a sense of security to the travellers. It is also desirabl e 
to extend the highway from Agartala to Sabroom, the southern border of the State as has 
been recommended by the Working Group set-up by the Ministry of Home Affairs. 
Considering the importance of NH-44 in the economic development of the State it should be 
c<Jnverted into a double-lane Highway in line with Meghalaya and Assam. 
116. The Committee notes that the present surface route from Agartala to Calcutta is 
about 1500 kms., whereas the transit route through Bangladesh is roughly 300 kms. The 
Committee feels that Government should take up the. matter with that country for opening of 
such a transit route. 
Government's Policy and steps taken to control Insurgency 
117. The policy of the Government of India has been to deal firmly with those indulging 
in violent activities on the one hand und to encourage them to join the national mainstream 
on the other, provided they abjure violence and agree to work within the framew ork of the 
Const itution of India. 

27 
118. Government have taken the following steps to control insurgency in the North­
Eastern States:-
A. Insurgency and other law and order problems: 
(a) With a view to meeting the genuine demands and redressal of grievances of 
the tribal people, agreements/accords were signed with the Nagas in 1975, 
Mizo National Front (MNF) in 1986, Tripura National Volunteers (TNV) in 
1988 and Assam Accord in 1985. 
(b) The NSCN, Meitei Extremist Groups (PLA, PREPAK, KCP and UNLF), 
BDSF, and ULFA have been banned under the Unlawful Activities 
(Prevention) Act, 1967. 
(c) Insurgency-affected areas/States, viz. the whole of Manipur, Nagaland, Assam 
and Tirap and Changlang Districts of Arunachal Pradesh and a 20 km. belt 
from Assam in the neighbouring States have been declared as "disturbed 
areas" under the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 1958, as amended in 
1972. 
(d) The North-Eastern State Governments have been provided units of CPMFs 
and Army units, inducted from time to time for the aid of civil authorities. 
(e) In addition to the normal Central grants under the Scheme for Modernisation 
of State Police Forces, speciai Central assistance amounting to Rs. 14.70 crores 
to Assam,· Rs. 10.50 crores to Manipur and Rs. 7.40 crores to Nagaland was 
provided in the year 1993-94. Government of Manipur was also sanctioned Rs. 
00.50 crores in February, 1995 for repair/maintenance of State Police vehicles. 
During 1994-95, allocation under the Modernisation Scheme was doubled to all 
the seven North-Eastern States. 
(f) Collection and sharing of intelligence/information with the States/Security 
Forces have been improved. 
(g) Two India Reserve Battalions for Assam and one Battalion each for Manipur 
and Mizoram were sanctioned in 1993. 
(h) To facilitate co-ordination between the State administration/Police, Central 
Para-Military Forces and the Army, mechanism for co-ordination has been 
established, both for co-ordination within a State as also for ·the inter-state co­
ordination. 
(i) The situation in the North-Eastern States is also· reviewed at various levels 
from time to time. The Union Home Minister met the Chief Ministers of 
North-Eastern States on the 22nd January and 19th July, 1994. The Minister of 
State (IS) also reviewed the situation with North-Eastern Chief Ministers on 
the 29th April, 1995. The situation is also reviewed periodically in the meetings 
of North-East Regional Security Co-ordination Conference with Chief 
Secretaries/DGPs and senior officers of, Central Agencies. The last such review 
was held on the 28th April, 1995 at Shillong. Decisions taken in these meetings 
are followed up. Some of the major decisions taken/followed up are ots 
under:-
(i) Need for optimum co-ordination between States and Ce.ntral Security 
Agencies; 
(ii) Optimum use of units of Central Para-Military Forces for effective counter­
insurgency duties; 
(iii) Strengthening of jail security; 

28 
(iv) Effective implementation of legal provisions, particularly the Unlawful Activities 
(Prevention) Act, 1967; 
(v) Effe.ctive prosecutions/transfer of hardcore detenues outside the North-Eastern 
States; 
(vi) Sharing of actionable intelligence; and 
(vii) Constituting Special Squads to prevent extortions etc. 
B. Economic Development: 
In view of weak fin~ncial resource base of the States of North-Eastern region, in 
addition to the Plan expenditure, assistance to meet the non-Plan expenditure has also been 
provided. All the seven States have been declared special category States for Central 
assistance. For speedier economic development of whole of the region, the North-Eastern 
Council had also invested an amount of Rs. 2474 crores till March, 1995. It may be noted 
that 87% of this amount has been spent on the development of two major infrastructure 
sectors viz. power, transport and communications. 
C. Initiatives with neighbouring countries: 
With a view to take up matters of mutual concern at various levels with the 
Governments of Bangladesh and Myanmar, an Indo-Bangladesh Joint Working Group was 
set-up in 1994 and an Agreement for maintenance of peace and tranquility on the lndo­
Myanmar border was signed in January, 1994 with the Government of Myanmar. Two 
national level meetings at the level of Home Secretary and five sectoral level meetings have 
been held with Myanmar. This initiative has been very successful. The Myanmar authorities 
and army have, in recent months, been providing good co-operation. With Bangladesh, one 
meeting at the level of Home Secretary and two meetings at the Joint Working Group level 
have been held. There has been partial success only in the initiative so far. Initiatives have 
also been taken with Thailand,' as some insurgent groups have been procur ing arms from 
that country. 
RECOMMENDATIONS AND CONCLUSIONS 
119. The Committee is of the view that despite a number of measures taken by 
Government to control insurgency and to improve the law and order situation in the North­
Eastern region, the situation demands a Jot more to be done. Government is duty-bound to 
guarantee a secured life to its people. The Committee notes with serious concern that a 
number of Ministers in Manipur are under threat to life and are not feeling secure despite 
tight security. The Committee, therefore, feels that first and foremost. the local police, 
which is a demoralised Jot today, has to be given a morale boosting. They must be well­
equipped with matching arms and training. They need adequate number uf vehicles. The 
intelligence network needs urgent improvement for effective collection. collation and 
dissemination of intelligence information. The affected States must be provided with 
adequate police force, Central Para-Military forces and other security forces and there 
should be harmonious co-ordination between them. The kith and kin of the local policemen 
require adequate security so that they can work fearlessly in discharging their d~ties. It is 
suggested that a separate police housing colony may be set-up for the families o_f the police 
personnel in each of the insurgency-affected States. All the necessary funds should be made 
available for this purpose. 
120. The problem of insurgency cannot be solved by force alone. ll must be combined 

29 
with dialogue and negotlatton with various insurgent groups, in an atmosphere of mutual 
trust and understanding. The Committee is fully convinced that a permanent solution to the 
insurgency problem in the region can be found only through political negotiations. The 
Committee, theref ore, takes this opportunity to call upon the Government to try to create a 
conduc ive atmosphere for bringing all toe insurgent groups across the table for a dialogue, 
without any precondition. The insurgent groups must also understand that violence is no 
solution to any problem and it is only through dialogue that they can put forth their 
demands before Government and evolve an amicable solution. 
121. The existence of basic transport infrastructure such as rail, road and air link is the 
pre-requisite for economic and industrial development of the region. There is no denying the 
fact that most of the North-Eastern region is underdeveloped due to lack of proper air, rail 
and road network. Most of the places are not easily accessible. Even within the same State, 
it is extreme ly difficult to reach from one point to another. Transportation of goods is 
equally difficult. Communication network is in a bad shape. Power is also in short supply. 
Unless these difficulties are removed , all efforts for bringing about development of the 
region would be retarded. It is in this context that the Comm ittee feels that constr uction of 
roads, laying of new rail lines and adequate air service in the region need highest priority. 
The Committee is of the view that laying of a rail line from Danshree to Imphal shou ld be 
considered on a priority basis to improve the trade and commerce in the region. The North­
Eastern States have to be placed on a different footing in this regard. Action in these areas 
need to be taken in a time bound programme. 
122. The Committee also notes that the newly introdu ced Pawan Hans helicopter service 
with subsidy from Central Government in the States of Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland has 
not been fully operational. The Committee feels that frequency of these services should be 
enhanced and larg er helicopters (24 seater) instead of the present one (8 seater) be 
introduced immediately not only in the existing routes but also in other States/areas of the 
North-Eastern region, having regard to the needs of the people. 
123. The North-Eastern States are faced with the problem of large scale unemployment , 
especially amongst the youth. These yout hs, who are without jobs, fall an easy prey to 
insurgent activities. It is very essential that these youths are used for constructive work and 
brought in the mainstream of national life. If we are able to properly channelise their 
services in productive work, it will be, on the one hand, a serious blow to the insurgent 
activities, and on the other, it will lead to the economic development of the region. lt is, 
therefore , an immense need of the hour that these youths ttrc provided with gainful 
employment under various employment/self employment schtmes/program mes of the 
Government. Further, these programmes/schemes require periodic review and the follow -up 
action of their outcome is also essentially required. The small scale industries would also 
have to be developed in a big way to utilise the manpower potehtial. Government should 
establish recruitment Centres and launch recruitment drive in the region for Government 
undertakings such a~ Civil Aviation, Railways and Post & Telegraph etc., so that the 
unemployed youth ge~ an opportun ity of employment. It will be better if recruitment boards 
of these undertaking!- have representation from the North-East also . Government must 
explore all the possibilities in this regard. 
124. The Committee feels that financial construints should not come in the wa~ of 
fighting insurgency and undertaking speedy economic development of the North-Eastern 
region . insurgency i~ a nat ional problem and everyone will be required to make sacrif ice to 
solve this problem . The Committee has been apprised that there has been no proper 
utilisation of funds, with the result that the benefits intended- (or the common peop1e have 

30 
not reached them. The Committee, therefore, opines that there should be regular and close 
monitoring of funds to ensure their proper utilisation. 
125. There are reports that the NSCN (I) and other insurgent groups like ULFA , PLA , 
UNLF, ATTF, NLFT, TRA etc. have been enjoying training and other facilities in 
Bangladesh. The NSCN (Khaplang) is having its training camps on the Burmese side. There 
are reports of smuggling of arms by insurgent groups from Thailand via Bangladesh and then 
through the Indo-Myanmar borders in Mizoram and Manipur. Besides, the insurgents of 
insurgency affected States are setting up their training camps and sanctuaries in the 
comparatively peaceful neighbouring States. The Committee is seriously perturbed over this 
and urges upon Government to take urgent effective steps to tackle the situation. The 
Committee feels that efforts of Government in this regard have not yielded the desired 
results as the movement of illicit arms, narcotics and the insurgent outfits from across the 
borders is going on unabated. To combat the problem it is essential to take immediate steps 
for sealing of the border totally by providing fencing and increasing vigil by security force. 
The Committee is also of the view that to mitigate the discontentment among the inhabitants 
of these insurgency afflicted States, various accords signed by the Central Government with 
various insurgent groups like the Shillong Accord, MNF Accord, TNV Accord, A TTF 
Accord and Assam Accord etc., need to be implemented in true spirit. 
126. There are wide ethnic, religious and cultural diversities in the entire Region. 
Numerous tribes, sub-tribes in the region perceive their status in danger in remaining with 
other groups/tribes in that district/State. The problem has been aggravated due to poor vigil 
on our borders, resulting in illegal infiltrations and demographic changes. This situation has 
led to frustration, discontentment and insecurity among the original inhabitants of that State. 
This is why, a demand is now being raised for an ethnographic survey of the North-Eastern 
Region. The Committee, therefore, feels that · this problem needs immediate attention with 
due care for Constitutional safeguards. 
127. In its note, the Government of Assam has -stressed the need for a fresh legislation 
consequent upon the repeal of Terrorists and Disruptive Activities Act (TADA) to deal with 
insurgency in the State. A suggestion in this regard was earlier forwarded by it to the 
Government of India. The Committee desires that this suggestion be examined to see 
whether any fresh legislation is required or existing legislations are sufficient to deal with the 
insurgency situation in the entire North-Eastern Region. 
128. The Study Group was informed that Meghalaya has a combined All India Service 
Cadre with Assam while in Arunachal Pradesh UT Cadre Officers of All India Services are 
postea who are generally not acquainted with the local customs and traditions of the State 
arid remain ignorant of developmental needs of the local people. Government should, 
therefore, consider to create a Separate All India Service Cadre for these States. 
129. The Chakmas and Hajong refugees problem is a burning problem in Arunachal 
Pradesh and to some extent in Mizoram and Tripura. Government should devise ways and 
means for an amicable solution of the problem before the situation aggravates into a 
complicated law and order problem. 
130. The Members of the Study Group were informed that a number of . proposals 
submitted by the Governments of North-Eastern States including· rai.s(ng. of strength of 
Assam Rifles and more l.R. Bns. for North-Eastern States have been pending with the 
Central Government for years. Government should take action for expeditious clearance of 
those proposals. 
131. Government should provide adequate protection and security to the business and 

31 
trading community from other States carrying on thier business activities in the North­
Eastern States. Government should take steps for protection of life and property and also 
ensure immediate compensation and return of business premises of the traders whose 
premises were ransacked and destroyed. 
132. Government should ensure proper allocation of funds for enabling the Autonomous 
District Councils entrusted with the development of the Scheduled Tribes and preserving 
with their own traditions, customs and cultures to meet their requirements. For sanction of 
Funds for Tribal Autonomou s District Councils a separate yard-stick may be fixed by the 
Planning Commission. Government may , therefore , take up the matter with the Planning 
Commi ssion, so that the demand is suitably considered while sanctioning Plan allocations. 
133. Government should take steps to prevent alleged diversion of Central Development 
Funds for the rehabilitation of surrendered militants. Since the internal resources of all the 
North-Eastern States are limited, Centre should come forward with an economic package to 
assist the State Governments, in rehabilitation of these surrendered extremists. 
134. To strengthen National Integration and to boost economic development, the 
Regional Council needs to be strengthened. The North-Eastern Council should be 
reconstituted with the Union Home Minister/Dy. Chairman , Planning Commission as 
Chairman. In the Council, Union Ministers of Finance, Agriculture, Railway, Surface 
Transport, Welfare, Rural Development etc. should be included as members alongwith Chief 
Ministers of all the North-Eastern States. The Council should hold regular meetings. These 
meetings should be held in each State Capital by rotation. 
135. At the end, the Committee feels that the problem of insurgency in the North­
Eastern Region has become a national problem with multifaced dimensions. The problem 
needs to be viewed as the problem of the entire region, not confined to one State and 
should be tackled accordingly. This requires a concerted and sincere effort on the part of all 
concerned, rising above narrow considerations and without making any prestige issue , in the 
intere st of the country.

REPORT 
The Ministry of Home Affairs has been entrusted broadly with the following functions: 
(a) To deal with all matters relating to internal security; 
(b) To deal with all matters relating to Centre-State relations and Inter-State 
relations; 
(c) Implementation of the provisions of the Constitution relating to Official 
Language and the provisions of the Official Language Act, 1963; 
(d) To discharge certain basiC'-functions like notification of assumption of office by 
the President and the Vice-PreSident; notification of appointment of the Prime 
Minister and other Ministers; notification of appointment, resignation and 
removal of Governors and Lt. Governors, appointment of Lt. Governors, Chief 
Commissioners and Administrative Officers in Union Territories; and 
(e) To deal with matters like citizenship and naturalisation, census of population·, 
National Anthem, National Flag of India, etc. 
2. To discharge the above functions,. the Ministry has been divided into four 
Departments:-
(i) Department of Internal Security-to deal with Police, Law and Order and 
rehabilitation; 
(ii) Department of States-to deal with Centre-State relations, inter-State relations, 
Union Territories and Freedom Fighters' Pension; 
(iii) Department of Official Language-to deal with the implementation of the 
provisions of the Constitution relating to Official Language and the provisions 
of the Official Language Act, 1963; and 
(iv) Department of Home-to deal with the notification of assumption of office by 
the President and Vice-President, notification of appointment of the Prime 
Minister and other Ministers, etc.

12. The Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs made a detailed presentation before the 
o1 Committee on 26th March, 1997 in the cours~ of which he explained the broad thrust of the 
demands relating to his Ministry, the reasons for variation in these demands as compared to 
the Revised Estimates of the previous year (1996-97), the nature of allocation for important 
sector such as housing needs of CPMF personnel, modernisation of police forces and dwelt 
at some length on the general internal security situation obtaining in the country. The 
Committee brought to his notice that as against total outlay of Rs. 7547.36 crores provided 
for the Ministry at the RE stage during the year 1996-97, budgetary provision of 
Rs. 7440.72 crores had been made for the Ministry for the year 1997-98 which was 
comparatively Rs. 107 crores lesser than the Revised Estimates of 1996-97. Similarly 
Demand Nos. 45 and 46 reflected allocations as proposed for 1997-98 on a considerably 
lower side. On the contrary, the budgetary outlay as proposed for the year 1997-98 for the· 
Union Territories (without Legislature) namely Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Dadra & 
Nagar Haveli, Daman & Diu and Lakshadweep showed an upward trend. The Secretary was 
asked to clarify this phenomenon underlying the Demands of this Ministry. The Secretary 
pointed out that the reasons for lesser allocations as proposed for 1997-98 vis-o-vis the 
Revised Estimates of 1996-97 were manifold in that parliamentary elections coupled with 
assembly elections in some States necessitated movement of para military personnel from 
one State to another involving additional cost; two additional battalions-one each in BSF 
and CRPF-had to be raised specially for recruitment of surrendered militants in Jammu & 
Kashmir a sum of Rs. 85 crores was earmarked, pursuant to Delhi High Court decision, to 
pay compensation to the victims of 1984 anti-Sikh riots; and additional provision to meet the 
expenditure on providing relief/succour to the victims of riots between the Bodos and 
Santhals had also to be made. This was one time expenditure involving substantial amount 
of additionality at the RE stage in 1996-97 and if this is excluded, then the outlay for 
1997-98, is higher by Rs. 355.35 crores (5%) over the Budget Estimates of 1996-97. 
Responding to a query from the Committee about the higher allocations for most of the 
Union Territories (without Legislature), it was explained by the Secretary that more 
attention was being given to Andaman & Nicobar Islands and enhanced allocat~ons were 
also made to take care of the normal growth.

plan component of Rs. 368.66 crores (as against projected demand of Ministry of Home

more. In some of the States people feel aggrieved on account of incessant flow of foreigners 
from across the borders and agitate for their detection and deportation. One of the reasons 
for their feeling agitated is· that the phenomenon of influx of foreigners on a large scale has a 
bearing on the demographic character of the State as also their cultural ethos. It is, 
therefore, very important that their illegal entry into the country is thoroughly checked on 
immediate time bound basis and those already having entered illegally should be detected

and deported. The Committee, in its 32nd Report had touched upon this issue and.:had 
observed that the Photo Identity Cards if issued on a national plan will be of immense :use to 
the citizens in many ways particularly from the point ofview of internal security. They will 
also help in identification of the illegal foreign migrants who could be deported back to the 
countries of their origin. A look in its entirety had, therefore, to be had on this issue and a 
time-frame could be laid down for issuance of Photo Identity Cards to all the people. It is 
doubtfull whether providing Photo Identity Cards to the people would solve the problem of 
illegal e'ntry of foreigners into our country in toto but they will definitely go a long way in 
their identification and subsequent <leportation. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its 
earlier recommendation that the exercise of issuance of Photo Identity Cards on a national 
plan be undertaken and completed in a time bound manner. The Government should 
impress upon the State Governments concerned to accord this exercise top priority. Identity 
Cards in identified border areas of Rajasthan, Punjab, Gujarat, Andaman & Nicobar Islands 
and North-Eastern States under the Pilot schemes of the Government may also be taken up 
on priority basis and completed in a definite time frame. 
MODERNISATION OF POLICE FORCE 
22. There is a scheme of the Ministry of Home Affairs for modernisation of police 
forces under which financial assistance is provided to the State Governments in th~ form of 
50% grants-in-aid and 50% loan to be utilised for expenditure of non-recurring nature qn 
purchase of vehicles, wireless equipments, computers and other sophisticated equipments. 
This scheme has been in operation since 1969-70. During 1996-97, an allocation of Rs. 55 
crores was made at the RE stage under this scheme and an outlay of Rs. 50 crores has been 
provided for during 1997-98. The Secretary, in the course of his submissions before the 
Committee, conceded that while modernisation of police force is very important, it has been 
neglected over the years. In this context, he cited the example of Nagaland which is in the 
throes of insurgency, where during the last 15 years not a single additional constable has 
been recruited and even police stations are put up in rented houses or thatched houses. 
Being deprived of the faciiity of accommodation, the police personnel have per force to live 
with . the villagers or urban population as the case may be, as a result of which they are 
exposed to all kinds of threats from militant groups. The police there does not have proper 
arms, proper shoes, proper communication system and proper vehicles and the whole thing 
appears to be in a mess. The. feeling there is perhaps that with the army being called upon to 
tackle insurgency, there is not much of a role for policemen. But, the matter cannot be set 
right alone by the army unless there is increased role for police which can provide vital input 
in terms of intelligence. In any case in a democratic . set-up it is the duty of civil 
administration to maintain law and order and provide security to the citizens. Army has only 
a limited role and that too in emergencies. Army can not be and should not be deployed on 
long term basis. At a time when Naxalite problem is spreading its tentacles to the States like 
Andhra Pradesh, Bihar and parts of Madhya Pradesh and Orissa and the various 
organisations involved in these activities are networking with other militant groups in other 
States, the issue of modernisation of police forces is to be attached highest priority, 
23. The Committee feels that in the present context when the terrorist and extremist 
activities are on the increase and sophisticated weapons and explosive devices are reaching 
their hands, there is all the more greater need for modernisation of our police forces so that 
they can effectively deal with such elements. The Committee is aware that Government is not 
oblivious of this problem and at various stages, steps have been taken to equip police forces 
with latest weaponry and production of arms in our ordnance factories for police forces has 
also been upgraded, but the progress in this regard is not altogether satisfactory. Our police

forces in many of the States are still ill-equipped to face extremist groups. No doubt, police 
administration rests with the State Governments' concerned and onus is primarily on them to 
keep them well equipped, but as pointed out by the Secretary of the Ministry, it is a national 
problem and has to be dealt with utmost priority. The Committee had earlier also dealt with 
this issue in its lStb and 32nd Reports and emphasised the need to suitably enhance the

24. Traffic management is one of the assigned tasks of Delhi Police and the Committee 
drew the attention of the Secretary of the Ministry to the chaotic conditions on Delhi roads, 
long traffic snarls, failure of traffic light signals and the measures being taken to redeem the 
sitution. The Committee was informed that there has been a phenomenal growth in the 
vehicular traffic in Delhi over the past two decades and the number of vehicles has increased 
from 3.12 lakhs in 1976 to 26.82 lakhs in 1996. As per a study conducted by the Indian Road 
Congress, the optimum capacity o·f a three lane road is 4500 vehicles per hour. However in 
Delhi the figure goes upto 15,680 at places like ITO bridge. The number of vehicles on 
Delhi roads is in fact greater than the combined strength of vehicles in Madras, Calcutta and 
Bombay. 
25. This volume of traffic on Delhi roads and unruly driving have resulted in road 
accidents more than in any of the remaining metropolitan cities. The number of road 
accidents which occurred in Delhi during 1995 and 1996 were of the order of 10,141 and 
11,310 respectively, which include 1,981 and 1,953 fatal road accidents during the respective 
years. 
26. The Ministry also submitted that though the number of vehicles in Delhi outnumber 
the vehicles in the three other major metros taken together, yet the number of traffic 
policemen to handle this mammoth number is less than that in any of them. A significant 
number of road accidents involve red and blue line buses and a special drive to rein in these 
buses . has been continuing in coordination with the State Transport Authority since 13th 
October, 1995. During the period 1.1.1996 to 28.2.1997, 343 permits of these buses were 
suspended. Besides during the year 1996, 1363 red and blue line bus drivers were tested, out 
of which 391 were found not upto the mark. Further , about 30,000 vehicles were checked for 
pollution, out of which 20,795 were found not having the "pollution under control" 
certificate and were prosecuted. 
27. As intimated to the committee, Delhi Tra.ffic Police has taken a number of 
measures to improve the traffic situation in Delhi which include:-
(i) Speed checking 
(ii) Parking discipline 
(iii) Roundabout discipline 
(iv) Lane discipline 
(v) Surveillance of vehicles 
(vi) Mobile patrolling 
(vii) Installation of latest road traffic signal techniques 
(viii) Restrictions on plying of goods vehicles on various roads

(ix) Education to general public about traffic rules and other policing aspects through 
print and electronic media, hoardings and literature, imparting training to 
professional drivers and training of school children to manage traffic in front of 
their schools. 
28. A Traffic Management Task Force has also been constituted by the Lt. Governor to 
examine traffic related problems and to evolve solutions thereto. Further, in an effort to 
decongest roads and to provide a non-polluting and efficient and affordable mode of 
transport rail based Mass Rapid Transit System for the National Capital Territory of Delhi 
duly integrated with other modes of transport has been under consideration of the

29. The Committee feels concerned that with all types of vehicles operating on Delhi 
roads and adherence to the traffic rules thrown to the winds, sane driving on the roads is a 
nightmarish experience. As a matter 1of fact the volume of traffic is so much that the roads are 
unable to bear the burden and skeleton traffic staff find it unmanageble to cope with the 
magnitude of the problem. The problem becomes aggravated particularly at important 
trijunctions in the event of traffic light going out of order, which now a days is a common 
sight. The measures which have been initiated by traffic police do not appear to go far beyond 
and strike at the root cause of the problem. What is needed most is an integrated . and 
coordinated approach to the problem and need for a perspective long term plan aimed 
particularly at finding other modes of transport and planning futuristic roads as m.ay 
withstand the volume of traffic which is bound to increase manifold in coming years. 
Construction of Oyovers at important trijunctions should be undertaken in a time·bound 
programme to ensure smooth and uninterrupted Oow of traffic. In the view of the Committee 
it would be quite useful to undertake a study in respect of Oow and behaviour of traffic in 
Delhi so that the points of obstructions could be identified and coorective measures taken. For· 
this the Delhi Police should closely inter-act with the Delhi Administration and necessary 
action taken within this year. The problem of managing traffic on Delhi roads is quite a 
serious one requiring a gigantic effort and the requirements of manpower to augment the Oeet 
of traffic police be seriously examined to ensure that earnest efforts in this direction are not 
hampered on account of shortage of manpower. The Committee has noted that the incidence 
of accidents on Delhi roads is particularly of staggering proportion and most of the time it is 
the blue line or red line buses involved in such accidents. It appears to the committee that the 
primary reason for this increasing phenomenon of accidents is the highly untrained drivers of 
such vehicles who manage to procure driving licences without having proper skills/training. 
The Committee feels that this menace can be suitably dealt with if the licencing regime is 
made more strict and accountable and a premier driving school is established in Delhi 
particularly to teach driving techniques to drivers of commercial vehicles. It could perhaps be 
more advantageous if similar driving schools are established in other States as well for 
highway driving. The Committee also feels that the policemen manning traffic should be given 
better training.

REHABILITATION OF 1947 REFUGEES IN J&K 
61. In the course of the meeting of the Committee on March, 26 and April 9, 1997 
points were raised to the effect that in the wake of Pakistani aggression in J&K in the year 
1947, thousands of families from former West Pakistan and areas now under the illegal 
occupation of Pakistan migrated to J&K, but they have yet not be properly rehabilitated. 
People who came from Sialkot have no right to vote for the State Legislature and are not 
even considered as citizens of the State. 
62. The Ministry has clarified that displaced persons from the Pak Occupied Kashmir 
have not been given any compensation under the Displaced Persons (Compensation & 
Rehabilitation) Act, as the whole of Jammu and Kashmir has always been considered an 
integral part of India and the areas presently under the occupation of Pakistan are 
considered to be under illegal occupation. The claims in respect of the properties left behind 
by these displaced persons could not be verified. Pak occupied areas are part of India and 
the 'Evacuee Property Law' as such does not apply to that State. In view of this, 
Government decided that these families may be given ex-gratia payment which had nothing 

23 
to do with the value/quantum of properties )eft by these displaced persons in PAK. 
Accordingly; · Ex-gratia payment was made as per the following scale:-
(i) Urban families · Rs. 3,5(}()1- per family 
(ii) Agricultural families Rs. 1 ,000'- plus 2 to 3 acres of irrigated or 4 to 6 
acres of unirrigated land, depending upon the 
strength of each family. 
63. However, these displaced persons have been making representations from time to 
time ..regarding: · 
(i) Compensation for properties left behind in PoK; 
(ii) Removal of deficiency in their land allotments; and 
(iii) Improvement in living conditions in their colonies. 
· 64. These demands have been examined by the Government from time to time. 
However, it has not been found feasible to accede to these demands on the grounds that 
(i) the amount of Rs. 350(¥- paid to these families in 1960 would compare favounibly with 
what they have been demanding ' subsequently, (ii) these families were provided such 
assistance long back and they now ought to be treated to have been absorbed in the national 
mainstream, and (iii) any reconsideration of their demands may trigger similar demands 
from o~her quarters. However, the Government of India has agreed, on the recommenda­
tions of 1he National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) to consider payment of cash 
compensation to 8409 families in lieu of deficiency in their allottable units of land in 
consultation with the State Government of Jammu and Kashmir. The matter is being 
processed in consultation with the State Government. 
65. With regard to the displaced persons from former West Pakistan, who had been 
settled in Jammu and Kashmir State, the Ministry has stated that they were paid 
compensation under the Displac~d Persons (Compensation & Rehabilitation) Act/Rules 
1954/1955 for the properties left behind by them in West Pakistan. These displaced persons 
were also allotted land by the State Government of Jammu and Kashmir and were also 
allotted house, shops etc. like displaced families from PoK. However, these persons are not 
treated as permanent residents of the State of Jammu and Kashmir in terms of the 
Constitution of Jammu and Kashmir and, therefore, are not citizens of the State, although 
they are citizens of India and can a.Iso vote in the Lok Sabha elections. A writ petition was 
filed by the West Pak displaced persons in the Hon'ble Supreme Court in this regard. The 
Hon'ble Supreme Court observed that it is for the State Legislature to make suitable 
amendment in the State Laws to provide relief to these persons without amending the 
Constitution of J&K. The Government of India is of the view that it would be most 
appropriate if the , amendment to the State Laws is left to the Jammu and Kashmir State

66. The Committee feels that the matter of settlement of migrapts from Pakistan has 
lingered on far too long and they continue to be in lurch being deprived of their rights. It is 
really very strange that they are staying in the State of J&K, owing land, are treated as 
citizens of India and c_an vote in Parliamentary elections but cannot participate in the elections 
to the State Assembly. The Committee strongly feels that this state of affairs must come to an 
end and all the rights due to the citizens in J & K should be made available to them including 
the right to vote· in Assembly/Municipal elections. The dividing line which has been drawn 
between the displaced persons from Pakistan and /the displaced persons from Pak occupied, 
Kashmir may, though, for technical reasons hold good but in the view of the Committee the 
persons from Pak occupied Kashmir had perforce to leave their ancestral homes and 
properties behind and they are being deprived of their legitimate -claims for so long which 
tantamounts to heaping further misery on them. What is needed most is to adopt a

OVERVIEW 
1. The Ministry of Law and Justice comprises 
(i) Department of Legal Affairs, 
(ii) Legislative Department, and 
(iii) Department of Justice 
the following Departments:-
2. The main functions of the Department of Legal Affairs are:-
(i) To render advice to the various Ministries/Departments of the Government of 
India on legal matters. 
(ii) To carry out the conveyancing work of the Central Government; 
(iii) To attend the litigation work in the Supreme Court, High Courts and some of the 
subordinate courts; 
(iv) To handle the treaties and agreements with foreign countries in matters of Civil 
Law; 
(v) To authorise officers to execute contracts and assurances of property on behalf of 
the President under Article 299 (1) of the Constitution. 
(vi) To sanction grants-in-aids to certain institutions engaged in research in the field of 
law. 
3. The Department of Legal Affairs is further concerned with appointment of the -Law 
Officers, namely the Attorney-General of India, the Solicitor-Genera] of India and the Additional 
Solicitors-General of India, etc. It is also administratively incharge of the Foreign Exchange 
Regulation Appellate Board. 
4. The Legal Affairs Department has a two-tier organisational set-up, namely, the main 
Secretariat at New Delhi and the Branch Secretariats at Mumbai, Calcutta, Madras and 
Bangalore. 
5. The Legislative Department is concerned mainly with the following matters:-
(i) Scrutiny of Notes for the Cabinet in relation to all legislative proposals from 
drafting and constitutional points of view; 
(ii) Drafting of all Government Bills including Constitution (Amendment) Bills before 
introduction in Parliament; translation of all such Bills into Hindi and forwarding 
both English and Hindi versions of the Bills to the Parliament Secretariat; drafting 
of non-official amendments and rendering of assistance to Administrative 
Ministries to decide on the acceptability or otherwise of non-official amendments; 
(iii) Rendering assistance to Parliament and Joint, Select or Standing Committees of 
Parliament at all stages through which a Bill passes before enactment. This 
includes scrutiny of and/or preparation of reports of such Committees, and Hindi 
Translations of such reports and minutes of dissent; · 
(iv) Drafting of Ordinances to be promulgated by the President. 
(v) Drafting of legislations to be enacted as President's Acts in respect of States under 
President's rule; 
(vi) Drafting of Regulations to be made by the President; 
(vii) Drafting of Constitution Orders, i.e., Orders required to be issued under the 
Constitution; 
(viii) Scrutiny of all statutory rules, orders and notifications and their translation into 
Hindi; . 
(ix) Scrutiny of State Legislation in the Concurrent field which requires assent of the 
President under article 254 of the Constitution; 
(x) Scrutiny of legislations to be enacted by Union Territory Legislatures; 
(xi) Election of ParliaJTlent, Legislatures of States and Union Territories and Offices of 
the President and Vice-President;

Justice it is under the administrative contro l of Ministry of Home Affairs. The Committee in its 
thirty-first Report had recommended that this state of affairs gave an anomalous picture which 
needed to be set right. The Committee in the said Report bad recommended that the 
Department of Justice should be placed under the Ministry of Law and Justice for all purposes 
thereby dispensing with the administrat ive control of the Ministry of Home Affairs. But so far no 
change bas been made in that set-up.

13. The Committee having considered all aspects makes recommendations/observations in 
respect of the following: 
DEPARTMENT OF LEGAL AFFAIRS 
National Legal Services Authority 
14. From the information provided by the Legal Affairs Department, the Committee notes 
that the main object of the National Legal Services Authority Act, 1987 (enforced w.e.f. 
9.11.1995) is to provide free and competent legal services to the weaker sections of the society on 
a uniform basis throughout the country. Under the Legal Services Authorities Act, free legal aid 
is admissible to every citizen whose income is less than Rs. 9000/per annum in cases before 
subordinate Courts and High Courts and Rs. 12,000/ in cases before the Supreme Court of India. 
The limitation as to income is however not applicable in case of persons belonging to the 
Scheduled Castes, the Scheduled Tribes, women, children, handicapped persons, etc. 

4 
A budgetary provision of Rs. 5 crores has been made for grants under this Act in the Budget 
Estimates for the year 1997-98 keeping in line with the recommendations made by the Committee 
in its 34th Report. 
15. The Committee was informed that the implementation of the provisions of Chapter ill of 
Legal Services Authorities Act, which deals with free legal aid to be poor bas been extended to 
sixteen States in the country. The Committee recommends that the implementation of the Chapter 
in rest of the States be carried out with utmost priority keeping in tune with the object of the Act. 
The Committee also observes that amount allocated for the scheme of free legal aid to the poor for 
the year 1997-98 is quite inadequate. 
16. The Committee also expresses its concern over the low rate of fee being paid to advocates 
taking up cases under the free legal aid scheme. The Committee, therefore, would like to reiterate 
that the rate of fee to advocates be suitably revised. It has been noted by the Committee that the 
recommendation to this effect has been forwarded to the State Legal Aid and Advice Boards by 
the Department. But the matter needs to be pursued with a positive attitude in order to attract 
talented advocates, thereby creating an ele!'flent of confidence in the minds of beneficiaries of this 
scheme. 
LOK ADALAT 
17. In a written reply to the point raised by the Committee, the Department of Legal Affairs 
has stated that since its inception in October-November, 1985, there have been 15,570 Lok 
Adalats held in different parts of the country settling 64,91,660 cases. The Committee is, 
however, constrained to observe that in spite of settling about 65 lakh cases by the Lok Adalats , 
there has not been any significant improvement in the pendency of cases in the courts. The 
Committee was informed that the Lok Adalats are being organised by the States from time to 
time. The Committee recommends that the Department should take more effective steps to 
popularise the Lok Adalats and persuade the States to hold Lok Adalats on regular basis. The 
Committee appreciates that steps have been taken for settlement of disputes of tribal 
communities through Lok Adalats and such Lok Adalats have been held in many States where 
there is concentration of tribal communities. The Committee has, However, noted that the 
concept of Lok Adalats has yet not taken shape in the States of Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland 
and the Union Territories of Andaman & Nicobar Islands, Daman & Diu, Dadra & Nagar Haveli 
and Lakshadweep. Where no Lok Adalats have been held so far , the Committee recommends 
that Government should make concerted efforts to organise Lok Adalats in these StatesiUT s 
also. The Committee has gathered that in cases involving Citizens vs. State coming up before the 
Lok Adalats, often the competent officers from the Government side, having powers to take 
decisions, are not present. This causes unnecessary delay in settlement of cases. The Committee 
recommends that Government should issue necessary instructions in this regard to ensur e 
presence of such officers on the spot. 
INCOME TAX APPELLATE TRIBUNAL (ITAT) 
18. The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal constituted under the Income-Tax Act deals with 
second appeals in all the matters relating to direct taxes and with appeals in revision against ord er 
of the Commissioners as well as orders of acquisition of properties under Chapter XX-A of the 
Income Tax Act. The ITAT is headed by the President who is assisted by one Senior Vice­

The Committee would also like to reiterate that steps should be taken to ensure that the two Judicial

LAW COMMISSION 
21. The Law Commission of India is a non- statutory body constituted by the Government from 
time to time. The Commission was originally constituted in 1955 and is reconstituted every three 
years. The administrative control of the Law Commission vests with the Department of Legal 
Affairs. The terms of reference of the Law Commission are also determined by the Department of 
Legal Affairs. The Law Commission presents its reports on various subjects to the Government 
which are then processed by the Department of Legal Affairs for placing them on the Tables of 
Parliament. These reports are thereafter forwarded to the various Ministries/Departments of 
Government of India who are administratively concerned with their implementation. A total of Rs. 
95.29 lakhs Budgetary provision has been made for the expenses of Law Commission for the year 
1997-98. 
22. The Committee was informed that its recommendations in the 34th Report regarding 
revision of Code of Civil Procedure has been forwarded to the Law Commission. It is, however , not 
given to understand the course of action being taken by the Law Commission. The Committee is of 
the view that it would be appropriate to conduct a study before any Bill to propose comprehensive 
amendments in the O.P.C. is introduced in the Parliament. 
23. The Committee is constrained to note that the recommendations of the Law Commission 
made in its !44th Report and onwards are still under consideration of various Ministries/ 
Departments of the Government. The Committee recommends that the Department of Legal Affairs 
should impress upon the concerned Ministries/Departments to ensure that the Reports are given due 
importance and measures to suitably amend the relevant Acts are brought before the Parliament. The 
Committee feels that the matter should be discussed by holding inter-Ministerial meetings and a view 
evolved at the earliest. 
24. The Committee would like to reiterate that a study must be condu~ted on the customary 
practices and conventions prevalent in different parts of the country . It has been noted by the 
Committee that at times these customary practices and conventions are quicker and more effective in 
imparting justice. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Government should make efforts to 
codify these customary practices and conventions in order to give legal sanctity to them and create 
necessary institutional framework to put these into effect. This is of special significance in matters of 
dispute resolution as distinct from dispute adjudication. 
ALTERNATIVE DISPUTE RESOLUTION 
25. The Committee has been informed that the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 has for 
the first time defined the law relating to conciliation and has paved the way for recognising these 
traditional and cultural approaches to dispute resolution. 
26. The Committee notes with dissatisfaction that the annual report and statement of accounts of 
the International Centre for Alternative Dispute Resolution, New Delhi (ICADR), a registered 
society under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, has not been laid in the Parliament so far. The 
Committee urges upon the Government to ensure timely submission of annual report and statement 
of accounts of ICADR to the Parliament. 
GENERAL RECOMMENDATIONS 
27. The Committee is of the opinion that in the wake of World Trade Organisation arrangement 
and the consequent likelihood of technical and scientific subjects coming up in dispute, the 
Government should take adequate steps to meet the new challenge thrown to the legal fraternity. 
The Committee recommends that a process and prog'ramme for training experts in technical subjects 
be initiated irnmedia tely. 
28. The Committee regrets to note that satisfactory action has not been initiated on it~ 
recommendation in the 34th Report regarding the performance of the Government lawyers. The 
Committee recommends that a scheme be evolved for monitoring the performance of Government 
lawyers so that they are made accountable for the cases entrusted to them. 

6 
LEGISLATIVE DEPARTMENT 
29. One of the responsibilities entrusted to the Legislative Department is to provide 
translated version of Acts in various languages. However, the Committee feels that there is a lot 
more to be achieved in this field. It is the considered view of the Committee that there is a 
serious lacun ae in the availability of various Acts in regional languages mentioned in the Eighth 
SchedUle of the Constitution. 
30. The Committee is of the opinion that a time-frame should be evolved for translation of 
Acts and the same must be adhered to strictly. The Committee notes with regret that over the 
last four years, the work relating to publication of authoritative texts of Central Acts in different 
regional languages has consistently gone down with only 16 Acts being authenticated in 1996-97. 
The Committee has been informed that Central Government spends a huge amount on account 
of reimbursement of translation charges (@Rs.l60/- per standard page) and printing charges to 
various States. Hence the Committee recommends that instead of simply holding the State 
Governments responsible for not submitting the translation of Central Acts, the Central 
Government should stress upon the concerned State Governments to expedite the work. 
31. The Committee desired to know details about the introduction of Photo Identity Cards. 
Committee was informed that as regards conduct of elections in August 1993, the Election 
Commission of India had introduced the scheme of Photo Identity Cards and it had directed that 
all the States, except the State of Jammu & Kashmir , would arrange for issue of Photo Identity 
Cards to all electors. The Commission initially fixed 30th November, 1994 as the deadline for the 
completion of the scheme which has had extended from time to time. However, the Commission 
stipulated in November, 1994 that it would not hold elections after 31st January, 1995, unless 
Photo Identity Cards were issued to all voters. At that time, general elections to State Assemblies 
were due in many States. Hence, certain private parties in the State of Bihar and Orissa filed writ 
petition in the Supreme Court challenging the stand taken by Election Commission. The Supreme 
Court vide its interim order dated 17.1.1995 directed the Election Commission not to withhold 
the elections of State Legislative Assemblies on the ground that the State Governments have not 
been able to complete the process of issuance of Photo Identity Cards by the deadline prescribed 
by the Election Commission. Hence, the issuance of Photo Identity Cards did not ramaio a pre­
condition for holding elections. However, the Committee has been informed that the Election 
Commission is of the view that the scheme of Photo Identity Cards for election needs to be 
continued and the issue of Identity Cards to all registered electors be completed as soon as 
possible. The Secretary of the Department during his deposition before the Committee stated 
that 48.98% work with regard to issue of Identity Cards to voters has been completed in the 
country. However, the Committee was of the view that when the Supreme Court had given such 
judgement regarding the Photo Identity Cards, it was incumbent on the part of the concerned 
department to examine the implications of the judgement and to suggest some measures &O as to 
make it compulsory to issue Photo Identity Cards to voters. The Committee took serious note of 
the fact that the concerned department did not take any initiative in this direction. The 
Committee is of the view th~t the multipurpose usage of the Identity Card creates a need for 
completion of the task of issuing the same to all adults in the country on a war footing. The 
importance of an Identity Card assumes significance specially in the border areas of the country 
from security point of view. Hence the Committee recommends that a time-frame should be 
evolved to complete the work relating to issuance of Photo Identity Cards. This· work should be 
completed by the year end in all the States. The Committee further recommends that it should be 
the responsibility of Government to ensure that defect-free Identity Cards are issued to all the 
citizens and if a card is not issued to any person, the officer concerned should be made 
accountable. The Committee recommends that an enactment, if necessary, should be brought to 
this effect. 
32. On a point raised by the Committee regarding the Sugar Export Promotion (Repeal) 
Ordinance, 1996, which repealed the Sugar Export Act, 1958, the Secretary of the Legislative 
Department · in his written reply informed the Committee that the Ministry of Food in 
consultation with the Legislative Department has decided that in case of an Ordinance repealing 
an existing Act , a replacement Bill is not necessary. Accordingly, the Sugar Export Promotion 
Act, 1958, has been repealed without getting the Bill to replace the Ordinance passed. The 
Committee expresses its disagreement with this view of the Ministry of Law and Justice. The 

7 
Committee expresses its serious concern over the manner in which an Act has been repealed by 
an Ordinance without taking the Parliament into confidence. Undoing of Acts passed by 
Parliament through Ordinances is not a healthy practice either morally or legally and goes against 
the spirit of the Constitution and democracy both. 
33. The Committee has observed that many of the subordinate legislations are at variance 
with the main Acts. The Committee, therefore, emphasises the need for a comprehensive review of 
aU subordinate legislation in the country. 
34. It has been brought to the notice of the Committee that in certain cases the judgements 
passed by the different High Courts and the Supreme Court pointed out some anomalies in the 
law itself. The Committee expresses its displeasure that the Legislative Department did not make 
any effort to monitor such judgements. Moreover, the Department has not conducted any study 
on the judgements which pointed out infirmities and anomalies in various laws. The Committee 
recommends that Government should monitor all such judgements on a regular basis and ensure 
that timely corrective actions are taken. 
35. The Committee is constrained to note that there are so many vacancies in the Vidhi 
Sahitya Prakashan (VSP) due to which the publication is lagging behind. As a measure to bring 
out the publication in time, the Committee suggests that the Department should seriously consider 
preparation of Camara Ready Copy o~ the manuscript to be published in order to make the 
publication work of VSP more efficacious. Necessary inputs like installation of computer system 
and networking towards achieving the above objective in the VSP b€ "'lstl undertaken. The 
Committee further suggests th~t proper training sho••ld be jmparted to the £ for working on 
computers, alternatively, trained personnel be recruited to man the machines. The Committee 
recommends that Government should create an inhouse printing facility at least upto the stage of 
type-setting. 
DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE 
36. The Committee, in its 34th Report, had expressed its concern over the pendency of cases 
in the courts. The Committee stressed that some time-frame should be prescribed for the disposal 
of cases. While expressing concern over the pendency of cases, the Committee had observed that 
mere filling up all the vacancies of judges in Supreme Court and different High Courts would not 
solve the problem. Number of benches should be increased. The Committee had suggested that 
the Benches of High Courts could be set up according to the distance or the areas of the 
population they cover. The Committee had specifically referred to the State of Uttar Pradesh and 
stated that Seventy-five percent of the cases in the Allahabad High Court pertained to the 
Western part of Uttar Pradesh which accounted for one third of the State, population-wise and 
one fourth area-wise. The Committee had stressed that there was a long standing demand for 
setting up a Bench of Allahabad High Court in Western Uttar Pradesh. The Committee notes 
with concern that no concrete steps have so far been taken with regard to the pendency of cases 
and regarding setting-up of a bench of Allahabad High Court in Western Uttar Pradesh. The 
Committee recommends that a system should be evolved for creation of High Court Benches on the 
basis of the population of the States. · 
37. The Committee suggests that pendency of cases in the various courts should be reduced. 
The Committee has been informed that t\Je lower courts in the country function under the 
supervision of · the High Courts of various States. However, the cases in High Courts and 
Supreme Court are being monitored by the Central Government. The Committee has been given 
Lo understand that the Allahabad High Court alone contributes to about 30% of the total 
pendency of cases. While the Gujarat and Madras High Courts have the lowest pendency of 
cases. The Committee suggests that Government should make study on the reasons for such 
variance in the disposal of cases by different courts. One of the reasons for the pendency of cases is 
the vacancies on the benches which remain vacant for a long time. The Committee recommends 
that the process for f.tlling the vacancies of judges of Supreme Court and High Courts should 
commence at least six months before the date of vacancy so that the new incumbant joins as soon 
the vacancy occurs. The Committee is of the view that the strength of the judges in High Courts 
and Supreme Court be increased. The Committee is of the opinion that another causative factor 

8 
for such high pendency of cases in the courts is the traditional method of issuing summons. The 
process is age-old and needs to be reviewed in the context of the present day scenario. The moderu 
methods of communications wherein much faster and quicker modes of communication are 
available should be adopted. The Committee also recommends that specific limit for completion of 
each stage of the case has to be fiXed. 
38. The Committee is of the considered view that Government should study the feasibility to 
set up more tribunals to deal with more categories of cases. Efforts need to be taken towards 
setting up of tribunals related to education, companies, election disputes / petitions :<!tc. This will 
save valuable time of the courts and also lessen the burd en on the courts . 
39. The Committee has observed that in many cases, the case is adjourned without assigning 
any particular reason. In such instances the saying 'justice delayed is justice denied' hold s 
grounds. The Committee strongly recommends that some yardstick in this regard needs to be laid 
down. The Committee further recommends that proper reason should be assigned, in writing, for 
adjourning a case without proper pleading. 
CENTRALLY SPONSERED SCHEME FOR DEVELOPMENT OF INFRASTRUCTURAL 
FACILITIES FOR THE JUDICIARY 
40. A centrally sponsered scheme relating to development of infrastructural facilities for the 
judiciary is being implemented by the Department of Justice from the year 1993-94. The sche me 
has been formulated with a view to augment the sou rces of the State Government/Union 
Territory Administration. The schem e envisages construct ion of court buildings and residences of 
Judges/Judicial Officers covering High Courts and subordinate Courts. As per the present set up, 
the expenditure under the scheme is to be shared by the Central and State Governments on 50-50 
basis. 
41. ln the current financial year an amount of Rs. 50 crores has been allocat ed for this 
scheme. The Committee is of the view that the allocation for the purpose is quite on the lower 
side and this sphere of activity needs to be given more importance. The implementation of the 
scheme is definite to boost the morale of the functionaries. The Committee strongly recommends 
that the amount needs to be enhanced to the tune of Rs. 200 crores. The Committee urges the 
Government to impress upon the Planning Commission to enhance allocation for the scheme. The 
Committee is of the view that the enhancement of the allocation for this activity will also facilitate 
the setting up of additional Benches of High Courts in diffenent parts of the country. 
DEMAND NO. 60 - ELECTION COMMISSION OF INDIA 
42. The Election Commission of India and Electoral Reforms come under the purview of the 
Legislative Department of the Ministry. The Demands for Grants of the Election Commission do 
not form part of the composite Demand No. 59. Demand No. 60 has separately been assigned to 
Election Commission. The Expenditure of the Election Commission is 'Voted'. Budgetary 
allocation of a total of 5.83 crore rupees bas been made for the year 1997-98 as against 5.47 
crores allocated under the Revised Esti mat es for the year 1996-97. 
DEMAND NO. 61 - SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
43. Demand No. 61 in the detailed Demands for Grants of the Ministry has been assigned to 
the Supreme Court of India. The expenditure to be incurred on the Supreme Court of India is 
'Charged'. As regards the Committee's concern regarding pendency of cases, the Committee _has 
been informed that at present there are only four vacancies in the Supreme Court and the 
pendency position has improved to a great extent dur ing the recent past. The number of pending 
cases which was over one lakh on 1st December, 1995, has come down to 37,000. The total 
Budget Estimates of the Supreme Court of India under the Revenue are Rs. 16.11 crores as 
against Rs. 16.36 crores of Revised Estimates for the year 1996-97.
