REPORT 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Home Affairs, having been authorised by the 
Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Fortieth Report of the 
Committee, relating to the Lokpal Bill, 1996*. 
2. In pursuance of the Rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha, in consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha 
referred** the Lokpal Bill, 1996, as introduced in the Lok Sabha on the 13th September, 
1996 and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and Report. 
3. The institution of Lokpal, as the Statement of Objects and Reasons appended to the 
Bill says, has been sought to be established on the basis of the recommendations of the 
Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC) contained in its interim Report on the 
"Problem of Redress of Citizens' Grievances". This Report of the ARC was submitted in 
1966 and the earlier attempts at legislation for setting up such an institution could not 
fructify in 1968, 1971, 1977, 1985 and 1989 for various reasons. The current Bill, as the 
Statement of Objects and Reasons goes on to say, seeks to carry out the object and purpose 
of the recommendations 'of ARC for enabling the citizens to have recourse to a convenient 
and effective forum for determination of complaints and thereby save him from pursuing his 
remedy through the process of Courts, which may prove to be expertsive or dilatory and may 
not facilitate speedy determination. 
4. The concept of having an institution like the Lokpal arises from the need for 
redressal of citizens' grievances. The term Lokpal is akin to the English term 'Ombudsman' 
which has been described in Chamber's Dictionary as a 'grievance man'. Ombudsman means 
an official who is appointed to investigate complaints against the administration. In other 
woi'Qs, Ombudsman is an officer who investigates complaints of citizens of unfair treatment 
meted out to them by Government Departments and suggests remedy thereof, if he finds 
that a complaint is justified. The institution of Ombudsman came into being in 1713 in 
Sweden when Chancellor of justice was appointed by the King to act as an invigilator to look 
into the functioning of the war time Government. In the year 1809, provision was made for 
the appointment of Ombudsman by the legislature. The institution remained mainly confined 
to the Scandinavian countries such as Finland and Denmark, In 1962 New Zealand also 
adopted the system of Ombudsman. Great Britain also did not lag behind and a slightly 
modified version of the institution in the form of the office of Parliamentary Commissioner 
came into being through an Act of Parliament in 1967. This was followed by other countries 
such . as Canada, Australia, U.S.A., France and several newly independent countries of 
Africa and Asia. 
5. A study of the system of Ombudsman or similar institutions in Sweden, United 
Kingdom, Zambia and Nigeria brings into focus the fact that mainly complaints of mal­
administration are looked into by the Ombudsman there and Ministers etc. do not seem to 
*Published in the Gazette of India Extraordinary Part-11, Section 2, dated the 13th September, 1996 . 
.. Rajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin Part-ll dated the 25th September, 1996. 
1 

I ' 
2 
have been brought within their purview. However, in Denmark all administrative matters 
concerning all units of State administration including Ministers and in Norway administrative 
aspects of acts of Ministers have been brought within the purview of Ombudsman. In 
Tanzania and Uganda the areas of jurisdiction for the institutions which are known as Anti 
Corruption Squad and Inspector General of Government, respectively, are mainly targetted 
at corruption and abuse of public office. The thrust of the system of Ombudsman as 
obtaining in these countries is mainly on redressal of public grievances arising mainly out of 
their complaints of mal-administration. 
6. In so far as India is concerned animated discussions both inside Parliament as well as 
outside took place preceding examination of the issue by the Administrative Reforms 
Commission, on the need for setting up an Ombudsman like institution to investigate and 
report on complaints pertaining to corruption. Coupled with this was the felt necessity for 
the establishment of an independent authority for the redressal of public grievances. The 
idea, however, could not be formalised till the Administrative Reforms Commission in its 
interim Report submitted in 1966 suggested that: 
"The special circumstances relating to our country can be fully met by providing 
for two special institutions for the redress of citizens' grievances. There should be 
one authority dealing with complaints against the administrative acts of Ministers 
or Secretaries to Government at the Centre and in the States. There should be 
another authority in each State and at the Centre for dealing with complaints 
against the administrative acts of other officials... The setting up of these 
authorities should not, however, be taken to be a complete answer to the problem 
of redress of citizens' grievances. They ·only provide the ultimate set-up for such 
redress as has not been available through the normal departmental or 
governmental machinery and do not absolve the department from fulfilling its 
obligations to the citize9: for administering its affairs without generating, as far as 
possible, any legitimate .sense· of grievance. Thus, the administration itself must 
play the major role in reducing the area of grievances and providing remedies 
wherever necessary and feasible ... When this machinery (in-built departmental 
machinery) functions effectively, the number of cases which will have to go to an 
authority outside the Ministry or the Department should be comparatively smail in 
number." 
7. The Administrative Reforms Commission thus contemplated a very limited role for 
the proposed creation of an institution like the Lokpal which would only inquire into 
complaints against a specified category of persons and not be a forum to deal with all 
complaints of citizens' grievances. As the Administrative Reforms Commission itself 
emphasised that 'the responsibility of the Departments to deal adequately with public 
grievances must squarely be faced by them', the· institution of Lokpal was thought of 
something in the nature of a set up for redress as has not been available through the normal 
departmental or governmental machinery. The Administrative Reforms Commission also 
underscored an important point when it referred to the special circumstances relating to our 
country's vastness and enormous size of population which would virtually make it quite 
stupendous, if not impossible, for a single agency to deal with the vast magnitude of 
complaints of public grievances and provide a remedy therefor. The proposed Lokpal Bill, 
there{ore, has mainly been devised to provide a forum to the citizens to make complaints of 
corruption against public functionaries who have been defined to mean persons who hold or 
have held the office of the Prime Minister, Minister of State or Deputy Minister of the 
Union and are or have been Members of either House of Parliament. 

3 
8. The Committee held twelve sittings in all to consider and finalise its report on this 
Bill. 
9. In its first sitting held on October 8, 1996 the Committee discussed the Bill in general 
and having regard to the special importance of th~ Bill which sought to . establish an 
institution of this kind at the national level, the Committee decided to invite memoranda 
from the individuals/organisations/institutions etc. interested in the subject matter of the 
Bill. The Committee also decided to issue a Press communique in this behalf fixing 
November 18, 1996 as the last date for the receipt of memoranda. On the lOth October, 
1996 the Director General, Doordarshan and All India Radio were also requested to 
telecast/broadcast the matter repeatedly to give it wide publicity so as to elicit public 
opinion on the Bill. 
10. In all 110 memoranda containing comments and suggestions· on the provisions of the 
Bill were received by the Committee from various organisations, associations and individuals 
etc. (see list of organisations/individuals, etc. at Appendix-!). At its sitting held on February 
6, 1997 the Committee heard the Secretary of the administrative Ministry concerned with the 
Bill, namely the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions on the Bill. At its 
sittings held on the 19th February and 3rd,4th,l7th,18th,19th and 20th March, 1997, the 
Committee heard the views of some former bureaucrats, joumalists and represent~tives of 
various political parties and institutions and organisations on the subject (vide list at 
Appendix-III). The Committee wishes to express its thanks to all the persons who either 
appeared before it or sent their valuable suggestions/views on the provisions of the Bill for 
the benefit of the Committee. 
11. The Committee considered various papers and memoranda placed before it and also 
the views expressed by the witnesses on the Bill. 
12. At its sittings held on the 29th April and 1st May, 1997 the Committee took up 
clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill. 
13. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its sitting held on the 6tb 
May, 1997. 
14. The observations of the Committee with regard to the principal changes proposed in 
the Bill are given below:-
Clause 3 
The Committee is of the view that sub-clause (b) of clause 3(2) be substituted to read as 
follows:-
"two Members who are, or have been, judges of the Supreme Court or the Chief 
Justices of the High Courts" 
Clause 4 
The Committee notes that the seven Member Committee, which has been proposed for 
recommending the names for appointment as Chairman and Members of the Lokpal, seems 
to be heavily loaded in favour of the party/parties in Government, giving excessive leverage

to the ruling party/combine in the appointment process, and as such it would not inspire 
public confidence. The Committee is, therefore, of the view that the first proviso to clause 
4(1) be substituted to read as follows:-
Provided that every appointment under this sub-section shall be made after 
obtaining the recommendations of a Committee consisting of-

Clause 6 
The Members of the Lokpal have been ensured a fixed tenure of 5 years. The 
Committee feels that no mechanism has been envisaged in the Bill to evaluate the 
performance of the Lokpal and in that context the fixed tenure of 5 years appears to be 
rather too long. Besides, in case the retired Chief Justice or judges of the Supreme Court 
are appointed as. the Chairman/Members of the Lokpal well past the age of 65 years, their 
continuance upts> the age of 70 years would perhaps be a factor to reckon with. The 
Committee, therefore,. recommends that the term of office of the Members of the Lokpal be 
reduced to 3 years and Clause 6 be amended accordingly. 
Clause 7 
The Committee has noted that under this Clause a member of the Lokpal can be 
removed from his office only by an order made by thePresident on the ground of proved 
misbehaviour of incapacity after an inquiry made by the Chief Justice of India or as the case 
may be, by such other judge of the Supreme Court as the Chief Justice of India may 
nominate in this behalf. Clause 3(2)(a) stipulates that the Chairman of the Lokpal shall be a 
person who is or has been a Chief Justice or judge of the Supreme Court. Similarly, Clause 
3(2)(b) prescribes that the members ofthe Lokpal shall be persons who are or have been or 
are qualified to be a judge of the Supreme Court (recommended by the Committee to be 
amended). The existing procedure for removal of judges of the Supreme Court and the High 
Courts as laid down under Articles 124 (4) and (5) read with Article 218 of the Constitution 
is by an order of the President on an Address being presented to him by requisite number of 
members of each House of Parliament. The Committee feels that the status of Chairman and 
the members of the Lokpal as envisaged under the scheme of the Bill is akin to the Chief 
Justice/judges of the Supreme Court and hence the procedure for their removal should be 
more stringent if not analogous to the one as laid down in the Constitution. The Committee, 
accordingly, is of the view that the inquiry against a member of the Lokpal as contemplated 
under Clause 7 for his removal should be made by the Chief Justice of India and the two 
senior-most judges of the Supreme Court. Clause 7 may be amended accordingly. 
Clause 8 
The Committee has noted that the Lokpal has inter-alia beerl empowered vide Clause 
8(2)(i) to secure the services of any officer or employee or investigating agency of the 
Central Government or the State Government with the concurrence of that Government for 
the purpose of dealing with any complaints or any classes of complaints. Similarly, it has 
been ensured vide Clause 8(2)(ii) that the Lokpal does not suffer in any way in the 
F-28 718/R 
' 

5 
investigation of the complaints made to it and for that purpose, if need be, tt can secure the 
services of any other person or agency which implies even private persons or agencies. The 
Committee expressed the apprehension that ·the p{ovision relating to seeking the 
concurrence of concerned Governments for securing services of any officer may delay the 
investigation. Hence the Committee is of the view that in order to remove any 
apprehensions on this score, steps may be taken to ensure that the services of officers, etc. 
to the Lokpal are provided with due promptness and necessary procedure in this regard may 
be provided in the rules to be framed under this Act. 
Clause 9 
The Committee feels that the amplitude of the discretionary power vested in the Lokpal 
under Clause 9(1) by the usage of the words 'the Lokpal may' is far too large. The 
Committee is accordingly of the view that subject to thl- other provisions of this Act the 
Lokpal should be under a mandatory obligation to inquire into the subject matter of the 
complaint. The word "may" in sub-clause (1) of this clause may be substituted by the word 
"shall". The Committee also feels that when the complaints about allegations of corruption 
against public functionaries are sought to be brought within the purview of the Lokpal, there 
is no reason for such complaints being taken up at any other forum such as the Commissions 
of Inquiry. The Committee is, therefore, of the opinion that the amount of discretion 
conferred on the Lokpal vide sub-clause (3) of clause 9 in the matter of referring any 
complaint for inquiry under the Commissions of Inquiry Act, 1952, is not desirable and the 
words 'except on the r~commendfition, or with the concurrence, of the Lokpal' occuring 
therein be deleted. Clause 9 may be amended accordingiy. 
Clause 10 
In view of the recommendation made by the Committee for omitting the discretionary 
aspect of Lokpal from sub-clause (3) of clause 9, sub-clause (2) of clause 10 becomes 
redundant and hence it may be deleted. 
In terms of sub clause (3) of clause 10, the jurisdiction of Lokpal is restricted to 
inquiring into complaints in respect of offences which are alleged to have been· committed 
during the previous five years. The Committee has, however, noted that some times 
information about corruption cases of immense proportions surfaces very late and national 
interest demands that truth must come out and the guilty be brought to book. Besides, the 
Committee is given to understand that in some of the Lok Ayukta Acts in force in some of 
the States, the provision exists for inquiry into complaints in respect of offences alleged to 
have been committed upto ten years earlier. The Committee, therefore, is of the opinion 
that the period of five years occurring in sub-clause (3) of clause 10 be substituted to read as 
ten years. 
Clause 11 
The Committee has noted that under sub-clause (3) of clause 11, it is enjoined upon the 
complainant to make a deposit of a sum of rupees one thousand but the manner of making 
this deposit and the authority or agency with which the deposit is to be made are left to be 
prescribed in the rules to be framed under clause 32. The Committee is of the opinion that if 
a fixed amount is prescribed in the Act itself, the concerned authority will have to come " 
before Parliament every time they wish to enhance/modify the fee which very often becomes 
essential because of the changing value of money. Hence, the Committee is of the opinion 
that this can be taken care of in the rules. The Committee feels, that this provision should 
be amended accordingly. 

I ' 
6 
Clause 12 
In view of the change proposed by the Committee in sub-clause (3) of clause 10 for 
raising the period of limitation for complaints from 5 years 'o 10 years, consequential change 
should be made in clause 12(1)(a) and the period of 5 years mentioned therein be 
·substituted to read as 10 years. Likewise, since the Committee has recommended deletion of 
sub-dause (2) of clause 10 consequential change in clause 12(1)(b) should also be effected. 
The Committee is of the view that the wording of sub-clauses (c) and (d) of clause 12(1) 
coRfers unguided and arbitrary powers of in-limine rejection of complaints on the Lokpal. It 
is in public interest that the complaints should be properly investigated and disposed of 
rather than nipped in the bud. Sub-~lause. (1)(c) should accordingly be reworded to read 
'that the complaint is manifestly false and vexatious' and sub-clause (1)(d) should be deleted 
in toto. 
Clause 13 
Sub-clause (2) of clause 13 stipulates that every inquiry shall be conducted in camera by 
the Chairman and the Members of the Lokpal sitting jointly. The Committee feels that this 
is not in consonance with the system of open court hearings currently prevalent in our 
country. One of the essential ingredients of democratic functioning of Government is 
increased participation of people in the governance of the country and their right to 
information. The very nature of conducting proceedings or trials by the judicial or quasi­
judicial organs in camera leads one to believe that truth is being shrouded in mystery. The 
Committee, therefore, feels that people of the country have a right to know about the acts 
of the public functionaries and accordingly they should have access to the inquiries being 
conducted by the Lokpal. The Committee, then!fore, recommends that sub-clause (2) of 
clause 13 be amended and the words in camera be substituted by the words in open and a 
proviso be added thereto as foJlows: 
"Provided that the Chairman and the Members of the Lokpal may conduct an 
inquiry in camera in exceptional circumstances for reasons to be recorded in 
writing." 
Clause 14 
The Committee has noted that by the powers conferred under clause 14, the Lokpal can 
stop investigations being pursued by the Polic_e Qfficials under the Code of Criminal 
Procedure, 1973, solely on the ground that such investigations might prejudicially affect the 
conduct of inquiry in respect of complaints made to it. The. Committee feels that it will not 
be proper to allow the Lokpal, whose jurisdiction is restricted to making inquiry into 
allegations of corruption, to hamper investigations being conducted under the normal 
criminal law of the country. The Committee is accordingly of the opinion that clause 14 be 
omitted from the Bill. 
Clause 15 
The Committee has noted that under sub-clause (4) of clause 15, information as may be 
relevant or useful· to the conduct of an inquiry by the Lokpal can be withheld on various 
grounds as mentioned thereunder so much so that the Secretary to the Government of India 
or Chief Secretary of the State Government have been given extensive powers to refuse to 
make available necessary information to the Lokpal. The Committee is of the opinion that 
sub-clause ( 4) is inconsistent with the nature of the proceedings before the Lokpal. Denial of 

7 
such information will reduce the institution of Lokpal to a mockery and will create doubts in 
the public mind. Therefore, sub-clause (4) nf clause 15 should be deleted. In view of this 
recommendation of the Committee, sub-clause (3~ of clause 15 should also be 
consequentially amended. 
Clause 16 
The Committee feels that the powers conferred on the Lokpal under the provisions of 
clause 16(1) and (2) for purposes of search and seizure of documents, which may be useful 
for or relevant to any inquiry being conducted by it, are quite adequate. The proviso may, 
however, be modified to read as follows: 
"Provided that in cases where such documents are required to be returned, the 
Lokpal shall return the documents after retaining copies thereof with due 
authentication." 
The Explanation added after the proviso appears to be unnecessary to the Committee 
and hence it should be deleted. 
Clause 17 
The Committee has noted that sub-clause (a) of clause 11 {1) confers power on the 
Lokpal to close the cases in the event of the allegations made in the complaint not being 
substantiated either wholly or partly. Sub-clause (b) of clause 17(1), on the other hand, 
enjoins upon it to make a Report in writing to the competent authority in case all or any of 
the allegations made in the complaint have or has been substantiated either wholly or partly. 
The Committee feels that after inquiry, whether the offences alleged in the complaint are 
found to have been substantiated or not, either wholly or partly it should be incum~ent upon 
the Lokpal to make a Report of its findings to the competent authority and in~lmate the 
complainant "nd the public functionary abou~ its having made the Report. 
The Committee is also of the view that the Lokpal should, while communicating its 
findings and recommendations in its Report to the competent authority, clearly specify the 
action to be taken against the public functionary against whom the offence alleged in the 
complaint has been found to be substantiated, either wholly or partly. Rather, the 
functioning of the Lokpal should be made more transparent and its pronouncements should 
be made public and under no circumstances it should be empowered to record a finding, 
closing the case which can at best be confined tu stating tllat, upon inquiry the offences 
alleged in the complaint have not been substantiated, either wholly or partly. In this manner 
the public functionary would get due justice. The Committee,· accordingly, recommends that 
sub-claus·es (a) and (b) of clause 17(1) inay be combined into one clause to read as 
follows:-
"At the conclusion of the inquiry, the Lokpal shall determine whether all or any of 
the offences alleged in the complaints have or has been proved to its satisfaction. 
The Lokpal shall. report its findings to the complainant, the public functionary and 
the competent authority." 
Consequential amendment in this clause be made accordingly to re-number it as 17(1) 
instead of 17(1)(a) and (b). 
The Committee has noted that in terms of sub-clause 17(2), the examination of a 
Report in respect of Prime Minister received from the Lokpal by the competent authority 
and communication of a decision th~reon to the Lokpal within the prescribed period seems 
to have been precluded. The matter is left vide sub-clause (3) of clause 17 to the discretion 

I_' t 
8 
of the House of the People or the Council of States to which the Prime Minister belongs 
merely by the laying of the Report. The Committee feels that the Act has to be uniformly 
applicable to all the public functionaries including the Prime Minster and accordingly 
recommends that the words "other than the Prime Minister" occurring in sub-clause (2) of 
clause 17 should be deleted. The Committee is also of the opinion that the period of 90 days 
prescribed under sub:..clause (3) for laying of the Report of the Lokpal before the House of 
. the People or the Council of States, as the case may be, read with the Explanation appended 
, thereto, is quite upreasonable and it should be omitted from the clause along with the 
Explanation. Instead sub-clause (3) may be amended to provide for laying of the Report 
· after its receipt before the House of the people or the Council of States, as the case may be, 
· within the first week on their. assembling for a Session. The Committee feels that since sub­
. clause (3) of clause 17 relates to the laying of Reports in respect of complaints against public 
. functionaries received from the Lokpal 1 it should have precedence for chronological reasons 
over sub-clause (2) and accordingly, sub-clause (3), as amended, be re-numbered as sub­
clause (2) and sub-clause (2) be re-numbered as sub-clause (3) 
Clause 18 
In the view of the Committee, clause-18 which provides for declaration of assets by the 
Members of Parliament, before the Lokpal every year, should be amended to provide for 
furnishing of return by the members within a period of 90 days on· their becoming members 
and annually thereafter, within 90 days . of commencement of each Financial Year. An 
explanation should also be added to the clause to define the family as including both the 
·spouse and dependent children. 
The Committee has also noted that clause-18 is too general in nature and does not refer 
to the consequences as may flow in case the members of parliament either do not furnish a 
return of assets to the Lokpal or furnish incomplete or false return. The Committee 
accordingly recommends that a provision be made in the Bill to include, that the details of 
the returns filed by the Members of Parliament will be reported by the Lokpal to the 
Chairpersons of the .House of the People and the Council of States. A deterrent clause may 
also be inserted to deal with cases of non-filing or delayed filing of returns by the Members 
of Parliament or their filing them in an incomplete or falsified manner. 
C/ause-19 
The Committee feels that the 1language of clause-19 be slightly modified in the interest 
of clarity to substitute the words "the Members"· with the words "the Chairman and the 
Members of the Lokpal". 
C/ause-20 
This clause provides for secrecy of information and evidence collected during any 
inquiry by the Lokpal. Even courts also cannot have any access to this evidence. The 
Committee feels that this clause negates the concept of transparency in the fun~ioning of 
the institution of Lokpal. There is no denying the fact that the evidence collected by the 
Lokpal will be at tremendous cost of men and material and keeping in view the fact that 
Lokpal under the proposed scheme of the Bill will not be the prosecuting or punishing 
authority against public functionaries held guilty, the bar placed on the use of evidence by 
the courts is not justified. On the contrary, allowing the Courts to have access to the 
evidence or information collected by the Lokpal will save them considerable time and 
botheration. Taking a view in its totality about clause 20, the Committee holds that as it is 
too secretive and bars flow of information, it should be deleted. 

• 
9 
Clause-21 
The Committee is in broad agreement with the provisions of clause 21 as the dignity of. 
the office of the Lokpal is to be respected and protected. The Committee, however, is of the 
view that sub-clause (2) of Clause 21 is too wide in its language and may well be an 
unreasonable restriction on free speech. Besides, the purpose contemplated under sub-clause 
(2) is by and large achieved by sub-clauses (1) and (3) and hence there does not appear to 
be any need to retain sub-clause (2). Hence, it should be deleted. Consequentially, the 
reference to sub-clause (2) in sub-clause (3) be deleted. 
Clause-22 
This clause seeks to confer powers on the Lokpal to try certain offences summarily and 
punish the persons who tender false evidence before it. The Committee however, feels that 
provisions for summary trails for offences of this nature already exist in the Code of 
Criminal Procedure, 1973 and there does not appear to be any need to specifically provide 
sub-clause (1) for this purpose. Hence, it should be deleted. Likewise, the Committee feels 
that in sub-clause (2) of clause 22 reference to sections 175, 178, 179 and 180 of the Indian 
Penal Code is unnecessary and the words occurring therein from "in Section 175, ...... to the 
Indian Penal Code" be substituted by the words "in clause 21(1) of this Act". 
The Committee has noted that under sub-clause (4) of clause 22 an appeal has been 
allowed to be made to the High Court by persons convicted under clause 22 by the Lokpal. 
This, however, does not appear to be proper as the status of the Chairman and Members of 
the Lokpal is equivalent to the status of the Chief Justice and Judges of the Supreme Court 
and accordingly, an appeal against the conviction pronounced by the Lokpal should lie to 
the Supreme Court and not to the High Court. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
sub-clause(4) may be amended to provide for appeals to the Supreme Court and the 
Explanation to this clause which consequently becomes redundant should also be deleted. 
Clauses 23, 24 and 25 
Clause 23 makes printing or publication of any information in relation to any complaint 
before the inquiry under the Act has reached its definitive stage, an offence triable 
summarily by the Lokpal. The ground on which this is based is that disclosure of information 
in such a manner causes irreparable damage to the public functionaries, particularly, in cases 
where the public functionary has been absolved of the charges against him. Similarly clause 
24 provides for the punishment which may be awarded by the Lokpal to a person making a 
complaint which is found by the Lokpal to be false. In cases, both under clauses 23 and 24 
provision for appeal against sentence of conviction pronounced by the Lokpal has been 
made to the Supreme Court. Clause 25 has been provided for the modified application of 
the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure for the trial of offences under clauses 22. 
23 and 24. 
The Committee has already recommended holding of inquiries by the Lokpal in the 
open, save in exceptional circumstances for reasons to be recorded in writing for in camera 
proceedings. The Committee has also stressed that there has to be transparency in the 
functioning of the Lokpal. Clause 23 on the contrary, seems to put unnecessary fetters on 
the right of expression and freedom of speech of the people by making the proceedings of 
the Lokpal too secretive and conferring extensive powers on it to punish the persons who 
may be adjudged guilty. Similarly, clause 24 is too severe. The Committee feels that the 
Lokpal should not convert itself into a criminal court except for the purposes of punishing 
ex-facie cases of contempt under clause 21(1). It sounds logical that if the Lokpal h.as no 

I 'I 
10 
power to punish a guilty public functionary, he should have no power to prosecute and 
punish the complainant or any witness. Such persons may be left to be prosecuted under the 
Indian Penal Code in the normal course. Therefore, in view of the recommendation of the 
Committee for open inquiry by the Lokpal and the fact that the sweep of the penal 
· provisions under clauses 23 and 24 is too wide, the Committee recommends that clauses 23 
and 24 may be dropped. As the Committee has recommended dropping of clauses 23 and 
24, clause 25 consequentially becomes redundant and it may also be dropped. 1 
Clause 26 
Clau~e 26 places a bar on prosecution in respect of allegations not proved or not 
substantiated before the Lokpal. This clause appears to be too draconian in nature and 
substance as it makes the Lokpal or the competent authority the final arbiters in determining 
the complaints of corruption against public functionaries. It is well known that even under 
the ordinary law of the land appeals have been provided at various stages in the courts and 
here, under this clause, the complainants who may not be satisfied with the decision of the 
Lokpal have been left high and dry as they cannot approach any court against the decision 
of the Lokpal or the competent authority. The Committee, therefore, feels that this clause in 
not in consonance with the judicial system of a democratic polity and it may be dropped 
altogether. It should be left to the complainants to approach the courts against the decision 
of the Lokpallcompetent authority to seek appropriate remedies. 
Clause 27 
Clause 27 requires the Lokpal to inquire .into any ·allegation as may be the subject 
matter of a complaint under this Act on an order being issued by the President and subject 
to such conditions or limitations as may be specified therein notwithstanding anything 
contained in the Act. The implication of the wording of this clause is perhaps that the only 
limitation of this Act which applies to the order issued by the President is that the alfegation 
which is referred to the Lokpal for inquiry has to be only in respect of which a complaint 
may be made and no other provisions of the Act seem to apply while determining the 
truthfulness or otherwise of the allegation. It may perhaps be that the allegation cited h the 
complaint may relate to a matter more than 10 years old. The Committee is, therefore, of 
the view that the words "notwithstanding anything contained in this Act" occurring in clfluse 
27 be substituted by the words "subject to the provisions of clause 12". 
Clauses 28 and 29 
Clause 28 provides for the disposal of deposits made by the complainants and clause 29 
provides for compensation or reward or both, pa'yable to complainant in the event of all or 
any of the allegations made in a complaint being substantiated. The Committee feels that the 
areas covered by clauses 28 and 29 are somewhat inter-linked and it will be more 
appropriate if both these clauses are combined into one and provision is made for the 
amount of compensation/reward or punishment to be decided by the Lokpal while 
concluding its findings. The Committee is also of the view that the words occurring at the 
end of clause 29. (which may be· combined with clause 28 in appropriate form) viz. "and the 
Central Government shall pay, the amount or amounts so determined, to the complainant" 
be substituted by the words "and the Lokpal shall determine the person by whom the said 
compensation or award shall be paid after giving that person a reasonable opportunity of 
being heard". 

11 
aause 30 
The Committee has noted that sub-clause (2) of clause 30 bars court's jurisdiction on the 
proceedings or decisions of the Lokpal. The Commi1:tee understands that the Supreme Court 
under Article 32 and the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution have inherent 
writ jurisdiction and aggrieved citizens can always approach these courts in matters where 
their rights have been encroached upon. Viewed in that context and in view of the fact that 
the Committee has already .reconunended deletion of clause 26, sub-clause (2) of clause 30 
may be dropped. 
Clause 11 
The Committee feels that in view of the recommendation made by it for dropping sub­
clause (1) of clause 22 and clauses 23 and 24, consequential changes may be made in clause 
31. 
Clause 33 
Sub-clause (b) of clause 33 bars any inquiry suo-motu by the Lokpal into cases of 
corruption by public functionaries corning to his notice through media or otherwise. The 
Committee feels that the basic objective of the creation of an institution of Lokpal is to 
cleanse public life from the scourge of corruption and, therefore, the Lokpal should not be 
fettered in being barred from jurisdiction to make inquiry upon its own knowledge and 
information. It should be given powers to take suo-motu notice of cases of corruption by 
public functionaries and accordingly sub-clause (b) of clause 33 may be deleted. 
Clause 35 
The Committee feels that clause 35 be suitably amended to take care of the amendment 
suggested by it in sub-clause (3) of clause 9. 
Clause 1, the Enacting Formula and the Title 
The Committee is of the view that the consequential changes in respect of Clause 1, the 
Enacting Formula and the Title with reference to the year of enactment as indicated therein 
may also be carried out. 
15. The Committee agrees with the provisions contained in the remaining clauses of the 
Bill. 
16. In view of the above recommendations/observations some necessary changes of 
consequential or drafting nature may also have to be carried out in the Bill and some of the 
clauses may also have to be renumbered. 
17. The Committee recommends that the Bill be passed after incorporating the 
amendments suggested by it.

Clause 4 
The Committee noted that the 7 Member Committee as proposed in this Clause for 
recommending the names for appointment as Chairman and Members of the Lokpal seemed 
to be heavily loaded in favour of the party I parties in Government, giving excessive leverage 
to the ruling party I combine in the appointment process, and as such it would not inspire 
public confidence. The Committee, accordingly, felt that the first proviso to clause 4(1) 
should be amended and the Committee provided thereunder should comprise Vice-President 
of India as the Chairman and the Prime Minister, Speaker of the House of the people and 
the Leaders of Opposition in the House of the people and the Council of States as its

Clause 5 
The Committee felt that no change/ amendment was required m this clause. 
Clause 6 
The Committee felt that the term of office of 5 years provided under this clause for the 
Members of the Lokpal is rather too long and it should be reduced to three years. 
Clause 7 
The Committee noted that the status of the Chairman and the members of the Lokpal 
as envisaged in the Bill is akin to the Chief Justice/ Judges of the Supreme Court and the 
procedure for their removal should accordingly be more stringent vis-a-vis the one provided 
for under clause 7, if not analogous to the one lnid down under article 124 (4) and (5) of the 
Constitution. The Committee, therefore, expressed the view that clause 7 should be 
amended to provide for an inquiry against a member of the Lokpal for his removal to be 
made by the Chief Justice of India and the two senior-most judges of the Supreme Court. 
Clause 8 
The Committee was in broad agreement with the provisions made under this clause. 
The Committee, however, was of the view that lest there be any apprehensions about the 
Central Government or State Government taking inordinately long time in giving their 
concurrence for providing the services of any ·officer or employee or investigating agency to 
the Lokpal as prescribed under sub-clause (2) (ii) of clause 8, adequate provision be made in 
the rules to be framed under this Act vide clause 32 to epsure that the services of officers 
etc. by the Central Government or the State Government, as the case may be, are provided 
to the Lokpal with due promptness. 
Clause 9 
The Committee felt that it should be obligatory for the Lokpal to inquire into the 
subject matter of the complaint made to it under this Act and accordingly the word 'may' 
occurring in sub clause (1) of clause 9 should be substituted by the word 'shall'. The 
Committee also expressed the view that the discretion conferred on the Lokpal under sub­
clause (3) of clause 9 to refer any matter cited in the complaint for inquiry under the 
Commissions of Inquiry Act, 1952, was not desirable and accordingly the words 'except on 
the recommendation, or with the concurrence, of the Lokpal' occurring therein should be 
deleted.

Clause 10 
The Committee felt that having regard to the view expressed by it to do away with the 
powers conferred on the Lokpal vide clause 9 (3) for referring any matter cited in the 
complaint for inquiry under the Commissions of Inquiry Act, 1952, sub clause (2) of clause 
10 would become redundant and hence it should also be deleted. 
The Committee also discussed at some length the provision contained in clause 10 (3) 
empowering the Lokpal to inquire into only complaints in respect of offences alleged to have 
been committed during the previous five years. The Committee was of the opinion that the 
limitation period of complaints needs to be enhanced to make it 10 years as many a time 
cases of corruption of immense proportions surface very late and national interest demands 
that they must be inquired into to bring the guilty to book. Besides, there already exist 
provisions in Lok Ayukta Acts of some States for inquiry into complaints in respect of 
offences alleged to have been committed upto 10 years earlier. 
Clause 11 
The Committee broadly agreed with the provisions of clause 11. tt, however, felt that 
the provision of making a deposit of Rs. lOOCY- under sub-clause (3) for filing a complaint 
need not be provided for in the Act, itself, because every time the fee is required to be 
enhanced I modified, the concerned authority would have to come before Parliament. It 
should instead be left to be provided for in the rules.

Clause 12 
The Committee felt that in view of the change proposed by it in sub-clause {3) of clau<>e

change should be made in clause 12{l){a) and the period of 5 years mentioned therein be

The Committee also noted that the wording of sub-clauses (c) and {d) of clause 12 {11 
confers unguided and arbitrary powers of in-limine rejection of complaints on the Lokpal. 
The Committee felt that it would be in the public interest to ensure proper investigation of 
complaints and accordingly it was necessary that the language of sub-clause {1) (c) of clause 
12 should be reworded to read 'that the complaint is manifestly false and vexatious' and sub­
clause {l){d) should llltogether be deleted. 
Clause 13 
The Committee expressed the view that the provision of in camera proceedings by the 
Lokpal as provided vide sub-clause (2) of clause 13 was not in consonance with the system 
128 

129 
of open court hearings currently prevalent in our country. Besides, it created unnecessary 
apprehensions in the minds of the people about the fairness of inquiry. The Committee, 
accordingly, felt that sub-clause (2) of clause 13 should be amended and the words in 
camera occurring therein should be substituted by the words in open and a proviso be 
added thereto as follows: 
'Provided that the Chairman and the Members of the Lokpal may conduct an 
inquiry in camera in exceptional circumstances for reasons to be recor<ted in 
writing.' 
Clause 14 
The Committee felt that as under Clause 14 the Lokpal could scuttle investigations 
being pursued by the Police officials under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, it 
should be deleted. 
Clause 15 
The Committee noted that under sub-clause (4) of clause 15 information as may be 
relevant or useful to the conduct of inquiry by the Lokpal can be withheld on various 
grounds as mentioned thereunder so much so that the Secretary to the Government of 
India or the Chief Secretary of the State Government have been given extensive powers 
to prevent disclosure of information to the Lokpal. The Committee felt that as sub-clause 
( 4) was inconsistent with the nature of proceedings before the Lokpal and denial of 
information would reduce the institution of Lokpal to a mockery, sub-clause (4) of clause 
15 should be deleted. The Committee also felt that in view of the deletion of sub-clause 
(4), consequential amendment in sub-clause (3) of clause 15 would become necessary. 
Clause 16 
The Committee was in broad agreement with the prov1s1ons of this clause. It was, 
however, of the view that the proviso to sub-clause (2) of clause 16 may be modified to 
provide that in cases where the documents seized by the Lokpal are required t.o be 
returned, the Lokpal shall return the same after retaining the copies thereof with due 
authentication. The Committee also felt that the explanation added to sub-clause (2) of 
clause 16 should be dropped. 
Clause 17 
The Committee considered the provisions of this clause in detail. It was of the view 
that after inquiry, the Lokpal should make a Report of its findings to the competent 
authority whether the offences alleged in the complaint have been found to be 
substantiated or not either wholly or partly and under no circumSlances it should be 
empowered to close the case. The complainant and the public functionary concerned 
should also be informed by the Lokpal about its having made such a Report. The 
Committee also felt that the Lokpal should, while communicating its findings and 
recommendations to the competent authority, clearly specify the action to be taken 
against the pubhc functionary against whom the offence alleged in the complaint has been 
found to be substantiated. either wholly or partly. The Committee was also of the 
opinion that as in substance sub-clauses (u) and (b) of clause 17 (1) related to findings of 
the Lokpal on the conclusion of inquiry, they could be combined together and brought 
under claw:e 17(1). 
The Committee was also of the opinion that sub-clause (3) may also be amended to 
provide for laying of the Report received from the Lokpal before the House of the 
People or the Council of States. as the cuse may be. within thr first week (instead of 

130 
within a period of 90 days as presently stipulated in the Act) on their assembling for a 
Session and for chronological reasons, the Committee suggested renumbering of sub­
clause (3) as amended, as sub-clause (2) and sub-clause {2), as sub-clause {3). 
Clause 18 
The Committee noted that clause 18 is too general in nature and accordingly felt 
that it should be amended to provide for -
(i) Furnishing of return of assets by the members within a period of 90 days on 
their becoming members and annually thereafter, within 90 days of 
commencement of each Financial Year; 
(ii) addition of an Explanation to- the clause to define the family as including both 
the spouse and dependent children; 
(iii) Reporting by the Lokpal of the details of the returns filed by the Members of 
Parliament to the Chairpersons of the House of the People and the Council of 
States; and 
(iv) a deterrent clause to deal with cases of non-filing or delayed filing of returns 
by the Members of Parliament or their filing them in an incomplete or falsified 
manner. 
Clause 19 
The Committee felt that the language of clause 19 should be slightly modified in 
the interest of clarity and the words 'the Members' occurring therein should be 
substituted with the words 'the Chairman and the Members of the Lokpal'. 
Clause 20 
The Committee was of the view that the bar placed on the courts to use evidence 
collected by the Lokpal under this clause was not justified and hence this clause should 
be deleted. 
Clause 21 
The Committee was in broad agreement with the provisions of clause 21 as it was 
necessary to respect and protect the dignity of the office of the Lokpal. The 
Committee, however, expressed the view that the sweep of sub-clause (2) of clause 21 
is too wide and tantamounts to an unreasonable restriction on free speech. The 
Committee felt that even otherwise the purpose contemplated under sub-clause (2) is by 
and large achieved by sub-clauses {1) and (3) and hence sub-clause (2) should be 
deleted. Reference to sub-clause (2) in sub-clause (3) consequentially would also have to 
go. 
Clause 22 
The Committee was of the view that sub-clause (1) of clause 22 should be deleted 
as provisions for summary trials for offences of the nature sought to be covered 
thereunder already exist in the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973. Accordingly, reference 
to Sections 175, 178, 179 and 180 of the Indian Penal Code in sub-clause (2) of clause 
22 becomes unnecessary and the words from 'in Section 175... to the Indian Penal 
Code' occurring therein be substituted by the words 'in clause 21{1) of this Act'. 
The Committee also felt that having regard to the status of the Chairman and 
Members of the Lokpal which is akin to the Chief Justice and Judges of the Supreme 
Courts, sub-clause (4) of clause 22 should be amended to provide for appeals against 
the convictions pronounced by the Lokpal to the Supreme Court (and not to the High 

131 
Court). The Explanation to sub-clause (4) would consequently become redundant and hence 
it should be deleted. 
Clauses 23, 24 & 25 
The Committee noted that Clauses 23 and 24 confer powers on the Lokpal to try 
offences arising out of printing or publication of any information in relation to any complaint 
or making of such complaints as are held by it to be false. Clause 25 has been provided for 
modified application of the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure for the trial of 
offences under clauses 22, 23 and 24. 
The Committee felt that there has to be transparency in the functioning of the Lokpal 
and it should not convert itself into a criminal court except for the purpose of punishing ex­
facie cases of contempt under clause 21(1). Clause 23 tends to make the proceedings of the 
Lokpal too confidential and clause 24 confers penal jurisdiction on the Lokpal to punish 
complainant whose complaints are held to be false. The Committee observed that on the 
analogy of the Lokpal having no powers to prosecute or punish guilty public functionary, no 
powers should be vested in it to prosecute or punish the complainant or any witness who 
could at best be left to be prosecuted under the Indian Penal Code in the normal course. 
The Committee, accordingly felt that clauses 23 and 24 should be dropped and clause 25 
which would consequentially become redundant should also be deleted. 
Clause 26 
The Committee noted that the bar placed on prosecution under this clause in respect of 
allegations not proved or .substantiated before the Lokpal and the courts being barred from 
taking cognizance of such allegations was contrary to the spirit of the ordinary law of the 
land which provided for appeals at various stages in the courts. The Committee, accordingly, 
felt that the complainants should have a right to go to the courts to seek appropriate 
remedies in case they are not satisfied with the decision of the LokpaVcompetent authority 
and clause 26 should, therefore, be dropped. 
Clause 27 
The Committee was of the view that for the words 'notwithstanding anything contained 
in this Act' occurring in clause 27 (1) the words 'subject to the provisions of clause 12' 
should be substituted to set at rest any apprehensions arising from the orders issued by the 
President requiring the Lokpal to inquire into any allegation subject to the conditions or 
limitations specified therein. 
Clauses 28 & 29 
The Committee was of the view that the areas covered by clauses 28 and 29 were 
somewhat similar in nature and inter-linked and hence it would be more appropriate if both 
these cluuses were combined into one and provision was made for the amount of 
compensation/reward or punishment to be decided by the Lokpal while concluding its 
findings. The Committee also felt that the words 'and the Central Government shall pay, the 
amount or amounts so determined, to the complainant' occuning at the end of clause 29 
should be substituted by the words and the Lokpal shall determine the person by whom the 
said compensation or award shall be paid after giving that person a reasonable opportunity 
of being heard'. 
Clause 30 
The Committee noted that it has already favoured deletion oi clause 26 and accordingly 
felt that sub-clause (2) of clause 30 which bars Courts jurisdiction on the proceedings or 
decision of the Lokpal should also be dropped.

1, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Home Affairs, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its

Supreme Court Judges (Conditions of Service) Amendment Bill, 1998.*

2. In pursuance of the Rules relating to Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha in consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha
referred** the High Court and Supreme Court Judges (Conditions of Service) Amendment
Bill, 1998 as introduced in the Lok Sabha on the 28th May, 1998 and pending therein, to the
Committee for examination and report by the 3rd July, 1998.

3. The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill states that the salaries of the
Judges of the Supreme Court and the Judges of the High Courts were last revised with effect
from 1५ April, 1986 under the Constitution (Fifty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1986 as
indicated below:—

Chief Justice of India Rs. 10,000 per month
Judges of the Supreme Court Rs. 9,000 per month
Chief Justice of a High Court Rs. 9,000 per month
Judges of High Courts Rs. 8,000 per month

3.1 The Statement further states that the Fifth Central Pay Commission had recom-
mended the revision in the salaries and allowances of the Central Government employees
including the members of All India Services and the Government accepted the majority of
the recommendations. The notification dated the 30th September, 1997 amending the
existing pay rules, namely, the Central Civil Services (Revised Pay), Rules, 1997 had also
been issued and the revised pay rules deemed to have come into force on the Ist day of
January, 1996, The Statement further adds that having considered all aspects of the matter,
a necessity was felt to increase the salaries of the Judges with effect from
Ist January 1996 as detailed below:—

Chief Justice of India Rs. 33,000 per month
Judges of the Supreme Court Rs. 30,000 per month
Chief Justice of a High Court Rs. 30,000 per month
Judges of High Courts Rs. 26,000 per month

3.2. The Statement also states that since the Parliament was not in session, the
President promulgated the High Court and Supreme Court Judges (Conditions of Service)
Amendment Ordinance, 1998 on the 24th April, 1998 to give effect to the increase in the
salaries of the Judges. The Bill seeks to replace the said Ordinance.

4. The financial Memorandum of the Bill states that the additional expenditure on
account of revision in salaries in case of Judges of the Supreme Court, Delhi High Court and
6% (approximately) for Punjab and Haryana High Court will be charged on the
Consolidated Fund of India. The additional expenditure in respect of the Judges of other
High Courts will be charged on the Consolidated Fund of respective States. The sanctioned
strength of Judges of the Supreme Court, the Delhi High Court and the Punjab and Haryana
High Court is at present 26 and 31 (including 6 additional Judges) and 37 (including 7
additional Judges), respectively. On an average there will be an increase of Rs. 10,000 per
month per Judge. Thus, additional expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India on
account of revision of salaries would be about Rs. 71 lakhs per annum. No other
expenditure, either recurring or non-recurring, is likely to be incurred.

5. In its meeting held on the 25th June, 1998, the Committee heard the Additional
Secretary, Department of Justice, Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs on various
aspects of the Bill. ‘fhe Committee was informed that the Bill seeks to replace the
Ordinance promulgated on the 24th April, 1998 which is to expire after six weeks of
reassembly of the Parliament session. The Parliament's session commenced on the 27th May,
1998 and the six week period would be over on 8th July, 1998 and as such the Bill is to be
passed by both the Houses of Parliament before that date.

5.1 The Committee noted that the recommendations of the Fifth Central Pay
Commission were accepted by the Government in September, 1997 and it failed to
understand why the Government could not bring a Bill to amend the relevant Acts to effect
the enhancement in the salaries of the Judges of the Supreme Court and the High Courts.
The Committee did not appreciate the recourse taken by the Department in promulgating an
Ordinance which if not converted into an Act by 8th July, 1998, would result in an
anamolous situation in asmuchas the salaries of the Judges would revert back to the pre-
revised scales until the current session of Parliament was prorogued cn or after August 14,
1998 and another Ordinance promulgated on the subject. Such a situation could be very
awkward and embarassing for Parliament in view of the provisions of Articles 125 and 221
of the Constitution in terms of which the allowances etc. of the Judges of the Supreme Court
and High Courts shall not be varied to their disadvantage after their appointment.

5.2 Members sought clarifications from the representatives of the Department of Justice
on the various provisions of the Bill which were replied to.

5.3 The Chairman of the Committee informed that he had received a copy of a
representation dated 3rd June, 1998 from the All India Judges Association regarding the
revision of salaries of the Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts. The Committee
was apprised of the issues raised therein. The said representation has been forwarded to the
Department of Justice for their consideration. In this connection the Committee urges upon
the Government to seriously consider the suggestions made in the representation expediti-
ously. The Committee recommends that the Government should have a second look at the
salaries and allowances of the Judges of the Supreme Court and the High Courts and take
decisions in that regard at the eartiest.

6. The Committee considered and adopted this Report in its sitting held on the 30th
June, 1998.

7. The Committee agreed to the amendments proposed to be effected by Clauses 2, 3
and 4 of the Bill in the High Court Judges (Conditions of Service) Act, 1954 and adopted
them without any change.

8. The Committee also agreed to the amendments proposed to be effected in the
Supreme Court Judges (Conditions of Service) Act, 1958 by Clauses 5, 6 and 7 of the Bill
and adopted them without any change.

9. Clauses 8 and 9 of the Bill were adopted without any amendment.
10. Clause 1, the Enacting Formula and the Title were adopted.
11. The Committee recommends that the Bill as reported by it, be passed.

3. The Ministry has submitted that the conduct of certain types of lonery trade 10 the

the Lotteries (Regulation) Ordinance, 1997 was promulgated by the President on October l,

6. Keeping in view the public importance and urgency the Committee (J 997-98) in its

8. The Commillee in its, sitting held on June 30, 1998 briefly discussed the Bill and felt

Commillee thereafter took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill. 
10. The Commillee considered and adopted this Report in its silting held on the Jrd 
July, 1998. 
II. The Commillee notes with serious concern the adverse effec ts cast by the lottery 
trade on the public in general and persons belonging to the economically weaker sections of 
our society in particular. It observes that persons from middle income group, low income 
group and a large number of daily wage earners are lured most by the idea of making quick 
buck without sweating. The Committee notes that draws of lotteries are held every half an 
hour or 45 minutes and the lottery buye~ sit for the whole day purchasing tickets and 
waiting with a hope for a prize . This has the effect of turning people away from productive 
and purposeful avenues of employment. A large number of persons have been ruined on 
accou'nt of this trade. Cases of suicides by persons who lost everythin in hope of good 
fortune through purchase of lottery tickets are also coming to light at regular intervals. 
12. The Committee does not feel conv inced about the arguments advanced in favour of 
lollery trade which inter alia include providing employment to unemployed, being a source 
of revenue for the States organising them and investment of the profits earned through this 
trade on development and social welfare activities. The Committee disapproves 
development/welfare activities of this n:Hure which in turn does more harm to the society 
than good. The Committee is of the considered view that instead of providing employment 
through lottery trade Government should endeavour to find alternative productive 
employment for the unemployed persons. 
13. The ComrRittee notes the frequent incidents of irregularities and malpractices 
·wolved in the lottery trade and how unsuspecting buyer of lottery ticket is duped and 
cheated by the lottery mafia.

14. The Committee note that the Government has been seized of the question of lottery 
trade since 1960s, if not earlier . The Committee suo moto took up consideration of the 
subject and it heard the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs in its meeting held on the 11th 
July, 1997. II also invited public opinion and views/comments from State Governments and 
Union Territory AdminislTations. Public notices to this effect were also published. Whilst the 
subject was still under consideration of the Committee and the Ministry of Home Affairs was 
aware of the exercise undertaken by it, the first Ordinance on lotteries was promulgated on 
October 1, 1997. This was followed by two successive Ordinances. The Committee strongly 
disapproves this course of action and considers it as an act of impropriety inasmuch as the 
Government did not wait for the recommendations of the Committee. When the evil was 
already prevalent in the society for quite some time~ what was the rationality of 
promulgating the Ordinance in haste when the subject was pending with the Parliamentary 
Standing Committee? 
15. Having considered the maner in all its aspects the Commiltee recommends thot as a 
first step the pre.sent Bill may be passed with some amendments as suggested in the 
succeeding paras. At the same time, in the light of the overwhelming view in the Committee 
for across the board ban on all kinds of lonerics, it strongly recommends to Government to 
come forward with a comprehensive Bill at the earliest in consultation with all the State 
Governments and the Union Territory administrations imposing complete ban on the lottery 
trade in the country having regard to the feasibility of effective implementation of the 
recommended legislation. 
16. The principal changes suggested by the Commiltee in the Bill and the reasons 
therefor are set out hereinafter:-
CLAUSE 4 
The Cause enumerates tbe conditions subject to which a lollery may be organised, 
conducted or promoted by a State Government. 
Sub-clause (e) of the clause provides that the prize money unclaimed within ~uch a time 
as may be prescribed by the State Government or not otherwise distributed, shall become 
the property of that Government. 
One of the conditions laid down by Supreme Court in the case of State of Haryana v/s. 
Suman Enterprises [1994 {4~ SSC 217) was that the sale proceed of the tickets either sold in 
retail or wholesale should be credited to the funds of the Government, however, the clause 
does not contain any such provisions. The Ministry of Home Atrnirs has stated that since the 
Bill relates to organisation, conduct and promotion of lolleries by the State Governments it 
is implied that the sale proceed of the louery tickets will get credited to the funds of the 
State Government concerned. The Commillee is not satisfied with the explanation and 
rec<>mmends that explicit provision in this regard may be incorporated in the Clause. 
Sub-clause (i) of the Cause provides that the number of bumper draws of a lottery shall 
not be more than six in a calender year. The Committee observes that the term "bumper 
draw" has not been defined in the Bill, as a result of which it can be interpreted differently 
by different organisers of the louery trade to escape from the effect of this provision. The 
Commillee understands that the intentio n of this provision is to limit the frequency of 
lotteries offering big prizes and thereby luring the common man for a quick buck. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the term "bumper draw" should be defined suitably 
to achieve the desired objective. 

4 
CLAUSES 
It empowen a State Government to prohibit within its territorial jurisdiction the sale of 
tickets of a lottery organised, conducted or promoted by another State. As this appears to 
be an enabling provision , one State Government may show favour towards the lottery 
orpniled by a particular State by not prohibiting it in its territory while banning the lotto·ry 
of another State Government. The Committee notes that as per proviso to Article 298 of lhe 
Constitution, the executive power of each State shall, in so far as a trade or business or such 
purpose is oot one wilh respect to which the State Legislature may make laws, be subject to 
legislation by Parliament. The Committee notes that as per Article 301, trade , commerce 
and intercoune throughout the territory of India shall be free, subject however , to other 
provisious of Part XD1 of the Constitution. The Committee fu~er notes that under Article 
302, Parliament may by law impose such restrictions on the freedom of trade , commerce or 
intercourse between one State and another or within any part of the to:rritory of India as 
may be required in the public interest . Notwithstanding the provisions of Article 302, Article 
303 imposes restrictions on the legislative powen of the Union and of lhe States with regard 
to trade and commerce on grounds of giving preferential treatment to one State over 
another or discriminating between one State and another, by virtue of any entry relating to 
trade and commerce in any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule. 
The Clause appean to be violative ul Arti _cle 303. It is prr st discrirninawry . The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that this clause may be suitably modified with a view to 
ensuring its uniform application by all the States . 
CLAUSE 7 
The Qause provides for penal provisions for any person who acts as an agent, promoter 
or trader in any lottery organised, conducted or promoted in contravention of the provisions 
of this Act or sells, distributes or purchases the ticket of such lottery . Primary entity in the 
legislation is 'State'. U the State decides to itself organise lotteries then the violation of the 
provisions of the Bill by the concerned Government o£ficen is not punishable. The Clause 
may be suitably modified so as to include State authorities in addition to othen.

CLAUSE S

INTERNAL SECURITY-AN OVERVIEW 
13. The Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs made a detailed presentution before the 
Committee on June 22, 1998 in the course of which he explained the broad thrust of the 
Demands relating to his Ministry. A major portion of his presentation was devoted to the 
internal security scenario, left wing extremism, insurgency , ethnic conflicts in the North · 
East, communal violence, caste clashes and other extremisvterrorist activities in the country. 
The Home Secretary apprised the Committee that out of the 535 districts in the country, 210 
districts are affected by one crisis or the other. Out of the 14 districts in Jammu and 
Kashmir, 10 are affected by militancy. Out of 69 districts in the North-Eastern region, as 
many as 48 are affected by insurgency or ethnic violence. The situation in Assam is worse 
because 23 of its districts are badly affected by violer.ce, the Home Secretary stated. He 
further stated that in Jammu and Kashmir during the period 1990-1998. Indian Security 
Forces arrested 4397 Pak trained militants and intercepted 711 gangs of Pak trained militants 
from the border. The Security Forces killed 1501 terrorists and arrested 1031. Besides, 2820 
militants of various outfits , including 1003 Pak trained , surr endered to the authorities, the 
Home Secretary informed the Committee. He went on to apprise the Committee that 
Pakistan has shifted its focus towards Nepal which is a porous border. lSI agents in 
Kathnwndu and Dhaka have been imparting training to youth in border areas, particularly 
on Indo-Nepal border and the interceptions have revealed that not only funds flow from that 
route, but unwanted el~ments also are intruding through that route. In the North-East, while 
the situation in Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh and Mcghalaya is comparatively peaceful as 
compared to other States, the situation in Assam is pretty bad. The situation in Nagaland is

PRISON REFORMS 
93. In the meeting of the Committee held on Jun~ 22, 1998 a point was raised regarding 
the problems of prisons in the country and the reforms undertaking by the Gov~ ~rnment. In 
this respect, the Committee was informed that a 'Prisons' is a State subject the Central 
Government h·ave been interacting with the State Governments on the various issues relating 
to prisons and prisoners. As a result of reviews being conduct.ed by the Government and the 
periodical interactions with repersenatives of the State Governments the following problem 
have come to ! tne fore:- · · 
(i) The State Governments are according very low priority to the prison administration 
and there is no systematic monitoring of prison conditions in the States due to frequent 
transfers of officers at the senior level. Even the funds being released by the Central 
Government under the scheme of modernisation of prison administration are not being 
utilised; 
(ii) The high percentage of under-trials also affects the living conditions of prisoners. In 
most of the States, the under-trials population in the prisons nmges from 80% to 90%. The 
wider use of alter~atives to imprisonment and the reduction of under-trials in the prison 

23 
population are the two main areas that assume high priority in any action meant to ·reduce 
overcrowding in prisons; · 
(iii) Even though some of the State Government have·upgraded the basic amenities and · 
facilities in recent years with regard to food, clothing, medical care etc. the requirement~ ~(' ·· 
sanitation, water supply-, electrification etc . are yet to be adequately met; · 
(iv) There is also need for bringing improvement in the service conditions of prison 
personnel. The recruitment policy, recruitment procedures and promotional prospects are 
not properly orierited to attract the requisite talent. There is also problem of residential 
accommodation and schools for the children of prison personnel in most of the States; ·and 
I 
(v) The criminals who are lodged in jails for petty crimes come out as hardened 
criminals. 
94 .. The Committee was informed that in order to address . the aforesaid problems and 
keeping the importance of correctional administration in mind the Central Government have· 
been sending senior officers of the Ministry of Home Affairs frequently to States in order to 
assess the conditions of prisoners. In order to tackle the problem of und~r-trials, the Central 
Government has been stressing the need for devising effective procedures so that the 
periodical meetings of the representatives of the judiciary, district administration, poliqe 
department and prison authorities are conducted. A qu:uterly statement of under-trials is 
submitted to the High courts which in turn issues necessary instructions to the Courts for 
speedy disposal of cases and initiate suitable steps for setting up of special courts. The State 
Governments from time to time have also been advised to resort to the use of alternative 
measures to imprisonment such a the grant of bail, release of prisoners on probation, parole, 
grant of remission etc. and also to encourage the setting up of open prisons where the work 
release programmes help the prisoners to earn money to be used for their accommodation in 
the prisons and for the suppor~ of their family. 
95. The Committee was also informed that the Central Government had constituted a 
high pgwet committee known as AIJ India Jail Reforms Committee in 1980 under the 
Chairmanship of Justice A.N. Mullah (Retd.) to study various aspects of prison 
administra tion in the country and to suggest ·remedial measures to improve living conditions 
in prisons. The Mullah Committee made ·650 recommendation in 1983 majority of which 
pertained to the State Governments. Only 10% of the recommendations concerned the 
Central~ Government. The recommendation on which action was to be taken by the State 
Governments were forwar ded for their necessary action. The recommendations for which the 
Central Government had to take action mainly rehited to providing a financial assistance for 
strengthening of security , training of the prison staff, vocational training and rehabilitation, 
provision of medical and psychiatric services' etc. The Mullah Committee in its report, inter 
alia also recommended that all 'the Acts per.taining to prison administration should be 
consolidated and a new uniform and comprehensive legislation be enacted by Parliament for 
the entire coun try. In 1986 the Government of India also set up a Special Group with Shri 
R.K. Kapoor, former Director , IB, as Chairman to examine and review various aspects of 
administration and management of prisons. The group recommended better communication 
system, watch towers, wire fencing etc. In pursuance of recommendations of Mullah 
Committee and the Kapoor Group a scheme for modernisation of prison administration vras1 
introduced in 1987. Under this scheme an amount of about 100 crores have been rele~sed · to 
the various St(lte Governments. Besides, this the lOth Finance Commission have also 
recomr11ended ~n amount of Rs. 66.31 crore~ covering the period 1996-2000 for upgradation 
of.Jail Administration : The Ministry has also been interacting with National Human Rights 

24 
Commissi_on and the National Commission for Women. A proposal for enactment of 
legislation for transfer of foreign convicted nationals has also been under consideration so 
that they could be transferred to their Home Countries to serve the remaining period of jail 
terms. 
96. As far as the aspect of overcrowding in Central jail, Tihar, was concerned, the 
Committee was informed that Tihar had an authorised capacity of 3237 prisoners, while as 
on 19.6.98, there were 8767 prisoners in the jail. The Government of National Capital 
Territory of Delhi, in order to overcome the problem of overcrowding have taken steps to 
construct six new jails. These include four jails with a capacity of 1800 prisoners in the Tihar 
Jail Comp -lex, another jail with a capacity of 2000 prisoners at Mandoli and a jail at Rohini 
for lodging 950 prisoners. These jails are at present in various stages of construction and it is 
expected that one jail will be ready every year from 1998 onwards. The prisoners are 
provided round the clock medical services and separate medical faci 'ity also exists for women 
prisoners. Over 100 NGOs are engaged in providing vocational training to the prisoners. The 
prisoners are also encouraged to take parts in the games, sports and cultural activities 
organised for their benefit. A Committee in this respect appointed under the Chairmanship 
of Justice Santosh Duggal had since presented its Report. The recommendation made by this 
Committee have been accepted and implemented by the Government of Delhi. 
97. The Committee is dismayed over the sluggish pace of reforms in the Prison 
administration. It feels that the prevailing reforms are inadequate to meet the basic amenities 
of the swelling population of the prison inmates. The Committee notes with distress that the 
undertrials who are lodged in the prisons on charge of petty crimes, come out as hardened 
criminals. The Committee is shocked at the overcrowding in most of the prisons and expects 
that the Government will come out with well defined policies to decongest the prison premises 
and give a humane face to the prisons.

104. In pursuance of the recommendations contained in 37th Report of the Committee , 
the Committee sought information from the Ministry whether the Home Ministers' Advisory 
Committee (HMACs) had become functional in the UTs of Daman & Diu and Dadra & 
Nagar Haveli and the position in regard to notification of HMACs in the UTs of

(HMACs) for the Union Territories of Daman & Diu and Dadra & Nagar Haveli were 
constituted on the 21st November, 1996. The process of nomination of members to the said 
Committees has also been completed and duly notified. However, it has not been possible, 
for vary ing reasons, to convene a meeting of the two Committees. It is the Government's 
endeavour to hold a meeting of these Committees within a month or so. The Committee was 
also informed that these Committees have also been constituted for the Union Territories of 
Cha!ldigarh, Lakshadweep and Andaman & Nicobar Islands. However, the nomination of 
members to these Committees has not been so far completed. The meeting of these 
Committees would be convened soon after the nomination process is extended. 
106. The Committee in its Thirty-seventh Report had appreciated the steps taken by. the 
Ministry in this respect and had expected that the formalities relating to composition and 
nomination would be completed soon. However, the Commillce expresses dissatisfaction over 
the routine approach of t.~e Ministry in this regard and observes that even when the 
formalities have been completed in respect of JII\1ACs for Daman and Diu and Dadra and 
Nagar Haveli meetings have still not been convened, although one year ancl seven months have 
elapsed since their constitution. The Committee also expresses its concern over the cont inuing 
delay in completing the formalities of nomination of memher s on the Committee in respect of 
Union Territories of Chandigarh, Lal<shadweep and Andaman & Nicohar Islands. The 
Committee urges upon the Ministry to make all the five Committees functional and convene 
their meetings imme~iately and in no case later than 60 days.

tha,Cconsequent on the 73rd amendment to the Constitution the MPs and MLAs were made the· 
members of the Municipal Corporation, Zila Parish ad etc., but in Chandigarh an anomalous 
situation bas arisen in that. MLAs (even though there is no Legislature or MLAs) continue to be

Union Territory of Chandigarh being transitory in nature, it is only expedient that the law as
