within three months this issue with be resolved. The Committee accordingly, hopes that 
anomalous situation will be rectified within the indicated time-frame. 
RESERVATION BENEFITS TO SCHEDULED CASTES RESIDING IN CHANDIGARH 
113. In the meeting of the Committee held on 22nd June, 1998, a point was raised to 
review the Government's instructions under which the memebrs of Scheduled Castes 
communities residing in Chandigarh cannot avail of the reservation benefits unless they were 
residing in Chandigarh prior to 1.11.1966. 
114. The Committee has been informed that the matter was examined by th\! 
Chandigarh Administration tast year in consultation with the Ministry of Personnel, Public 
Grievances and Pensions and it was opined by the latter that since the verification was 
required to be made on the basis of revenue records maintained by the Revenue authority of 
the district concerned, it was not possible to extend the benefit to those who migrated to 
Chandigarh after the issue of Presidential notification on 1st November, 1966. The Ministry 
has assured to take up the matter again with the Ministries concerned with the subject 
matter so that the issue could be resolved. 
115. The Committee is not satisfied with the explanation given by the Ministry and 
unable to appreciate the logic behind the stand of the Administration. The Committee notes 
that the Secretary of the Ministry has assured the Committee in its meeting held on 25th 
June, 1998 that the issue will be resolved within three months and hopes that the members of 
the Scheduled Caste communities residing in Chandigarh prior to 1.11.1966 will be able to 
avail the reservation benefits.

law of the Parliament.

REPORT 
The management of personnel policies in Government of India, to begin with, was the 
joint responsibility of the Ministries of Home Affairs (Services and Establishment Wing) and 
Finance (Establishment Division) with· Union Public Service Commission playintz an 
important advisory role. The Establishment Officer to the Government of India, functioning 
under the Cabinet Secretary had an important role to play in the senior appointments under 
the Government of India. All this made for improper division of responsibility and lack of a 
unified central direction. 
2. To plug this organisational loophole, the Estimates Committee of the Third Lok 
Sabba in its 93rd Report (April 1966) observed that "the ever expanding role of the 
Government in a welfare state with its natural concomitant of a large civil service calls for 
effective personnel control through a singJ.e agency". • The Administrative Reforms Commi­
ssion too urged upon the Government to set up a separate Department of Personnel, to be 
placed directly under the Prime Minister to serve as a nodal agency for the personnel 
functions of the Government. 
3. The Union Government accepted this recommendation and. as a consequence the 
'Department of Personnel' was set up in August, 1970 and placed within the Cabinet 
Secretariat. In February 1973, the Department of Administrative Reforms, tilr then with the 
Ministry of Home Affairs, was amalgamated with the Department of Personnel and the 
newly created department was christened, the 'Department of Personnel and Administrative 
Reforms'. In 1977, this department was transferred to the Ministry of Home affairs. In 
March, 1985 a full fledged 'Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions' was 
created. The Ministry comprises three departments, namely:-
1. Department of Personnel and Training. 
2. Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances. 
3. Department of Pensions and Pensioners' Welfare. 
4. The Ministry is under the overall charge of the Prime Minister~ assisted by a Minister 
of State. All th~ three departments are functioning under the charge of Secretary 
(Personnel) assisted. by four additional Secretaries, three Joint Secretaries and other officers 
and staff. 
5. Functionally, the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions is divided 
into the following seven divisions:-
- Establishment officer 
- Establishment 
- Administrative Tribunal and Administration 
-Training 
- Pension and Central Services 
- Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances 
6. DEPARTMENT OF PERSONNEL AND TRAINING AND THE VARIOUS AGEN.CIES 
UNDER ITS ADMINISTRATIVE CONTROL 
6.1 The role of the Department of Personnel and Training can be conceptually divided 
into two paos. In its larger nodal role, it acts as the formulator of policy and the watch dog 
*Ninety-third Report of the Estimates Committee (Third Lok Sabha), New Delhi, Lok Sabha Secretariat, 1966, 
pp 18-19. 
1 

2 
or tlie Government ensuring that certain accepted standards and norms, as laid down by it, 
are followed by all Ministries/Departments in the recruitment, regulation of service 
conditions and deputation of personnel as well as other related issues. Towards this end, 
guidelines are issued by it for the benefit of all Ministries/Departments and it monitors the 
implementation of these guidelines. It also advises all organisations of the Central 
Government on issues of personnel management. At a more immediate level, the 
Department has the direct responsibility of being the cadre controlling authority for the 
Indian Administrative Service (lAS) and the Central Secretariat Service (CSS). The 
Department also operates the Central Staffing Scheme under which suitable officers from All 
India Services and Group 'A' Central Services are selected and then placed in posts at the 
level of Deputy Secretary/Director and Joint Secretary, on the basis of tenure deputation. 
The Department also deals with cases of appointment to posts of Chairman, Managing 
Director, full-time functional Director/Member of the Board of Management of various 
public sector undertakings/enterprises, corporations, banks and financial institutions. It also 
deals with the assignment of Indian experts to various developing countries. 
Recruitment Agencies 
6.2 The two organisations through which the Department ensures recruitment of 
personnel for the Government are the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) and the' 
Staff Selection Commission (SSC). The former is constituted under a provision of the 
Constitution and is responsible for conducting examinations for appointment to the higher 
civil services and civil posts under the Union Government, including recruitment to the All 
India Services. There is a mandatory provision for consulting the Commission on all matters 
relating to methods of recruitment, principles to be followed in making promotions and 
transfers from one service to another and all the disciplinary matters. The sse is responsible 
for making recruitment to subordinate staff such as Assistants, Stenographers etc. 
Training Institutions 
6.3 Two major training institutions directly under the administrative control of the 
Department are the Lal Bahadur Shastri Nlltional Academy of Administration (LBSNAA), 
Mussoorie and the Institute of Secretariat Training and Management (ISTM), New Delhi. 
The former is mainly responsible for providing induction training to recruits to the Indian 
Administrative 'Service and other All India Services and Central Services. The Institute of 
Secretariat Training and Management provides induction as well as in-service training to 
members of the Central Secretariat Service. 
Senior Appointments under the Government of India 
6.4 All proposals for senior appointments under the Government of India, which 
require the approval of the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC) are processed 
through the Establishment Officer as Secretary of the ACC. These include board level 
appointments to Central Public Sector Undertakings and appointments of Joint Secretaries, 
Directors and Deputy Secretaries in the Ministries/Departments. In addition, all 
appointments by promotion, which require the approval of the ACC are also processed 
through the Establishment Officer. 
Public Enterprises Selection Board 
6.5 The Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB) is entrusted with the responsibility 
of making recommendations for appointment to the full-time Board level posts· of Chief 
Executive and functional Directors and part-time Chairman in the Central Public Under­
takings. 

3 
Administrative Vigilance 
6.6 The Department of Personnel and Training determines Government policy for the 
maintenance of integrity of the public services and eradication of corruption and CC?Ordinates 
the activities of various Ministries/Departments in that area. 
Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) 
6.7 Advice on all vigilance matters is provided by the Central Vigilance Commissbn. It 
has jurisdiction and power in respect of all matters to which the executive power of the 
Union Government extends. The Commission enjoys the same measure of independence and 
autonomy as the Union P"!blic Service Commission. 
Central Bureau of Investigation 
6.8 The CBI is the premier investigating agency of the country. Originally set up as an 
anti-corruption agency of the Government of India, the role of CBI has undergone a sea 
change. It is now dealing with a variety of offences which include anti-corruption, special 
crimes, economic offences, major financial frauds, terrorist crimes and other serious crimes 
having inter-state and international ramifications. A large number of such cases are now 
referred to the CBI by High Courts and the Supreme Court. 
Joint Consultative Machinery 
6.9 There is a well-structured machinery for joint consultation between the Central 
Government and its employees on a wide variety of service matters having a bearing on the 
administration and the general interests of the Government employees. It is a three-tier 
machinery consisting of the National Council, the Departmental Council and the Regional! 
Office Council. Service matters pertaining to the interests of the generality of employees or 
specific groups of them are dealt with by this machinery. 
Central Administrative Tribunal 
6.10 In order to provide speedy and inexpensive justice to employees aggrieved by 
Government decisions, the Government set up the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) 
in 1985, which now deals with all cases relating to service matters which were previously 
dealt with by Courts upto and including the High Courts. There are now 17 regular Benches 
of the CAT functioning in various parts of the country, including its Principal Bench in 
Delhi. 
Staff Welfare 
6.11 The Department supports various staff welfare programmes, which are provided _in 
various Ministries/Departments, Central Government Employees Welfare Coordination 
Committees in Central Government Offices located outside Delhi, Residents' Welfare 
Associations! Area Welfare Officers; Benevolent Fund and Departmental Canteens. 
Department of Personnel and Training is the nodal agency for three registered societies set 
up for the welfare of the Government employees and their families. These societies are the 
Central Civil Services Cultural and Sports Board, Grih Kalyan Kendra and Kendriya 
Bhandar. As a welfare measure, the Government had also decided, during the course of the 
year, to have a Civil Services Officers Institute in Delhi which has been set up as a 
registered society. 
DEPARTMENT OF PENSION AND PENSIONERS' WELFARE 
7. The Department of Pension & Pensioners' Welfare is the nodal agency of the 
Government of India for formulation of general policy on pension and other retirement 
benefits, as also for redressal of grievances on retirement benefits. The Department was set 

4 
up in 1985 as a part of Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions and has been 
rendering service for the benefit of pensioners since then. Department has taken a number 
of steps over the years for streamlining the pension administration system, for greater 
convenience and welfare of the pensioners. 
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEVANCES 
8. 1be Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances is the nodal 
agency of the Government of India for administrative reforms as well as redressal of public 
grievances relating to the State in general and grievances pertaining to Central Government 
agencies in particular . The Department disseminates information on important activities of 
the Government relating to administrative reforms and public grievance redressal through 
Management Publications and Documentation. It also undertakes activities in the field of 
international co-operation and exchanges to promote public service reforms. 
9. Demand No. 66 which pertains to the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances & 
Pensions includes requirements of funds for the Department of Personnel & Training, the 
Department of Administrative Reforms & Public Grievances, the Department of Pension & 
Pensioners' Welfare, the Central Administrative Tribunals, the Staff Selection Commission, 
the Central Bureau of Investigation (including lnterpool and Coordination Wing), the 
Institute of Secretariat Training & Management, the LaJ Bahadur Shastri National Academy 
of Administration, Training Schemes, the Central Vigilance Commission, the Public 
Enterprises Selecti~n Board, loans to State Government for payment of House Building 
Advance to All India Services Officers and purchase of land for construction of residential 
flats for the All India Service Officers posted in the North Eastern Region.

PUBLIC GRIEVANCE REDRESSAL 
33. Public grievance redressal remains an area of concern. It is a major cause of 
public dissatisfaction and the subject of criticism by elected representatives. Inaccessibility of 
officials, failure to acknowledge applications, unwarranted delays and non-enforcement of 
time limits, ignorance of procedures and forms and the unsympathetic attitude of officials at 
all levels only serve to further accentuate the problem of public grievances and their non­
redressal. The Committee understands that the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and 
Pensions had issued an office memorandum on 31st October, 1996 to all Ministries! 
Departments asking them to fix time limits for dispos:tl of grievances and endorsing a copy 
of the instructions issued in this regard to the Ministry. The Committee would like to be 
apprised of the action taken in the matter. 
34 .. The Committee has been taking up the issue of inadequate redressal of public 
grievances repeatedly. In response, the Ministry had been taking the plea that the process of 
public grievance redressal has necessarily to be decentralised for making it more effective. 
The argument of the Ministry is well taken but the Committee feels that the Department of 
Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances (DAR&PG) in its nodal role, should ascertain 
whether the policy of decentralisation of public grievance redressal is yielding desirable 
results. The fact that Directorate of Public Grievances in the Cabinet Secretariat and the 
Prime Minister's Office also have to take up the issue of public grievance redressal indicates 
some inadequacy in the existing mechanism. The Committee expects that the DAR&PG would 
take up a pro-active approach in the matter and induce the introduction of necessary 
corrective steps. 
CITIZEN'S CHARTER 
35. The Citizen's Charter concept was adopted as a pro-active instrument to achieve 
responsive administration. It indicates the commitments for improved service and grievance 
redress machinery of the organisation. The Ministry informed the Committer that these 
charters are indicative and that they are non-justiciable in nature. The Committee welcomes 
the concept of Citizen's Charters but it is of the view that their non-justiciable nature and

The Committee feels that a system of Administrative Courts should be set up to look into and

integrity and merit. The Citizen's Charters' should be made a justiciable document so as to 
empower the citizens with a view to introduce efficiency and transparency in administration 
by ensuring accountability. 
FREEDOM OF INFORMATION 
)6. In January 1997, Government had constituted a "Working Group on Right to 
Information and Promotion of Open and Transparent Government" under the Chairmanship 
of Shri H.D. Shourie. The Working Group submitted its Report to the Government on the 
21st May, 1997, which contained a draft "Freedom of Information Bill". The Group has 
recommended amendments to Section 5 of the Offical Secrets Act, 1923, Section 123 and 
124 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 together with consequential amendments in the Code 
of Civil Procedure, 1908 and in the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973, Rule 11 of the CCS 
(Conduct) Rules, 1964 and the Manual of Departmental Security Instructions relating to 
classification of information. The draft Bill, thus submitted has been circulated to all State 
Governments/Union Territory Administration and the Ministries/Departments of the Union 
Government for their views/comments. 
37. The Committee had inquired of the Ministry the reasons for bringing forth a 
'Freedom of Information Bill' and not a 'Right to Information Bill'. The Ministry contends 
that t,he u~e of the word "Right" in a "Right to Information Bill", has connotations which 
may ·make the legislation susceptible to avoidable litigation. The Working Group has 
explained that "the right to inf~rm~\ion has already received judicial recognition as a part of 

12 
the fundamental right to free speech and expression and the purpose in enacting the 
freedom of Information Act is mainly to provide a statutory framework for this right". 
38. Be that as it may, the Committee feels that explicitly providing for a 'Right to 
Information" will enable the citizenry to ensure accountability in administration. Moreover, 
the draft Bill on 'Freedom of Information Bill' as proposed by the Working Group bas a

more appropriate appellate body would be the 'Administrative Courts' as proposed by it

the Right to Information Act. The Committee would like to be apprised of the applicability of 
the Union Legislation to such States and situation arising therefrom. It would be necessary to

SENIOR APPOINTMENTS AND PERSONNEL POLICY 
43. The Department of Personnel and Training deals with the senior appointments and 
personnel policies in the Government of India, DoPT is also charged with the responsibility 
of Cadre Management in respect of certain services namely, the lAS, the Central Secretariat 
Service (CSS) etc. The Establishment Officer and the Additional Secretary in the 
department is nodal officer who oversees the senior appointments, personnel policies and 
cadre management and he also serves as Secretary to the Appointments Committee of the 
Cabinet (ACC). All proposals for senior appointment under the Government of India which 
require approval of the ACC under the Government of India (Transaction of Business) 
Rules, 1961, are processed through the Secretary of the ACC. The appointments inter-alia : 
include Joint Secretaries, Directors and Deputy Secretaries in the Ministries and Department 
of the Government of India. 
44. The Committee was informed that in order to regulate the posting of officers of 
various cadres at different levels-Deputy Secretary, Director, Joint Secretary, Addtional 
Secretary, Secretary-the Union Government has administratively devised a procedure 
known as the 'Central Staffing Scheme', which has been in operation' for over three decades 
now. Under this scheme, a modality has been laid down by which the officers on offer, at 
different levels from different cadres, are systematically considered for appointment to 
Secretariat and non-Secretariat posts governed by the Central Staffing Scheme. The 
significant features of the procedure so prescribed are, as under:-
(a) Keeping in view the academic background, work experience, seniority, 
representation of different cadres at a particular level in the Central Secretariat, a 
panel of three names is offered to the Ministry /Department for consideration; 
(b) These three names are discussed and considered by the Civil Services Board at its 
next Meeting, and a choice in order of preference is made of the candidates; 

14 
(c) Thereafter, the Ministry concerned obtains the formal approval of the Minister-in­
Charge to the officer placed first in the order of preference. In case the Minister does 
not approve the officer placed first in the order of preference, the Ministry has to 
furnish detailed reasons for choosing the second or the third officer in order of 
preference; and 
(d) After the selection by the Ministry..f)epartment is received, a suitable note is 
submitted through the Cabinet Secretary, to the ACC comprising, the Home Minister 
and the Prime Minister. 
45. The Ministry also submitted that only the All India Services, viz. Indian

47. Similary the Committee do not agree with the rationale given by the DoPT regarding

48. In this connection the Committee would emphasize that DoPT has not appreciated the 
fact that how much time is taken by that department in empanelling the Officers of the CSS and

for consideration for promotion to higher level but were left out on account of the 
Establishment Officer not forwarding names to the concerned Division (CS Division) of the

the DoPT should have a re-look at promotiopal avenues of the CSS Officers particularly at the 
level of Director, Joint Secretary and Additidnal Secretary so that these Officers are empanelled 
and appointed within a time-frame to be specified by them.

4?. In regard to reply given by the DoJYf to para 43 of its Thirty-eighth Report the 
Committee deeply regret to observe that its vie\vs-tecommendations have not been considered 
in its true perspective. The DoPT have wrongly interpreted the recommendations made by the 
Committee in this para that the amendments of CSS Rules, 1962 to bring the post of Director 
and above within its purview would tantamount to earmarking of post for CSS in the Central 
Secretariat. The CSS Rules were framed in the year 1962 i.e. about 36 years ago. The DoJYf 
have not bother ed to have a fresh look on the various provisions of these Rules keeping in 
view the past experience and operation of these Rules during the last 36 years. In this 
connection, the Committee has noted that the AIS and even the various Central Group 'A' 
services have their own set of service rules. And whenever any need has arisen in the past 
necessary amendments are being'had been made in the rules applicable to these services. the 
amendment to the service rules and earmarking of posts are two distinct issues. Whenever any 
amendment is carried out in the rules it does not necessarily mean that such an amendment 
would amount to earmarking of post for a particular service. 
50. The basic objective of the Central Staffing Scheme is to provide a systematic 
arrangement for selection and appointment of officers to senior administrative posts at the 
Centre, excluding posts which are specifically encadred within the organised Group 'A' 
Services or filled by recruitment through the UPSC. Under the Central Staffing Scheme 
officers from the AIS and participating Group 'A' Services, which are havig their own service 
rules, are borrowed for manning posts for a specified tenure and the cardinal principle being 
that all such officers who are so borrowed will serve the government of India for a stipulated 
tenure on deputation and, thereafter, return to their parent cadre. 
51. It is a well recognized fact that officers of the CSS have always been and or been 
manning the posts at the level of Director, Joint Secretary and Additional Secretary in the 
Government of India and acquitted themselves with distinction . When such officers can be 
appointed to these posts the Committee fails to understand why such posts could not be 
brought within the purview of the CSS Rules, 1962 by making suitable amendments to these 
rules. The Committee do not agree with the conclusion reached by the DOPT that if 
earmarking of posts is to be done in favour of a particular service, AIS might also demand 
earmarkign of posts to the extent of Central Deputation Reserve. The Central Staffing Scheme 
does not prescrib e earmarking of any post for any particular service including the AIS. The 
Central Deputation Reserve of AIS Officers of various State cadres varies from State to State . 
In Certain States the Central Deputation Reserve is over-utilised whereas in other States the 
Central Deputation Reserve is extremely under-utilised. Moreover, over-utilisation or under­
utilisation of quota of Central Deputation Reserve of a particular State cadre depends upon 
the number of names of officers sponsored by the respective State Governments for Central 
Deputation . It is, therefore, wrong to say that if the necessary amendments to the CSS Rules 
is carried out this will amount to earmarking of posts for this service, giving rise to demands 
for such earmarking by various other services. It is relevant to note here that Central Staffing 
Scheme provides that the growth , development and career prospects of the officers brought on 
deputation to the Centre, will be mainly in their own service. 
52. The Central Secretariat Service Rules, 1962 have become quite old .and the 
Committee is of the strong view that there is an urgent need to review these rules and carry 
out necessar,Y amendments in these rules in light of their operation during the last 36 years 
and to include the post of Director, Joint Secretary and Additional Secretary within the 
purview of these rules as the officers of this service have been holding these posts during the 
last so many years. The Committee, therefore, recommends accordingly. 
53. Keeping in view the above mentioned facts the Committee is of the view that the

OVERVIEW 
1. The Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs comprises the following 
Departments:-
(i) Department of Legal Affairs, 
(ii) Legislative Department, 
(iii) Department of Justice, and 
(iv) Department of Company Affairs. 
2. The main functions of the Department of Legal Affairs are:-
(i) To render advice to the various Ministnes!Departments of the 
Government of India on legal matters; 
(ii) To carry out the conveyancing work of the Central Government; 
(iii) To attend the litigation work in the Supreme Court, High Courts and 
some of the subordinate courts; 
(iv) To handle the treaties and agreements with foreign countries in matters 
of Civil Law; 
(v) To authorise officers to execute contracts and assurances of property on 
behalf of the President under Article 299 (1) of the Constitution; 
(vi) To sanction grants-in-aids to certain institutions engaged in research in the 
field of law. 
3. The Department of Legal Affairs in further concerned with appointment of the 
Law Officers, narr.~ly the Attorney-General of India, the Solicitor-General of India 
and the Additional Solicitors-General of India, etc. It is also administratively incharge 
of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Appellate Board. 
4. The Legal Affairs Department has a two-tier organisational set-up, namely, the 
main Secretariat at New Delhi and the Branch Secretanats at Mumbai, Calcutta, 
Madras and Bangalore. 
5. The Legislative Department is concerned mainly with the following matters:­
(i) Scrutiny of Notes for the Cabinet in relation to all Legislative proposals 
from drafting and constitutional points of view; 
(ii) Drafting of all Government Bill including Constitution (Amendment) Bills 
before introduction in Parliament; translation of all such Bills into Hindi 
and forwarding both English and Hindi versions of the Bills to the 
Parliament Secretariat; drafting of non-official amendments and rendering 
of assistance to Administrative Ministries to decide on the acceptability or 
otherwise of non-official amendments; 
(iii) Rendering assistance to Parliament and Joint, Select or Standing 
Committees of Parliament at all stages through which a Bill passes before 
enactment. This includes scrutiny of and/or preparation of reports of such 
Committees, and Hindi Translations of such reports ar.d minutes of 
dissent; 
(iv) Drafting of Ordinances to be promulgated by the President;

(v) Drafting of legislations to be enacted as President's Acts in respect of States 
under President's rule; 
(vi) Drafting of Regulations to be made by the President; 
(vii) Drafting of Constitution Orders, i.e. Orders required to · be issued under the 
Constitution; 
(viii) Scrutiny of all statutory rules, orders and notifications and their translation 
into Hindi; 
(ix) Scrutiny of States Legislation in the Concurrent field which requires assent of

(x) Scrutiny of legislations to be enacted by Union Territory Legislatures; 
(xi) Election of Parliament Legislatures of States and Union Territories and Office.s

(xv) Translation of Central Acts in the regional languages enumerated in the

6. The Department of Justice deals with the constitutional organisation of the Supreme 
Court and the High Courts and the appointment of Judges thereto, conditions of their 
service and with the administration of Judicial services in the Union Territories. Besides, it is 
the nodal Department in so far as -the administration of justice in States is concerned, 
although the actual responsibility of judicial administration below the High Court level rests 
with the concerned State Governments and High Courts. Though this department forms a 
part of Ministry of Law and Justice it is under the administr-ative control of Ministry of 
Home Affairs. Till 1992-93 the budget of the Department of Justice was salary oriented. 
From 1993-94, the Demands of the Department of Justice also included provision for the 
Centrally Sponsored Scheme relating to infrastructural facilities for the judiciary and 
National Judicial Academy. From the financial year 1996-97 provision has also been made 
for the National Judicial Pay Commission. In the year 1998-99 Rs. 58.00 lakhs are being 
allocated for the Commission as against Rs. 55 lakhs for the last year. 
7. The Department of Company Affairs is the primary agency respo.nsible for the 
orderly growth and functioning of Joint Stock Companies. Functions of the Department 
include administration of the Companies Act, 1956 and the Monopolies and Restrictive 
Trade Practices Act, 1969 (MRTP Act), Indian Partnership Act, 1937, and the Societies 
Registration Act, 1960, and to exercise supervision over the activities of the Institute of 
Chartered Accountants. Besides, it also holds administrative control over the Institute of 
Company Secretaries and the Institute of Costs and Works Accountants.

12. The Committee having considered all aspects makes recommendations/observations 
in respect of the following: 
DEPARTMENT OF LEGAL AFFAIRS 
Central Agency Section (CAS) 
13. The Central Agency Section (CAS) was set up in the year 1950. It is responsible for 
the conduct of litigation work in the Supreme Court on behalf of all Ministries/Departments 
of the Union Government and Administration of the Union Territories and performs 
functions of an Advocate-on-record. Government Advocates in the Central Agency Section 
are Advocates-on-record of the Supreme Court. They appear before the Supreme Court in 
all matters as per the Supreme Court Rules and whenever necessary, engage the Law 
Officers and other Advocates from the panel of Central Government Counsels. The 
Counsels are paid fees prescribed by the Union Government. The fee bills of the Counsels 
are scrutinised and the fees payable is certified by the Government Advocates of the Central 
Agency Sections. As per Annual Report (1997-98) of the Ministry of Law, Justice and 
Company Affairs, during the period from 1st April, 1997 to 31st March, 1998, the Central 
Agency Sections received 2929 new cases from various Departments of the Government of 
India as well as the Union Territories in which the Union of India or Union Territories were 

4 
either petitioners or respondents. The Department of Legal Affairs, in its written replies to 
the queries of the Committee stated that, "As on date 3,300 cases are pending and from 
1997 till date 4,176 cases were disposed of by the Central Agency Section". While 
appreciating the rate of disposal of cases by the Central Agency Section of the Department of 
Legal Affairs, the Committee urges upo'n the Departm~nt to chalk out a time bound 
programme for arranging litigation work in the pending cases in the Supreme Court on behalf 
of the Ministries/Departments of the Central Government and Union Territory 
Administrations, so that the litigation work of the Central Government and Union Territory 
Administrations in the Apex Court gets accelerated. 
LITIGATION (HIGH COURT) SECTION 
14. The litigation work in Delhi High Court and Central Administrative Tribunal 
(CAT), Principal Bench at New Delhi on behalf of all Ministries/Departments of the 
Government of India except Railways and Income Tax Departments is handled by the 
Litigation (High Court) Section. The cases dealt with, generally relate to Civil and Criminal 
Writ Petitions under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution of India, letters patent 
Appeals, Suits, Appeals, Reviews, Division Bench Appeals, Company Applications, 
Execution Applications and Criminal Miscellaneous and Service matters. There is a panel of 
Central Government Standing Counsels and Government Counsel who are nominated for 
contesting the cases. In most important matters, Senior Counsels are also engaged at the 
request of the Ministries/Departments concerned. In some matters of public importance and 
also in complicated matters one of the Law Officers, namely, Attorney-General of India, 
Solicitor-General of India or Additional Solicitors-General of India is also engaged. On 
receipt of requests from the Ministries/Departments, action is taken by the Department of 
Legal Affairs for engaging a suitable Counsel to appear on their behalf in the cases. Close 
liaison is maintained with various Departments by the counsels to safeguard interest of the 
Government in the litigation in the High Court at Delhi and Central Administrative 
Tribunal. Fee bills received from the Counsels are scrutinised having regard to the terms and 
conditions of their appointments before certifying for payments at prescribed scales. As per 
the Annual Report (1997-98) of the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs, during 
the period from 1st January, 1997 to 31st March, 1998, Litigation (High Court) Section 
engaged Counsel in 4922 cases to safeguard the interest of the Government litigation before 
Delhi High Court and the Central Administrative Tribunal. The Department of Legal 
Affairs informed that at the end of the year 1997-98 in the Litigation (High Court) Section 
21453 cases were pending while 602 cases were disposed of during that period. The 
Committee impresses upon the Department to initiate steps in coordinating the litigation work 
in the pending cases in the Delhi High Court and CAT, Principal Bench, New Delhi, on behalf 
of all Ministries/Departments of Government of India, except Railways and Income Tax 
Department. As the number of cases pending in the Section is very high, a time schedule may 
be prepared and strictly adhered to. 
LITIGATION (LOWER COURT) SECTION 
15. The main functions of the Litigation (Lower Court) Section are:-
(i) to engage a Union Government counsel from the panel for conduct of the Union 
Government cases at Delhi and New Delhi, excluding cases relating to the Railways 
and the Income Tax Department; 
(ii) to keep day-to-day watch on all the matters being conducted at Subordinate 
Courts/Tribunals in which the interests of the Union of India are involved, and to 
intimate the progress in such matters to the concerned Ministries/Departments of 
the Government; and 

5 
(iii) to certify and make the payment of fee bills of the Union Government Standing 
Counsels and to maintain regular accounts/records relating thereto. 
A~ per Annual Report of (1997-98) of the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company 
Affairs during the period from 1st January, 1997 to 31st March, 1998, 876 new cases were 
re~.:eived and 338 cases were disposed of by the Litigation (Lower Court) Section. The 
Department of Legal Affairs informed that at the end of the year 1997-98, 8884 cases were 
pending and 265 cases were disposed of during that period. The Committee recommends to 
the Department to initiate time bound programme of action to facilitate the conduct of 
pending cases and coordination, monitoring thereof in different subordinate courts, Tribunals 
at Delhi and New Delhi on behalf of the Union Government. 
NATIONAL LEGAL SERVICES AUTHORITY (NALSA) 
16. Since the year 1952, the Government of India has been taking steps for providing 
legal aid to the poor in as much as equality before law is a fundamental constitutional right. 
Article 39A of the Constitution of India enjoins upon the Government to provide legal aid 
to the poor and weaker sections of society to ensure equal justice for all , the cardinal 
principle on which the Administration of justice is based . The Legal Services Authorities 
Act. 1987 (as amended by the Act of 1994) aims at establishing a nationwide network for 
providing free and comprehensive legal services to the weaker sections of the society on 
uniform basis. National Legal Services Authorities, a statutory body constituted under the 
Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 to monitor and oversee the legal aid programmes 
throughout the country, has become fully functional in January, 1998. The various functions 
to be performed by the Authority, inter-alia include organising Lok Adalats and legal aid 
to the persons declared eligible under Section 12 of the Legal Services Authorities 
Act , 1987. 
17. From a perusal of the papers, it is seen that NALSA has become fully functional 
only in January/February, 1998 and prior to that it was functioning with skeleton staff. The 
working of NALSA is being supervised by the Chief Justice of India who is its Patron-in­
chief and by Dr. Justice A.S. Anand, Judge, Supreme Court of India who is the Executive 
Chairman of the Authority. The Committee recommends that the Annual Report and 
Audited Statement of Accounts of NALSA should be laid on the Table of the Houses of 
Parliament. 
The income criteria for imparting Legal Aid to the poor was fixed way back in 1987 by 
the Committee for Implementing Legal Aid Scheme (CILAS). It is high time that the income 
criteria is reviewed by the Government without delay. 
A budgetary provision of Rs. 5 crores was made in 1997-98 B.E. stage for carrying on 
the activities of NALSA. The Committee in its 39th Report on the Demands for Grants 
(1997-98) of the Ministry of Law & Justice had observed that the said amount allocated for 
the Scheme for free Legal Aid to the poor was quite inadequate. Despite this observation of 
the Committee, the grant was reduced at the R.E. stage to Rs. 3.38 crores. A provision of 
Rs. 4 crores has been made in B.E. 1998-99. The Committee, accordingly, recommends that 
the Government should at least increase the allocation to Rs. 5 crores so as to restore it to the 
1997-98 B.E. stage and thereafter review the allocation with a view to enhancing it even 
beyond 5 crores. 
LOK ADALATS 
18. The Committee was informed that Lok Adalats had got the statutory status under 
the Legal Services Authorities Act , 1987. 22,452 Lok Adalats have been held in different 
part of the country settling , since its inception in October-November 1985, approximately 66 
lakhs cases as on 31st January, 1998. The Committee was also informed that during 1997-98,

steps to popularise Lok Adalats and pursuade State Governments/Union Territories to h~ld

LAW COMMISSION 
20. The Law Commission of India is a non-statutory body constituted by the 
Government from time to time. The Commission was originally constituted in 1955. It is 
reconstituted every three years. The present Law Commission (15th Law Commission) was 
constituted with effect from 1st September, 1997 for a period of three years. The Law 
O;>mmission has so far submitted 158 reports on different subjects, out of which 80 reports 
have been fully implemented and 17 reports were not accepted. The remaining reports are 
under consideration of the Government. The 14th Law Commission had submitted two 
reports viz. 155th and 156th. The Commission had submitted 154th Report on "the Code of 
Criminal Procedure, 1973" and 156th Report on the "the Indian Penal Code"wherein various 
important amendments have been recommended. Both the 154th and 156th Reports have 
been forwarded to the Ministry of Home Affairs for implementation. The Committee has 
been informed that the Department of Legal Affairs has a cell dealing with implementation 
of the recommendations of the Law Commission, legal profession and the administration of 
the Advocates Act, 1961. 
21. From the facts made available by the Government, the Committee is constrained to 
note that the special cell of the Department of Legal Affairs dealing with the implementation 
of the recommendations of the Law Commission has yielded the least result since 
approximately 60 reports of the Commission are yet to be implemented and that Government 
has failed to ensure the accountability of the administrative Ministries of the Government for 
implementation of the accepted recommendations. The Committee also recommends for 
containing the growth of expenditure of the Commission under the head 'Foreign Travel'. The 

7 
Committee also impresses upon the Government to ask the Law Commission to study and 
recommend in the matter of speedy disposal of election petitions, at the earliest. The Committee 
also feels that the Law Commission should undertake a comprehensive study of cases of 
undertrials in respect of whom trials are yet to commence in any court of law. 
INCOME-TAX APPELLATE TRIBUNAL (ITAT) 
22. The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, constituted under the Income Tax Act, deals 
with second appeals in all matter s relating to direct taxes, and with appeals against orders in 
revision of commissions as well as orders of acquisition of properties under Chapter XXA of 
the Income Tax Act. The Tribunal is headed by the President who is assisted by one senior 
Vice President and three Vice Presidents. As per Annual Report (1997-98) of the Ministry of 
Law, Justice and Company Affairs, there are 106 Members for 53 Benches spread over 24 
cities. Earlier there were 38 benches of the Tribunal spread over 19 cities. The Government 
created 15 additional benches on 1.4.1997. The Committee was informed that out of 15 
additional benches, only one bench in Rajkot had started functioning and efforts were bejng 
made to locate suitable office premises for housing the remaining 14 benches. The 
Government informed the Committee that there were 10 vacancies of Juditial Members and 
I4 vac<mcies of Accountant Members in the Tribunal. The Committee was also informed that 
there were more than three lakh pending cases before the Tribunal. Regarding the growing 
trend in the expenditure under the head 'Domestic Travel Expenses' for the Tribunal, the 
Government informed the Committee that the increase was due to the necessity to send more 
Members on tours to places where there were no regular bench of the Tribunal and also due 
to general rise in travel costs. The (Jovernment further stated that the substantial increase in 
BE for 1998-99 under the head 'Travel Expenses' was due to the fact that 15 additional 
benches were likely to become functional during the current financial year. 
23. The Committee is astonished to note that out of 15 benches of Income Tax Appellate 
Tribunal , 14 benches are yet to start tunctioning while more than three lakh cases are pending. 
The Committee is also not convinced with the explanation of the Government in this regard and 
recommends that all the benches should be made functional without any further delay. The 
Committee also recommends that all the vacancies in the Tribunal should be filled up with 
utmost expediency. The Committee would also urge the Government to contain the expenditure 
of IT AT particularly under the heads 'Domestic Travel', and 'Other Administrative expenses 
(Hospitality)'. 
INTERNATIONAL CENTRE FOR ALTERNATIVE DISPUTE RESOLUTION (ICADR) 
24. In India number of cases filed in the Courts has mushroomed in recent times for 
variety of reasons thereby indicating the urgency for alternative dispute resolution. It is in this 
context. that a resolution was adopted by all the Chief Ministers and the Chief Justices of the 
High Courts in a meeting held on 4th December, 1993 under the Chairmanship of the then 
Prime Minister and presided over by the then Chief Justice of India, emphasising the 
desirability of disputants taking advantage of alternative dispute resolution which provided 
procedural flexibility, saved valuable time and money and avoided the stress of a conventional 
trial. The first major steps in the direction of settlement of dispute by arbitration and 
conciliation was the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 which came into force w.e.f. 22nd 
August, 1996. This Act has showed the way for the growth of the Alternative Dispute 
Resolution (ADR) movement in India on scientific lines. It is in this backdrop that "the 
International Centre for Alternative Dispute Resolution" (ICADR)-an autonomous 
organisation under the aegis of the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs was 
registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 on 31.5.1995 with the following main 

8 
objective~:-
(i) To propagate, promote and popularise the settlement of domestic and 
international disputes by different. modes of ADR; 
(ii) To provide facilities and administrative lind other support services for holding 
conciliation, mediation arbitration proceedings; 
(iii) To promote reform in the system of settlement of disputes and its healthy 
development suitable to the social, economic lind other needs of the community; 
(iv) To appoint conciliators, mediators, arbitrators, etc., when so requested by the 
parties; 
(v) To undertake teaching in ADR and related matters and to award diplomas, 
certificates and other academic or professional distinction; 
(vi) To develop infrastructure for education, research and training in the field of 
ADR; and 
(vii) To impart training in ADR and related matters and to arrange for fellowships, 
scholarships, stipends and prizes. 
25. The Committee is optimistic that the ICADR would be able to successfully translate 
its charter of duties into reality. The Committee in its 39th Report on the Demands for Grants 
(1997-98) had urged upon the Government to ensure timely submission of Annual Report and 
Statement of Accounts of ICADR to Parliament. The Committee is happy to note that the 
First Annual Report and Accounts (1995-96) of ICADR have since been laid. However, the 
Committee urges upon the Department to make sincere efforts also to lay on the Table of the 
Houses, the remaining Annual Reports and Accounts at the earliest.

26. The Committee has been informed that 41 complaints were ,received by the 
Government against the Central Government Counsels, out of which a senior panel Counsel

functioning of Government lawyers. 
27. The Committee notes with concern the sudden spurt in filing of the Public Interest 
Litigations. The Committee recommends that the whole issue pertaining to the Public Interest

time frame. 
2~. Under the World Trade Organisation regime, the country is entering into important 
international agreements which will have tremendous impact on our normal commercial 
activities. For example laws relating to the intellectual property rights, laws relating to trade 
and investment. which were not very much in focus until the recent past, have become 
priority items in the economic agenda of the country. In the light of this background the 
Committee recommends that the Law Commission should undertake study in this field and 
come out with appropriate recommendations within a given time frame.

DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE 
31. The Department of Justice was created in the year 1971. The subjects handled by 
the Department are constitution and organisation of the Supreme Court and the High 
Courts. appointment of Judges in the High Courts and the Supreme Court and their service 
conditions. Judges strength, administration of justice in Union Territories and monitoring of 
pendem:y of cases in courts. Courts in the country are at three levels. At the district level, 
there is subordinate judiciary, at the Stitte level, High Courts and finally the apex court at 
the Union level. As per the provisions of Articles 233, 234 and 235 of the Constitution, the 
supervision. control and appointment of subordinate judiciary is done at the level of tl)e 
State Governments and the concerned High Court. The Union Government is concerned 
only with the appointment of Judges in High Courts and the Supreme Court. At present 
there are lS High Courts in the wuntry. 11 States and 0ne Union Territory have separate 
High Courts. Six High Courts, namely Punjab and Haryana, Bombay, Kerala, .Madras, 
Calcutta and Guwahati High Courts have jurisdiction over more than one State." 
32. The Committee, in its 17th, 31st, 34th and 39th Reports had taken a serious view of 
the anomaly to the effect that the Demands for Grants of the Department of Justice is met 
from that of the Ministry of Law. Justice and Company Affairs whereas the Department is 
under the administrative control of the Ministry of Home Affairs. The Committee was 
informed that the Department of Justice is a small Department having a sanctioned staff 
strength of 37 only and it being under the administrative control of Ministry of Home 
Affairs. there were few advantage and that arrangement had been working for quite a long 
time. The Committee was further informed that its earlier recommendations in the matter 
would be taken into wnsideration for further action. The Committee reiterates its earlier 
recommendation that the Department of Justice should be placed under the administrative 
control of Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs. 
33. According to the Annual Report (1997-98) of the Ministry of Law, Justice and 
Company Affairs, the duties of the Department of Justice include the administration of 
Justice and the processing of appointment of the Judges to the Suprement Court and High 
Courts. Apart from this the Ministry of Law. Justice and Company Affairs is answerable to 
the Parliament in the matters of Supreme Court and High Courts. The Demands for Grants 
of the Supreme Court is accounted in the name of this Ministry. Till 1994-95, the Demand 
for Grants of Election Commission and Supreme Court formed part of the Demands for 
Grants of the Department of Legal Affairs, Legislative Department and the Department of 
Justice (i.e. Demand No. 57 for 1994-95). This year, during the -course of examination of the 
Demands for Grants (1998-99) of the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs the 
Department of Justice was. requested to furnish the explanatory note on the Demands for 
Grants (1998-99) and other associated papers in respect of Supreme Court (Demand No. 61 
of the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs), but the same were not received. The 
Committee, therefore, could not discuss the Demands for Grants of the Supreme Court. 
34. The Committee feels that it is the duty of the concerned Ministry to make available 
all the documents of the organisation whose Demands for Grants are a«:eounted for in the 
name of the Ministry . The CommiUee recommends that in future the Department should 

10 
ensure that all the documents relating to the Budget provisions made in the Demands for 
Grants (1998-99) of the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs are made available to 
the Committee and in time for consideration and discussion.

FOR TIJE JUDICIARY 
35. The Centrally Sponsored Scheme approved by ~ government relating to 
infrastructural facilities for the judiciary includes construction of court buildings and 
residential accommodation for judicial officers/judges covering High Court and subordinate 
court!ii. The expenditure on the scheme is to be shared by the Union and the State 
Governments on 50:50 basis. The Central share is, however, restricted to the amount 
allocated for this purpose by the Planning Commission, which has to be distributed as per 
the guidelines laid down by them. The expenditure in respect of the Union Territories is to 
be metJully by the Government of India. Rs. 70 crores has been allocated for this purpose

Governments like Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Kerala, Maharashtra, Punjab, Haryana, 
Sikkim, Uttar Pradesh who have spent more amount than they were required to, had

was not ~ceded to. The Committee has also been informed that under the scheme, Rs. 1200 
crores was proposed to be spent of which Rs. 600 crores would be the share of the Union 
Government in the Eight Fi.,e Year Plan. However, it would continue in the Ninth plan 
period. 
36. The Committee, while appriciating the Centrally Sponsored Scheme relating to the 
infrastructural facilities for the judiciary recommends that the Union Government assistance 
should not be confined to 50:50 basis and if some State Governments are able t0'3utilize more 
funds than their due share, then the Union Government should also increase the allocation 
whi~h will be in addition to the normal allocation. 
NATIONAL JUDICIAL ACADEMY 
37. The Eleventh Law Commission in its 117th Report in Nov. 1986 had recommended 
for the setting up of a Central Academy for providing formal training to judicial officers of 
various States. In August-September, 1985, in a joint conference of Chief Justice, Chief 
Ministers and Law Ministers held in New Delhi had also adopted the resolution for setting 
up an institute or an academy for Judicial Officers. The Judgment of Supreme Court dated 
the 13th November 1991 in the matter of All India Judges' Association and Others versus 
Union of India and other State Governments was inter-alia related to setting up of an All 
India in-service training Institute for Judicial Officers. Keeping in view these facts and 
pursuant to the decision 9f the Cabinet, the National Judicial Academy was registered under 
the Societies Registration Act, 1860 with the Registrar of Societies, Delhi on 17th August, 
.. l993 which is being funded as a central project. For 1998-99, Rs. 18 crores have been 
allocated for the Academy. The Registered Office of the Academy is located in the Supreme 
Court premises at New Delhi. The Government of Madhya Pradesh gave 60 acres of land 
free of cost in Bhopal and the Academy will be located at Bhopal where the building 
complex is under constrcution since Jan., 1997 and is expected to be completed in 1999. 
38. The Committee while appreciating the purpose of th~ National Judicial Academy 
recommends that the expenditure for the academy should not form part of the Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme relating to the infrastructural facility for judiciary; rather it should be 
!JtV&rately allocated funds.

Commission include the examination of the present structure of emoluments and conditions of 
services, etc. of judicial officers in the States and Union Territories, taking into account the total 
package benefits available · to them and make suitable recommendations to the State 
Governments. The Committee in this context tails upon the Central Government to request the 
Commission to expedite its recommendations.

one of the items in the National Agenda for Governance of the country is to set up a National 
Judicial Commission to make recommendations for judicial appointments in the Supreme Court 
and the High Courts and draw up a code of ethics for the judiciary. 
41. The Committee has been informed that the total sanctioned strength of Judges in the 
High Courts as on 1st June, 1998 is 587 against which 474 judges are in position, thus leaving 113 
posts vacant. The Committee finds that the maximum number of vacancy exists in the 
Allahabad Hogh Court. As against the sanctioned strength of 71 judges, 48 judges are in

High Courts have 10, 11, 11 and 9 vacancies of Judges, respectively (see Annexure A). The 
Department has informed that they have received proposals of appointment of only 60 Judges 
from the Cheif Justices of High Courts. The Committee feels concerned over the number of the

42. The <lommittee has been informed that the pendencies at the High Court level are 
increasing. As on 31st December, 1993, there were 26.51lakh cases pending and it increased to 
31.74 lakhs as on 31st December, 1997 (see Annexure B). The Deapartment further informed 
that they had taken various steps in that direction. The Law Minister had written to the Chief 
Justice of India to place the matter before the Annual Conference of Chief Justices of High 
Courts and suggest measures to reduce the pendencies. The Department added that it was also 
trying to streamline the Civil Procedure Code and the Criminal Procedure Code. The 
Government had also written to the High Courts not to grant adjournments on frivolous 
grounds. 
43. The Committee views with serious concern the disturbing phenomenon of pendency of 
cases at the High Court level. It notes the various steps taken by the Department with a view to 
reducing the pendencies. In this context, it recommends to the Government to suggest the High 
Courts to follow the steps taken by the Supreme Court in bringing down the pendencies, such as 
grouping and clubbing of cases having the same question of law and listing of cases by compuiers 
etc. 
44. The Government informed the Committee that the pendency in the subordinate courts 
was 2.18 crores as on 31st December, 1995 and it decreased to 1.99 crores as on 31 December 
1996 following the judgement of the ·Supreme Court on 1st May, 1996 in which it d~rected the

Governments to appoint Special Magistrates under Section 13 and 18 of the Criminal Procedure 
Code for minor/petty offences and most of State Governments have appointed the special

pending cases in the subordinate judiciary, notes the steps taken by the Government in this

REPORT 
I. the Chairman of the Departmem-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Home Affairs, having been aut11orised by the Committee, present this Forty-seventh Report 
of the Commirtee relating to the Marriage Laws (Amendment) Bill, 1997. • 
2. ln pursuance of the rules relating to the Department -related Parliamentary Standing 
Comminees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha, referred** lhe Marriage Laws (Amendment) Bill, 
1997, as introdu ced in the Rajya Sabha on the 13th August, 19'!7 and pending therein , to the 
Comminee for examination and repon. 
3. While considering the bill, the Committee took note of the following documents/ 
information placed before it: 
(i) Background note on the Bill; and 
(ii) Note on the curative aspects of epilepsy furnished by the Ministry of Health & 
Family Welfare. 
4. The Ministry of Law, Justice .ami Company Affairs (Legislative Department) 
informed the CommiHee that the Law Commission of India in its 59th Report on "Hindu 
Marriage Act, 1955, and the Special Marriage Act, 1954," had recommended for amendment 
of Section 5 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, and Section S(b) of the Special Marriage Act, 
1954, so as to define the words "idiot and lunat ic" which inter-alia also suggested 
incorporating there in based on the English Law that at the time of marriage the party should 
not also be subject to recurrent attacks of insanity or epilepsy. However, the Law 
Commission in its Report had not given any reason for inclusion of the word 'epilepsy' in 
the relevant provision along with 'insanity'. They had recommended that a provision may be 
included on the lines of the English Law. As English Law provided for epilepsy a.lso, the 
same had been incorporated in the relevant provisions of our laws as well. The Acts were 
accordingly amended vide the Marriage Laws (Amendment) Act, 1976, which made the 
position with regard to the difficulties of interpretation for reckoning different degrees of 
lunacy, clear. 
4.1 Ever since the amendment had been made in 1976, the Government had been 
receiving representations from Neuro -surgeons, Members of Parliament and other prominent 
persons of the society and also from Women's Organisations, against the said amendment 
stating that the disease 'epilepsy' should not onder any circumstances, be equated with 
"insanity" and it would do great injustice to several patients suffering from epilepsy since the 
disease was completely controllable. It was, therefore , urged upon the Government to 
undertake necessary legislation to remove references to epilepsy from the matrimonial laws 
on the ground that epilepsy had become fully controllable by proper medical care and 
atte ntion. The National Commission for Women and the Women's Organisatio ns have also 
recommended for undertaking necessary legislation in this regard. In view thereof the 
Government considered it appropriate to undertake the necessary legislation to remove 
references to 'epilepsy' in the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, and the Special Marriage Act, 
1954, as a ground for obtaining a decree for nullity of marriage. 
5.The Committee (1997-98) considered the Bill and heard the then Secretary, Ministry 
of Law, Justice and Company Affairs (Legislative Department) thereon in its meeting held 
'Published in the Gazette of India, Extraordinary Part II , Section 2, dated the 13th August, 1997. 
''Rajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin Part U, dated the 2nd September, 1997.

on the 30L\t September, 1997. The Committee decided to hear Dr. Y. Lakshmi Prasad, 
Member, Rajya Sabha and Dr. M. Jagannath, Member, Lok Sabha who had introduced 
Private Members' Bills on the same subject in Rajya Sabhe and Lok Sabha, respectively on 
the 20th December, 1996. Sin.;e the bill sought to do away with the proviSion of epilepsy as 
a cqndition of nullity of marriages from the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, and the Special 
Marriage Act, 1954, the Committee also decided to hear medical experts of the country on 
~10 curative aspects of the disease. In the meontimc the Committee. however, got dissolxed 
on the dissolution of the Eleventh Lok Sabha on 4th December, 1997. 
5.1 The present Committee, accordingly, in its meeting held on the 14th August. 1998, 
heard Dr. M. Jagannath, former Member of Lok Sabha, Dr. Y. Laksbmi Prasad, Member. 
R.ajya Sabha, Dr. S.P. Agarwal, Director-general, Directorat~ General of Health Services. 
Ministry of Health and Family Wt;lfare, Government of lndhj}:Dr. M.C. Mahcshwari, Prof. 
and Head, Department of Neurology, AliMS, Dr. ftt.K. Ifanerjee, Director, Vidyasagar 
Instituto of Mentall-lealth & Neuro Sciences, New Delhi and pr. (Ms.) M. Gourie-Dcvi, 
Director, National fnstitute of Mental Health & NeuroSciences, Bangalore on the curative 
aspects of epilepsy. TI,Je medical experts in their deposition before the Committee opined 
that in a majority of cases (about 80 per cent) epilepsy could be well controlled with modern 
anti-epileptic drugs and as such pleaded that the reference to 'epilepsy' should be removed 
from the matrimonial laws of the country. ln this context it was pointed out by the medical 
experts that the words 'epilepsy is completely curable' were wrongly used tn the Statement 
of Objects and Reasons of the Bill and should be deleted therefrom. It was clarified that 
even though a lot of scicmiric information was available on a particular dtsease, yet the 
c:xpression 'complc1ely cur!lble' was not used. What the medical fraternity ~aid was that the 
majority of patients could be fairly well controlled to the extent of 80 per cent of the cases. 
It was, therefore , suggested that the words objected to may be substituted by the words 
'fairly well controllable in a majority of cases who can lead a normal life'. 
5.2 The Committee agrees in principle with the point raised by the Doctors with regard 
to use of expression 'fully curable' in the Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill. 
However, as mentioned in the Practice and Procedure of Parliament by Kaul and Shakdher 
(4th Edition, 1991, page 485), 'the Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill can be 
amended by the Member·in·charge of the Bill with the permission of the Presiding Officer at 
the tinle of introduction of the nm. Any lacuna in the Statement of Objects and Reasons 
must be pointed out at tbe time of introduction of the Bill; a point ntised in this regard at 
the consideration stage of the Bill is not valid'. 
5.3 ln view of the position stated above the Comminee feels that the best course 
available is that the Minister-m-charge of the J3ill may clarify the posttion m this regard in 
the House while moving the motion for consideration of the Bill. 
6. With regard to the recommendation of the Law Commission of India as contained in 
their 59th Report on 'The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 and the Special Marriage Act, 1954', 
for incorporating therein based on the English Luw that at the time of marriage the party 
should not be subject to recurrent attacks of im,anity or epilepsy, and the subsequent

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 
Dased on the recommendations of the Law Commission of India as contamed in 
their fifty-ninth Report on "Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 and Special Marriage Act, 
1954", section 5 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 and section 4 of the Special 
Marr iage Act, 1954 were amended vide the M"arriage Laws (Amendment) /\ct. 1971i

amendment came into force, the Central Government have been receiving 
representations from eminent medical experts, jurists <md Members of Parliament for 
omission of reference to "epilepsy" conta ined in the aforesaid Acts of 1955 and 1954 
on the ground that medical experts have found that epilepsy is fully curable and, 
therefore, equating "epilepsy" to "insanity'' would do great IDJUSrice to pat1ents 
suffering from epilepsy in matrimonial matters. The grounds for annulling a marriage

·:epilepsy" in section 5(ii) of the H indu Marriage Act , 1955 and section 4(b)(iii) of 
the Speciol Marriage Act, 1954 has the effect of non-availability of the ground of 
epilepsy for getting a decree of nullity of the marriage as well. ln order to mitigate 
the hardship> of the persons suffering from epilepsy on account of the aforesaid 
provisions, necessary amendments tO remove references to "epilepsy" in the 1955 and

REPORT 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Home Affairs, having been authorised by the 
Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Forty-ninth Report of the 
Committee on the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 1997*. 
2. In pursuance of the Rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committees, the Presiding Officer, Rajya Sabha referred**. The Code of Civil Procedure 
(Amendment) Bill, 1997 as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the 14th August, 1997 and 
pending therein, to the earlier Committee (1997-98) for examination and report . 
3. The Committee (1997-98) considered the Bill in its meeting held on 30th September, 
1997 and heard the Secretary of the Legislative Department, Ministry of Law, Justice and 
Company Affairs on the provisions contained in the Bill. 
4. In the said meeting of the Committee, having regard to the special importance of the 
Bill which sought to streamline the procedural delays in the judicial process a~d amend 
certain Sections and Orders of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, decided to invite 
memoranda from individuals/organisations/ins titutions etc. interested in the subject matter 
of Bill. The Committee directed that a Press Communique may be issued in this behalf 
fixing November 10, 1997 as the last date for the receipt of memoranda. An advertisement 
was, accordingly, published in all the leading English and Vernacular dailies on 11th 
October, 1997. The matter was also broadcast/telecast repeatedly on All India Radio and 
Doordarshan to give it wide publicity. 
S. Since the intended amendments were of far-reaching importance to the .community of 
lawyers and litigants and would have a significant impact on the administration of justice, it 
was also decided to .invite views/suggestions from the Bar Council of India, State Bar 
Councils and Bar Associations of Allahabad, Bombay, Calcutta , Delhi, Guwahati, Kerala, 
Madras and two District Bar Associations from each S tate. Accordingly, !hey were 
requested to send their views/suggestions on the Bill. 
6. Before the Committee (1997-98) could proceed further with the consideration of the 
Bill, it got dissolved consequent upon the dissolution of the Eleventh Lok Sabha on 
4.12.1997. 
6.1 While the ~arlier Committee started receiving a large number of memoranda from 
different quarters, it also received requests for extension of time from the Bar Council of 
India and some Bar Councils! Associations of a few States seeking extension of time for 
submission of their views on the Bill. Before those requests for extension could be 
considered, the Committee got dissolved as mentioned earlier and the same continued to 
remain pending. 
7. The present Committee (1998-99) was constituted on 5th June, 1998. Due to change 
in Government ' at the Centre, it was decided that a reference may be made to the 
Legislative Deparnnent to let the Secretariat know the views of the present Government

with regard to the enactment of the Bill in its present form. Accordingly, a reference was 
made to the Legislative Department . on 3rd August, 1998. In response thereto, the 
Legislative Department vide their communication dated 6th August, 1998 informed that the 
matter was under consideration of the Department and after the decision of the competent 
authority was obtained, a further communication in the matter would follow shortly. 
Consequently on 19th August 1998 that Department was reminded to expedite their 
response. The Department vide communication dated 3rd September, 1998 stated that 
instructions of the Cabinet were being sought for taking up the consideration of the Bill in 
Parliament. Thereafter on 28th October/3rd November, 1998 another reminder was sent to 
the Department in the matter. The Legislative Department vide their latest communication 
dated 5th November, 1998 stated that having obtained the Cabinet's approval, the 
Government proposed to further pursue the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 
1997 in Parliament. 
8. In the meetings of the Sub-Committee (of the Standing Committee on Home Affairs) 
on Judicial Reforms, held on 9th and lOth November, 1998, the Chairman of the Committee 
apprised the Members of the latest communication of the Ministry on the CPC 
(Amendment) Bill, 1997. The Sub-Committee briefly discussed about the consideration of 
the Bill by the full Committee. It was when decided that a meeting of the full Committee 
may be convened to take up further consideration of the Bill. 
9. The Committee in its meeting held on 24th November, 1998 took up further 
consideration of the Bill. The requests for extension of time for submission of views on the 
Bill, received from Bar Council of India, six Bar Councils of different States and one Bar 
Association, were considered by the Committee and it decided to give them another 
opportunity to submit their views within a week. In response thereto, the Bar Council. of 
India and the Madras Bar Association sent their views/suggestions on 4th and 7th 
December, respectively. 
9.1. In all 97 memoranda have been received from different quarters. Out of which only 
57 contained suggestions on the Bill while the rest of them are not directly related to the 
provisions of the Bill (See Annexure for list of 57 organisations/individuals).

11. The Bill contains 36 Clauses and seeks further to amend the Code of Civil 
Procedure, 1908, the Limitation Act, 1963 and the Court Fees Act, 1870. The Bill has been 
prepared by the Legislative Department in the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company 
Affairs with a view {o implementing the recommendations of Justice Malimath Committee
